elimination.verdict: That leaves assessing for infection and reviewing medications.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old tells the nurse she has stopped going to her book group because she cannot follow the conversation in a noisy room. Her hearing was tested last year and was normal for her age. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Explore what would let her keep attending
options.rationale: The expected change is real, and the loss of the activity is the problem nursing can act on.

options.text: Reassure her that difficulty in noisy rooms is an expected change
options.rationale: It is an expected change, and stopping an activity because of it is a functional loss that needs addressing.

options.text: Refer her for repeat audiometry before anything else
options.rationale: Her hearing was tested recently and the finding is consistent with expected change.

options.text: Suggest she find an activity that does not require hearing
options.rationale: This accepts the loss and narrows her life further.

questions.takeaway: An expected age-related change still produces a functional consequence, and the consequence is the nursing problem.
questions.strategy: The trap is that the physiology is normal. Normal physiology with a lost role is still something to act on.

strategies: Separate the change from its effect

steps.detail: She has given up a social role.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring what would let her keep attending.

questions.stem: A nurse suspects elder mistreatment when an 86-year-old arrives with bruises at different stages of healing and a daughter who answers every question for her. The daughter refuses to leave the room. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the suspicion to the appropriate agency immediately
options.rationale: Reporting is required, and the nurse first needs to speak with the patient alone to assess.

options.text: Ask the daughter directly how the bruises occurred
options.rationale: This gives the suspected person the account and warns her.

options.text: Create a reason to interview the patient alone
options.rationale: Assessment comes before reporting, and it cannot happen with the suspected person present.

options.text: Document the bruises and the daughter's behavior and continue the visit
options.rationale: Documentation without assessment or action leaves the patient where she is.

questions.takeaway: Nurses are mandated reporters. Reporting follows an assessment, and the assessment requires the patient alone.
questions.strategy: Reporting is required and it is not the first step. Assessment before intervention holds even when the law is involved.

strategies: Apply assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Any account from the patient herself.

elimination.verdict: That leaves finding a way to interview the patient alone.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old living alone manages her own medications and finances and has had no falls. Her son tells the nurse he wants her moved to assisted living because he worries constantly. She declines. Which action best reflects the nurse's role?

options.text: Support the son, since families usually recognize decline before the patient does
options.rationale: This substitutes the family's judgment for a competent patient's and is the ageist answer.

options.text: Explore what the son is afraid of and what would address it
options.rationale: His worry is real and the patient is competent. The nursing work is the fear, not her autonomy.

options.text: Arrange a cognitive screen to settle whether she can decide
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests impaired cognition, and screening her to override her is not neutral.

options.text: Tell the son the decision belongs to his mother and close the discussion
options.rationale: This is legally right and clinically incomplete, because it leaves the family unsupported.

questions.takeaway: Aging in place means supporting independence. A competent patient decides, and the family's distress is still a nursing problem.
questions.strategy: The weakest answer is the one that is technically correct and does nothing. Autonomy is the boundary, not the whole response.

strategies: Ask who has a problem

steps.detail: Frightened, and nobody has assessed why.

steps.action: Cut overriding her and cut dismissing him
steps.detail: One ignores autonomy, the other ignores the family.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring what the son fears.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is admitted after a fall. Which findings in her record are red flags rather than expected changes of aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confusion that began two days ago
options.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag at any age, and it is the one most often written off.

options.text: A slower reaction time than at age 40
options.rationale: Slowed reaction time is an expected change.

options.text: A new inability to manage her own medications
options.rationale: A sudden decline in function is a red flag and needs a cause.

options.text: Reduced bowel sounds on auscultation
options.rationale: Peristalsis slows with age, so reduced bowel sounds are expected.

options.text: Three falls in the past month with no previous history
options.rationale: New unexplained falls are a red flag, and previous falls predict future ones.

options.text: Skin that has lost resilience and moisture
options.rationale: Integumentary change is expected with aging.

options.text: A marked change in behavior reported by her daughter
options.rationale: A significant behavior change from baseline is a red flag.

questions.takeaway: Expected: slower reactions, sensory change, reduced peristalsis, skin change. Red flags: sudden confusion, sudden functional decline, new falls, behavior change.
questions.strategy: Every red flag in this list is sudden and every expected change is gradual. Sort by speed before sorting by system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sudden goes in one pile, gradual in the other.

elimination.verdict: The four sudden changes are selected.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old is going home on six medications. Which instructions reduce her risk of a medication problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bring every bottle to each visit, including anything bought over the counter
options.rationale: Over-the-counter and herbal products are the ones missing from the list, and bringing the bottles is what finds them.

options.text: Use one pharmacy for everything
options.rationale: A single pharmacy can catch an interaction that no one prescriber would see.

options.text: Ask before starting any new product, including supplements and sleep aids
options.rationale: Most dangerous additions in older adults are things nobody prescribed.

options.text: Report new dizziness, confusion or a fall, because these can come from the medications
options.rationale: These present as aging and are often the drug, which is the connection patients do not make.

options.text: Stop a medication once the symptom it was treating has gone
options.rationale: Stopping without advice is how control of a chronic condition is lost, and some drugs cannot be stopped abruptly.

options.text: Keep leftover antibiotics in case the same infection returns
options.rationale: Saved antibiotics lead to incorrect self-treatment and a partial course.

options.text: Use a weekly pill organizer filled on the same day each week
options.rationale: An organizer makes a missed or doubled dose visible rather than invisible.

questions.takeaway: Medication safety at home: one pharmacy, every product disclosed including what nobody prescribed, nothing started or stopped alone, and new confusion or falls treated as a possible drug effect.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are what people do with leftover medicine. Both substitute the patient's judgment for a prescriber's.

strategies: Ask who is making the decision in each option

steps.action: Bottles, one pharmacy, asking first, reporting, organizer
steps.detail: The patient and the prescriber together.

elimination.verdict: The five safe instructions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the 4 Ms to organize care for an 85-year-old admitted with pneumonia. Which assessments belong to the framework? Select all that apply.

options.text: What the patient wants from this admission
options.rationale: What Matters is the first M, and it is the one most often skipped.

options.text: Whether any medication affects mobility, mentation or what matters
options.rationale: Medication is assessed for its effect on the other three Ms, not in isolation.

options.text: Screening for delirium, dementia and depression
options.rationale: Mentation covers all three, and distinguishing them is the point.

options.text: How the patient moves and whether that has changed
options.rationale: Mobility covers function and safe movement.

options.text: The patient's insurance coverage and likely discharge date
options.rationale: Both matter to planning and neither is one of the 4 Ms.

options.text: The patient's primary medical diagnosis and prognosis
options.rationale: The 4 Ms deliberately organize care around function rather than diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: The 4 Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are things every chart contains. The framework exists because those are not what guides care for an older adult.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Medical, and the framework is built to look past them.

elimination.verdict: The four assessments matching the Ms are selected.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone takes oxybutynin for urge incontinence and has added an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine every night for the past three weeks. She now has a dry mouth, has not had a bowel movement in four days, becomes muddled in the evenings, and caught herself on the doorframe on the way to the bathroom last night. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Two medications are acting on the same receptors and the combined burden is producing all four findings
options.rationale: Dry mouth, constipation, confusion and unsteadiness are one anticholinergic picture, not four separate problems, and the aging brain tolerates that burden poorly.

options.text: Reduced fluid intake has produced dehydration
options.rationale: Possible, and it does not account for a change that began when a new drug did.

options.text: Her sleep pattern has changed with age and she is disoriented on waking
options.rationale: Age changes sleep. It does not produce constipation and a dry mouth.

options.text: Dementia is emerging, and that is why the confusion comes on later in the day and at night
options.rationale: Evening confusion fits the pattern and so does an anticholinergic peaking after the bedtime dose. A three-week onset with a clear drug trigger is not a progressive disease.

questions.takeaway: When several unrelated-looking findings start together, look for one cause. Over-the-counter drugs count as medications and nobody volunteers them.
questions.strategy: Two options explain the confusion. Only one explains the dry mouth and the constipation as well.

strategies: Find the explanation that covers every finding
elimination.verdict: Cumulative anticholinergic burden.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old long-term care resident arrives after falling twice in one day. Staff report she has been off since yesterday. She is normally oriented and today cannot say where she is. Temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate 96, respirations 22, blood pressure 108/64. Which conclusion does the nurse reach?

options.text: Infection has to be ruled out, because a normal temperature does not exclude it in an older adult
options.rationale: Older adults often mount no fever. Confusion, a rising respiratory rate and new falls are frequently the whole presentation, and the confusion preceded the falls.

options.text: The falls caused a head injury, and that is what is producing the confusion and disorientation she now shows
options.rationale: Head injury has to be assessed and it does not fit the sequence. She was off before she fell, so the confusion is a cause of the falls rather than a result.

options.text: This is an expected decline for her age
options.rationale: Age explains nothing. A sudden change in a previously oriented person is acute until proven otherwise.

options.text: Dementia has progressed to the point of disorientation
options.rationale: Dementia does not arrive overnight, and the stem gives a baseline of full orientation.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, infection presents as confusion, falls and functional decline before it presents as fever. Afebrile is not uninfected.
questions.strategy: The order of events decides it. Work out what came first, the confusion or the fall.

strategies: Build the timeline
elimination.verdict: Rule out infection.

questions.stem: Three days after abdominal surgery a patient lies still, answers in single words, eats almost nothing and asks for nothing. The previous shift charted her as quiet, cooperative and without complaints. Asked to say the months of the year backward, she loses her place after four months and starts over twice. Which interpretation does the nurse act on?

options.text: Oversedation from her analgesia
options.rationale: Opioids are a common precipitant and reviewing them belongs in the workup. Naming the drug names a possible cause, not what is in front of her.

options.text: Hypoactive delirium, because the inattention is what separates it from low mood
options.rationale: Inattention is the cardinal feature of delirium in any form. The quiet presentation is the one that gets charted as cooperative and missed.

options.text: Expected fatigue after major surgery
options.rationale: Fatigue makes a patient tired. It does not break attention.

options.text: Depression related to the surgery and her loss of independence
options.rationale: Depression fits the withdrawal and the poor intake. It does not produce a patient who cannot hold a sequence in mind, and it does not appear over three days.

questions.takeaway: Hypoactive delirium looks like a good patient. Test attention on anyone whose engagement has dropped, because inattention is the finding that forces the question.
questions.strategy: Two options explain a withdrawn patient. Only one explains a patient who cannot keep her place in a list.

strategies: Isolate the finding the others cannot explain
elimination.verdict: Hypoactive delirium.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man is admitted to a four-bed room where a television is on. He answers the first two interview questions appropriately. After that his answers stop matching the questions, and the nurse notices he is watching her mouth. What does she do next?

options.text: Ask his daughter in the hallway to supply the rest of the history so the admission is not delayed
options.rationale: It takes the patient out of his own assessment over a problem that takes two minutes to fix.

options.text: Document possible cognitive impairment and arrange a cognitive screen
options.rationale: Screening a patient who cannot hear the questions produces a score that measures the room. Correct the sensory barrier before you measure cognition.

options.text: Move to a quieter space, face him directly, lower the pitch of her voice, and ask the questions again
options.rationale: Age-related loss takes the high frequencies first, and background noise masks what is left. Watching her mouth says he is working to fill in what he cannot hear.

options.text: Raise her voice and carry on with the interview
options.rationale: Shouting raises pitch into the range he has lost and distorts the consonants. It makes him harder to understand, not easier.

questions.takeaway: Correct sensory barriers before you test cognition. Hearing loss that is mistaken for confusion follows an older adult through the whole admission.
questions.strategy: Two options respond to the same observation. Ask which one would produce a trustworthy result.

strategies: Ask what the finding really shows

steps.action: Read the detail about his eyes

elimination.verdict: Quiet space, face him, lower the pitch.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old admitted with pneumonia walked independently at home and is now on the third hospital day. Which nursing decisions reduce his risk of leaving the hospital less able than he arrived? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reviewing the medication list for anything causing sedation or orthostasis
options.rationale: The most common reason a hospitalized older adult stops walking safely is something that was started in the hospital.

options.text: Having him wear his own clothes and glasses during the day
options.rationale: Clothes and glasses orient a person and make moving around plausible. A gown keeps people in bed.

options.text: Applying a chair alarm so he does not stand without help
options.rationale: Alarms have not been shown to prevent falls and they teach a patient that standing up is the wrong thing to do.

options.text: Getting him up to a chair for meals
options.rationale: Sitting upright protects strength, swallowing and intake at the same time.

options.text: Keeping the urinary catheter until his gait is steadier
options.rationale: A catheter is a tether and an infection risk. It removes the reason to stand up, which is what makes the gait steadier.

options.text: Walking him to the bathroom with assistance rather than offering a bedpan
options.rationale: Every trip is practice. The bedpan saves the nurse ten minutes and costs him the walking he came in with.

options.text: Maintaining bed rest until physical therapy has evaluated him
options.rationale: Muscle is lost within days. Waiting for a consult to permit ordinary mobility is how function disappears during an admission.

questions.takeaway: Hospital-associated functional decline comes from the tethers and the waiting, not from the illness. Protect mobility like a vital sign.
questions.strategy: Three distractors sound cautious. Caution that keeps an older adult in bed is the mechanism of the harm.

strategies: Ask whether the option gets him moving or keeps him still
elimination.verdict: Walking, chair, own clothes, and the medication review are selected.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

sources.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients
sources.label: Iggy Ch. 5 · Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

questions.stem: A teenage boy hands in an intake form and the receptionist says his mother's and father's names are required. He says quietly that he has two dads, and she announces loudly that he does not have a mother. Heads turn and he starts for the door. What would have prevented this?

options.text: An intake form that asks for parent or guardian names rather than mother and father
options.rationale: The form created the problem before anyone spoke. Updating policies and forms is one of the five ways to build a safe space, and it removes the assumption at the point it is made.

options.text: Displaying symbols of inclusivity in the waiting area
options.rationale: Part of an inclusive environment, and a rainbow sticker does not change what the form demands.

options.text: Posting the clinic's nondiscrimination policy at the reception desk
options.rationale: A policy on the wall does not change what the form demanded of him. The exchange still happens.

options.text: Having him complete the form privately with a nurse instead of at the desk
options.rationale: Reduces the audience for the exchange. The form still asks the wrong question.

questions.takeaway: Foster an inclusive environment: update policies and forms, display symbols of inclusivity, and build sexual orientation and gender identity into records.
questions.strategy: Three options are visible gestures of inclusion. Only one removes the thing that forced him to correct the form at a public desk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The form asked for a mother and a father.
Both improve the response to a problem still built in.
Moves the exchange, not the question.

elimination.verdict: That leaves changing the form.

questions.stem: A receptionist loudly tells a teenage boy, in a full waiting area, that he does not have a mother, after he said he has two dads. She realizes what she has said. Which response is most appropriate at that moment?

options.text: Briefly say sorry, correct the record, and continue with the check-in
options.rationale: A short correction keeps the attention on him and signals that the mistake is routine rather than a crisis he has to manage.

options.text: Offer to move him to a private room to finish the conversation
options.rationale: Well meant, and it makes the moment larger and marks him out further in front of the people already looking.

options.text: Say nothing further and complete the form as he has described it
options.rationale: This comes across as not having noticed, or not caring. Acknowledgment is what matters, not how long you spend.

options.text: Apologize at length and explain that she did not mean anything by it
options.rationale: Makes him manage her distress. A long apology asks a patient in a waiting room to reassure the person who upset him.

questions.takeaway: Acknowledge briefly, correct, move on. The repair should cost the nurse something, not the patient.
questions.strategy: Every option except one enlarges the moment. Ask who ends up doing the emotional work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A long apology puts him in charge of her feelings.
Makes a small moment into a scene.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the brief correction.

questions.stem: A clinician asks a patient whether she is sexually active with men, women, or both. She answers that she is sexually active with one woman. He skips the questions about condom use. Her partner is a transgender woman. Which error has he made?

options.text: He used outdated terminology in the question itself
options.rationale: The question itself was framed reasonably: he asked about partners rather than labels. What went wrong came after she answered.

options.text: He should not have asked about sexual activity at all
options.rationale: The sexual history is appropriate care. The failure is in the reasoning that followed her answer.

options.text: He failed to ask about the number of partners
options.rationale: She told him there is one. The omission is about what happens, not how many.

options.text: He inferred the anatomy involved from the gender of the partner
options.rationale: Sexual health risk follows anatomy and practices, not the gender of either person. Assuming from the label is what skipped a question she needed.

questions.takeaway: Assess anatomy and practices rather than inferring them from gender or orientation. Avoid assumptions.
questions.strategy: Three options criticize the question. The stem tells you the question was answered, then something was skipped.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He assumed what her partner's body was.

steps.action: Cut the options about the question
steps.detail: The question was asked and answered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the inference from gender to anatomy.

questions.stem: A clinician who is openly gay skipped his center's training on LGBTQ+ care, saying he already knew the subject. He then assumed a patient with a female partner needed no questions about condom use. What does this illustrate?

options.text: The training should have been mandatory rather than optional
options.rationale: A reasonable policy conclusion, and it names an administrative fix rather than what the case shows.

options.text: Belonging to a community does not substitute for training
options.rationale: Personal identity gives lived experience, not clinical knowledge of every population under an umbrella. Ongoing training is the first of the five safe-space practices.

options.text: The error was one of attitude rather than knowledge
options.rationale: His attitude let him skip the training, and what harmed the patient was a specific knowledge gap.

options.text: Clinicians who are themselves LGBTQ+ should not care for LGBTQ+ patients
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he should be excluded. Identity did not give him what training would have.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself: learn the terminology, know the specific health issues, and take part in ongoing training. Every team member needs it.
questions.strategy: Two options draw policy or personnel conclusions. Ask what the missing training would have given him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He did not know to assess anatomy over label.

steps.action: Cut the policy and attitude options

elimination.verdict: That leaves identity not substituting for training.

questions.stem: A patient's chart lists a legal name different from the one on the referral letter. Which actions create a safe space? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask what name and pronouns the patient uses and record them where staff will see
options.rationale: Affirming language starts with asking rather than guessing, and recording it means every subsequent staff member gets it right.

options.text: Ask which surgeries the patient has had, to know how to refer to them
options.rationale: Surgical history is relevant when it bears on the care being given. Asking to satisfy curiosity about someone's body is not assessment.

options.text: Keep the legal name in the record for billing and identification
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record. The legal name is needed for insurance and identification; the used name is needed for care.

options.text: Wait for the patient to raise the difference before mentioning names
options.rationale: Leaves the patient to correct staff repeatedly, which is the burden the practice exists to remove.

options.text: Use the name the patient gives from that point on, in every interaction
options.rationale: Consistency is what makes it affirming. Asking and then not using it is worse than not asking.

options.text: Explain to colleagues why the patient's name differs from the chart
options.rationale: Discloses information that is the patient's to share. Respect privacy is part of affirming communication.

questions.takeaway: Affirming communication: use preferred names and pronouns, avoid assumptions, be mindful of nonverbal cues, and respect privacy.
questions.strategy: Two distractors involve telling someone else, or asking about a body without a clinical reason.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staff need the name, not the explanation.
Privacy is part of affirming care.

elimination.verdict: A, C, and E are selected.

questions.scenario: A clinic manager reviews practice after two patients did not return following a first visit.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate which of the five safe-space practices it represents.

rows.text: Adds a field for gender identity and pronouns to the electronic record
rows.rationale: Building identity into records and forms is part of the environment, not of any single conversation.

rows.text: A nurse notices she assumed a patient's partner was a man and examines why
rows.rationale: She is examining her own assumption and holding herself accountable for it, which is self-reflection.

rows.text: Sends a survey asking patients what would make the clinic feel safer
rows.rationale: She is asking patients what would help instead of deciding for them, which puts the patient's priorities first.

rows.text: Schedules quarterly training on terminology and population-specific health issues
rows.rationale: Scheduled training on terminology and population-specific health issues is how staff educate themselves rather than guessing.

rows.text: Introduces herself with her own pronouns before asking the patient's
rows.rationale: Makes the question routine rather than singling anyone out, and it avoids the assumption.

rows.text: Displays a visible inclusivity symbol at the reception desk
rows.rationale: A signal built into the space, which is what the environment practice covers.

questions.takeaway: Five safe-space practices: educate yourself, self-reflection, affirming communication, inclusive environment, prioritize patient needs.
questions.strategy: Two rows are both environment. Ask whether the action changes the space, the conversation, or the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The space, the words, or the nurse herself.
Forms and symbols are both environment.

elimination.verdict: Environment, self-reflection, patient needs, education, communication, environment.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria attends clinic with a parent and asks when hormone therapy can start. Which response is accurate according to current practice?

options.text: Hormone therapy may be started at any age once dysphoria is diagnosed
options.rationale: A diagnosis does not by itself start hormones, and the typical threshold is 18.

options.text: Hormone therapy requires the parent's consent regardless of the patient's age
options.rationale: Consent requirements vary, and it is not what determines the timing described here.

options.text: Hormone therapy is typically not prescribed until at least 18 years of age
options.rationale: That is the threshold, and the intervening years involve mental health care, medical care, and social services rather than nothing.

options.text: Hormone therapy is unsafe for anyone under 18 and should not be discussed
options.rationale: It is safe for youth and adults with provider supervision. The threshold is about prescribing practice, not a safety prohibition on the conversation.

questions.takeaway: Hormone replacement therapy is typically not prescribed until at least 18. It is safe for youth and adults with supervision and appropriate management.
questions.strategy: One distractor removes the threshold, one turns it into a safety prohibition, one substitutes a consent rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diagnosis alone does not start it.

steps.action: Cut the option that calls it unsafe
steps.detail: It is safe with provider supervision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the threshold of at least 18.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why gender-affirming care is described as medically necessary rather than elective. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: It restores fertility that was lost through hormone therapy
options.rationale: Fertility is part of the informed consent discussion because it may be affected, not something the care restores.

options.text: It improves mental health and overall wellbeing
options.rationale: Dysphoria, depression and anxiety all drop measurably with treatment. Those are outcomes, not preferences.

options.text: It is limited to surgical procedures
options.rationale: It covers a wide range of services including mental health care, medical care, and social services.

options.text: It is potentially life-saving for transgender people
options.rationale: This is stated directly, and it reflects the mortality that follows untreated dysphoria.

options.text: It is supported by strong scientific evidence
options.rationale: There is a strong evidence base behind this care, and that evidence is what moves it out of the elective category.

options.text: It reduces suicidal ideation and suicide attempts
options.rationale: This is an outcome, and it is the clearest basis for the word necessary.

questions.takeaway: Gender-affirming care is medically necessary and potentially life-saving, supported by strong evidence, and it spans mental health, medical, and social services.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses what the consent discussion says about fertility. One narrows the care to surgery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mental health, medical, and social services.
Consent covers fertility risk, not restoration.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted for a hip fracture. Her partner of 41 years is not listed as next of kin, and she declines to say who should be contacted. Which factor most likely explains her hesitation?

options.text: Her partner's own preference not to be involved in decisions
options.rationale: This is possible, and the stem describes her hesitation rather than her partner's wishes. Nothing says the partner wants to stay out of it.

options.text: Reluctance to burden family during an acute admission
options.rationale: A real reason people give, but it does not explain a 41-year relationship going unnamed.

options.text: A lifetime of discrimination that has taught her disclosure carries risk
options.rationale: This generation lived through criminalization and open hostility. Historical discrimination and lifetime exposure to stigma shape whether disclosure feels safe today.

options.text: Cognitive changes affecting her recall of who to contact
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests impairment, and she is declining rather than failing to remember.

questions.takeaway: LGBTQ+ older adults carry historical discrimination and lifetime exposure to stigma and violence. Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services at all.
questions.strategy: Two distractors offer ordinary explanations that do not account for the length of the relationship.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the partner and burden options

elimination.verdict: That leaves a lifetime of learned risk around disclosure.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she has not seen a provider in four years. She explains that at her last clinic staff repeatedly used the wrong name and asked questions she found intrusive, so she stopped going. Which action takes priority at this visit?

options.text: Apologize for the previous clinic and reassure her that this one is different
options.rationale: Warmth that changes nothing clinically. Four years of missed care is still sitting in front of you.

options.text: Review which routine screenings and preventive care she has missed in those four years
options.rationale: Avoidance after a non-affirming experience is how conditions get found late. The gap in care is the clinical problem her story created.

options.text: Document the previous clinic's conduct in the chart
options.rationale: This records the history instead of acting on it, and the chart is not where that complaint belongs.

options.text: Ask her to describe in detail what happened at the previous clinic
options.rationale: This turns her visit into a debrief of her worst experience. She has already told you enough to act on.

questions.takeaway: A non-affirming environment drives avoidance, and avoidance shows up as a gap in screening and preventive care. Close the gap.
questions.strategy: One distractor is warmth, one is documentation, one is more history. Only one of them treats the four years as the finding.

strategies: Ask which option changes her care today

steps.action: Find the clinical finding in the stem
Cut the apology and the detailed history

elimination.verdict: That leaves reviewing the screenings and preventive care she has missed.

questions.nursesNote: 0930: Patient is 31, admitted for elective surgery. Transgender man. Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use; he asks to be called Sam. Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns since arrival. He is on testosterone therapy and has not had a cervical screening in six years. He has no documented primary care provider. He says he stopped going to clinics after a receptionist argued with him about his name. Vital signs stable. He has arranged his own transport home and has a friend staying overnight.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require nursing action before this admission proceeds.

segments.text: On testosterone therapy
segments.rationale: Part of his medical history and relevant to his care. It is not in itself a finding requiring action.

segments.text: Stopped going to clinics after a receptionist argued with him about his name
segments.rationale: Explains the screening gap and the missing provider. It is the finding that connects the others.

segments.text: Chart lists a legal name the patient does not use; he asks to be called Sam
segments.rationale: Both names belong in the record. Recording the name he uses is what stops the next staff member repeating the error.

segments.text: No documented primary care provider
segments.rationale: A gap in continuity, and with the clinic history it points to avoidance of care rather than preference.

segments.text: Has arranged his own transport home and has a friend staying overnight
segments.rationale: The discharge arrangements are in place. This is the part that is going well.

segments.text: Two staff members have used incorrect pronouns since arrival
segments.rationale: A pattern rather than a slip. It needs correcting with the staff, briefly and away from the patient.

segments.text: Has not had a cervical screening in six years
segments.rationale: Screening follows the organs a person has, not their gender. Reproductive and sexual health needs are frequently overlooked in this population.

segments.text: Vital signs stable
segments.rationale: Stable vital signs are a normal finding. Nothing here needs acting on before the admission proceeds.

questions.takeaway: Screening follows anatomy. Avoidance of care after a bad encounter shows up as missed screening and no regular provider.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal, planned, or part of his history. One finding explains two others, and all three belong in the selection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The clinic argument explains the gaps.

elimination.verdict: s2, s3, s4, s6, and s7: the reason behind them, the name, no provider, pronouns, and screening.

questions.stem: A nurse is taking a sexual history from a new patient. Which approach best reflects the recommended practice?

options.text: Ask about anatomy and specific practices rather than inferring from gender
options.rationale: Risk follows what a person has and what they do. Her flowsheet notes that transgender and non-binary patients may prefer non-gendered terms for their sex organs.

options.text: Ask whether the patient is sexually active with men, women, or both, and proceed from the answer
options.rationale: A reasonable opening that becomes a problem when the answer is used to infer anatomy rather than asking about it.

options.text: Ask only the questions relevant to the presenting complaint
options.rationale: Narrows the history to the reason for the visit and misses screening needs, which is how this population's needs get overlooked.

options.text: Defer the sexual history until a relationship has been established over several visits
options.rationale: Well intentioned, and it delays screening for a group already presenting late. The way to make it safe is how you ask, not whether.

questions.takeaway: Assess anatomy and practices. Avoid inferring what a person has, or what they do, from how they describe themselves.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a reasonable opening question that becomes wrong the moment its answer is used to infer anatomy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves asking about anatomy and practices directly.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses a transgender patient's care with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Gender-affirming care includes mental health and social services, not just surgery."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Most gender-affirming care is mental health care and social services, and surgery is a small part of it.

options.text: "Transitioning is private, personal, and individualized, so I should not assume the steps."
options.rationale: This is accurate. There is no required sequence and no required endpoint, so you do not assume which steps someone has taken.

options.text: "I should ask what name and pronouns he uses and put them in the record."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Recording the name and pronouns is what makes the affirmation hold across every staff member who opens the chart.

options.text: "Since he takes testosterone, he no longer needs cervical screening."
options.rationale: Screening follows the organs a person has. Hormone therapy does not remove a cervix, and this is exactly the need that gets overlooked.

questions.takeaway: Reproductive and sexual health needs are frequently overlooked in this population. Screening is determined by anatomy, not by hormones or identity.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth uses hormone therapy to cancel a screening need.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Names, scope of care, individualized transition.
Testosterone does not remove a cervix.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the cervical screening statement.

questions.stem: A birth center's quality committee is asked why its LGBTQ+ patients report worse birthing experiences and outcomes than other patients. Which recognized contributing factors should the committee address? Select all that apply.

options.text: A higher rate of underlying obstetric complications in this population
options.rationale: The poor outcomes trace to how care is delivered and received, not to an inherent obstetric difference.

options.text: Heterocentric policies
options.rationale: Forms and policies written around an assumed mother and father exclude a patient before anyone has said a word to them.

options.text: Invalidation as parents
options.rationale: Having your parental role questioned or dismissed during pregnancy and birth is a recognized harm, and the non-gestational parent takes most of it.

options.text: Inexperienced physicians
options.rationale: A contributing factor, and it connects directly to the gap in clinician training.

options.text: Bias or discrimination during care
options.rationale: It shapes whether a person returns for the rest of their care.

options.text: Reluctance to disclose pregnancy intentions to an employer
options.rationale: This is plausible as a life stressor, but it is not one of the recognized contributors. The recognized ones happen inside the care encounter itself.

options.text: Disruptions in hormone therapy
options.rationale: Interruptions in hormone therapy are a specific problem for transgender and non-binary parents during pregnancy, and an unplanned gap is a clinical event.

questions.takeaway: Contributing factors include bias and discrimination, heterocentric policies, invalidation as parents, hormone therapy disruption, birth trauma, postpartum difficulties, dysphoria, and inexperienced clinicians.
questions.strategy: One distractor locates the problem in the patients' bodies rather than in the care they receive. That distinction runs through the whole chapter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Places the cause in the patient.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague refer to a patient by the wrong pronoun during handover. He is not present. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the patient afterwards that the error occurred
options.rationale: Hands him a problem he can do nothing about and adds to the burden the practice exists to remove.

options.text: Correct it briefly at the time and continue the handover
options.rationale: The correction has to happen where the error happened, or every nurse on the next shift inherits it. Brief keeps it about the patient rather than the colleague.

options.text: Raise it with the manager after the handover is complete
options.rationale: Going to the manager fits a repeated pattern. It also leaves the incoming shift working from the wrong pronoun all night.

options.text: Say nothing, since the patient is not there to hear it
options.rationale: The pronoun used in handover becomes the pronoun used at the bedside. An uncorrected error propagates.

questions.takeaway: Affirming language has to be consistent across the team. Correct briefly, in the moment, and move on.
questions.strategy: Two options defer the correction. One transfers it to the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what happens to an uncorrected pronoun

steps.detail: The next shift acts on it tonight.
Adds a burden he cannot act on.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the brief correction during handover.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned a transgender patient, tells the charge nurse that affirming care conflicts with the nurse's personal beliefs, and asks to be reassigned. Which basis for the obligation to care for this patient comes from the nursing profession itself?

options.text: Facility policy requires staff to use patients' stated names and pronouns
options.rationale: Real and binding, and it comes from the employer rather than from the profession.

options.text: The Code of Ethics requires respect for every patient's dignity
options.rationale: It is not conditional on agreement, comfort, or the nurse's own views. The obligation attaches to every patient.

options.text: State law protects patients from discrimination in health care settings
options.rationale: Real and binding, and it comes from the legislature rather than from the profession.

options.text: Affirming care improves patient satisfaction survey scores
options.rationale: This is true, but it is the wrong basis. Dignity is not owed to a patient because respecting it scores well on a survey.

questions.takeaway: The Code of Ethics: compassion, respect for dignity, and the worth of every patient. Not conditional and not variable by jurisdiction.
questions.strategy: Three options name real reasons to do it. Ask which one is the professional obligation rather than an external requirement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the Code of Ethics.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse prepares to care for a transgender patient.

Gender-affirming care is the treatment for a diagnosis of [[1]].

A nurse who examines her own assumptions before an encounter is practicing [[2]].

Adding pronoun fields to the intake form is an example of [[3]].

Deciding what screening a patient needs is based on [[4]].

options.text: gender dysphoria
options.rationale: Gender-affirming care treats a diagnosis of gender dysphoria. Dysphoria is the distress, and it is what gets treated.

options.text: sexual orientation
options.rationale: Sexual orientation is who a person is attracted to. It is not a diagnosis and it is unrelated to gender identity.

options.text: gender expression
options.rationale: Gender expression is how someone presents outwardly. It is not a diagnosis either.

options.text: gender identity
options.rationale: Identity is who a person is. It is not a diagnosis and does not require treatment.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Self-reflection means examining your own biases and holding yourself accountable for them. That is inward work.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: Affirming communication is what happens out loud in the conversation. This describes something the nurse does in her own head.

options.text: prioritizing patient needs
options.rationale: Prioritizing the patient means listening, respecting and asking for feedback. It is directed at the patient rather than at yourself.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Educating yourself is learning terminology and health issues. It points outward at the content, not inward at your assumptions.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: The near-miss. Pronouns are used in communication, and changing the form changes the space rather than the conversation.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Self-reflection is inward work on your own assumptions. Changing a form is not that.

options.text: fostering an inclusive environment
options.rationale: Updating policies and building identity fields into the record is how the environment itself becomes inclusive.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Educating yourself is training and terminology. This describes changing the system rather than changing what you know.

options.text: the sex recorded at birth
options.rationale: Closer, and still wrong after surgery. What matters is what is there now.

options.text: the patient's gender identity
options.rationale: Gender identity does not tell you which organs are present. Screening follows anatomy, not the marker in the chart.

options.text: whether the patient takes hormone therapy
options.rationale: Hormone therapy changes physiology and removes nothing. A patient on testosterone who still has a cervix still needs screening.

options.text: the organs the patient has
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy. A transgender man with a cervix still needs cervical screening.

questions.takeaway: Gender dysphoria is the diagnosis. Identity, expression and orientation are not diagnoses. Screening follows anatomy.
questions.strategy: Blank 3 has a genuine near-miss: pronouns belong to communication, and putting a field on a form changes the environment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The nurse, the words, or the space.

elimination.verdict: Gender dysphoria, self-reflection, inclusive environment, organs present.

questions.stem: Which reason best explains why LGBTQ+ health matters specifically to nursing?

options.text: Nurses are often the first contact, which shapes whether patients return
options.rationale: First point of contact, better outcomes and ethical responsibility are the three reasons, and the first is what makes the other two possible.

options.text: Nurses are responsible for prescribing gender-affirming hormone therapy
options.rationale: Outside the registered nurse's scope. The nurse's role is assessment, support, education, and advocacy.

options.text: Nurses must document sexual orientation for every patient on admission
options.rationale: Incorporating identity into records is a system practice, and it is not a mandatory field for every patient.

options.text: Nurses should refer LGBTQ+ patients to specialist clinicians where possible
options.rationale: Reasonable-sounding, but it routes patients away from the care in front of them, which is how needs get overlooked.

questions.takeaway: Three reasons: nurses are the first point of contact, they improve health outcomes, and they hold an ethical responsibility.
questions.strategy: One distractor exceeds nursing scope. One routes the patient elsewhere, which is the opposite of the point.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves being the first point of contact.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she has put off a mammogram for three years, because at her last visit staff repeatedly asked questions about her partner. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that staff attitudes have improved since then
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot keep and that asks her to trust an institution that has already failed her.

options.text: Document that the patient declined screening for three years
options.rationale: This records the gap without doing anything about it, and declined misstates what happened. She was driven away, not asked and refused.

options.text: Explain the importance of regular screening and the risks of delay
options.rationale: This is correct teaching that assumes the barrier is knowledge. She knows why screening matters; she is avoiding the experience of getting it.

options.text: Acknowledge what happened and arrange the screening with the concern addressed
options.rationale: The barrier is the previous encounter. Naming it and changing what happens this time is what makes the screening possible.

questions.takeaway: Avoidance after a bad encounter is an access problem. Address what happened before addressing the screening.
questions.strategy: One option teaches, one documents, one reassures. None of them changes what she is afraid will happen again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves acknowledging it and arranging the screening differently.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old is admitted for a scheduled procedure. She lives with the woman she calls her partner of 30 years, who is not listed anywhere in the record. During admission she asks twice whether her partner will be allowed to stay, and says a previous hospital sent her partner home at the end of visiting hours while family members of other patients remained. She has not had a primary care visit in four years.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Confirm with her what the visiting arrangements are and tell the team
options.rationale: Answers the question she has now asked twice, and makes the arrangement known to the people who will enforce it.

options.text: Ask who she wants documented as her support person and record it where staff will see
options.rationale: Records that assume a family structure are what produced the exclusion last time. Writing down the support person she names is what stops it repeating.

options.text: Reassure her that this hospital does not discriminate
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot enforce, offered instead of the documentation and communication that would actually secure it.

options.text: Document that the patient appears anxious about visiting policy
options.rationale: This records her anxiety as a finding and leaves the cause of it untouched. She will be just as anxious with it charted.

options.text: Knowledge deficit regarding hospital visiting policy
options.rationale: Frames it as not knowing the rules. She knows what happened last time; the issue is whether it happens again.

options.text: Lack of family support during hospitalization
options.rationale: She has support. The risk is that the institution will not recognize it.

options.text: Anxiety related to the upcoming procedure
options.rationale: This is plausible and it is not what she asked about. Both of her questions were about her partner, not the operation.

options.text: Anticipated exclusion of her partner, based on a previous experience
options.rationale: She has asked twice and told you why. The problem is a reasonable expectation built from what happened before.

options.text: Whether her vital signs remain stable before the procedure
options.rationale: Stable vital signs are a real parameter and they evaluate nothing you changed. Nothing in the plan was aimed at her blood pressure.

options.text: Whether she can state the hospital's visiting policy
options.rationale: Tests recall of a rule. The problem was never that she did not know one.

options.text: Whether her partner is recorded and treated as her support person by all staff
options.rationale: This measures whether the documentation actually changed how staff behaved, which is the only thing that matters to her.

options.text: Whether she raises the question again
options.rationale: She asked twice. If she stops asking, the question has been answered to her satisfaction.

questions.takeaway: Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services. A partner unrecognized by the record is how that exclusion happens in practice.
questions.strategy: Two problem options relocate the issue into her, as anxiety or as not knowing. She told you it is about what happened last time.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Twice, about her partner, with a reason.

steps.action: Cut the options that relocate it

steps.detail: You documented and you told the team.

elimination.verdict: Document and communicate, for anticipated exclusion, evaluated by staff behavior and whether she asks again.

questions.stem: A clinic schedules every patient for a 15-minute visit and sends every patient home with the same printed handout. A nurse points out that patients who need an interpreter receive less information in that time than patients who do not. Which principle supports the concern?

options.text: Health equity
options.rationale: Equity asks what a patient needs to reach the same outcome. The interpreted visit needs more minutes to deliver the same teaching, so identical scheduling produces unequal care.

options.text: Health equality
options.rationale: The emotionally satisfying answer and the wrong one. Equality is exactly what the clinic is already doing, and it is what created the gap.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: This is true of the nurse's motive, but too broad to name the problem. Beneficence does not explain why giving everyone the same thing fails here.

options.text: Cultural competence
options.rationale: Knowledge about groups would not add the minutes back. The barrier is structural rather than informational.

questions.takeaway: Equality gives everyone the same. Equity gives each patient what it takes to reach the same outcome. Identical treatment can produce unequal care.
questions.strategy: When an option restates the policy that caused the problem, it is the distractor.

strategies: Name what the policy already does

steps.action: Notice the clinic is treating everyone alike
Choose the principle that accounts for need

elimination.verdict: Health equity is the answer.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted to a long-term care facility. The record lists her partner of 40 years as a friend. She asks the nurse not to mention the relationship to the rest of the staff. Which nursing action best addresses the concern behind that request?

options.text: Correct the record so the relationship is listed accurately
options.rationale: Accuracy serves the patient only when the patient wants it. Overriding the request hands out information the patient deliberately withheld.

options.text: Document the request and hold the limits the patient set
options.rationale: Disclosure belongs to the patient. Older LGBTQ+ patients entering congregate care often return to concealment because they expect worse treatment, and the nurse's job is to make the limit hold rather than test it.

options.text: Reassure the patient that staff here are trained to be inclusive
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot verify, and it answers a fear with optimism instead of control.

options.text: Encourage disclosure so the partner can be fully involved
options.rationale: Well meant pressure is still pressure. It asks the patient to accept a risk for the nurse's idea of better care.

questions.takeaway: Disclosure is the patient's to control. Entering a facility is exactly when an older LGBTQ+ patient is most likely to re-conceal, and the nurse protects that choice rather than correcting it.
questions.strategy: Options that make the patient more visible feel like advocacy. Ask who carries the risk if they are wrong.

strategies: Ask who owns the information

steps.action: Cut the options that widen disclosure
steps.detail: Correcting the record and encouraging it both do.

elimination.verdict: Document the request and hold the limit.

questions.stem: A patient who is transgender is admitted for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. While taking the surgical history, the nurse considers how to ask about previous gender-affirming surgery. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Ask about prior abdominal and pelvic surgeries only
options.rationale: Ask what bears on this operation. Previous abdominal or pelvic surgery of any kind raises the chance of adhesions, and that is a surgical fact rather than a question about gender.

options.text: Ask about all gender-affirming surgeries for completeness
options.rationale: Completeness is the stated reason and curiosity is the usual one. A chest reconstruction has no bearing on a gallbladder.

options.text: Avoid the surgical history entirely to protect privacy
options.rationale: Avoidance is not respect. Skipping relevant history puts the patient at risk in the operating room.

options.text: Review the record instead of asking the patient directly
options.rationale: Records are frequently incomplete or wrong on this. The patient is the better source, and this question is clinically relevant to an abdominal operation.

questions.takeaway: Ask about anatomy and procedures that affect the care in front of you. Gender-affirming surgery is relevant when the site is relevant, and not otherwise.
questions.strategy: Two options sound protective. Neither gets the clinical information this operation requires.

strategies: Tie each question to this admission

steps.action: Ask what affects a laparoscopic approach

elimination.verdict: Ask about abdominal and pelvic surgeries.

questions.stem: A patient's chart lists a legal name and sex that do not match the name and pronouns he gave at the desk. He is being moved to a ward bed. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Ask him what name and pronouns staff should use and record both in the chart
options.rationale: Recording both keeps the legal name for billing and identification while every clinician sees what to use at the bedside.

options.text: Use his legal name for identification and his chosen name in conversation
options.rationale: This splits the practice so that each new clinician gets it wrong once before learning.

options.text: Ask the charge nurse which room assignment is appropriate
options.rationale: This turns his identity into a logistics problem before anyone has asked him anything.

options.text: Correct the legal name in the chart to the name he uses
options.rationale: The legal name is required for identification and billing, and the nurse cannot change it.

questions.takeaway: Record the chosen name and pronouns alongside the legal name. One is for the system, the other is for the person.
questions.strategy: Three options pick one name and lose the other. The item is asking whether you can keep both.

strategies: Ask what each name is for

steps.detail: Identification and billing, cannot be deleted.

steps.action: Cut the options that discard one

elimination.verdict: That leaves recording both.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted to long-term care. Her partner of 40 years is listed in the record as a friend. She asks the nurse not to correct it. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Correct the record, since accurate relationship data improves care
options.rationale: Accuracy matters and overriding her request removes the control she is asking for.

options.text: Leave the record alone and say nothing further
options.rationale: This respects the request and leaves the reason for it unexamined.

options.text: Ask what makes disclosure feel unsafe here
options.rationale: Her request is a report of expected discrimination, and that is the assessable problem.

options.text: Explain that staff are required to treat everyone equally
options.rationale: This answers a fear with a policy and tells her the concern is unfounded.

questions.takeaway: A request for concealment from a patient of this generation is usually about safety, not privacy. Assess the fear before changing anything.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the record. The question is about why she asked, not what the record says.

strategies: Ask what the request is telling you
elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what makes disclosure feel unsafe.

questions.stem: A nurse is taking a sexual history from a new patient who says she is sexually active with one woman. Which action is correct?

options.text: Ask about sexual practices and about condom and barrier use
options.rationale: Practices determine risk, and partner gender does not. This is the step most often skipped.

options.text: Move on, since the risk of sexually transmitted infection is lower
options.rationale: This is the assumption the case is built to catch, and it skips the assessment.

options.text: Ask whether she has ever had a male partner
options.rationale: This treats male partners as the only source of risk and reduces her to a history.

options.text: Document her orientation and continue with the rest of the history
options.rationale: Orientation is not the assessment. What she does is.

questions.takeaway: Risk follows practices, not identity. The questions about barriers get asked of everyone.
questions.strategy: Three options stop the assessment early. Each stops for a different reason, and all three are the same error.

strategies: Ask what determines risk

steps.action: Cut every option that stops asking

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking about practices and barrier use.

questions.stem: A transgender patient on hormone therapy is admitted for an unrelated surgery. The surgical team plans to hold the hormones perioperatively. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Support the plan, since hormone therapy raises perioperative clotting risk
options.rationale: There is a clotting consideration, and holding it without discussion is what the item is testing.

options.text: Confirm that the patient has been told and consulted about the interruption
options.rationale: Disruption of hormone therapy is a known harm, and the patient has a stake in a decision made about her body.

options.text: Request that the hormones be continued through the admission
options.rationale: Advocating for one clinical answer oversteps, and the decision is not the nurse's to make.

options.text: Document the plan and reinforce that it is temporary
options.rationale: Documenting and reassuring skips whether she knows at all.

questions.takeaway: Disruption of hormone therapy is a recognized harm. The nursing action is making sure the patient is part of the decision.
questions.strategy: Two options pick a side of a clinical argument that is not the nurse's to settle. Ask what the nurse owns here.

strategies: Ask what the nurse owns
elimination.verdict: That leaves confirming she has been consulted.

questions.stem: A transgender man is admitted for pneumonia and will be placed in a shared room. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask him what room placement would feel safest and act on his answer
options.rationale: Placement affects his safety and his privacy, and he is the only one who knows what feels safe on this unit.

options.text: Place him in a room with other male patients, since that matches his gender identity
options.rationale: Reasonable as a default, but it still decides something for him that he may have a view about.

options.text: Place him in a private room regardless of availability to avoid any difficulty
options.rationale: Automatic isolation treats him as a problem to be managed and can read as exclusion.

options.text: Place him according to the sex recorded on his insurance record
options.rationale: A record field does not determine where a person is safe.

questions.takeaway: Where the law and the facility allow a choice, the patient decides what is safe for him. Do not place by a record field, and do not isolate by default.
questions.strategy: Placing him by his gender identity is defensible and still skips him. Being right about his gender does not substitute for asking about his safety.

strategies: Ask who holds the information
elimination.verdict: That leaves asking him.

questions.stem: A nurse reads that LGBTQ+ older adults have higher rates of chronic conditions and worse overall health than their peers. A colleague says this must reflect lifestyle. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Lifestyle factors account for most of the difference in this population
options.rationale: This is the colleague's assumption and it misplaces the cause.

options.text: The difference reflects higher rates of underlying genetic risk
options.rationale: Nothing supports a genetic explanation for this disparity.

options.text: Lifetime exposure to stigma and avoidance of care account for much of it
options.rationale: Discrimination over a lifetime, isolation, and avoiding a system that has not affirmed them drive the disparity.

options.text: The data largely reflect underreporting in comparison groups
options.rationale: This dismisses a measured disparity as an artifact.

questions.takeaway: The disparity traces to stigma, isolation, and lack of affirmation discouraging people from using services.
questions.strategy: Three options relocate the cause into the patient. Ask whether the explanation sits in the person or in what the person has met.

strategies: Ask where the cause is placed

steps.detail: Outside, in what they have encountered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stigma and avoidance of care.

questions.stem: A nursing student says she treats all her patients exactly the same regardless of identity, and that this is what equity means. Which response is accurate?

options.text: She is describing equity correctly, since identical treatment removes bias
options.rationale: Identical treatment is equality, and it is not the same thing.

options.text: She is describing equality; equity adjusts so each patient reaches the same outcome
options.rationale: Equality gives everyone the same thing. Equity gives each person what they need to reach the same place.

options.text: She is describing cultural competence, which requires treating everyone identically
options.rationale: Cultural competence requires responding to difference, not ignoring it.

options.text: She is correct, provided she also documents each patient's identity accurately
options.rationale: Documentation does not convert identical treatment into equity.

questions.takeaway: Equality is the same input. Equity is adjusted input so the outcome can be the same.
questions.strategy: The student's statement sounds like fairness. The item turns on whether you can name which kind.

strategies: Define both terms before reading the options
elimination.verdict: That leaves the option that names it as equality.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to reduce the barriers LGBTQ+ patients report to accessing care. Which changes address barriers that patients themselves identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Training all staff, including reception, in affirming care
options.rationale: Fear of stigma is the most commonly reported barrier, and it is met at the front desk first.

options.text: Revising intake forms to capture gender identity and chosen name
options.rationale: Heterocentric forms are a recognized barrier and are the first thing a patient encounters.

options.text: Displaying symbols of inclusivity in public areas
options.rationale: Visible signals of inclusion are a recognized element of creating a safe space.

options.text: Hiring more clinicians who identify as LGBTQ+
options.rationale: Shared identity does not substitute for training, and patients name training rather than staff identity.

options.text: Adding evening and weekend appointment slots
options.rationale: Extended hours help everyone and are not among the barriers this population names.

options.text: Reviewing insurance coverage for gender-affirming services
options.rationale: Cost and coverage are recognized by both patients and providers as a barrier.

questions.takeaway: Patient-reported barriers: fear of stigma, distrust of the system, cost and coverage. Provider-reported: coverage, policy environment, lack of training.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are genuine improvements to a clinic. Ask whether patients name them as the barrier.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A general improvement, not a recognized barrier.

elimination.verdict: The four changes matching named barriers are selected.

questions.stem: A transgender man is admitted for abdominal pain. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask which terms he uses for his own anatomy before the examination
options.rationale: Patients may prefer non-gendered terms for their organs, and asking first prevents a distressing exam.

options.text: Base the assessment on the organs he has rather than his recorded sex
options.rationale: Anatomy present determines what is assessed, whatever the chart says.

options.text: Ask about his surgical history as part of the assessment
options.rationale: Surgical history is relevant to abdominal pain and is asked of any patient with that complaint.

options.text: Ask about the details of his transition out of general interest
options.rationale: Transition is private, personal and individualized, and curiosity is not an assessment.

options.text: Explain his gender identity to the oncoming nurse during handover
options.rationale: Handover covers what the next nurse needs clinically, including name and pronouns, not an explanation of his identity.

options.text: Use his chosen name and pronouns with every member of the team
options.rationale: Consistency across the team is what makes the affirmation real rather than individual.

questions.takeaway: Assess the anatomy present, ask what words to use, and keep name and pronouns consistent. Transition details are only relevant when they bear on the problem.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are things a curious or well-meaning nurse does. Ask whether the patient's care requires it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the abdominal pain requires
Cut explaining his identity at handover

elimination.verdict: The four appropriate actions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse examines her own practice after a transgender patient tells her the admission felt uncomfortable. Which of these are elements of creating a safe space? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reflecting on her own assumptions before the encounter
options.rationale: Self-reflection and examining personal bias are recognized first in creating a safe space.

options.text: Being mindful of her nonverbal behavior
options.rationale: Nonverbal cues are recognized alongside language, and they often carry more than the words.

options.text: Seeking feedback from patients about their experience
options.rationale: Prioritizing patient needs includes asking patients and acting on what they say.

options.text: Avoiding any mention of gender identity to prevent discomfort
options.rationale: Avoidance is not neutrality, and it leaves identity unaddressed in the record and the care.

options.text: Participating in ongoing training rather than a single session
options.rationale: Education is ongoing rather than a single session, and a one-off is where this most often fails.

options.text: Relying on a colleague who shares the patient's identity to take over
options.rationale: Transferring the patient removes the nurse's responsibility to learn and singles the patient out.

questions.takeaway: Creating a safe space: educate yourself, reflect on bias, use affirming language and nonverbal behavior, build an inclusive environment, prioritize patient needs.
questions.strategy: Both distractors feel considerate. Ask whether the action develops the nurse or avoids the discomfort.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: The four elements are selected.

questions.stem: A patient who told the admitting nurse about his husband asks the day nurse not to mention it when the surgical team rounds. The day nurse knows the relationship is already recorded in the chart and that the team will see it. What does she do?

options.text: Reassure him that the surgical team are professionals who will not judge him
options.rationale: Whether they will judge him is not hers to promise, and the reassurance ends the conversation before he says why he asked.

options.text: Explain that the information is already documented, so the team will have it regardless once they open the chart
options.rationale: True, and it answers a question he did not ask. He is telling her about this conversation with these people, and the reply hands the decision back to the record.

options.text: Remove the information from the chart at his request
options.rationale: Clinically relevant information is not deleted, and altering the record is not how a privacy concern is handled.

options.text: Honor the request for this conversation and ask him what he wants shared, with whom, and when
options.rationale: Disclosure is decided again in every room and with every team. The right nursing action is finding out where his line is rather than assuming one disclosure settled it.

questions.takeaway: Coming out is not an event that happens once. A patient controls what is said, to whom, in each situation, and documentation does not transfer that consent.
questions.strategy: The accurate option and the correct option are different things here. Ask what he was asking for.

strategies: Ask what the patient requested
elimination.verdict: Honor it and ask what he wants shared.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old transgender man is admitted with abdominal pain. His record carries a male sex marker. He has had chest surgery and no other procedures. His hemoglobin returns and the system has not flagged it, although the value sits below the range used for women. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Treat the unflagged value as normal, since the laboratory applies the range in the record
options.rationale: The system compared his result to the wrong population. A missing flag is not a normal result.

options.text: Record gender identity and an inventory of the organs he has as separate fields, so results are interpreted correctly and screening is not dropped
options.rationale: Reference ranges and screening both follow anatomy and physiology. Recording them separately from identity is what lets the record be right about both things at once.

options.text: Change the sex marker in the record to female, so that his laboratory values flag correctly against the right reference range for every test from now on
options.rationale: It fixes one flag by misgendering him in every other screen, document and conversation. The marker is not the tool for this problem and it is not the nurse's to change.

options.text: Report the value to the provider without comment and wait for direction
options.rationale: Passing along a number without the context that makes it meaningful leaves the same error in place.

questions.takeaway: Identity and anatomy are two different pieces of data and the record needs both. Laboratory ranges and screening follow the body; names and pronouns follow the person.
questions.strategy: One option solves the immediate problem and creates a larger one. Ask what else the change would touch.

strategies: Trace the consequence of each action
elimination.verdict: Record identity and organ inventory separately.

questions.stem: An unconscious patient's partner of twenty years is at the bedside. A brother arrives, states that the partner has no legal standing, and asks to be consulted on decisions instead. There is no advance directive in the record. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Defer to the partner, since twenty years means he knows the patient's wishes better than anyone
