questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is prescribed home oxygen at 2 L/min. On a home visit the concentrator is set at 5 L/min, and he is drowsy, difficult to rouse, and has a respiratory rate of 8. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply a non-rebreather mask and increase the flow further
options.rationale: Would deepen the problem. This patient is hypoventilating on too much oxygen, and more oxygen removes what is left of the drive to breathe.

options.text: Reduce the flow to the prescribed rate and rouse
options.rationale: The cause is in front of the nurse and is reversible in seconds. Correct the flow and stimulate respiration, then escalate while reassessing.

options.text: Obtain an arterial blood gas sample for analysis
options.rationale: Will confirm what the respiratory rate of 8 already says. Correct but premature when the cause is visible and fixable now.

options.text: Document the finding and notify the prescribing provider
options.rationale: Notification is coming and documenting first is acting on the chart while the patient hypoventilates.

questions.takeaway: In chronic carbon dioxide retention, excess oxygen suppresses the respiratory drive. A drowsy patient with a rate of 8 on more oxygen than prescribed needs the flow corrected, not increased.
questions.strategy: Only one option makes the patient worse, and it is the one that looks most like treating hypoxia. Ask what the extra oxygen is doing.

strategies: ABCs
Reverse the cause when it is visible

steps.action: Link the drowsiness to the flow
Cut the gas and the documentation

elimination.verdict: Reduce the flow and rouse the patient.

questions.stem: A man has provided all the care at home for his wife with advanced dementia for three years. He has lost 6 kg, has not seen a provider in two years, sleeps in a chair at her bedside, and says it is all manageable. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Assess the spouse for depression and unmet health needs
options.rationale: Weight loss, no care of their own, and broken sleep is a caregiver in trouble who is reporting none of it. You find out what is happening before choosing what to arrange.

options.text: Arrange respite care so the spouse can rest
options.rationale: The most compelling option and the one most likely to be chosen. It may be exactly right, and the nurse does not yet know what the need is.

options.text: Praise the spouse's commitment to the patient
options.rationale: This is warm, and it closes the conversation. He has already minimized once, and praise tells him to keep doing that.

options.text: Teach techniques that reduce the daily workload
options.rationale: Assumes the problem is technique. The findings point to the caregiver's own health.

questions.takeaway: Caregiver strain gets assessed before it gets solved. A caregiver who says it is manageable while losing weight is giving you the reason to assess, not the reason to accept it.
questions.strategy: The intervention options feel more satisfying than the assessment option. That is usually the sign you are being pulled toward the wrong one.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Notice the report and the findings disagree
steps.detail: Manageable versus 6 kg and no provider.
Both pick an intervention before the need is known.

elimination.verdict: Assess the caregiver.

questions.stem: Two patients have the same ejection fraction and the same medication list for heart failure. One has stopped attending church and describes himself as a burden. The other has adjusted his routine and says little has changed. Which distinction does this illustrate?

options.text: One is adherent and the other is not
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem describes either man's adherence.

options.text: Chronic disease is the same in both, and chronic illness differs
options.rationale: Chronic disease is the diagnosed pathological process. Chronic illness is how a person feels, adapts and lives with it.

options.text: One has a comorbid depressive disorder
options.rationale: Possible, and the stem supplies no diagnosis and the distinction being tested is not psychiatric.

options.text: Ejection fraction is an unreliable measure of severity
options.rationale: The measure is not what differs. The experience is.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease is the clinical process. Chronic illness is the personal and social experience of living with it.
questions.strategy: Identical clinical data with different lives is the setup. Resist diagnosing the difference and name it.

strategies: Ask what is identical and what differs
elimination.verdict: That leaves disease against illness.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old caring for her husband with dementia for two years in their shared home tells the nurse she is managing. Which finding most strongly indicates she is at risk for poor health?

options.text: She describes the caregiving as rewarding most days
options.rationale: A positive appraisal does not remove the risk and is not itself a risk factor.

options.text: She has not seen her own provider in eighteen months
options.rationale: Missed care is a consequence, and the recognized risk factors are about the caregiving situation itself.

options.text: She is 70 and has cared for him at home for over a year
options.rationale: Three risk factors stack here: age 65 or over, living with the recipient, and caregiving beyond one year, with dementia care on top.

options.text: Her husband needs help with all activities of daily living
options.rationale: Significant need is one risk factor. The option naming three carries more weight.

questions.takeaway: Caregiver risk factors: caring over a year, age 65 or over, caring for someone with significant needs, dementia care, and living with the recipient.
questions.strategy: Two options each name a real factor. The strongest answer is the one that stacks several.

strategies: Count the named factors in each option
elimination.verdict: That leaves the option naming three.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has been told conflicting things by three clinics and has stopped attending any of them. Which Chronic Care Model component has failed?

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Self-management support teaches the patient to manage daily care. He is not failing to manage, he is failing to be coordinated.

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: Shared information is what would have let three clinics say the same thing.

options.text: Decision support
options.rationale: Decision support puts evidence in front of clinicians. The problem is not what they knew, it is that they did not share it.

options.text: Community resources
options.rationale: Nothing here concerns resources outside the health system.

questions.takeaway: Chronic Care Model: community, health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems.
questions.strategy: Three clinics disagreeing is a data problem before it is a teaching problem. Ask what would have prevented the contradiction.

strategies: Ask what would have prevented it

steps.detail: He is not the failing part.
Each clinic may have been individually right.

elimination.verdict: That leaves clinical information systems.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with ulcerative colitis says the hardest part is that she looks well, so people assume she is exaggerating. Which aspect of chronic illness is she describing?

options.text: Social isolation resulting from her symptoms
options.rationale: Isolation may follow, and what she is naming is why.

options.text: A knowledge deficit among her family and friends
options.rationale: Framing it as other people's ignorance misses that this is her experience of the illness.

options.text: Stigma attached to a gastrointestinal diagnosis
options.rationale: Stigma is about the condition being judged. She describes not being believed.

options.text: The invisible nature of many chronic symptoms
options.rationale: Invisible symptoms are a recognized aspect of chronic illness, and disbelief from others is the consequence she reports.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness includes invisible symptoms, mental health effects, fatigue and navigating social change.
questions.strategy: Three options name real phenomena. Match the option to what she said rather than to what might follow from it.

strategies: Quote her back

steps.detail: Both are consequences, not what she named.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the invisible nature of her symptoms.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old with multiple sclerosis works full time and has two children under ten. She has stopped taking her afternoon dose because it makes her too drowsy to collect them from school. Which nursing consideration matters most?

options.text: She is nonadherent and needs teaching about the consequences of missed doses
options.rationale: She made a reasoned trade and calling it nonadherence ends the conversation that would fix it.

options.text: Her developmental stage shapes what the regimen has to fit around, so the plan is built around work and parenting
options.rationale: At this stage the roles are the life, and a regimen that costs her those roles will keep losing.

options.text: Her disease severity should be reassessed before the regimen is changed
options.rationale: Severity has not changed. What is colliding is the schedule.

options.text: The family should take over the school collection so she can take the dose
options.rationale: Reorganizing her family around the drug reverses the order of the problem.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness is managed inside a life. Ask what the regimen is competing with at this stage, then build around it.
questions.strategy: Nonadherence is the label waiting to be used. She told you exactly why, which means the problem is solvable.

strategies: Ask why she stopped

steps.action: It cost her the school run

elimination.verdict: That leaves building around her stage of life.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure is admitted for the third time this year. The unit has no current heart failure pathway, and each nurse teaches discharge weights differently depending on what she was taught.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: The patient is not refusing to manage. The staff cannot agree on what to teach him.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: Delivery system design is about how visits and roles are organized, and the failure here is in what guides the care rather than who delivers it.

options.text: Decision support
options.rationale: Evidence-based guidelines embedded where care happens are what is missing, and without them practice varies by whoever is on.

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: The records are not the problem. The guidance is.

questions.takeaway: Decision support puts current evidence at the point of care. Delivery system design arranges who does what and when. Without the first, practice varies with whoever is working.
questions.strategy: Both middle options describe something organizational. Ask whether what is missing is the arrangement of the care or the guidance behind it.

strategies: Ask what is missing

steps.detail: Roles and visits are not the issue.
He is not the one failing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves decision support.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes asks whether she caused this by being overweight. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Weight is the main driver, and losing it is where to start
options.rationale: This confirms blame and oversimplifies a multifactorial disease.

options.text: Several factors interact, including genetics, environment and lifestyle, and none of them acts alone
options.rationale: Chronic disease is multifactorial, and this answers the blame without dismissing the role of weight.

options.text: No, diabetes is genetic and not related to weight
options.rationale: This is inaccurate and swaps one oversimplification for another.

options.text: The cause matters less than the management from here
options.rationale: True, but it refuses her question, which was about blame.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease is multifactorial: genetic, environmental, lifestyle, physical and psychological factors interacting.
questions.strategy: The last distractor is the kind, evasive answer. Ask whether the response addresses what she asked.

strategies: Ask what she wants to know
elimination.verdict: That leaves the multifactorial answer.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has heart failure, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes. Which assessments are nursing implications specific to chronic illness? Select all that apply.

options.text: How she manages her symptoms on a bad day
options.rationale: Symptom management is a recognized nursing implication and it is where chronic and acute care differ most.

options.text: Whether she takes her medications and what interferes
options.rationale: Adherence is recognized, and the barrier matters more than the fact.

options.text: Her tobacco and alcohol use
options.rationale: Both are recognized lifestyle assessments in chronic illness care.

options.text: Her ejection fraction and most recent A1C
options.rationale: Clinical values are part of the medical picture. The nursing implications concern how she lives with the conditions.

options.text: How the three conditions together affect her daily activities
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is the norm and the interaction is what the nurse assesses.

options.text: Which specialist is managing each condition
options.rationale: Useful for coordination and not a nursing implication of chronic illness itself.

questions.takeaway: Nursing implications in chronic illness: assessment, adherence, symptom management, tobacco, alcohol, lifestyle, and the effect on daily life.
questions.strategy: Two distractors belong in the chart. Ask whether the item describes the disease or the life being lived with it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The human response, not the pathology.

elimination.verdict: The four nursing assessments are selected.

questions.stem: A patient has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which factors reflect the multifactorial nature of chronic disease? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thirty years working in a textile mill
options.rationale: Occupational exposure is an environmental factor and it is the one most often missed.

options.text: A parent and a sibling with the same diagnosis
options.rationale: Genetic influence and family history are recognized.

options.text: A forty-year smoking history
options.rationale: Tobacco use is one of lifestyle and risk factors.

options.text: The age at which his first symptom appeared
options.rationale: Age of onset describes the course of the disease rather than contributing to it.

options.text: Poor nutrition over many years
options.rationale: Nutrition is one of the contributing factors.

options.text: His score on a quality of life questionnaire
options.rationale: That measures the impact of the disease, not what produced it.

questions.takeaway: Multifactorial: genetic influence and family history, environmental exposure, tobacco, alcohol, nutrition.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe the disease rather than its causes. Ask whether the item came before the disease or after it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut age of onset and quality of life
steps.detail: Both describe the disease once it exists.

elimination.verdict: The four contributing factors are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with three chronic conditions will manage a complex regimen at home. Which actions support self-management? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching him to recognize early signs of fluid overload and what to do
options.rationale: Recognizing and acting on early change is the core of self-management support.

options.text: Agreeing with him which single change he will make first
options.rationale: Involving the patient in setting the goal is what makes it his rather than the team's.

options.text: Giving him a written action plan with thresholds for calling
options.rationale: A plan with thresholds converts knowledge into a decision he can make at home.

options.text: Arranging daily phone calls from the clinic to check adherence
options.rationale: Monitoring by the clinic replaces self-management rather than supporting it.

options.text: Connecting him with a community program for people with the same condition
options.rationale: Community resources are a recognized component and they extend support beyond the clinic.

options.text: Simplifying the regimen by stopping the medication he finds hardest
options.rationale: Stopping a prescribed medication is not a nursing decision and it is not self-management.

questions.takeaway: Self-management support: teach recognition and response, set goals with the patient, give an action plan, link to community resources.
questions.strategy: Two distractors look supportive. Ask whether the patient ends up more capable or more supervised.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who holds the decision afterwards

elimination.verdict: The four supporting actions are selected.

questions.stem: A man with heart failure has not taken his diuretic for eight days. He can state what it does and what happens without it. He stopped because on the days he takes it he cannot leave the house, and he drives his wife to dialysis three mornings a week. Which nursing action fits the problem?

options.text: Document the nonadherence in the record and notify the provider that he has not been taking it
options.rationale: Accurate as a label and it hands over a judgment instead of a reason. The provider gets no information that leads anywhere.

options.text: Reteach the purpose of the diuretic, how it works, and why taking it at the same time every day matters, since missed doses are a common reason for readmission
options.rationale: Teaching treats a knowledge gap. He described the mechanism correctly, so repeating it tells him something he used to decide.

options.text: Treat it as a reasoned trade-off, find a dosing time that fits the mornings he drives, and tell the provider what changed and why
options.rationale: He made a choice between two things he values. The intervention has to change the fit between the regimen and the day, because nothing about his understanding needs changing.

options.text: Set up a weekly pill organizer and arrange daily reminder calls from the clinic
options.rationale: A solution for forgetting, applied to a man who did not forget.

questions.takeaway: Find out whether the patient could not or chose not. Unintentional nonadherence needs reminders and skills. Intentional nonadherence needs the regimen renegotiated against the life it has to fit inside.
questions.strategy: Three options assume a deficit the stem has already ruled out. Read what he knows before choosing.

strategies: Ask what is missing
elimination.verdict: Renegotiate the timing.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old with several chronic conditions takes two glucose-lowering medications aimed at a tight target. She has had three episodes of lightheadedness in a month, one on standing in her kitchen. She tells the nurse the only thing she wants is to keep going to her grandson's games on Saturdays. What does the nurse bring to the provider?

options.text: A plan to teach her hypoglycemia symptoms and recheck in a month
options.rationale: Education applied to a dosing problem. She can learn the symptoms and still fall on a Saturday.

options.text: A recommendation to discontinue one of the two agents
options.rationale: Probably the right clinical direction, and it skips the part that makes the conversation work. Handing over a conclusion without her goal and the episodes behind it invites a yes or a no rather than a rethink.

options.text: A request to add a third agent so that the target is reached more consistently through the day and through the night as well
options.rationale: It treats the number as the goal in a patient whose risk from a fall exceeds her risk from a slightly higher value.

options.text: The three episodes, what she said she is aiming for, and the question of whether the target still fits her
options.rationale: She has given the goal that the plan should be measured against, and the episodes are the data that makes the question answerable. Framing it as a question keeps the decision where it belongs and still forces it.

questions.takeaway: In chronic illness the target serves the patient's goal, not the other way around. Bring the goal and the data, and let the question be asked rather than answered for the provider.
questions.strategy: Two options point the same clinical direction. Ask which one brings the reasoning with it.

strategies: Ask what the provider receives
elimination.verdict: Bring the episodes, the goal, and the question.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure and kidney disease has been admitted twice in three months. In that period he saw a cardiologist, a nephrologist and his primary provider, all within one health system using one shared record that each of them read. Each changed a medication without reference to the others, and no one list matched. Which part of the chronic care model failed here?

options.text: Decision support
options.rationale: Decision support puts current evidence in front of clinicians. Each change may have been evidence-based on its own, and they still collided.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Keeping three specialists aligned is not a task the patient should be carrying, and calling it his failure misplaces the problem.

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: The strongest distractor and the stem closes it. One record, shared, and each of them read it. The information was present and nobody owned the coordination.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: This component decides who does what, who coordinates, and how a patient moves between clinicians. Three people acting independently with no one holding the whole is a design failure.

questions.takeaway: Information available to everyone and coordinated by nobody is a design problem. Ask who was responsible for the whole patient before blaming the record or the patient.
questions.strategy: The detail about the shared record is placed there to eliminate the tempting answer. Read it.

strategies: Look for the detail that rules out a distractor
elimination.verdict: Delivery system design.

questions.stem: A man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease performed pursed-lip breathing correctly twice in clinic. He tells the nurse he cannot do it at home, because by the time he is breathless he has forgotten how. Which approach is most likely to change that?

options.text: Show him a recording of another patient with the same diagnosis using it during exertion
options.rationale: Watching someone similar succeed does raise confidence and it is weaker than doing it. Use it when the patient cannot attempt the task yet.

options.text: Explain how pursed-lip breathing keeps the small airways open
options.rationale: Understanding why is not the gap. He knows the technique and does not believe he can produce it when breathless.

options.text: Have him walk the corridor until he is short of breath and use the technique there, with the nurse alongside, until it works
options.rationale: A success under the conditions where he needs it is the strongest source of confidence. Performing it calm and seated proves nothing about the moment that matters.

options.text: Tell him he has done it correctly twice already and that he is a good deal more capable of doing it at home than he believes
options.rationale: Encouragement is the weakest of the routes to confidence and it tends to evaporate at the first failure.

questions.takeaway: Confidence in a skill comes mostly from having done it, and it has to be done under the conditions it is for. Watching and encouragement are second and third.
questions.strategy: All four are real teaching strategies. Rank them by strength, then check which matches the condition he described.

strategies: Rank the strategies, then match the gap

steps.action: Rank doing against watching and telling

elimination.verdict: Practice it while breathless.

questions.stem: Which findings point to treatment burden rather than to a knowledge deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: He asks what the newest medication on his list is for
options.rationale: A direct knowledge gap and an easy one to close.

options.text: He says he spends about two hours a day on his health and has stopped seeing friends
options.rationale: The regimen has taken over the life it exists to protect. That cost is the burden itself.

options.text: He names every medication and the time each is due, and takes about half of them
options.rationale: Knowing and not doing is the signature. Something other than understanding is stopping him.

options.text: He cannot name his inhaler and his technique with it is wrong in several steps
options.rationale: Skill and knowledge, both teachable.

options.text: He has four appointments in two weeks at three locations and misses the third
options.rationale: The schedule exceeds what one person with his transport and energy can execute.

options.text: The drug he stopped is the one requiring monthly bloodwork, not the most expensive one
options.rationale: He dropped the one with the highest effort cost. The pattern of what gets abandoned tells you what the burden is made of.

questions.takeaway: Treatment burden is the work a regimen demands. When a patient knows the plan and cannot run it, teaching harder makes the burden heavier.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into cannot and will not. Knowledge gaps are cannot, and they look different from a plan that costs too much.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: The four burden findings are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient is 27, diagnosed with type 2 diabetes two years ago and now requires insulin. Admitted with a blood glucose of 322 mg/dL; the target range is 80 to 130. HbA1c 11%, target 7% or less. Became unhoused after losing a job and health insurance. Currently living in shelter-provided housing. Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months. Previous providers documented that the patient verbalized understanding of the diabetes management but has difficulty following the treatment plan. Alert and oriented. Answers questions readily.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent social determinants affecting her ability to manage her diabetes.

segments.text: Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months
segments.rationale: The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

segments.text: Lost the health insurance
segments.rationale: Losing her insurance is health care access, and both the insulin and the supplies depend on it.

segments.text: Living in shelter-provided housing
segments.rationale: Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely.

segments.text: Alert and oriented, answers questions readily
segments.rationale: Alert and oriented is a normal finding, and it rules cognition out as an explanation for any of this.

segments.text: Became unhoused after losing a job
segments.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion.

segments.text: HbA1c 11%
segments.rationale: An A1c of 11 percent is a clinical measure. It tells you the problem has run for months without naming its cause.

segments.text: Verbalized understanding of the diabetes management
segments.rationale: Documented knowledge. It is the finding that rules out a knowledge deficit, which makes it important and not a determinant.

segments.text: Blood glucose 322 mg/dL
segments.rationale: A clinical value describing the disease. It is the consequence of the determinants rather than one of them.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants are the non-medical conditions where a person lives, learns, works and ages. The glucose is what they produce, not what they are.
questions.strategy: Two findings are laboratory values and two rule out the easy explanations. If she understands and is oriented, the barrier is elsewhere.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1, s2, s3, and s5: the four conditions surrounding her care.

questions.stem: A nursing student is caring for a patient with type 2 diabetes who is living in a shelter. The student teaches her the importance of taking insulin as prescribed and how to make healthy food choices. She nods and says she has no questions. Which assessment should the student have made first?

options.text: The patient's health literacy before the teaching begins
options.rationale: Literacy shapes how you teach, and the stem gives you nothing about her reading or her understanding. What it does give you is where she lives.

options.text: What gets in the way of the plan at home
options.rationale: The one concrete fact you have is that she lives in a shelter, where refrigeration, meal timing and a safe place for supplies are not hers to control. The plan being taught assumes all three.

options.text: Whether the insulin has been stored correctly at home
options.rationale: Storage is one of the barriers a shelter creates. Asking only about it misses meal timing, supplies and safekeeping.

options.text: Readiness to learn about diabetes self-management
options.rationale: Readiness belongs before teaching, and nothing here suggests she is unwilling. Nodding without questions is not evidence either way.

questions.takeaway: Before teaching a plan, find out whether the plan can be carried out where the patient lives. A shelter changes refrigeration, meal timing and storage.
questions.strategy: Three options assess the learner. The stem says nothing about the learner and one thing about her circumstances, and that is where the barrier is.

strategies: Work from what the stem gives you

steps.action: The only detail about her life

steps.detail: Nothing in the stem points at either.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what gets in the way.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient with type 2 diabetes who is living in a shelter about insulin storage. She explains that the shelter has one shared refrigerator that is often full, meals are served at fixed times she cannot always attend, and her supplies are kept in a locker. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The housing situation directly affects storage, meal timing, and access
options.rationale: Every element of her regimen depends on conditions she does not control. Neighborhood and built environment is a determinant with concrete clinical consequences.

options.text: The patient is nonadherent with the prescribed diabetes regimen
options.rationale: This describes the outcome and blames her for it. The stem has just explained what stands in the way of her doing it.

options.text: More intensive education about insulin storage is required
options.rationale: She has just described the problem accurately, which means she understands the requirement and cannot meet it.

options.text: A referral to a diabetes specialist is the priority
options.rationale: Specialist input may help eventually, and it does not change a shared refrigerator or fixed mealtimes.

questions.takeaway: Housing instability affects insulin storage, meal timing, and medication adherence directly. The regimen assumes conditions she does not have.
questions.strategy: One distractor labels her. One sends her to a specialist for a problem the specialist cannot change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared fridge, fixed meals, a locker.

steps.action: Cut the label and the referral
steps.detail: One blames her, one misses the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves housing affecting storage, timing and access.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse prepares for a difficult conversation with a patient whose beliefs about treatment differ from her own.

Agreeing a plan that keeps the patient's traditional remedies alongside the prescribed treatment is the [[1]] step of LEARN.

Saying "tell me more about what you think is causing this" is the [[2]] step.

Pointing out that they both want to avoid another admission is the [[3]] step.

A nurse who examines her own assumptions before entering the room is demonstrating [[4]].

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Acknowledge compares perceptions. It does not build the plan.

options.text: Negotiate
options.rationale: Negotiate a treatment plan, incorporating selected aspects of the patient's culture into it.

options.text: Recommend
options.rationale: This is the near miss. Recommending offers the options; negotiating settles on one you both accept.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Explain is where you give your perception of the problem, which is earlier in the model.

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Acknowledge compares the two views once both are already on the table. Nothing has been heard yet.

options.text: Listen
options.rationale: Listen to the patient's perception of the problem, nonjudgmentally, using encouraging comments such as tell me more.

options.text: Negotiate
options.rationale: Negotiate is the last step, where the plan gets agreed. It cannot come first.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Explain is where you give your own perception, and it comes after listening.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Explaining is giving your own view. This step is about comparing the two views side by side.

options.text: Listen
options.rationale: Listening has already happened by this point in the model.

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Recognize the differences and build on the similarities. Naming a shared goal is exactly that.

options.text: Recommend
options.rationale: Recommend offers the options, and it comes after the differences have been named.

options.text: cultural awareness
options.rationale: This is the first Campinha-Bacote construct: examining your own background and biases before anything else.

options.text: cultural knowledge
options.rationale: Knowledge is what you learn about other groups, which is outward rather than inward.

options.text: cultural skill
options.rationale: Skill is the doing: taking the history, performing the assessment, working with an interpreter. This describes looking inward.

options.text: cultural desire
options.rationale: Desire is the genuine wish to engage rather than the act of self-examination.

questions.takeaway: LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire.
questions.strategy: Recommend and Negotiate are the pair that gets confused. Recommending offers options; negotiating lands on a plan the patient accepts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Listen, Acknowledge, Negotiate, cultural awareness.

questions.stem: A nurse catches herself assuming a patient will decline a blood transfusion because of his surname. She stops and asks him directly. Which describes what she recognized?

options.text: Stereotyping
options.rationale: This is close. Stereotyping is the assumed belief itself; what she caught was the unconscious process that produced it before she noticed.

options.text: Cultural knowledge
options.rationale: Knowledge about a group applied without checking becomes the problem rather than the solution.

options.text: A failure of cultural desire
options.rationale: Desire is the genuine wish to engage. Hers is evident in stopping to ask.

options.text: Implicit bias
options.rationale: Unconscious, outside our control, and it drives quick judgments. She is responsible for recognizing and managing it, which is what she did.

questions.takeaway: Implicit bias is unconscious and outside our control. Recognizing and managing it is the part we are responsible for.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is stereotyping. One names the unconscious process, the other names the belief it produces.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An automatic assumption, before conscious thought.
That is the belief, not the process.

elimination.verdict: That leaves implicit bias.

questions.stem: A nurse reads that a particular cultural group commonly involves family elders in medical decisions. She assumes a patient from that background will want a parent present and arranges it without asking. What error has she made?

options.text: She applied group knowledge to an individual without checking
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is one of the five constructs, but it becomes stereotyping the moment it is applied without asking. Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values.

options.text: She should not have read about cultural practices at all
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is part of competence. The problem is applying it without verifying it.

options.text: She demonstrated a lack of cultural awareness
options.rationale: Awareness is self-examination. She may lack it, and what the stem shows is misapplied knowledge.

options.text: She failed to obtain the patient's consent for the arrangement
options.rationale: Consent is a real issue here, but it follows from the underlying error rather than being the error itself.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values. Group knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: One distractor concludes that learning about cultures is itself the mistake. Ask what turned useful knowledge into an error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what she did with the knowledge

elimination.verdict: That leaves applying group knowledge without checking.

questions.stem: Which domains are included in the five social determinants of health in Healthy People 2030? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment
options.rationale: Neighborhood and built environment is one of the five, covering housing, food access and whether the streets are safe to walk.

options.text: Social and community context
options.rationale: Social and community context is one of the five, covering support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Digital access and health technology literacy
options.rationale: Affects care, but it is not one of the five domains. It sits inside health care access and quality rather than beside it.

options.text: Economic stability
options.rationale: Economic stability is one of the five: income, employment and whether basic needs can be met.

options.text: Education access and quality
options.rationale: Education access and quality is one of the five, and it connects to both health literacy and lifetime earnings.

options.text: Genetic predisposition to disease
options.rationale: A real influence on health, but it is a biological factor rather than a social determinant. Determinants are the non-medical conditions around the patient.

options.text: Health care access and quality
options.rationale: Health care access and quality is one of the five, covering insurance, transport and having a provider at all.

questions.takeaway: Five domains: economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real health influence that is biological rather than social. Determinants are non-medical by definition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work and age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and G are selected.

questions.scenario: Four patients attend the same clinic, all with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within the past year.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the barrier most likely to affect their diabetes management.

rows.text: A 25-year-old who is unhoused and uses a shelter
rows.rationale: Housing and income shape everything else, including whether insulin can be stored and meals eaten on time.

rows.text: A 32-year-old executive whose church community treats illness as a private matter she does not discuss
rows.rationale: Resources and access are not the problem. Her support network is a place she cannot bring this.

rows.text: An 85-year-old retired nurse in rural Alabama, 50 miles from the nearest endocrinologist
rows.rationale: She has the knowledge and the means. What she lacks is a service she can physically reach.

rows.text: An undocumented mother who avoids clinics for fear of immigration consequences
rows.rationale: The service exists and she cannot safely use it. Fear functions as an access barrier.

questions.takeaway: The same diagnosis meets four different lives. Intersectionality is why identical treatment plans produce different outcomes.
questions.strategy: Two patients share a domain for opposite reasons: one cannot reach the service, the other cannot safely use it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Money, distance, safety, or someone to tell.
Distance and fear both block use.
The executive lacks a place to be open.

elimination.verdict: Economic, access, community, access.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a patient who is undocumented, uninsured, and the only caregiver for a disabled child. A colleague says the insurance is the real problem, so fix that first and the rest will follow. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Identities accumulate, so more marginalized identities produce proportionally worse outcomes
options.rationale: Treats them as additive. The framework describes interlocking systems rather than a running total.

options.text: Overlapping identities interact, so privilege and oppression work as interlocking systems
options.rationale: The identities do not add up. A person can hold advantage in one dimension and disadvantage in another, and the combination shapes the outcome.

options.text: The most significant identity should be identified and addressed first
options.rationale: Ranking identities misses the point that they operate together and cannot be separated.

options.text: Patients with shared identities will have comparable health experiences
options.rationale: This contradicts the framework, and it is exactly the assumption that produces stereotyping.

questions.takeaway: Intersectionality: social identities overlap, and privilege and oppression interlock rather than adding up.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns it into arithmetic. One turns it into a ranking. Both simplify what the framework exists to describe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves interlocking systems.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient whose first language is not English. She speaks slowly, uses simple words, and asks the patient's adult son to interpret the consent discussion. Which action requires correction?

options.text: Speaking slowly and clearly during the conversation
options.rationale: Speaking slowly and clearly is reasonable, and it helps anyone working in a second language. It is not the error here.

options.text: Using plain language instead of clinical terminology
options.rationale: Plain language instead of clinical terms is a recognized cultural skill, and it applies whatever language the patient speaks.

options.text: Continuing the conversation in English with support
options.rationale: Not itself wrong. What is wrong is who was asked to bridge the gap for a consent discussion.

options.text: Using the patient's son to interpret the consent discussion
options.rationale: Working with interpreters is a recognized cultural skill, and family members bring their own views, may edit what is said, and are not accountable for accuracy.

questions.takeaway: Working with qualified interpreters is a cultural skill. Family members are not interpreters, particularly for consent.
questions.strategy: Three options describe reasonable communication technique. Ask who is being asked to carry the responsibility.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slow speech and plain language are fine.

elimination.verdict: That leaves using the son to interpret.

questions.stem: A patient says she has been managing her blood pressure with a herbal preparation her mother used, and that she never started the prescribed medication. Which response reflects the LEARN model?

options.text: "That preparation has not been shown to lower blood pressure."
options.rationale: Explaining your own perception before hearing hers, which inverts the order and usually ends the conversation.

options.text: "We can keep the herbal preparation if you also take the medication."
options.rationale: Negotiation offered as the opening move. It may well be where you end up, and arriving there first skips the steps that make it stick.

options.text: "Tell me more about what the preparation does for you."
options.rationale: Listen is the first step, nonjudgmentally, using encouraging comments such as tell me more. You cannot negotiate a plan before you know what you are negotiating with.

options.text: "What matters is that your blood pressure comes down, however we do it."
options.rationale: This sounds flexible and it dismisses the thing she has just told you matters to her. Negotiating means her preference stays in the plan.

questions.takeaway: LEARN begins with Listen: the patient's perception of the problem, nonjudgmentally, before you offer yours.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are steps from later in the model offered too early. Ask what has to happen before you can negotiate anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves tell me more.

questions.stem: A health system is planning services for the next three decades. Which projected demographic change should most shape that planning?

options.text: Racial and ethnic minority groups approach a third of the population
options.rationale: The projection that changes practice. When a third of the population is from minority groups, culturally congruent care stops being a specialty skill and becomes the ordinary case.

options.text: The population aged 65 and over will remain roughly stable
options.rationale: The opposite of the projection. The over-65 group is the fastest-growing segment, and that growth is most of why service demand rises.

options.text: The multiracial population will decline over the same period
options.rationale: The multiracial population is projected to roughly double. Declining is the reverse of the trend.

options.text: The Asian population will fall by roughly half
options.rationale: Projected to grow substantially, and it is the largest proportional change among the groups rather than a decline.

questions.takeaway: By 2060: racial and ethnic minority population 32%, multiracial up 200%, Asian population doubling, and those aged 65 and over from 49 million to 95 million.
questions.strategy: Three distractors reverse the direction of a projected change. Every figure quoted points to growth.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the decline and the halving

steps.detail: The 65 and over group roughly doubles.

elimination.verdict: That leaves 32%.

questions.stem: A patient with a new diagnosis of epilepsy tells the nurse she has not told anyone in her community, because of how the condition is viewed there. Which concept best describes what she is experiencing?

options.text: Illness
options.rationale: Disease is the biological malfunction; illness is the individual and family reaction to it. Cultural stigma is part of the illness experience, not part of the pathology.

options.text: Acculturation
options.rationale: Acculturation is adopting a new culture while keeping your own. Nothing here describes a cultural transition.

options.text: Implicit bias
options.rationale: Community attitudes are involved, and implicit bias describes unconscious processes in the person providing care.

options.text: Disease
options.rationale: This describes the biological process. She is describing what having the condition means where she lives, which is illness.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the biological or psychological malfunction. Illness is the individual and family reaction, including cultural stigma and socially constructed meaning.
questions.strategy: One distractor names the pathology. One misapplies a term about the nurse to the community.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the process from the meaning

elimination.verdict: That leaves illness with its socially constructed meaning.

questions.stem: A patient who moved to the United States twelve years ago celebrates holidays from both his birth country and the United States, cooks traditional food, and speaks both languages at home. Which term describes this?

options.text: Assimilation
options.rationale: The near-miss. Assimilation replaces the original culture rather than adding to it, and his has not been replaced.

options.text: Acculturation
options.rationale: Adopting aspects of a new culture while retaining one's own. The original practices survive, which is the giveaway.

options.text: Cultural competence
options.rationale: A capability of health care professionals, not a description of a patient's cultural position.

options.text: Intersectionality
options.rationale: Intersectionality describes how overlapping identities interact. It is not about how someone relates to a new culture.

questions.takeaway: Acculturation keeps your own culture while adopting a new one. Assimilation replaces it. The test is whether the original practices survive.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is assimilation. Check whether anything was given up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One is about clinicians, one is about identity interaction.

elimination.verdict: That leaves acculturation.

questions.stem: A patient's background differs from the nurse's own. Which actions demonstrate cultural skill while taking the history? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assessing health literacy
options.rationale: Assessing health literacy is a recognized skill, and it decides how everything afterwards gets communicated.

options.text: Asking the patient's preferred name and goals for the visit
options.rationale: Asking her preferred name and what she wants from the visit is recognized, and it starts the encounter on her terms.

options.text: Reading about the patient's culture and planning the encounter around what you find
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is a separate construct, and used this way it produces the assumption that skill is meant to prevent.

options.text: Self-exploration before the encounter
options.rationale: Self-exploration before you walk in is recognized first. It is where awareness turns into practice.

options.text: Recording the patient's ethnicity to guide the plan of care
options.rationale: This sounds thorough and it plans care from a category instead of a person. Cultural skill means asking this patient rather than inferring.

options.text: Arranging a qualified interpreter when needed
options.rationale: Arranging a qualified interpreter is recognized, and working with one well is a skill in itself.

options.text: Using teach-back and plain language
options.rationale: Teach-back and plain language are recognized, and teach-back is what tells you whether anything landed.

questions.takeaway: Cultural skill: self-exploration, preferred name and goals, storytelling, history, health literacy, culturally based assessment, teach-back, plain language, interpreters.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns knowledge into a script for the encounter, which is how competence becomes stereotyping.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A hospital implements core measures for the management of myocardial infarction. A nurse asks what these are intended to achieve. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Individualized protocols adapted to each patient's cultural preferences
options.rationale: The opposite of what they are. Their value comes from being applied consistently.

options.text: Internal quality targets set by each hospital for its own improvement
options.rationale: Externally set by CMS and The Joint Commission rather than by the organization.

options.text: Evidence-based standards applied to every patient, intended to reduce disparities in care
options.rationale: Set by CMS and The Joint Commission, and the aim is to standardize care regardless of background so that outcomes depend less on who the patient is.

options.text: Guidelines for nurses working with patients who need interpreters
options.rationale: Interpreter use is a cultural skill. Core measures are clinical standards of care.

questions.takeaway: Core measures are evidence-based, scientifically researched standards set by CMS and The Joint Commission, aimed at reducing disparities and standardizing care regardless of background.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes them individualized, which is the opposite of the mechanism. Standardization is how they reduce disparity.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut internal targets and interpreter guidance
steps.detail: One is external, one is a different topic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves standardized evidence-based measures reducing disparities.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses cultural care with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Once I have learned about a culture, I can apply that knowledge to patients from that background."
options.rationale: Cultural competence is an ongoing process rather than a finished state, and culturally congruent care is based on the individual rather than the group.

options.text: "Self-awareness is where cultural competence starts."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it matches the first Campinha-Bacote construct. Awareness comes before knowledge.

options.text: "Disease is the biological process and illness is how the person and family react to it."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and the illness side includes cultural stigma and the meaning the condition carries.

options.text: "Implicit bias is unconscious, and I am still responsible for managing it."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Having bias is outside your control; managing it is not.

questions.takeaway: Cultural competence is an ongoing process, not an achievement. Group knowledge tells you what to ask, never what to assume.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth treats competence as something that can be completed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Group knowledge applied as a rule.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement about applying learned knowledge.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old attends a follow-up after a myocardial infarction and has not started the prescribed statin. The patient says a sibling took one and that it 'ruined the muscles', and that in the family heart trouble is managed with diet and rest. The patient can describe the personal risk factors accurately, and has attended every appointment since discharge.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Document that the patient declines the prescribed statin
options.rationale: This records the outcome without exploring it, and declines misstates a belief nobody has asked him about yet.

options.text: Explain the evidence for statins after myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Explain is a real LEARN step and it comes second, not first. Offered before listening it becomes a correction rather than a conversation.

options.text: Work with him toward a plan that keeps the diet changes and addresses the statin concern
options.rationale: Negotiate, the final LEARN step. Incorporating selected aspects of the patient's own approach is what makes a plan he will follow.

options.text: Ask what he understands about what happened to his brother
options.rationale: Listen, the first LEARN step. His belief has a specific source, and you cannot address it until you know what it is.

options.text: A health belief formed from family experience that conflicts with the plan
options.rationale: He has a specific reason rooted in what happened to his brother and how his family manages heart trouble. That is a belief, not a gap.

options.text: Nonadherence to the prescribed medication regimen
options.rationale: Names the outcome and explains nothing, and it locates the failure in him.

options.text: Lack of engagement with his follow-up care
options.rationale: He has attended every appointment since discharge, which is the opposite of disengagement.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about his cardiac risk factors
options.rationale: He describes his own risk factors accurately. The stem rules a knowledge gap out directly.

options.text: Whether his cholesterol has fallen at the next visit
options.rationale: A real clinical outcome, and it lags behind and does not tell you whether the conversation worked.

options.text: Whether he raises further concerns rather than stopping silently
options.rationale: The relationship outcome. A patient who tells you when something worries him is one you can work with.

options.text: Whether he has started and continued the agreed medication plan
options.rationale: This measures whether the plan you negotiated is one he could actually accept and keep to.

options.text: Whether he can list three benefits of statin therapy
options.rationale: Tests recall, when the obstacle was never that he did not know what statins are for.

questions.takeaway: Health beliefs come from somewhere specific. LEARN starts with listening because you cannot negotiate with a belief you have not heard.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out two distractors explicitly: he describes his risk factors accurately and he attends every appointment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the source of the belief
steps.detail: His brother, and his family's approach.

elimination.verdict: Listen and negotiate, for a family-formed health belief, evaluated by uptake and by disclosure.

questions.stem: Where does cultural competence begin?

options.text: With learning the health beliefs of the groups served by the hospital
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is one of the five constructs, but it is the second one. Knowledge without awareness becomes assumption.

options.text: With building experience through repeated cross-cultural encounters
options.rationale: Cultural encounters is a construct, and encounters without self-examination tend to confirm what you already believed.

options.text: With self-awareness, examining one's own beliefs and assumptions
options.rationale: Cultural awareness is the first Campinha-Bacote construct and her stated key point. Self-exploration precedes the encounter.

options.text: With a genuine wish to provide equitable care
options.rationale: Cultural desire is a construct and arguably what motivates the rest. It is not where the process starts.

questions.takeaway: Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire. Self-awareness is the starting point.
questions.strategy: All four options name real constructs from the same model. Ask which one comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what must precede the rest

elimination.verdict: That leaves cultural awareness.

questions.stem: Rural patients in one state have higher mortality and worse access to substance use treatment than urban patients. Which term describes this?

options.text: A social determinant of health
options.rationale: Determinants are the conditions producing the difference. The difference itself is the disparity.

options.text: Implicit bias
options.rationale: Bias may contribute, and the data describes an outcome gap rather than a mechanism.

options.text: A failure of cultural competence
options.rationale: Assigns a cause the data does not support, and rural disparities trace largely to access and resources.

options.text: A health disparity
options.rationale: This is measurable and it sits between defined groups. The measurability is what lets it be tracked and targeted.

questions.takeaway: A health disparity is a measurable difference in health between specific population groups. Social determinants are the conditions that produce it.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is social determinants. One names the cause, the other names the gap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both assign mechanisms the data does not show.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a health disparity.

questions.stem: A nurse notices she spends less time at the bedside of patients who need an interpreter, and that her assessments on those patients are shorter. Which does this describe?

options.text: Implicit bias
options.rationale: Implicit bias is the unexamined attitude. What is being described is the care that resulted from it.

options.text: Stereotyping
options.rationale: Stereotyping is the belief about the group. Again, this describes what she did.

options.text: Discrimination
options.rationale: When an attitude becomes unequal treatment, it is discrimination, whether or not it was intended.

options.text: Prejudice
options.rationale: Prejudice is the judgment held. The finding here is measurable in the care delivered.

questions.takeaway: Bias, stereotype and prejudice all live in the head. Discrimination is what shows up in the care, and intent does not change the label.
questions.strategy: Three options describe attitudes. The stem gives you a difference in what patients received, which is behavior.

strategies: Ask whether the finding is an attitude or an action
elimination.verdict: That leaves discrimination.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she has been taking a tea her grandmother made for her blood pressure and has not started the prescribed medication. Which response reflects the Negotiate step of LEARN?

options.text: Tell me more about the tea and what it does for you
options.rationale: That is Listen, the first step, and it comes before anything is negotiated.

options.text: The medication lowers pressure in a way the tea cannot
options.rationale: That is Explain, where the nurse offers her own perception.

options.text: We both want your pressure down, and you have kept it in mind for months
options.rationale: That is Acknowledge, naming the similarity between the two views.

options.text: Could we keep the tea and add the medication, then check the pressure in two weeks?
options.rationale: Negotiate builds a plan that incorporates part of the patient's culture, and this one does.

questions.takeaway: LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Negotiate produces a plan with the patient's practice inside it.
questions.strategy: All four options are good practice and each is a different step. The item tests whether you can place them in order.

strategies: Label each option with its step
elimination.verdict: That leaves the option that builds the combined plan.

questions.stem: A patient who came to the United States at age six now speaks only English, observes none of the holidays her parents kept, and says she thinks of herself simply as American. Which term describes this?

options.text: Assimilation
options.rationale: Assimilation is the full adoption of the new culture with the original given up.

options.text: Acculturation
options.rationale: Acculturation adds the new culture while the original is retained in some form, and hers is not.

options.text: Biculturalism
options.rationale: Biculturalism means operating in both, and she describes only one.

options.text: Ethnocentrism
options.rationale: Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures against your own, which is not described.

questions.takeaway: Acculturation adds, assimilation replaces, biculturalism holds both. What decides it is whether the original culture is still there.
questions.strategy: Acculturation is the answer students reach for whenever someone has adapted. Ask what is left of the first culture.

strategies: Ask what remains of the original culture

steps.detail: Both require the original to persist.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assimilation.

questions.stem: A nurse is told a patient will want family present for all decisions because of his culture. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange for family to be present at every discussion
options.rationale: This acts on a generalization and may remove the patient's own preference.

options.text: Ask the patient who he wants involved in decisions about his care
options.rationale: Not everyone from a culture communicates the same way, and the only reliable source is the patient.

options.text: Document the cultural preference and proceed accordingly
options.rationale: Documenting a generalization makes it travel to every clinician who reads the chart.

options.text: Ask the family what role they expect to take
options.rationale: This asks everyone except the person whose care it is.

questions.takeaway: Cultural knowledge describes groups. Cultural skill asks this patient. Knowledge applied without asking becomes stereotyping.
questions.strategy: The advice in the stem may well be true of this patient. The item tests whether you check before acting on it.

strategies: Ask who can confirm it

steps.action: Cut the options that act on the generalization

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking the patient.

questions.stem: A rural county has higher cardiac mortality than the neighboring urban county. Investigation finds fewer cardiologists, longer ambulance times, and one grocery store serving the whole area. Which statement most accurately separates the concepts?

options.text: The mortality difference is the disparity and the access and food conditions are the determinants
options.rationale: The measurable difference between groups is the disparity. The conditions producing it are the determinants.

options.text: Both the mortality difference and the conditions are social determinants
options.rationale: Determinants are conditions. A mortality rate is an outcome.

options.text: The conditions are disparities and the mortality difference is the health outcome
options.rationale: This reverses the terms. The conditions are the determinants and the mortality difference is the disparity.

options.text: Both are health disparities, measured at different levels
options.rationale: A grocery store is not a measurable difference in health.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants are the non-medical conditions. Health disparities are the measurable differences in health those conditions produce.
questions.strategy: The two terms get used interchangeably in conversation. Sort them by cause and measurement before reading the options.

strategies: Sort into cause and measurement

steps.action: Cut the options that merge or reverse them

elimination.verdict: That leaves the option that separates them correctly.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her care of a patient whose beliefs about treatment differed sharply from her own. Which stage of Campinha-Bacote's model is she engaged in?

options.text: Cultural knowledge
options.rationale: Knowledge is learning about groups and their beliefs.

options.text: Cultural skill
options.rationale: Skill is the ability to collect the history and perform the assessment.

options.text: Cultural awareness
options.rationale: Awareness is the self-examination of one's own biases and assumptions, which is what reviewing her own reaction is.

options.text: Cultural encounters
options.rationale: Encounters are the direct interactions themselves, and she is reflecting after one.

questions.takeaway: Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire. Awareness is the one pointed at yourself.
questions.strategy: Four of the five stages concern the patient. Only one concerns the nurse, and that is where reflection goes.

strategies: Ask who the stage examines

steps.detail: That is the interaction, not the reflection.

elimination.verdict: That leaves cultural awareness.

questions.stem: A patient declines a recommended treatment for reasons grounded in her family's beliefs. She repeats the risks back accurately. The nurse notices she is irritated with the patient. Which action should she take first?

options.text: Ask a colleague who shares the patient's background to speak with her
options.rationale: This transfers the patient and avoids the nurse's own reaction.

options.text: Recognize the irritation as her own bias surfacing and set it aside before continuing
options.rationale: Awareness of her own response is the first step, and acting while irritated is how bias reaches the care.

options.text: Document the refusal and notify the provider
options.rationale: Both will happen, and neither addresses what is interfering right now.

options.text: Explain the risks again to be sure she has understood
options.rationale: She has repeated them accurately, so repeating them treats a value as a knowledge gap.

questions.takeaway: Self-examination before the encounter continues. Bias acted on without being noticed is how it reaches care.
questions.strategy: Three options are things to do about the patient. The stem told you about the nurse for a reason.

strategies: Ask what the stem reported that was unusual
elimination.verdict: That leaves recognizing the bias.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to keep her own bias from affecting the care she gives. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Noticing when she feels irritation or impatience with a patient and asking where it came from
options.rationale: Bias usually arrives as a feeling before it arrives as a thought, and that feeling is the only early signal.

options.text: Slowing down when she is rushed, because snap judgments carry the most assumption
options.rationale: Time pressure is when bias does most of its work.

options.text: Asking the patient about his own practices rather than predicting them from his background
options.rationale: The individual account replaces the group assumption with a fact.

options.text: Reading about a patient's cultural group and planning care from what she reads
options.rationale: Group knowledge applied to an individual is how a stereotype gets delivered as care.

options.text: Comparing how much time and explanation she gives different patients
options.rationale: Bias shows in what was delivered, which can be measured even when the attitude cannot.

options.text: Treating every patient exactly the same regardless of what they need
options.rationale: Identical treatment ignores different needs and produces unequal outcomes.

options.text: Asking a colleague to tell her when something she said landed badly
options.rationale: She cannot see her own blind spot, and someone else can.

questions.takeaway: Bias is managed by noticing the feeling, slowing down, asking the individual, measuring what you delivered, and letting someone else tell you.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options sound like fairness and professionalism. One substitutes a group for a person, and the other calls identical treatment equitable.

strategies: Ask whether the action looks at this patient or at a category
elimination.verdict: The five actions are selected.

questions.stem: A patient is undocumented, uninsured, speaks limited English, and is the sole caregiver for a disabled child. Which statements reflect intersectionality? Select all that apply.

options.text: Her identities interact rather than adding up
options.rationale: Intersectionality holds that overlapping identities interact as interlocking systems.

options.text: Privilege and oppression operate together in her situation
options.rationale: Privilege and oppression as interlocking systems is the framework's core claim.

options.text: Another patient with the same diagnosis may have a different experience of it
options.rationale: Shared diagnosis with different identities produces different experiences, which is the point of the four-patient comparison.

options.text: The most limiting identity should be identified and addressed first
options.rationale: Ranking identities treats them as separable, which is what the framework denies.

options.text: Her care plan should account for several identities at once
options.rationale: Acting on the interaction rather than on one factor is what the framework asks for.

options.text: Patients sharing her immigration status will have comparable experiences
options.rationale: Shared membership of one group does not produce a shared experience.

questions.takeaway: Intersectionality: overlapping identities interact, privilege and oppression are interlocking, and shared diagnosis does not mean shared experience.
questions.strategy: Both distractors simplify the framework in opposite directions. One ranks identities, the other groups people by one of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identities interact rather than stack or substitute.

elimination.verdict: The four statements are selected.

questions.stem: A patient speaks limited English. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using a trained interpreter for the consent discussion
options.rationale: Consent requires accurate two-way communication, and a trained interpreter is the standard.

options.text: Speaking to the patient rather than to the interpreter
options.rationale: The conversation is with the patient, and directing it at the interpreter removes her from it.

options.text: Using teach-back to confirm what the patient understood
options.rationale: Teach-back is recognized within cultural skill and it does not rely on the patient saying yes.

options.text: Speaking more loudly to aid comprehension
options.rationale: Volume does not help with language and it signals impatience.

options.text: Allowing extra time for the interview
options.rationale: Interpreted conversations take longer, and rushing them produces the gaps.

options.text: Asking the patient's adult son to interpret for routine questions
options.rationale: Even for routine questions a family interpreter changes what the patient will say and may filter the answers.

questions.takeaway: Working with interpreters: use a trained one, address the patient, allow time, and confirm with teach-back.
questions.strategy: The family interpreter distractor is limited to routine questions, which is what makes it tempting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trained interpreter, direct address, time, teach-back.

elimination.verdict: The four actions are selected.

questions.stem: A woman newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse the illness began with a shock she had two years ago, when her brother died. Which question opens her understanding of the illness rather than replacing it?

options.text: Do you believe the medication will work?
options.rationale: Closed, and it jumps to adherence before anyone knows what she thinks she is treating.

options.text: What do you think the illness is doing inside your body?
options.rationale: It asks for her model of the illness, which is what she will be reasoning from when she decides whether to take a tablet every morning for the rest of her life.

options.text: Would it help if I explained what causes type 2 diabetes?
options.rationale: Correcting her before you have heard her tells her the conversation is about who is right. The explanation is the second move, not the first.

options.text: Has anyone else in your family had the same condition?
options.rationale: A useful history question that collects facts rather than meaning.

questions.takeaway: Find out what the patient thinks the illness is, what caused it, what it is doing, and what she fears. You cannot negotiate a plan with a belief you have not heard.
questions.strategy: Two options are about the cause of diabetes. One asks her, one tells her.

strategies: Ask which question produces her reasoning
elimination.verdict: Ask what she thinks it is doing.

questions.stem: A nurse says she treats every patient exactly the same no matter where they come from, and that paying attention to a patient's background is where bias starts. Which does this describe?

options.text: Cultural blindness, which produces unequal outcomes by refusing to see the differences that affect care
options.rationale: Identical treatment is not equal treatment when patients arrive with different barriers. The refusal to notice is what lets a disparity pass as fairness.

options.text: Cultural competence, because equal treatment is the goal
options.rationale: Competence adapts care so different patients can reach the same outcome. Sameness of input is the opposite of that.

options.text: Cultural imposition, because she is applying her own standard of care to every patient
options.rationale: The closest option. Imposition is pressing your own beliefs and practices onto a patient. She is not pressing anything, she is declining to look.

options.text: Ethnocentrism, because she believes her own culture is superior
options.rationale: She has made no claim about superiority. Ethnocentrism ranks cultures and she is denying that they matter.

questions.takeaway: I treat everyone the same is a disparity waiting to happen. Equity means adjusting what you give so patients can reach the same result.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real concepts. Match the definition to what she said, not to what it sounds like.

strategies: Hold each definition against her exact words
elimination.verdict: Cultural blindness.

questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin drinks a herbal tea his sister-in-law prepares for him every day and has done so for years. He tells the nurse he will not stop it. Which response fits?

options.text: Tell him that he has to stop drinking the tea for as long as he remains on warfarin, and explain that the combination can make his level unpredictable
options.rationale: Clinically tidy and it ends the conversation. He will drink it anyway and will stop mentioning it, which removes the only safeguard he had.

options.text: Find out what is in it and how much he drinks, tell him what it does to his bleeding risk, and plan closer monitoring with him
options.rationale: It keeps him talking, gets the information the team needs, states the risk plainly, and ends in a plan he has agreed to. Negotiation is the step that produces a plan both sides can live with.

options.text: Reassure him that herbal preparations are generally safe when they are taken in small amounts
