options.rationale: Untrue in this case and it closes the subject with false comfort.

options.text: Document that he declines to stop it and notify the provider of his decision
options.rationale: Accurate and inert. Nobody learns what is in the tea and nothing changes about his monitoring.

questions.takeaway: Negotiate rather than prohibit. A practice the patient will keep either way is safer inside the plan than outside it.
questions.strategy: The strictest option looks safest. Ask what he will do after each response.

strategies: Predict the patient's behavior after each reply
elimination.verdict: Get the details, state the risk, negotiate monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient who is Deaf and communicates in American Sign Language is being consented for surgery. The surgeon is behind and suggests writing notes back and forth, pointing out that the patient reads. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Agree to written notes, since he can read and the information will be in writing for him to keep
options.rationale: Reading ability is not fluency, and a written record of something not understood is still not consent.

options.text: Arrange a qualified sign language interpreter before the consent conversation goes ahead
options.rationale: For many people whose first language is a signed one, written English is a second language. Consent requires comprehension, and notes passed under time pressure do not establish it.

options.text: Speak slowly and clearly facing him so he can lip read
options.rationale: Only a fraction of speech is visible on the lips, and none of the detail that makes a risk discussion meaningful.

options.text: Ask the family member in the waiting room who signs to interpret
options.rationale: A family member is not a qualified interpreter, and consent is the conversation where that matters most.

questions.takeaway: A qualified interpreter is required for consent. Convenience, a willing relative, and the patient's reading ability are the three reasons it gets skipped.
questions.strategy: Every distractor is a workaround that would move things along. Ask which one produces understanding.

strategies: Ask what establishes comprehension
elimination.verdict: Qualified interpreter first.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes taking metformin and a sulfonylurea tells the nurse he intends to fast from dawn to sunset for the coming month, as he does every year. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask who he consults about religious questions and whether he would like that person involved in the planning
options.rationale: Many traditions have established guidance for people with chronic illness, and the person who carries that authority for him can make the plan workable.

options.text: Ask what his fasting usually looks like and bring it to the provider so the regimen can be reviewed before the month begins
options.rationale: The medications, not the fast, are what need adjusting, and the time to do it is before rather than after the first hypoglycemic episode.

options.text: Arrange monitoring supplies and set a schedule for checking across the fasting hours
options.rationale: Measurement replaces the warning signs that a fasting patient on a sulfonylurea most needs.

options.text: Document that he is declining medical advice about the fast
options.rationale: Nothing has been declined. Recording it that way frames the patient as the problem and closes the planning.

options.text: Suggest that he take both of his medications at dawn so that the whole of the fasting day is covered without needing a second dose later
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea at dawn with no food until sunset is the exact setup for hypoglycemia. Timing is a prescribing decision and this is the wrong one.

options.text: Explain that fasting is not safe for a person with diabetes and advise him against it this year
options.rationale: It presents a yearly religious obligation as a choice he should drop, and it guarantees he will fast without telling anyone.

options.text: Teach him the symptoms that mean he must break the fast, and that breaking it for illness is permitted within the practice
options.rationale: Knowing the exemption exists is often what makes a patient willing to act on symptoms instead of pushing through them.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care plans around the practice rather than against it. Move the medication, not the fast, and build in measurement where symptoms will be unreliable.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options sound protective. Ask whether each one would still be followed in week three of the fast.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Review, teach the exemption, monitor, and involve his adviser.

chapters.title: The Nursing Process and Clinical Judgment
chapters.subtitle: Critical thinking, assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation

sources.title: Critical Thinking and Clinical Judgment
sources.label: Potter Ch. 15 · Critical Thinking and Clinical Judgment

questions.stem: A nurse finds that a patient's respiratory rate has risen from 18 to 28, with neck muscles being used to breathe and an inability to finish a sentence. Yesterday the patient spoke in full sentences. She concludes the breathing is deteriorating and calls the provider. Which term names what she has demonstrated?

options.text: The nursing process
options.rationale: The nursing process is the framework she worked inside. The question asks what capability she showed, not where she was standing.

options.text: Clinical judgment
options.rationale: Judgment is what you can see: she reached a conclusion and acted on it. The thinking that produced it happened out of sight.

options.text: Critical thinking
options.rationale: One of the two processes feeding the judgment, and it is not itself observable.

options.text: Clinical reasoning
options.rationale: Clinical reasoning is the thinking underneath the decision. Like critical thinking, it stays below the surface where nobody can see it.

questions.takeaway: Critical thinking and clinical reasoning are the processes. Clinical judgment is the observed outcome of both.
questions.strategy: The distinguishing word is observed. Two options name processes you cannot see; one names a framework.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A conclusion reached and acted on.

elimination.verdict: That leaves clinical judgment.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a patient's breathing has worsened, decides low oxygen is the likeliest cause, acts, and reassesses an hour later. A student asks whether she just used the nursing process or the clinical judgment model. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The nursing process is used in practice and the model is used only for examinations
options.rationale: The model describes real cognitive work. It is measured on the NCLEX because it happens at the bedside.

options.text: The clinical judgment model has replaced the nursing process in current practice
options.rationale: Neither replaces the other. They run in parallel, and each step of one lines up with a step of the other.

options.text: The nursing process describes what nurses do; the model describes how nurses think while doing it
options.rationale: This is how she described it herself. One organizes the work into steps, the other describes the reasoning running underneath.

options.text: The nursing process applies to stable patients and the model to emergencies
options.rationale: The nursing process is used with every patient, in every setting, every shift.

questions.takeaway: The nursing process is what nurses do. The clinical judgment model is how nurses think.
questions.strategy: Two distractors put the two in competition. Ask what each one is describing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the exam-only and emergency options

elimination.verdict: That leaves what nurses do against how they think.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for a post-operative patient who reports incisional pain at 5 of 10. The wound edges are slightly separated and the temperature is 99.5 F.
questions.stem: For each nurse activity, indicate which step of the clinical judgment model it represents.

rows.text: Reassesses 24 hours later, finds no further separation and a normal temperature
rows.rationale: She is measuring the result against what she expected and deciding whether to carry on. That is evaluating outcomes.

rows.text: Compares the findings with normal wound healing and clusters them toward risk for infection
rows.rationale: Interpreting the data, grouping it, and asking what is expected against what is not.

rows.text: Decides to increase wound checks to every four hours and sets a threshold for calling the provider
rows.rationale: Choosing what could be done and when to escalate, before anything is carried out.

rows.text: Performs the wound care, documents, and communicates the change at handoff
rows.rationale: She is carrying out the plan, and the handoff communication is part of carrying it out rather than a separate step.

rows.text: Notes the wound separation, the drainage and the elevated temperature
rows.rationale: She is gathering the findings that matter without yet saying what they mean. That is recognizing cues.

questions.takeaway: Six steps: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes.
questions.strategy: The step missing from these five is prioritizing hypotheses, which needs competing explanations to rank.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Data, meaning, a plan, an act, a verdict.
Decides is planning; performs is action.

elimination.verdict: Recognize, analyze, generate, act, evaluate.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a confused older adult lists four possible causes: low oxygen, a new medication, infection, and dehydration. She decides the oxygen saturation must be checked first. Which step of the clinical judgment model is this?

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: She has not decided what to do about any of the four yet. Generating solutions comes after she picks one.

options.text: Recognizing cues
options.rationale: The data gathering is finished. She is working with findings she already has.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Analysis is what produced the four possibilities. Choosing between them is the step after.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Four competing explanations ranked by likelihood and urgency. Ranking is what this step means, and the ABCs put oxygenation first.

questions.takeaway: Prioritizing hypotheses ranks competing explanations by likelihood and urgency, using the ABCs, Maslow, acute against chronic, and risk of deterioration.
questions.strategy: The giveaway is that there are four explanations and she is putting one first. Ranking needs competitors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One is later, one is earlier.

elimination.verdict: That leaves prioritizing hypotheses.

questions.stem: Forty minutes after a scheduled analgesic, a patient's pain is 7 of 10 rather than the expected 3. Which step does the nurse return to?

options.text: Recognizing cues
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data. An unmet outcome sends you back to gathering, not forward.

options.text: Taking action
options.rationale: Acting again before knowing why the first action failed, and the reason may not be the dose.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes
options.rationale: She has already evaluated, and the verdict was not met. The question is what she does next with that verdict.

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Changing the plan before reassessing skips the step that would tell you what to change it to.

questions.takeaway: The cycle is not one-way. Evaluation data becomes new assessment data, and the process begins its next loop immediately.
questions.strategy: Two distractors jump forward to fixing it. Ask what you need before you can choose a new plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves returning to recognizing cues.

questions.stem: Which sources contribute to the assessment database for a newly admitted patient? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diagnostic and laboratory data
options.rationale: It is part of the database rather than separate from it.

options.text: The nurse's interpretation of what the findings mean
options.rationale: That is the next step, not a source. Interpretation is analysis performed on the database once the database exists.

options.text: The patient's own account of the problem
options.rationale: His own account is subjective data, and he is the primary source for it. Nobody else can report his pain.

options.text: The nurse's impression of how motivated the patient seems
options.rationale: A judgment about the patient rather than data. It belongs nowhere in the database, and it shapes care if left unexamined.

options.text: Family caregivers and significant others
options.rationale: Family and significant others are a recognized source, and they often hold the baseline the patient cannot give you.

options.text: The health record and previous notes
options.rationale: The record and previous notes are a recognized source, and reviewing them is part of preparing for the interview.

options.text: The nurse's physical examination findings
options.rationale: What the nurse sees, hears and measures is objective data, and it is one of the seven sources.

questions.takeaway: The database draws on scientific data and theory, patient subjective and objective data, family and significant others, the health care team, health records, and diagnostic data.
questions.strategy: One distractor is an inference about the patient dressed as an observation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse begins an admission interview by introducing herself, explaining the purpose and confidentiality, and asking what the patient most wants to cover. Which phase is this?

options.text: Working phase
options.rationale: The working phase is data collection, and it starts once the ground rules are set. She is still setting them.

options.text: Orientation
options.rationale: Introduce yourself, explain purpose and confidentiality, and set an agenda around the patient's priorities so he becomes an active partner.

options.text: Preparation
options.rationale: The near-miss. Preparation is reviewing the record before the encounter, and it happens before the patient is in the room.

options.text: Termination
options.rationale: Termination is summarizing, checking accuracy, inviting last questions and saying when you will be back.

questions.takeaway: Three phases: orientation, working phase, termination. Preparation happens before the interview begins.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is preparation, which is real and happens before you walk in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: In the room, being introduced to.

elimination.verdict: That leaves orientation.

questions.scenario: A nurse completes an admission assessment on a 54-year-old with abdominal pain.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is subjective or objective data.

rows.text: The abdomen is distended and firm on palpation
rows.rationale: A distended, firm abdomen is what the examiner found by looking and feeling. That is objective.

rows.text: He is guarding the abdomen and grimacing when he moves
rows.rationale: Observation of behavior. You are recording what you see, not what he tells you he feels.

rows.text: He reports feeling frightened about what this means
rows.rationale: Fear is an emotion he reported. It is real data, and only he has access to it, which makes it subjective.

rows.text: The patient rates his pain at 7 of 10
rows.rationale: His own report of his experience. Attaching a number does not make it measurable by anyone else.

rows.text: He says the pain is worse after eating
rows.rationale: He is describing a pattern only he can perceive. That makes it subjective, however reliable it is.

rows.text: Temperature 38.2 C
rows.rationale: A measured temperature is objective. Anyone with the same thermometer gets the same number.

questions.takeaway: Subjective is what the patient reports. Objective is what you measure or observe. A pain score is subjective; guarding is objective.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about pain and they fall on opposite sides. What he says about it is subjective; what you watch him do is objective.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A number that only he can supply.

elimination.verdict: Three subjective, three objective.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse everything is fine, while he sits rigidly, guards his abdomen, and grimaces when he shifts position. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Record that the patient denies pain
options.rationale: Documents one source and discards the other. The two findings together are the finding.

options.text: Record the objective findings and disregard his statement
options.rationale: The reverse error. His account is data even when it conflicts with what you see.

options.text: Name the discrepancy and invite him to say more about it
options.rationale: Validating is part of the working phase. Clarifying and summarizing checks your understanding rather than choosing which piece of data to believe.

options.text: Ask a direct closed question about whether he has pain
options.rationale: Rushing to yes or no questions masks the real problem, which is exactly the trap here.

questions.takeaway: When subjective and objective data conflict, the conflict is the finding. Clarify and validate rather than choosing a side.
questions.strategy: Two distractors pick one source and discard the other. One narrows the question too soon.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: What he says and what you see.

elimination.verdict: That leaves naming the discrepancy.

questions.stem: During an interview a patient pauses after describing the symptoms. The nurse says nothing, nods, and waits. Which technique is she using?

options.text: Back-channeling
options.rationale: An interview technique. Small signals that you are listening keep the account going without steering it.

options.text: Probing
options.rationale: Probing means asking a follow-up question for detail. She has asked nothing at all.

options.text: Closed-ended questioning
options.rationale: A closed question invites a yes or no. Silence with a nod invites the patient to keep going.

options.text: A leading question
options.rationale: Leading questions are recognized among the things to avoid, and she has not asked anything.

questions.takeaway: Interview techniques: observation, open-ended questions, direct closed-ended questions, back-channeling, probing, and avoiding leading questions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors describe something the nurse says. She has said nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves back-channeling.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the care plan for a patient two days after abdominal surgery.
questions.stem: For each item, indicate which type of diagnosis or problem it represents.

rows.text: Monitoring for postoperative hemorrhage
rows.rationale: The nurse monitors and the provider treats. Both are required, and the focus is preventing a potential complication.

rows.text: Perforated appendix
rows.rationale: Identifies the disease, and it is what physicians and advanced practice providers treat.

rows.text: Monitoring for hypoglycemia during the insulin infusion
rows.rationale: Nursing surveillance of a potential complication that needs medical intervention if it occurs.

rows.text: Acute pain related to the surgical incision
rows.rationale: This names his response to the illness, and nurses treat it independently. That makes it a nursing diagnosis.

rows.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
rows.rationale: Type 2 diabetes is a disease process, diagnosed and managed medically. That makes it a medical diagnosis.

rows.text: Impaired physical mobility related to incisional pain
rows.rationale: A human response the nurse can act on directly through positioning, analgesia timing and assisted movement.

questions.takeaway: Medical diagnoses name the disease. Nursing diagnoses name the patient's response. Collaborative problems need both, and the nursing role is monitoring for complications.
questions.strategy: The word monitoring signals a collaborative problem. Ask whether the nurse can treat it alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A disease, a response, or a watch.

elimination.verdict: Two medical, two nursing, two collaborative.

questions.stem: A nurse finds that a patient cannot explain the prescribed diuretic, has not weighed in since discharge, and cannot name foods high in sodium. She groups these findings and names the problem. Which step has she completed?

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Only one problem has been named here. Prioritizing needs at least two things competing for first place.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Analysis interprets the data, clusters it, and names what it amounts to. Three separate gaps became one problem.

options.text: Recognizing cues
options.rationale: Recognizing produced the three findings. Grouping and naming them is the next step.

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Nothing has been planned yet. She has named the problem and stopped there.

questions.takeaway: Analyzing cues means data interpretation, clustering, and finding patterns. Naming the problem is where it lands.
questions.strategy: Three findings became one named problem. That move from data to meaning is analysis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the earlier and later steps

elimination.verdict: That leaves analyzing cues.

questions.stem: A nurse writes a nursing diagnosis for a patient who developed a pressure injury during a five-day period of bed rest. Which related factor is appropriate?

options.text: Related to inadequate repositioning by the previous shift
options.rationale: Implies legal liability and names a colleague. A related factor must not do either.

options.text: Related to a stage 2 pressure injury
options.rationale: The injury is the problem, not the factor related to it. This restates the diagnosis as its own cause.

options.text: Related to the patient's refusal to be turned
options.rationale: This blames the patient, and a refusal is itself something to assess rather than a cause to write into the diagnosis.

options.text: Related to prolonged immobility
options.rationale: Names the cause in a way the nurse can act on, and it assigns no blame to anyone.

questions.takeaway: The related factor names the cause after the words related to. It must be something nursing can address, and it must not imply blame or legal liability.
questions.strategy: Two distractors assign fault. One uses the problem as its own cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the factor must do
steps.detail: Name a cause nursing can address.
One names a colleague, one blames the patient.

elimination.verdict: That leaves prolonged immobility.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies four problems for a patient: impaired gas exchange with a saturation of 88%, acute pain at 6 of 10, anxiety about the diagnosis, and risk for constipation. Which is the priority?

options.text: Acute pain
options.rationale: Pain at 6 of 10 is real, actual and distressing. It does not threaten airway, breathing or circulation.

options.text: Risk for constipation
options.rationale: This is a potential problem. An actual problem outranks a risk, and the saturation is already abnormal.

options.text: Impaired gas exchange
options.rationale: The ABCs place breathing above everything else, and 88% is a current physiological threat rather than a potential one.

options.text: Anxiety about the diagnosis
options.rationale: This is a real problem, and psychosocial diagnoses are not the ones to dismiss. It still ranks below hypoxia.

questions.takeaway: Priority concepts: the ABCs, Maslow, acute against chronic, actual against potential, and risk of deterioration.
questions.strategy: All four are legitimate problems. Ask which one is both actual and threatens the ABCs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both actual, neither threatens the ABCs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves impaired gas exchange.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews the care plan for a patient who is withdrawn, eating little, and refusing to see her family. Every diagnosis marked high priority on the plan is physiological. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Classifying only physiological diagnoses as high priority is an error to avoid
options.rationale: This is stated directly. A psychosocial problem can be the most urgent thing for a particular patient at a particular moment.

options.text: Psychosocial diagnoses should be addressed only after discharge planning begins
options.rationale: This delays psychosocial problems indefinitely, and nothing supports hanging them on discharge planning.

options.text: Priority should be determined by the order in which problems were identified
options.rationale: The order in which you noticed problems has nothing to do with how urgent they are.

options.text: Physiological diagnoses are always ranked above psychosocial ones
options.rationale: The rule of thumb, stated as an absolute. Applying it that way is exactly the misuse to avoid.

questions.takeaway: Avoid classifying only physiological nursing diagnoses as high priority. Consider each patient's unique situation.
questions.strategy: One distractor states the general rule and drops the caveat that goes with it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Avoid ranking only physiological problems high.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the warning against physiological-only ranking.

questions.stem: A patient is learning to inject insulin. Which expected outcome is written correctly?

options.text: The patient will feel confident about managing the insulin at home
options.rationale: Confidence matters and it is not measurable. Nothing tells you whether it was met.

options.text: The patient will understand how to inject the insulin
options.rationale: Understanding cannot be observed, and two nurses would score it differently. Write a verb you can watch happen.

options.text: The patient will demonstrate correct injection technique unaided before discharge
options.rationale: This is specific, measurable by watching, achievable, relevant to the priority problem and tied to a deadline.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient correct injection technique
options.rationale: This describes what the nurse will do. An outcome states what the patient will achieve.

questions.takeaway: SMART outcomes: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Write what the patient will do, not what the nurse will do.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses a verb you cannot observe. One describes the nurse's activity instead of the patient's.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One option is about the nurse.

elimination.verdict: That leaves demonstrating unaided before discharge.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse writes outcomes for a patient recovering from a stroke.

Adding by the end of the week makes the outcome [[1]].

Checking that the goal fits a patient who could walk 10 feet yesterday makes it [[2]].

Saying exactly what the patient will do, rather than that the patient will improve, makes it [[3]].

Adding a distance of 20 feet makes it [[4]].

options.text: time-bound
options.rationale: Time-bound sets the deadline, and without one an outcome can never be judged unmet.

options.text: measurable
options.rationale: The distance already makes it countable. What this outcome is missing is a date.

options.text: achievable
options.rationale: Achievable is about whether it is realistic, not about when it should happen.

options.text: relevant
options.rationale: Relevant is about whether it matters to his priority problem, not about timing.

options.text: achievable
options.rationale: Achievable means realistic for this patient, judged against what he could manage yesterday.

options.text: measurable
options.rationale: The number is already in the outcome. This blank is about whether he can reach it.

options.text: specific
options.rationale: The action is already named. This blank is about whether it is realistic.

options.text: relevant
options.rationale: Relevance asks whether it addresses his priority problem, not whether he can reach it.

options.text: measurable
options.rationale: Measurable adds the number. This blank is about naming the action itself.

options.text: specific
options.rationale: Specific says exactly what will happen, leaving no room for two nurses to read it differently.

options.text: relevant
options.rationale: Relevant asks whether the outcome addresses the priority problem, not how clearly it is worded.

options.text: achievable
options.rationale: Achievable asks whether it is realistic for this patient, which is a different question.

options.text: measurable
options.rationale: A number you can check against. Twenty feet either happened or it did not.

options.text: time-bound
options.rationale: Time-bound adds the when. This blank is asking about how much.

options.text: specific
options.rationale: This is the near miss. Specific says what will happen; measurable says how much.

options.text: achievable
options.rationale: Achievable concerns whether it is realistic for him, not whether you can count it.

questions.takeaway: SMART: Specific is what, Measurable is how much, Achievable is whether he can, Relevant is whether it matters, Time-bound is when.
questions.strategy: Specific and measurable are the pair that gets confused. Specific names the action; measurable attaches a number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: By the end of the week.

elimination.verdict: Specific, measurable, achievable, time-bound.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from a stroke has difficulty swallowing, cannot manage the stairs at home, and struggles to make himself understood. Which consultation should the nurse arrange for the swallowing difficulty?

options.text: Occupational therapist
options.rationale: Occupational therapy addresses daily activities and adaptation, which is relevant to other parts of his care but not to swallowing.

options.text: Speech and language pathologist
options.rationale: Swallowing assessment and management sits with the speech and language pathologist, alongside communication.

options.text: Physical therapist
options.rationale: Physical therapy addresses the stairs and his mobility. Swallowing belongs to someone else.

options.text: Registered dietitian nutritionist
options.rationale: The near-miss. The dietitian determines what he should eat; the speech pathologist determines whether he can swallow it safely.

questions.takeaway: Consult the professional whose scope matches the problem. Swallowing and communication go to speech and language pathology.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is the dietitian. One decides what the diet should be, the other decides whether swallowing is safe at all.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each problem to a discipline

steps.detail: Decides the diet, not the safety of swallowing.
Both address other problems in the stem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the speech and language pathologist.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a shift with a patient whose saturation is 89%, whose pain is uncontrolled, who is anxious about surgery, and who is at risk for constipation, and she is also taking an admission. Which principles guide how she establishes priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Address problems in the order they were identified
options.rationale: The order you noticed problems in has nothing to do with how urgent they are. Discovery order is not a priority rule.

options.text: Consider this patient's unique situation
options.rationale: It is why two patients with identical problem lists may be prioritized differently.

options.text: Apply Maslow's hierarchy to the identified problems
options.rationale: Maslow orders needs by how fundamental they are, and it is one of the recognized ways to rank competing problems.

options.text: Manage her time and protect it from interruptions
options.rationale: Part of establishing priorities, because a plan she never reaches is not a priority.

options.text: Treat every physiological problem as higher priority than any psychosocial one
options.rationale: This is exactly what to avoid. Physiological problems usually rank high, and always is what makes it wrong.

options.text: Rank problems as high, intermediate or low using the ABCs
options.rationale: Airway, breathing and circulation order the physiological problems, and that ranking produces the high, intermediate and low tiers.

questions.takeaway: Establishing priorities: the ABCs, Maslow, the patient's unique situation, and time management. Avoid ranking only physiological diagnoses as high priority.
questions.strategy: One distractor states a good rule of thumb as an absolute. That word is what makes it the wrong answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: ABCs, Maslow, the individual, time management.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse writes an outcome that a patient will ambulate 50 feet twice daily by tomorrow. He walked 10 feet once today with two assistants. Which element of the outcome is the problem?

options.text: It is not achievable for this patient at this point
options.rationale: Achievable asks whether it is realistic for this patient. The gap between 10 feet with two assistants and 50 feet twice daily makes failure certain.

options.text: It is not measurable
options.rationale: Fifty feet and twice daily are both countable. Measurement is not the problem with this outcome.

options.text: It is not time-bound
options.rationale: By tomorrow is a deadline, so the outcome is time-bound. That is not what is wrong with it.

options.text: It is not specific enough about the activity
options.rationale: Ambulate 50 feet twice daily is entirely specific. The problem is that he managed 10 feet with two people today.

questions.takeaway: An outcome that cannot be reached is not a goal, it is a guaranteed failure. Achievable is judged against what this patient can do now.
questions.strategy: Three elements are plainly present in the outcome as written. Check each against the wording before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves achievable.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a planned bed bath and the patient becomes short of breath and asks to sit forward. He was assessed as stable at the start of the shift. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue with the head of the bed raised and monitor him
options.rationale: Better, and it still continues a non-urgent task through an unexplained change in breathing.

options.text: Stop, reassess, and act on the new finding before continuing
options.rationale: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment while performing care. A plan made an hour ago does not override what is happening now.

options.text: Complete the bath quickly so he can rest afterwards
options.rationale: This puts finishing the task ahead of a change in his condition. The bath can wait; the breathlessness cannot.

options.text: Document that the bath was not tolerated and reschedule it
options.rationale: This records the event and leaves the breathlessness unassessed. Rescheduling is not a response to a new symptom.

questions.takeaway: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment during care. A change mid-task sends you back to assessment.
questions.strategy: Two distractors continue the task in some form. Ask what has changed since the plan was made.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New breathlessness in a stable patient.
The task is not urgent; the change is.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping and reassessing.

questions.stem: A nurse gathers her equipment, reviews the steps, and confirms the patient's identity and allergies before starting a procedure she has performed many times. Which principle does this reflect?

options.text: Individualization takes precedence over standardization
options.rationale: That tension is real in implementation, but nothing here is being individualized. She is preparing, not adapting.

options.text: Standard interventions ensure evidence-based care
options.rationale: Standard interventions concern what the care is, not how she readies herself to give it.

options.text: Preparation reduces adverse events
options.rationale: Familiarity with a procedure is not a substitute for preparing for this instance of it.

options.text: Care coordination requires appropriate use of resources
options.rationale: Coordination is about communication, time and resources across the whole assignment. This is preparation for one procedure.

questions.takeaway: Preparation reduces adverse events. Care coordination skills are communication, time management, and appropriate use of resources.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real implementation principles that describe something other than what she did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves preparation reducing adverse events.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Nurse enters to perform a scheduled dressing change on a 66-year-old, second day after bowel surgery. Supplies gathered and identity confirmed. Patient states the pain is 8 of 10 and that no analgesia has been given since 0400. Diaphoretic. Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800. Wound edges approximated, no drainage. Temperature 36.9 C. Patient says it would be better to wait. Blood pressure 138/84.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should stop the nurse proceeding with the dressing change now.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84
segments.rationale: A blood pressure of 138/84 is acceptable and does not by itself require any action.

segments.text: Supplies gathered and identity confirmed
segments.rationale: Gathering supplies and confirming identity is correct preparation. Preparing well does not oblige you to go ahead.

segments.text: Says it would be better to wait
segments.rationale: The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800
segments.rationale: A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not.

segments.text: Diaphoretic
segments.rationale: A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change.

segments.text: Temperature 36.9 C
segments.rationale: Normal, and it makes infection less likely as the cause of the other findings.

segments.text: Pain 8 of 10 with no analgesia since 0400
segments.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm.

segments.text: Wound edges approximated, no drainage
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding, and it is why this dressing change is not urgent.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing reassessment during implementation means the plan can be stopped. A prepared nurse is still allowed to change her mind.
questions.strategy: One finding tells you the task is not urgent. Another shows the preparation was correct, which is a reason to feel committed and not a reason to proceed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the task is urgent

steps.detail: Pain, sweating, rate up from baseline.

elimination.verdict: s3, s4, s5, and s7: the patient's own request, rising rate, diaphoresis, and pain.

questions.stem: A nurse follows a standard turning schedule but adapts it for a patient who cannot lie on his left side after surgery. Which implementation principle does this show?

options.text: Standard interventions provide evidence-based care and must still be individualized
options.rationale: Both halves of the statement are correct. The standard gives the evidence base; the individual gives the constraints.

options.text: Nurses should develop an original plan for every patient
options.rationale: This throws away the evidence base that standard interventions carry. You adapt the standard rather than reinventing it.

options.text: Deviation from a standard requires a provider order
options.rationale: Adapting how nursing care is delivered sits inside nursing judgment. No order is needed to change which side he lies on.

options.text: Standard interventions should be followed exactly to ensure consistency
options.rationale: This removes individualization, and individualizing care is a requirement rather than a nicety.

questions.takeaway: Standard interventions help nurses provide evidence-based care, and care should be individualized. Both are required.
questions.strategy: Two distractors take one half of the principle and discard the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves standards individualized.

questions.stem: A nurse hands over a patient whose condition changed during the shift. Which activities are part of implementation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Writing the expected outcome the care is aimed at
options.rationale: Outcomes are written during planning, before any care is delivered. By implementation they already exist.

options.text: Communicating the change at handoff
options.rationale: Communication is one of the care coordination skills, and handoff is where it matters most.

options.text: Setting the priority order among the identified problems
options.rationale: Planning. Prioritizing happens before implementation, and it is the step most often misfiled into this one.

options.text: Reassessing the patient while performing the care
options.rationale: Reassessing while you deliver the care matters here. You do not wait until afterwards to look again.

options.text: Performing the wound care per protocol
options.rationale: Performing the wound care is the most visible form of taking action, which is what implementation means.

options.text: Beginning patient and family teaching
options.rationale: Teaching is an intervention being delivered, not a separate activity that sits outside implementation.

options.text: Documenting the findings and the care given
options.rationale: Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened.

questions.takeaway: Implementation: carry out the plan, individualize it, reassess while performing care, prepare properly, and coordinate through communication, time management and resources.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the step before. Ask when the outcome was written.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: B, D, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: An outcome states that a patient will walk 100 feet twice daily by day four. On day four he walks 60 feet once, having managed 20 feet on day one. Which evaluation is accurate?

options.text: Met
options.rationale: The outcome named 100 feet twice daily. Progress is not the same as achievement.

options.text: Partially met
options.rationale: Three verdicts exist: met, partially met, not met. Real progress that falls short of the target is what partially met describes.

options.text: Cannot be evaluated until he reaches his baseline
options.rationale: The outcome carried a deadline and day four has arrived. You evaluate against what was written, not against his baseline.

options.text: Not met
options.rationale: Technically accurate about the target, but it discards a tripling of his distance, which the plan revision needs to know.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the goal was met, partially met, or not met, and what data supports that conclusion.
questions.strategy: The middle verdict exists for exactly this situation. Two of the options collapse it into all or nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One ignores the target, one ignores the progress.

elimination.verdict: That leaves partially met.

questions.stem: A patient's mobility outcome was not met. Which actions does the nurse take when revising the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Select new or additional interventions
options.rationale: Choosing new or additional interventions is recognized, and it is what most people reach for first.

options.text: Reassess the patient for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written.

options.text: Continue the current plan for a further 48 hours before changing anything
options.rationale: This delays a revision the evaluation has already shown is needed. Another 48 hours buys nothing.

options.text: Adjust the goal, the outcome, or the target timeframe
options.rationale: Adjusting the goal, the outcome or the timeframe is recognized, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong.

options.text: Reconsider whether the nursing diagnosis is still the priority
options.rationale: It is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly.

options.text: Document that the patient was nonadherent with the mobility plan
options.rationale: Attributes the failure to the patient and closes the revision before it starts.

questions.takeaway: When an outcome is not met: reassess for new data, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust goals or timeframes, and select new interventions.
questions.strategy: One distractor blames the patient. One waits. Neither is among the four steps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The evaluation already answered the question.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E are selected.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old was admitted with pneumonia. An outcome stated that the patient would maintain an oxygen saturation above 92% on room air by day three. On day three the saturation is 89% on room air and 94% on 2 L by nasal cannula. The antibiotics are nearly complete, temperature is normal, and chest sounds have improved. The patient has been on bed rest since admission and has not mobilized.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 conclusion she reaches, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Extend the target date by a further three days
options.rationale: Adjusting the timeframe is a legitimate revision, and doing it alone assumes the plan would work given longer. Nothing suggests it would.

options.text: Document that the outcome was not met and continue the current plan
options.rationale: This records the verdict and changes nothing, which is the one thing evaluation exists to prevent.

options.text: Reassess for factors the original plan did not account for
options.rationale: The first step when an outcome is not met. His infection is resolving, so something else is keeping his saturation down.

options.text: Add mobilization and deep breathing to the plan of care
options.rationale: Selecting new or additional interventions. Three days of bed rest is the factor the original plan missed.

options.text: The antibiotic regimen has failed and should be reviewed
options.rationale: His temperature is normal and his chest sounds have improved. The infection is responding.

options.text: The outcome was met, since his saturation is 94%
options.rationale: The outcome specified room air. Meeting it with supplemental oxygen is not meeting it.

options.text: The outcome was partially met and the plan should continue unchanged
options.rationale: Partially met is defensible as a verdict, and continuing unchanged is not, since the evaluation has revealed something.

options.text: The outcome was not met, and the plan omitted a contributing factor
options.rationale: He needs oxygen to reach 94%, so the outcome as written was not achieved. The infection is treated and the immobility is not.

options.text: Distance mobilized and frequency of deep breathing exercises
options.rationale: Measures whether the added intervention is actually happening, which has to be true before it can work.

options.text: Whether he can describe the purpose of deep breathing
options.rationale: This tests knowledge. The outcome was about his oxygen saturation, not about what he can explain.

options.text: Oxygen saturation on room air after mobilization begins
options.rationale: This is the original outcome remeasured under the same conditions, after the new intervention has had a chance to work.

options.text: White cell count at the next blood test
options.rationale: Tracks the infection, which is already resolving and is not what the actions changed.

questions.takeaway: An unmet outcome is information. Reassess for what the plan missed before assuming the plan needs longer.
questions.strategy: The outcome specified room air, which is what makes 94% on oxygen a non-achievement. Two distractors track the infection, which is already resolving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Reassess and add mobilization, outcome not met with a missed factor, evaluated by room-air saturation and by uptake.

questions.stem: After an outcome is not met, a nurse reconsiders whether the nursing diagnosis she wrote is still accurate. Which step of the clinical judgment model has she returned to?

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Choosing new interventions is generating solutions. She is questioning the problem, not the plan.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Ranking competing explanations. She is asking whether the one she chose was right at all.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Questioning whether the problem was named correctly is a return to interpretation, one step further back than revising the plan.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes
options.rationale: Evaluating is the step that produced the verdict. Acting on that verdict is what comes next.

questions.takeaway: Revising the plan can send you back to different steps. New data goes to recognizing cues; a wrong diagnosis goes to analyzing cues; a wrong intervention goes to generating solutions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are also steps you can return to. Ask which part of the plan she is questioning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That would be doubting the intervention.
One just finished, one ranks rather than names.

elimination.verdict: That leaves analyzing cues.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates whether a patient met the outcome of demonstrating correct inhaler technique. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Observe him use the inhaler and compare against the correct steps
options.rationale: A psychomotor outcome is evaluated by watching it performed. Asking whether he understands does not show that he can.

options.text: Ask him to describe the steps in the correct order
options.rationale: This is the near miss. Describing the steps shows knowledge; the outcome asked him to perform them.

options.text: Confirm that the teaching session was completed and documented
options.rationale: This records what the nurse did. It says nothing about what the patient can now do.

options.text: Ask him whether he feels confident using the inhaler
options.rationale: Confidence is not competence, and the outcome specified a demonstration rather than a feeling.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an outcome by the method the outcome specified. Demonstration is evaluated by watching.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers what the nurse did as evidence of what the patient achieved. The near-miss tests knowledge instead of performance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves observing him use it.

questions.stem: A patient's heart rate has risen from 88 to 124, his temperature is 100.9 F, and his urine output is 15 mL over two hours. The nurse decides hypovolemia is the likelier cause than early infection and addresses it first. Which step of the clinical judgment model is this?

options.text: Recognizing cues
options.rationale: That step already happened when the nurse picked these three numbers out of the shift's data.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: The near miss. Analysis connects findings to possible explanations. This nurse has gone past that and ranked them.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Two explanations fit the same cues, and the nurse decided which one to act on first. Choosing between competing explanations is what this step is.

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: That comes after the hypothesis is chosen. Nothing in the stem names an intervention yet.

questions.takeaway: Analyzing cues connects findings to possible problems. Prioritizing hypotheses decides which problem you act on first when more than one fits.
questions.strategy: Find the last thing the nurse did. Earlier steps in the list are already complete.

strategies: Trace the model forward

steps.action: Check that no action was taken yet

elimination.verdict: Prioritizing hypotheses.

questions.stem: Two days after a stroke, a patient has left-sided weakness, coughs when she drinks thin liquids, and has lost four pounds since admission. Which statement is a nursing diagnosis the nurse can treat independently?

options.text: Impaired swallowing related to neuromuscular weakness
options.rationale: A human response to the illness, with a cause the nurse can name and interventions the nurse owns: positioning, texture, pacing, supervision at meals.

options.text: Cerebrovascular accident with left-sided hemiparesis
options.rationale: A medical diagnosis. The nurse manages its consequences and does not make or treat it.

options.text: Risk for aspiration requiring antibiotic prophylaxis
options.rationale: Starts as a nursing diagnosis and the intervention attached to it needs a prescriber, which makes it collaborative.

options.text: Dysphagia requiring a swallow study by speech therapy
options.rationale: This is collaborative too. The referral named inside the diagnosis is the giveaway, because she cannot resolve it alone.

questions.takeaway: A nursing diagnosis names a human response the nurse can treat with nursing interventions. If the fix requires another discipline's order, it is collaborative.
questions.strategy: Read what each option would have you do next. If that act needs someone else's signature, it is not independent.

strategies: Test each option for who acts

steps.action: Cut anything naming an order or referral
Keep the response with nursing interventions

elimination.verdict: Impaired swallowing is the answer.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a patient's urine output has fallen, considers dehydration and early kidney injury, decides dehydration is likelier given the fluid balance, and increases oral intake. Which step of the clinical judgment measurement model has she just completed when she chose dehydration?

options.text: Analyze cues
options.rationale: Analyzing cues is interpreting what the data means and clustering it. She has moved past that to choosing between explanations.

options.text: Prioritize hypotheses
options.rationale: She generated two possible explanations and decided which is likelier and more urgent, which is exactly this step.

options.text: Generate solutions
options.rationale: Generating solutions is deciding what to do, which is the oral intake.

options.text: Take actions
options.rationale: Taking action is increasing the intake, which came after.

questions.takeaway: Recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take actions, evaluate outcomes.
questions.strategy: The stem walks through four steps in one sentence. The question names one moment, so find it rather than naming the last thing she did.

strategies: Label each clause with its step
elimination.verdict: That leaves prioritize hypotheses.

questions.stem: A patient two days after bowel surgery has a temperature of 38.3 C, a wound with increasing serous drainage, and a white cell count of 14,000. Which statement is a nursing diagnosis the nurse can treat independently?

options.text: Risk for infection related to a surgical incision
options.rationale: A risk diagnosis describes a human response the nurse addresses independently through wound care, hygiene and monitoring.

options.text: Surgical site infection related to bowel surgery
options.rationale: That is a medical diagnosis and the nurse cannot diagnose or treat it.

options.text: Potential for sepsis requiring antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: This names a collaborative problem and the intervention belongs to the provider.

options.text: Elevated white cell count related to postoperative inflammation
options.rationale: A laboratory value is a cue, not a nursing diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Nurses diagnose and treat human responses. Medical diagnoses and collaborative problems require the provider.
questions.strategy: All four describe the same patient. Ask which one names something nursing can act on without an order.

strategies: Ask who treats each one
elimination.verdict: That leaves the risk diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient met the outcome of walking 150 feet twice daily by day five. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document that the outcome was met and continue the plan unchanged
options.rationale: Continuing an intervention for a resolved problem spends time the other problems need.

options.text: Discontinue that part of the plan and evaluate the remaining problems
options.rationale: A met outcome ends that intervention and frees attention for what is unresolved.

options.text: Write a more demanding mobility outcome before discharge
options.rationale: Raising the bar may be reasonable, but it is not automatic and it is not what evaluation requires.

options.text: Reassess the patient for cues that were missed when the plan was written
options.rationale: Reassessment for missed cues follows an outcome that was not met.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation closes a loop. Met means stop that intervention and move on. Not met sends you back to the cues and the diagnosis.
questions.strategy: Three options keep working on a problem that is solved. Ask what a met outcome entitles you to stop doing.

strategies: Ask what met means
elimination.verdict: That leaves discontinuing and moving on.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient what he thinks is causing his symptoms, then pauses rather than moving to the next question. Which combination of techniques is she using?

options.text: An open-ended question followed by probing
options.rationale: Probing requires a follow-up question, and she asked nothing further.

options.text: An open-ended question followed by silence
options.rationale: Asking what he thinks is causing it is recognized in the working phase, and the pause that lets him answer is silence.

options.text: Back-channeling followed by a leading question
options.rationale: Back-channeling is small signals that you are listening, and she asked no leading question.

options.text: A closed-ended question followed by clarification
options.rationale: The question is open, and she sought no clarification.

questions.takeaway: Working phase: open-ended questions, asking what the patient thinks is causing the symptoms, and allowing time to respond.
questions.strategy: Each option pairs two real techniques. The item tests whether you can name both halves of what she did.

strategies: Name each half separately

steps.action: Cut any option mismatching either half

elimination.verdict: That leaves an open question followed by silence.

questions.stem: A nurse must choose between four problems for a patient: a saturation of 90 percent on room air, acute pain rated 7, anxiety about discharge, and risk for falls. The patient's main worry is the discharge. Which problem takes priority?

options.text: Acute pain at 7
options.rationale: Pain is urgent and it is not the most immediate physiological threat on this list.

options.text: Anxiety about discharge
options.rationale: Patient preference shapes the plan and does not override an airway or breathing problem.

options.text: The saturation of 90 percent on room air
options.rationale: ABCs rank first. Breathing outranks pain, anxiety and a risk diagnosis.

options.text: Risk for falls
options.rationale: A risk diagnosis is potential. An actual physiological problem outranks it.

questions.takeaway: Priorities: ABCs first, then Maslow, then actual over potential, with the patient's own situation considered throughout.
questions.strategy: The stem adds the patient's preference specifically to see whether it displaces the ABCs. It informs the plan without reordering physiology.

strategies: Apply the ABCs first
elimination.verdict: That leaves the saturation.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes implementing a plan and the outcome was not met. The findings have not changed at all. Which action does she take first?

options.text: Extend the target date and continue the current interventions
options.rationale: Extending the time for interventions that have produced no change repeats the failure more slowly.

options.text: Reassess the patient for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: Revision begins with reassessment, because an unchanged finding often means the original diagnosis was wrong.

options.text: Select additional interventions to add to the plan
options.rationale: Adding interventions to a possibly wrong diagnosis compounds the error.

options.text: Document that the outcome was not met and hand over
options.rationale: Recording the failure is not revising the plan.

questions.takeaway: Revision order: reassess, reconsider whether the diagnosis is still accurate, adjust goals and timeframe, then select new interventions.
questions.strategy: Three options act on the plan. The nursing process restarts at assessment, not at intervention.

strategies: Ask where the cycle restarts
elimination.verdict: That leaves reassessing.

questions.stem: A nurse writes: the patient will understand his heart failure diet by discharge. Which revision corrects the outcome?

options.text: The patient will verbalize an understanding of his heart failure diet by discharge
options.rationale: Verbalizing an understanding is still not observable, and a patient can say it without being able to do it.

options.text: The patient will name three high-sodium foods and read one label correctly before discharge
options.rationale: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, and every part of it can be observed.

options.text: The patient will be taught about his heart failure diet before discharge
options.rationale: This states what the nurse will do, and outcomes describe the patient.

options.text: The patient will demonstrate improved understanding of his diet by discharge
options.rationale: Improved is not measurable and there is no baseline to improve from.

questions.takeaway: SMART outcomes are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, and they describe the patient rather than the nurse.
questions.strategy: Three revisions change the wording without fixing the problem. Ask what you would watch the patient do.

strategies: Ask what you would observe

steps.action: Name three foods, read a label

elimination.verdict: That leaves the specific behavioral outcome.

questions.stem: A nurse records a blood pressure of 78/44 on a patient who looks well and says he feels normal. Which actions validate the cue before she acts on it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Repeat the measurement in the other arm
options.rationale: A second site separates a true value from a measurement artifact.

options.text: Check that the cuff size matches the patient's arm
options.rationale: A cuff too large reads falsely low, which is the most common equipment cause.

options.text: Compare the value with his readings from earlier in the admission
options.rationale: A baseline turns a number into a change or a normal variant.

options.text: Take the pressure manually
options.rationale: A manual reading checks the automated device against a different method.

options.text: Ask him whether he feels lightheaded, especially on standing
options.rationale: Corroborating findings tell you whether the number matches the patient.

options.text: Chart the value and continue the planned care
options.rationale: Charting is not validation, and acting on an unvalidated cue is the error this step prevents.

options.text: Begin a fluid bolus while the value is being rechecked
options.rationale: Intervening before the cue is confirmed treats a number that may not exist.

questions.takeaway: Validate a cue that does not fit the patient before acting: another site, the right equipment, a different method, the baseline and a corroborating finding.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are the two ends of overreacting and underreacting. Validation sits between them.

strategies: Ask whether the action tests the cue

steps.action: Other arm, cuff size, baseline, manual, symptoms

elimination.verdict: The five validating actions are selected.

questions.stem: A patient has been taught to self-administer insulin. Which methods evaluate whether the outcome was met? Select all that apply.

options.text: Watching him draw up and give the dose
options.rationale: Return demonstration is the method for a psychomotor skill.

options.text: Asking him to explain each step in his own words
options.rationale: Teach-back confirms understanding alongside the demonstration.

options.text: Asking whether he feels confident with the injection
options.rationale: Confidence is a feeling and it does not establish that he can do it.

options.text: Reviewing his glucose readings since teaching began
options.rationale: An outcome measure that reflects whether the skill is being performed correctly at home.

options.text: Asking whether he has any questions
options.rationale: A patient with no questions may have understood everything or nothing.

options.text: Observing whether he rotates the site as taught
options.rationale: A specific observable element of the skill, and the one most often dropped.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation methods: observation, return demonstration, verbal explanation, and outcome data. Not whether the patient says yes.
questions.strategy: Both distractors are questions a nurse asks at the end of every teaching session. Neither produces evidence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both produce a yes or no.

elimination.verdict: The four methods are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is partway through a planned bed bath when the patient becomes short of breath. Which actions reflect correct implementation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stopping the bath and assessing the breathing
options.rationale: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment while performing care, and a change stops the task.

options.text: Repositioning him upright to ease the work of breathing
options.rationale: Acting on the reassessment is part of implementation rather than a departure from it.

options.text: Completing the bath quickly since it is already underway
options.rationale: Finishing a planned task through a change in condition is what reassessment during implementation exists to prevent.

options.text: Reporting the change to the provider
options.rationale: Communication and care coordination are recognized components of implementation.

options.text: Documenting the change and the actions taken
options.rationale: Documenting what happened and what was done is part of carrying out care.

options.text: Deferring the assessment until the planned care is complete
options.rationale: This defers the assessment that should have interrupted the task.

questions.takeaway: Implementation includes ongoing reassessment, individualizing care, communication, coordination and documentation.
questions.strategy: Both distractors prioritize finishing the plan. The plan was written before the patient changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both continue a plan the patient has outgrown.

elimination.verdict: The four actions are selected.

questions.stem: Which nursing diagnostic statement is correctly constructed?

options.text: Impaired physical mobility related to postoperative pain and lower limb weakness, as evidenced by inability to transfer without two staff
options.rationale: The problem is a human response, the related factors are things nursing can act on, and the evidence is observable.

options.text: Impaired physical mobility related to hip fracture, as evidenced by an inability to transfer without two members of staff
options.rationale: The closest distractor. The response and the evidence are fine and the related factor is a medical diagnosis, which nursing cannot treat. Name the pain and the weakness instead.

options.text: Risk for falls related to inadequate staffing on the unit
options.rationale: The related factor has to be something about the patient. Writing a staffing complaint into the record is both clinically useless and legally reckless.

options.text: Impaired physical mobility related to difficulty moving, as evidenced by reduced mobility
options.rationale: The statement says the same thing three times and names no cause anyone can address.

questions.takeaway: The related factor names something nursing can change. A medical diagnosis, a staffing problem, and a restatement of the problem are the three ways it goes wrong.
questions.strategy: Read only the words after related to. That phrase is where all three errors live.

strategies: Test the related factor alone
elimination.verdict: Pain and weakness.

questions.stem: A patient has a stage 2 sacral pressure injury and has just failed a bedside swallow screen after a stroke. The nurse is ranking impaired skin integrity against risk for aspiration. Which is the priority, and on what grounds?

options.text: Impaired skin integrity, because it is already causing harm while the aspiration has not happened and may never happen
options.rationale: The same reasoning worded as urgency. Harm that has already occurred is not the same as harm that is about to.

options.text: Risk for aspiration, because a potential problem outranks an actual one when what it threatens is the airway
options.rationale: Actual before potential is a tiebreaker, and the ABCs sit above it. A risk that would take the airway beats a problem already present in the skin.

options.text: Impaired skin integrity, because an actual problem always takes priority over a potential one
options.rationale: The rule is real and it is not the top rule. Applied without the ABCs above it, it ranks a wound over an airway.

options.text: Both rank equally and should be addressed together in one plan
options.rationale: Both do get addressed. The question asks which comes first, and declining to rank is how the airway waits.

questions.takeaway: Actual before potential is a tiebreaker, not the first rule. Airway, breathing and circulation sit above it, and a life-threatening risk outranks a non-urgent actual problem.
questions.strategy: Two options apply a rule you were taught correctly. The question is whether a higher rule applies first.

strategies: Stack the frameworks before applying one
elimination.verdict: Risk for aspiration.

questions.stem: Two days after a knee replacement a patient has a temperature of 37.8 C, heart rate 104, respirations 24, and oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air. The incision is clean with scant serous drainage, the calf is soft and nontender, he reports a sharp pain on deep breathing, and he took the compression sleeves off overnight because they were uncomfortable. Which cues cluster into the problem the nurse acts on first?

options.text: Temperature 37.8 C, heart rate 104, incision drainage, and postoperative day two
options.rationale: The tempting cluster, and the cues are the weak ones. Scant serous drainage from a clean incision is expected, a low-grade temperature on day two is common, and this grouping leaves the breathing out.

options.text: Respirations 24, saturation 91 percent, pain on deep breathing, and the compression sleeves removed overnight
options.rationale: Four cues from the same story: a postoperative patient without mechanical prophylaxis, now hypoxic with pleuritic pain and a rising respiratory rate.

options.text: Soft nontender calf, clean incision, and scant serous drainage
options.rationale: These are the findings that are reassuring, and a soft calf does not exclude a clot.

options.text: Heart rate 104, temperature 37.8 C, respirations 24, and saturation 91 percent, taken together as a deterioration pattern
options.rationale: A real deterioration pattern with the specific cue removed. Without the pleuritic pain and the missing prophylaxis it names that he is unwell without naming why.

questions.takeaway: Clustering means finding the cues that tell one story. The strongest cluster usually contains a cue about what was not done, not only the measurements.
questions.strategy: Two clusters are internally consistent. Ask which one includes the finding that only fits one diagnosis.

strategies: Find the cue that belongs to one problem only
elimination.verdict: The respiratory cluster.

questions.stem: A patient last seen six months ago for hypertension returns for a scheduled visit. The nurse collects current data and compares it against the record from that visit to see what has shifted. Which type of assessment is this?

options.text: Time-lapsed
options.rationale: Comparing current status against a baseline collected earlier, to find change over an interval, is what defines this type.

options.text: Emergency
options.rationale: That is a rapid assessment of life-threatening problems in an unstable patient.

options.text: Comprehensive
options.rationale: A comprehensive assessment builds the database rather than comparing against one, and it is usually done on first contact.

options.text: Problem-focused
options.rationale: The strongest distractor, since hypertension is a named problem. A problem-focused assessment examines one concern right now and is not built on comparison with a previous database.

questions.takeaway: What distinguishes the types is the purpose: build the database, examine one problem, find the immediate threat, or measure change since last time.
questions.strategy: Do not classify by the content. Classify by what the nurse is doing with the data.

strategies: Ask what the assessment is for
elimination.verdict: Time-lapsed.

questions.stem: Which of the following are independent nursing interventions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Consulting physical therapy under the unit's mobility protocol
options.rationale: Collaborative. The protocol permits it and the work is carried out with another discipline.

options.text: Administering the ordered intravenous antibiotic
options.rationale: Dependent. It exists because a provider wrote it, although the judgment about whether to give it stays with the nurse.

options.text: Repositioning a patient at risk for pressure injury every two hours
options.rationale: The nurse decides to teach, decides what to teach, and does it on her own authority. Nothing has to be ordered and nobody else has to be involved, which is what makes an intervention independent.

options.text: Teaching splinted coughing before abdominal surgery
options.rationale: Patient education is nurse-initiated and is not delegable or prescribable.

options.text: Raising the head of the bed for a patient reporting breathlessness
options.rationale: A positioning decision the nurse makes on her own assessment.

options.text: Titrating oxygen to keep the saturation inside a prescribed range
options.rationale: Dependent, because the range and the permission to adjust both come from an order.

options.text: Assessing pain before an intervention and again afterward
options.rationale: Assessment is the nurse's own and does not wait for authorization.

questions.takeaway: Independent interventions need no order. Dependent ones carry one out. Collaborative ones are shared with another discipline, and a protocol does not make an action independent.
questions.strategy: Ask of each one whether it could happen on a unit with no provider available. If not, it is not independent.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Repositioning, teaching, positioning, and pain assessment are selected.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse plans the assignment for a shift with one registered nurse, one licensed practical nurse, and one assistive personnel.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate whether it may be delegated to assistive personnel or must be retained by a licensed nurse.
columns: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

rows.text: Assessing a patient who has become newly short of breath
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Assessment of an unstable patient. Neither the task nor the circumstance permits delegation.

rows.text: Assisting a patient who ambulates independently to the bathroom
rows.rationale: Helping a patient to the bathroom when his mobility is known and stable is routine assistance, and it can be delegated.

rows.text: Teaching a newly diagnosed patient how to inject insulin
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Patient education requires assessment of readiness and understanding, and it cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met his mobility outcome
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Evaluation is a step of the nursing process and stays with the nurse, even when the walking itself was assisted by someone else.

rows.text: Taking vital signs on a patient whose condition has not changed
rows.rationale: Right circumstance is satisfied: the patient is stable. The nurse still interprets what comes back.

rows.text: Recording intake and output for a stable patient
rows.rationale: A routine measurement task on a stable patient, and it requires no clinical judgment to perform.

answer.r1: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r3: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r4: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

questions.takeaway: Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable patients stay with the nurse. Routine tasks on stable patients may be delegated.
questions.strategy: Two things decide it: what the task requires, and how stable the patient is. A delegable task on an unstable patient is no longer delegable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is

steps.detail: The walking can be delegated; the verdict cannot.
