elimination.verdict: Three delegable, three retained.

questions.stem: A nurse tells assistive personnel to get the vital signs on the patient in room 12 and walks away. The readings are taken an hour later and the patient's blood pressure has fallen to 86/50 without anyone reporting it. Which right of delegation was not met?

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Vital signs on a stable patient are appropriate to delegate. The task itself was fine.

options.text: Right directions and communication
options.rationale: Clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back. She gave a task and no parameters, so nobody knew 86/50 needed reporting.

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the assistive personnel were unqualified to take a blood pressure. What was missing was any instruction about when and what to report.

options.text: Right circumstance
options.rationale: The patient was stable when the task was assigned. What followed came from the missing instructions, not from the circumstance.

questions.takeaway: Five rights: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three of the five were satisfied. Ask what the assistive personnel would have needed to know to act differently.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Get the vital signs. Nothing else.
When to report, and what would count as abnormal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves right directions and communication.

questions.stem: During a bed bath delegated to assistive personnel, a patient's oxygen tubing is dislodged and not replaced, and his saturation falls. Who is accountable?

options.text: The assistive personnel
options.rationale: They answer for their own performance. That does not remove the nurse's accountability for the outcome.

options.text: Both equally
options.rationale: Accountability is not divided into halves. Each answers fully for their own part, and the nurse answers for the outcome.

options.text: The charge nurse
options.rationale: The charge nurse answers for the assignment. The nurse who delegated this task answers for this outcome.

options.text: The nurse
options.rationale: The task moves and the accountability does not. She delegated the bath, and she still answers for what happened during it.

questions.takeaway: Accountability means you own the outcome of what you do, even if you delegate it. The task transfers; the accountability does not.
questions.strategy: Two distractors move accountability elsewhere. One splits it. Ask what delegation transfers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the nurse who delegated.

questions.stem: A charge nurse considers delegating a task to assistive personnel. Which questions must she answer before doing so? Select all that apply.

options.text: Is this person competent and qualified to perform it
options.rationale: This is the right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks. A certificate is not the same as having done it well.

options.text: Will I monitor the outcome and follow up
options.rationale: This is the right supervision and evaluation, and it is the one people treat as optional. Delegating is not handing the task away.

options.text: Is the patient's condition stable and appropriate for delegation
options.rationale: This is the right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient stops being delegable.

options.text: Is this task appropriate to delegate
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no.

options.text: Whether the nurse would be comfortable performing it
options.rationale: Conscientious and irrelevant. The question is whether the delegate is competent, not how the nurse feels about the task.

options.text: Does the patient agree to the task being performed by assistive personnel
options.rationale: Consent concerns whether care happens, not who may lawfully perform it. It is not among the five rights.

options.text: Have I given clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back
options.rationale: This is the right directions and communication: what to do, what you expect, and when to come back to you.

questions.takeaway: Five rights of delegation: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: One distractor names something reasonable that is not one of the five.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and G are selected.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse is worried about a patient whose condition is changing.

Reporting the situation, background, assessment and recommendation to the provider uses [[1]].

Saying "I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue" uses [[2]].

Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support are the pillars of [[3]].

Her legal power to call the provider and question an order is [[4]].

options.text: the five rights
options.rationale: The five rights are a delegation checklist, not a way of structuring a report.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: CUS escalates a concern after reporting has failed to produce a response. Nothing has been reported yet.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: TeamSTEPPS is the wider framework with four pillars. It is not itself a report structure.

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation. That is the structure for handing information over.

options.text: shared governance
options.rationale: Shared governance is a structure for involving staff in decisions. It is not a communication tool.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue. Graded language for escalating when the first report did not work.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: TeamSTEPPS is the framework these tools sit inside, not the tool being described.

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: This is the near miss. SBAR reports the situation; CUS escalates after the report produced nothing.

options.text: the Magnet standards
options.rationale: The Magnet standards are shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being and professional development.

options.text: the decision-making framework
options.rationale: The decision-making framework is responsibility, autonomy, authority and accountability. Different list.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: Its four pillars are communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support.

options.text: the interprofessional competencies
options.rationale: The near-miss. Those four are values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

options.text: accountability
options.rationale: Accountability is owning the outcome of what you did. This blank is about the standing to act.

options.text: responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility is what you are supposed to do, the duties of the job.

options.text: authority
options.rationale: The legal power to act, including calling a provider and questioning an order.

options.text: autonomy
options.rationale: The near-miss. Autonomy is freedom to choose within scope; authority is the power to act on it.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. CUS escalates. TeamSTEPPS has four pillars. Authority is the legal power to act; autonomy is the freedom to choose.
questions.strategy: Two pairs of four get confused: TeamSTEPPS pillars against the interprofessional competencies, and authority against autonomy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the two sets of four

elimination.verdict: SBAR, CUS, TeamSTEPPS, authority.

questions.stem: Using a structured format, a nurse reports a patient's falling blood pressure and rising pulse to the provider. He says to continue monitoring. Which tool should she use next?

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: She already reported it using a structure. Repeating the same tool that did not work is unlikely to change the outcome.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS situation monitoring
options.rationale: Situation monitoring is what produced her concern. It does not communicate it to anyone.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: CUS exists for the moment when reporting has not produced a response. The graded language makes the concern impossible to file away.

options.text: The chain of command
options.rationale: Going over the provider's head fits if CUS fails. Skipping the graded language misses a step that usually works.

questions.takeaway: SBAR hands over information. CUS escalates when the handover has not produced a response.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is repeating SBAR. Ask what changed between the first call and the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reported it in a structured format.
It did not work the first time.
One does not communicate, one skips a step.

elimination.verdict: That leaves CUS.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a colleague about to give a medication to the wrong patient and says nothing, assuming the colleague has checked. Which TeamSTEPPS pillar was not applied?

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: Involved in the sense that she said nothing, and the pillar that names watching out for a colleague is mutual support.

options.text: Mutual support
options.rationale: Mutual support means team members watch out for each other and speak up. Assuming someone else has checked is how errors reach patients.

options.text: Situation monitoring
options.rationale: She did monitor the situation. She saw it. What failed was acting on what she saw.

options.text: Team leadership
options.rationale: Concerns how the team is directed and coordinated, rather than one member covering another.

questions.takeaway: TeamSTEPPS pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is situation monitoring, and the stem tells you she noticed. Noticing was not the failure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves mutual support.

questions.stem: A nurse decides that a patient's scheduled bath can wait because the patient is exhausted after physiotherapy. She makes the decision herself without consulting anyone. Which element of the decision-making framework is she exercising?

options.text: Authority
options.rationale: The near-miss. Authority is the power to act, such as calling a provider and questioning an order. Autonomy is choosing what to do within scope.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility is what she is supposed to do. The bath is one of those duties; deciding when is autonomy.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: She will own this decision, and accountability describes answering for it rather than making it.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Timing routine care is squarely within nursing judgment, and she made the call herself.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is what you are supposed to do. Autonomy is your freedom to choose within scope. Authority is your legal power to act. Accountability is owning the outcome.
questions.strategy: All four elements are present in any nursing decision. Ask which one names the act of deciding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chose, within her scope, without asking.
Power to act, not freedom to choose.
One is the duty, one is the aftermath.

elimination.verdict: That leaves autonomy.

questions.stem: A nurse questions an order for a dose she believes is unsafe, contacts the prescriber, and documents the conversation. Which elements of the decision-making framework does this demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Delegation
options.rationale: She did not hand the problem to anyone. She acted on it herself.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it.

options.text: Authority
options.rationale: Questioning an order is the textbook example of authority. She has the legal standing to challenge it.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy operating inside her scope.

questions.takeaway: The four elements are not alternatives. A single nursing action usually involves all of them at once.
questions.strategy: The distractor describes handing the problem on. Ask whether she transferred anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what she did with the problem

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A new graduate says she does not see herself as a leader because she manages no one. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Leading her own patient care requires judgment, delegation, and communication
options.rationale: These are ground-level skills every nurse needs. Leadership is framed as practical rather than positional.

options.text: Leadership skills develop naturally with more clinical experience
options.rationale: They are described as learnable and practical, which implies they are taught and practised rather than absorbed.

options.text: Leadership becomes relevant once she moves into a management role
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the point. Leadership is a bedside skill you use on your first shift, not a management track.

options.text: Her focus should remain on clinical skills until she is more experienced
options.rationale: Separates clinical work from leading it, when prioritizing and delegating are part of the clinical work itself.

questions.takeaway: Leadership skills are learnable and practical: clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication.
questions.strategy: Three distractors defer leadership to later, to a role, or to experience. Ask what she does on her own assignment today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the ground-level skills.

questions.stem: A patient is discharged from hospital to a rehabilitation facility and then home, with one person coordinating her care across all three settings. Which nursing care delivery model is in use?

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Someone coordinates care across multiple settings, which is the definition of the model.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One registered nurse follows a patient throughout, and it operates within a setting rather than across several. It is rare today because it is expensive.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: Team nursing is a group led by a registered nurse working together on one unit, within one shift. This crosses three settings.

options.text: Patient- and family-centered care
options.rationale: Treats the patient and family as partners. It describes the relationship rather than how care is organized across settings.

questions.takeaway: Team nursing is a group led by an RN. Primary nursing is one RN following a patient through. Case management coordinates across settings. Patient- and family-centered care treats them as partners.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is primary nursing, which also involves one person following a patient. The difference is whether it crosses settings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut team nursing and the partnership model
steps.detail: One is a unit group, one is a relationship.

elimination.verdict: That leaves case management.

questions.stem: A hospital applies for Magnet recognition. Which standards must it demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared decision-making
options.rationale: Shared decision-making is recognized first, and it is what connects Magnet to shared governance and decentralized authority.

options.text: Quality
options.rationale: Quality is one of the standards, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes rather than claimed.

options.text: Well-being
options.rationale: Well-being is one of the standards, and it covers nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Cost containment per patient day
options.rationale: A real organizational concern, but not among the Magnet standards. The standards concern how nursing is practised and supported.

options.text: Leadership
options.rationale: It reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout.

options.text: Nurse-to-patient ratios fixed by state statute
options.rationale: A staffing law in some states and not a Magnet standard. Magnet measures how a unit is led and how its nurses practise.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Safety is one of the six standards, and it is measured rather than asserted.

questions.takeaway: Magnet standards: shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, and professional development.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a legitimate hospital priority that is not one of the six.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, professional development.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient's daughter says staff make the decisions and tell the family afterwards. The unit's Professional Practice Model is built on patient- and family-centered care. Which set of elements is the unit failing to deliver?

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
options.rationale: The TeamSTEPPS pillars, which concern how the team works rather than how patients are engaged.

options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration
options.rationale: Her four core elements of patient- and family-centered care within the practice model.

options.text: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork
options.rationale: These are the four interprofessional competencies. They describe how a team works, not the practice model.

options.text: Responsibility, autonomy, authority, and accountability
options.rationale: This is the decision-making framework. It describes an individual nurse's standing, not a practice model.

questions.takeaway: Patient- and family-centered care: respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, collaboration. The practice model drives the nursing care delivery model.
questions.strategy: All four options are real sets of four from this chapter. Ask which set is about patients rather than about staff.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves respect, information sharing, participation, collaboration.

questions.stem: A nurse executive introduces a program inviting staff nurses to propose and trial changes to unit practice, with protected time to do so. Which characteristic of an empowered nursing team does this support?

options.text: Compliance with regulatory standards for nursing practice
options.rationale: Regulation sets the floor. Empowerment is about what a unit does above that floor.

options.text: Standardization of nursing care across the organization
options.rationale: This points the other way. The program invites variation on purpose so that improvements can be tested.

options.text: Clear separation between management and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance blur that line deliberately. Staff nurses making practice decisions is the point.

options.text: An environment that supports risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth
options.rationale: This is what an empowering environment does, and protected time is what turns the invitation into something real.

questions.takeaway: Empowering environments support risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth. A culture of autonomy, quality and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe control rather than empowerment. Ask what protected time to trial a change enables.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trying something that might not work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves risk-taking and innovation.

questions.stem: A nurse wants staff on the unit to have real authority over how admissions are scheduled, not just to be asked afterward. Which structure provides that?

options.text: A manager who consults staff before announcing decisions
options.rationale: Consultation is better than none and it keeps the decision in one place. Governance means staff hold part of it.

options.text: An annual satisfaction survey distributed to staff nurses
options.rationale: A survey collects views without handing anyone a decision. Being asked afterwards is exactly what she is trying to move past.

options.text: A unit council of staff nurses that decides care delivery
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance mean decisions move toward the people doing the work.

options.text: A central committee writing policy applied to every unit
options.rationale: A central committee writing policy for every unit is centralization, which is the thing shared governance moves away from.

questions.takeaway: Decentralization and shared governance move decision-making toward the staff who deliver the care.
questions.strategy: Two distractors gather opinions without transferring any decision. Ask who decides in each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both inform a decision held elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: That leaves staff sitting on the deciding council.

questions.stem: Interprofessional rounds include a physician, a pharmacist, a physical therapist and a social worker. Which interprofessional competencies are in use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
options.rationale: Values and ethics underlie the mutual respect that makes a round work at all, and it is one of the four competencies.

options.text: Interprofessional communication
options.rationale: Communication is the visible activity of a round, and it is one of the four competencies by name.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Roles and responsibilities is one of the four, and rounds only work when everyone knows what each discipline brings.

options.text: Delegation of tasks across disciplines
options.rationale: Delegation operates within nursing to appropriate personnel. Coordinating with other disciplines is collaboration rather than delegation.

options.text: Teams and teamwork
options.rationale: Teams and teamwork is one of the four, and it is what turns four disciplines into a single plan.

questions.takeaway: Four interprofessional competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies a nursing-specific concept to interdisciplinary work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Values and ethics, roles, communication, teamwork.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 0730: Charge nurse reviewing the shift. Unit has four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse, and two assistive personnel for 28 patients. One registered nurse is orienting on her second shift. Three patients are scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit today. A patient in room 14 was admitted overnight with chest pain and has not yet been assessed this shift. The assistive personnel were told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters given. A newly admitted patient in room 22 needs discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen, and this has been assigned to an assistive personnel. Two patients are stable and awaiting routine morning care.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the charge nurse must address before the shift proceeds.

segments.text: Discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen assigned to assistive personnel
segments.rationale: Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

segments.text: Three patients scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit
segments.rationale: Three planned transfers need coordinating. That is expected work rather than a safety problem.

segments.text: A registered nurse orienting on her second shift
segments.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support.

segments.text: Assistive personnel told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters
segments.rationale: This is the right directions and communication missing. Without parameters, an abnormal reading can sit unreported for hours.

segments.text: Four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse and two assistive personnel for 28 patients
segments.rationale: The staffing she has. It shapes every decision she makes and is not itself a finding she can correct this morning.

segments.text: Two stable patients awaiting routine morning care
segments.rationale: Routine care on stable patients. This is the work the shift exists to do.

segments.text: A patient admitted overnight with chest pain, not yet assessed this shift
segments.rationale: An unassessed patient with chest pain is the one nobody has laid eyes on this shift. Right now nobody knows his status.

questions.takeaway: Delegation errors and unassessed patients come first. Staffing constraints shape the plan rather than being a correctable finding.
questions.strategy: One finding is the constraint she is working inside rather than a problem to solve. Two describe expected work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The staffing number is the constraint.
No parameters, and teaching assigned to AP.

elimination.verdict: s1, s3, s4, and s7: the orientee, the unassessed patient, and two delegation errors.

questions.stem: During a staffing huddle, a nurse explains how accountability works once a task has been delegated. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Once I delegate a task, the person performing it becomes accountable for the outcome."
options.rationale: Accountability stays with the delegating nurse. The task transfers and the answerability does not.

options.text: "A task that is usually delegable may not be, if the patient is unstable."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the right circumstance. Instability takes a delegable task off the table.

options.text: "I need to tell them what to report back and when."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Saying what to report and when is the right directions and communication.

options.text: "I cannot delegate assessment, teaching or evaluation."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Assessment, teaching and evaluation need nursing judgment and stay with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegation transfers the task. Accountability for the outcome stays with the nurse who delegated it.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the rights correctly. The fourth moves accountability with the task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement transferring accountability.

questions.stem: A unit reports rising nurse turnover, frequent reports of moral distress, and falling patient satisfaction. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Recruitment should be the priority before addressing unit culture
options.rationale: Recruiting into a unit people are leaving addresses the symptom and refills a leaking bucket.

options.text: The findings reflect individual nurses' resilience and coping skills
options.rationale: Locates a unit-level pattern in individual character, which is the misreading that leaves the culture unchanged.

options.text: How a unit is led affects outcomes, satisfaction, and burnout
options.rationale: Her first key takeaway. These are not three separate problems, and leadership is the common factor.

options.text: Turnover and satisfaction are unrelated to clinical quality measures
options.rationale: They move together, so Magnet treats well-being as a standard alongside quality rather than a perk.

questions.takeaway: Leadership shapes care quality. Patient outcomes, nurse satisfaction and burnout move together rather than separately.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a unit pattern into a personal shortcoming. Ask what the three findings have in common.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All three sit on one unit.

steps.action: Cut the unrelated and recruitment options
steps.detail: One denies the link, one treats the symptom.

elimination.verdict: That leaves leadership affecting all three.

questions.scenario: A nurse reports to the provider that a patient's blood pressure has fallen from 132/78 to 94/56 over three hours, the pulse has risen from 78 to 118, and urine output has been 15 mL/hr for two hours. She uses a structured report. The provider says to continue monitoring and recheck in two hours. She remains concerned.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Notify the charge nurse and prepare to move up the chain of command
options.rationale: Her authority includes questioning an order and escalating. Preparing the next step is not going over anyone's head prematurely.

options.text: Recheck in two hours as instructed and document the conversation
options.rationale: Following an instruction that does not match the findings, and documenting it does not make two hours safe.

options.text: Escalate using graded language: concerned, uncomfortable, this is a safety issue
options.rationale: CUS exists for exactly this moment. She reported once and the response did not match the findings, so the next step is language that cannot be filed away.

options.text: Repeat the same structured report to the same provider
options.rationale: The report was already given clearly. Repeating the tool that did not work is unlikely to change the response.

options.text: A communication failure requiring a clearer handover
options.rationale: She communicated clearly using a structure. The failure is in the response, not in the report.

options.text: A deteriorating patient whose concern has not been acted on
options.rationale: Three parameters moving together in one direction, and a response that does not match them. Both halves are the problem.

options.text: An expected postoperative variation in vital signs
options.rationale: Falling pressure with rising pulse and oliguria is not expected variation in any context.

options.text: A conflict between the nurse and the provider
options.rationale: Frames a patient safety issue as an interpersonal one, which is how escalation gets delayed.

options.text: The provider's response to being escalated
options.rationale: Concerns the relationship rather than the patient, and escalation is judged by whether the patient was assessed.

options.text: Whether a provider has assessed the patient in person
options.rationale: This measures whether the escalation actually worked. A verbal instruction over the phone is not an assessment.

options.text: Whether the incident report has been completed
options.rationale: Administrative follow-up. It records what happened and does not evaluate whether he is safe now.

options.text: Blood pressure, pulse and urine output at short intervals
options.rationale: The three parameters that defined the deterioration, measured frequently enough to catch the next change.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports and CUS escalates. When the response does not match the findings, the graded language is the next tool, and the chain of command is behind it.
questions.strategy: Two distractors frame this as a communication or relationship problem. Three numbers are moving together, which makes it a patient problem.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Pressure down, pulse up, output 15 mL/hr.
Not a handover failure, not a conflict.

elimination.verdict: Escalate with CUS and prepare the chain of command, for a deteriorating patient, evaluated by the trends and by an in-person assessment.

questions.stem: At the start of the shift, report is given on four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A patient with a pain score of 8 of 10 awaiting analgesia
options.rationale: Distressing and the most emotionally compelling option on the list. Pain is urgent, and it is not airway.

options.text: A patient with a respiratory rate of 28 using accessory muscles
options.rationale: Accessory muscle use means the work of breathing has exceeded what the patient can sustain. That is the one finding on this list that can end in an arrest within the hour.

options.text: A patient with a blood glucose of 248 mg/dL due for insulin
options.rationale: Needs attention this shift. It is elevated and not an emergency, and insulin can follow the first assessment.

options.text: A patient whose family is waiting to discuss discharge plans
options.rationale: This matters to the family and it can move. Nothing deteriorates while they wait twenty minutes.

questions.takeaway: Accessory muscle use with a rate of 28 is respiratory failure in progress. Airway and breathing come before pain, glucose, and anything a family is waiting for.
questions.strategy: Pain at 8 of 10 is placed on these lists to be chosen. Rank by what kills first, not by what is most distressing.

strategies: ABCs

steps.action: Find the airway or breathing problem
Set glucose and the family aside

elimination.verdict: The patient using accessory muscles.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg on a patient admitted with dehydration, and add that he looks fine. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to repeat the measurement
options.rationale: Delegates the verification back to the same source. When delegated data is abnormal, the nurse is the one who confirms it.

options.text: Reassess the blood pressure and the patient personally
options.rationale: The nurse needs both the number and what the patient looks like, and looks fine from an unlicensed observer is not an assessment. One visit answers whether this is real.

options.text: Notify the provider of the reported reading
options.rationale: Escalating a number the nurse has not confirmed, with no assessment to report alongside it.

options.text: Review the record for the patient's baseline pressures
options.rationale: This is accurate and inert. Knowing yesterday's pressure tells you nothing about what is happening in the room right now.

questions.takeaway: Delegated data that falls outside normal gets verified by the nurse. Accountability for the outcome did not transfer with the task.
questions.strategy: Reviewing the chart feels thorough and produces no new information about the patient in front of you.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Verify delegated data

steps.action: Cut repeating it by the same person

steps.detail: Both act before the nurse has looked.

elimination.verdict: Reassess personally.

questions.stem: A charge nurse asks assistive personnel to remove a peripheral intravenous catheter from a patient being discharged. The assistive personnel has never done it and says so. Which right of delegation is at risk?

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Removal of a peripheral catheter may be delegated in many settings, so the task is not the problem.

options.text: Right circumstance
options.rationale: Discharge is a stable circumstance and does not make the delegation unsafe.

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Competence of the specific person is what fails here, and the person saying so is the safeguard working.

options.text: Right supervision
options.rationale: Supervision would matter after a valid delegation, but this one fails before that.

questions.takeaway: Five rights: task, circumstance, person, direction and communication, supervision and evaluation. A delegatable task given to someone not competent fails on the person.
questions.strategy: The task sounds like something only a nurse does, which pulls toward right task. The detail that decides it is that she has never done it.

strategies: Ask which right the stem puts under strain
elimination.verdict: That leaves right person.

questions.stem: A nurse challenges a prescribed dose she believes is ten times too high. The provider insists. She refuses to give it and calls the pharmacist. Which element of the decision-making framework is she exercising?

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility is the duty to give medications safely. It is what prompts her to act rather than what she exercises in acting.

options.text: Authority
options.rationale: Authority is the legal power to act, including calling a provider and questioning an order, which is what refusing and escalating is.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Accountability is owning the outcome, which follows the action rather than constituting it.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Autonomy is the freedom to make independent choices within scope. What she is using is the legal power to question and refuse an order, which is authority.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is the duty. Autonomy is the freedom to choose. Authority is the legal power to act. Accountability is owning the outcome.
questions.strategy: All four are in play in any such moment. The stem emphasizes challenging someone more senior, which is the authority element.

strategies: Ask what the stem emphasizes

steps.action: Refusing and escalating against a provider

steps.detail: The duty prompted it, but the act is the challenge.

elimination.verdict: That leaves authority.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the CUS tool with a surgeon who wants to proceed without a timeout. Which statement completes the escalation correctly?

options.text: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue
options.rationale: The three CUS statements escalate in that order and the third names it as a safety issue, which is what stops the line.

options.text: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation
options.rationale: That is SBAR, a handover structure rather than an escalation tool.

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support
options.rationale: Those are the TeamSTEPPS pillars, not a phrase set.

options.text: I am concerned, please stop, I am documenting this
options.rationale: Documenting is not an escalation step and the middle phrase is not part of the tool.

questions.takeaway: CUS: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue. SBAR hands over. TeamSTEPPS is the framework the tools sit in.
questions.strategy: Three options mix up three different tools. Keep straight which one escalates and which one hands over.

strategies: Match each option to its tool
elimination.verdict: That leaves the CUS statements.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a medication at the wrong time after a pump alarm silenced itself during a code. No harm results. The manager is deciding how to respond. Which approach reflects a just culture?

options.text: Counsel the nurse about time management so the error is not repeated
options.rationale: Counseling an individual for a system failure teaches the unit to stop reporting.

options.text: Examine why the alarm silenced itself and what the workload made unavoidable
options.rationale: A just culture separates the system from the individual and looks first at the conditions the error happened in.

options.text: Take no action, since the patient was not harmed
options.rationale: No harm is not no problem, and the hazard remains for the next patient.

options.text: Require the nurse to complete a medication safety module
options.rationale: A module addresses knowledge, and the nurse's knowledge was not what failed.

questions.takeaway: A just culture asks what in the system allowed this, holds people accountable for reckless choices, and never punishes an honest error into silence.
questions.strategy: Two options act on the nurse and one acts on nothing. Ask what would stop the next nurse having the same problem.

strategies: Ask what failed
elimination.verdict: That leaves examining the system.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a registered nurse is assigned a group of six patients with a licensed practical nurse and an assistive personnel working under her direction. She assigns tasks by license, supervises, and holds the overall plan. Which delivery model is this?

options.text: Total patient care
options.rationale: In total patient care, one nurse performs all the care for her patients during the shift, with no team under her.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: Primary nursing assigns one nurse accountability for a patient from admission to discharge, not a shift team.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: A registered nurse leading staff of different licenses to care for a group of patients is the defining structure.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Case management coordinates a patient's care across settings and over time rather than across one shift.

questions.takeaway: Team nursing is a registered nurse directing a mixed-skill group for a shift. Case management follows a patient across settings. Primary nursing follows one patient across the stay.
questions.strategy: All four put a nurse in charge of something. The difference is what she is in charge of: a shift team, a caseload, a patient's whole stay, or every task herself.

strategies: Ask what she is leading

steps.action: A mixed-license group for a shift

elimination.verdict: That leaves team nursing.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is deciding what to delegate to a licensed practical nurse and what to an assistive personnel. Which assignment is appropriate?

options.text: The LPN reinforces discharge teaching for a stable patient and the AP records intake and output
options.rationale: Reinforcing teaching for a stable patient is within LPN scope, and recording intake and output is a task for assistive personnel.

options.text: The LPN assesses a newly admitted patient and the AP ambulates a stable patient
options.rationale: Admission assessment stays with the registered nurse.

options.text: The LPN evaluates whether a dressing change was effective and the AP takes vital signs
options.rationale: Evaluation is interpretation and stays with the registered nurse.

options.text: The LPN develops the teaching plan and the AP reports abnormal vital signs to the provider
options.rationale: Planning stays with the registered nurse, and an AP reports to the nurse rather than the provider.

questions.takeaway: RN: unstable patients, assessment, evaluation, teaching, planning. LPN: reinforcing, monitoring, stable and discharge. AP: vital signs, ambulation, positioning, hygiene, intake and output.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option pairs one correct half with one incorrect half. Check both halves before choosing.

strategies: Check each half separately
elimination.verdict: That leaves the first pairing.

questions.stem: Staff on a unit are asked for their views on a new admission process after the decision has been made. A nurse says this is not shared governance. Which element is missing?

options.text: Responsibility for carrying out the new process
options.rationale: Staff will carry it out either way, so responsibility is not what is missing.

options.text: Authority to make the decision rather than comment on it
options.rationale: Shared governance decentralizes decision-making. Being consulted after the fact is consultation, not authority.

options.text: Accountability for the outcome of the process
options.rationale: Accountability follows the decision, and the decision was made elsewhere.

options.text: Autonomy in their individual clinical practice
options.rationale: Individual clinical autonomy is a different thing from a unit's governance structure.

questions.takeaway: Shared governance decentralizes decision-making. Being asked afterwards is consultation.
questions.strategy: All four terms are from the same framework. The stem describes timing, so ask which element timing destroys.

strategies: Ask what the timing changes
elimination.verdict: That leaves authority.

questions.stem: A nurse has delegated bathing and ambulation for four patients to assistive personnel. Which actions are part of her supervision? Select all that apply.

options.text: Telling the assistive personnel which findings to report and when
options.rationale: Reporting parameters are what make supervision possible rather than retrospective.

options.text: Checking in partway through the shift rather than only at the end
options.rationale: Supervision happens while the work is in progress, not after it.

options.text: Observing the first time a new assistive personnel performs a task
options.rationale: Competence is verified by watching it done, and that is especially so with someone unfamiliar.

options.text: Reassessing whether the task is still appropriate when a patient's condition changes
options.rationale: Delegation is reversible, and a change in stability withdraws it.

options.text: Giving feedback about what was done well and what needs to change
options.rationale: Feedback is part of supervision and it is the part most often skipped.

options.text: Documenting the bath in the record as though she had performed it
options.rationale: Documenting care she did not provide is falsification, whoever performed it.

options.text: Leaving the unit once the tasks are assigned, since the work is covered
options.rationale: Supervision requires availability, and the accountability does not leave with the task.

questions.takeaway: Supervision is direction, availability, monitoring during the work, feedback, and withdrawing the delegation when the patient changes.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options treat delegation as a handoff. It is a loan with the accountability still attached.

strategies: Ask what supervision requires
elimination.verdict: The five supervision actions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse starts a shift with five patients, two of whom need extensive care. Which actions reflect sound priority setting and time management? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reviewing all five patients before starting care on any of them
options.rationale: You cannot rank what you have not seen, and the sickest patient is not always the one who calls first.

options.text: Clustering care so each room is entered fewer times
options.rationale: Clustering saves the nurse's time and protects the patient's rest.

options.text: Identifying which tasks must happen at a fixed time and building around them
options.rationale: Time-critical work anchors the plan and everything else moves around it.

options.text: Delegating what may be delegated rather than doing everything herself
options.rationale: Retaining delegable work is a common reason nurses run out of time for what only they can do.

options.text: Working through the patients in room number order
options.rationale: Room order is not a priority system and it leaves ranking to the floor plan.

options.text: Reassessing the plan when a patient's condition changes
options.rationale: Priorities are not set once at the start of the shift.

options.text: Finishing all documentation before beginning patient care
options.rationale: Charting first delays assessment and the chart is written from care that has not happened yet.

questions.takeaway: Priorities come from seeing everyone first, ranking by urgency, anchoring the fixed points, delegating what you can, and re-ranking when something changes.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are ways of imposing an order that has nothing to do with the patients: the floor plan and the paperwork.

strategies: Ask what sets the order
elimination.verdict: The five sound actions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse explains what remains hers after she delegates a task. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: She remains accountable for the outcome
options.rationale: Accountability does not transfer with the task, and this is the point students most often miss.

options.text: She must verify the task was completed and the result reported
options.rationale: Right supervision and evaluation is part of delegating, not an optional follow-up.

options.text: She retains responsibility for assessing the patient
options.rationale: Assessment never transfers, so it stays hers whatever was delegated.

options.text: Accountability transfers to the person who performed the task
options.rationale: The person performing it is accountable for their own performance, and the delegating nurse still owns the outcome.

options.text: She must intervene if the task was performed incorrectly
options.rationale: Supervision includes acting on what the follow-up finds.

options.text: Delegation is complete once clear instructions have been given
options.rationale: Instructions are the fourth right. Supervision and evaluation is the fifth.

questions.takeaway: Accountability stays with the delegating nurse. Supervision and evaluation complete the delegation.
questions.strategy: Both distractors describe delegation as a handover that finishes. It does not finish until the outcome is checked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut both options that end the nurse's involvement

elimination.verdict: The four statements are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is handing off at the end of a shift and is interrupted three times. By the end she has covered the history, the current medications and the day's events, but has not said the two things she is worried could happen overnight. Which part of the handoff was lost?

options.text: The anticipated problems and what the next nurse should do if each one appears
options.rationale: Contingency planning is the piece that transfers the outgoing nurse's judgment. Everything else she covered is already in the record.

options.text: The receiving nurse's summary back of everything she has just heard and what she plans to watch for
options.rationale: The closest alternative and it is also missing. The question asks what she did not say, and she never got to the worries for the receiving nurse to repeat.

options.text: The assessment of the patient's condition as it stands now
options.rationale: Covered under the day's events and current status.

options.text: The background and context of the admission
options.rationale: She gave the history and the events, which is the background.

questions.takeaway: A handoff transfers what is not written down: what you are worried about and what to do if it happens. That is the part interruptions cut, because it comes last.
questions.strategy: Both of these are missing. Read the question carefully: it asks what she failed to say, not what the exchange failed to include.

strategies: Match what was covered against the structure
elimination.verdict: Anticipated problems and contingency plans.

questions.stem: Two nurses disagree about who should take the next admission. After several minutes one of them says she will take it so the discussion can end, though she still believes the assignment is unbalanced. Which approach to conflict is she using?

options.text: Compromising
options.rationale: The closest option. Compromise means both parties give something up. Here one person gave up everything and the other gave up nothing.

options.text: Collaborating
options.rationale: Collaboration produces a solution both sides consider better than their starting positions. Nothing was built here.

options.text: Avoiding
options.rationale: Avoiding means not engaging at all. She engaged, argued, and then conceded.

options.text: Accommodating
options.rationale: She has yielded entirely to keep the relationship smooth. The work is covered and her concern never enters the record of what happened.

questions.takeaway: Accommodating ends the conflict and keeps the problem. It is the approach most likely to be mistaken for teamwork, and it is why the same unfair pattern repeats next week.
questions.strategy: Count what each side gave up. One-sided yielding is accommodating; two-sided yielding is compromise.

strategies: Count the concessions
elimination.verdict: Accommodating.

questions.stem: At the start of the shift a nurse delegated vital signs on four stable patients to an experienced assistive personnel. Since then one of those patients has had a rapid response called and is now receiving a new infusion. The assistive personnel offers to carry on taking that patient's vital signs as planned. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Let her continue, since taking vital signs is within her role and she is competent at it
options.rationale: Right task and right person, which is what makes this tempting. Two of the five rights holding does not make a delegation safe when the third has changed.

options.text: Let her continue but have her report the numbers immediately
options.rationale: It adds a reporting rule to a delegation that should not be in place, and the delay is not the problem. The nurse needs to see the patient, not the numbers.

options.text: Take that patient's vital signs herself and tell the assistive personnel why the delegation changed
options.rationale: The task and the person were both appropriate and the circumstance was not. An unstable patient's vital signs are assessment data the nurse has to gather and interpret in the same moment.

options.text: Reassign all four patients' vital signs to herself
options.rationale: The other three patients have not changed. Pulling back work that is still appropriate wastes the only help she has.

questions.takeaway: The five rights are checked continuously, not once. The right that most often changes during a shift is the circumstance, and a patient becoming unstable revokes the delegation.
questions.strategy: Three options are about the assistive personnel. The thing that changed is the patient.

strategies: Check which of the five rights moved
elimination.verdict: Take that patient's vital signs herself.

questions.stem: At 0800 a nurse has four things waiting. A breakfast tray has arrived for a patient whose mealtime insulin is due. A patient admitted overnight has not yet been assessed and his daughter is at the desk asking for an update. A dressing change is scheduled for this hour. The laboratory telephones a potassium of 6.1 mmol/L on her fourth patient. What does she do first?

options.text: Contact the provider about the potassium
options.rationale: A critical potassium threatens the cardiac rhythm, and it is an actual finding rather than a scheduled task. Nothing else on the list can kill him in the next twenty minutes.

options.text: Assess the patient who has not been seen
options.rationale: Assessment before intervention is the right instinct and the wrong application. An unassessed patient is an unknown risk; the potassium is a known one.

options.text: Give the mealtime insulin while the tray is in front of the patient
options.rationale: Time-critical, and the window is measured in minutes rather than seconds. The tray will keep for the five minutes this call takes.

options.text: Update the daughter, since it will take two minutes
options.rationale: Short does not mean first. Quick tasks get done between the things that cannot wait, not before them.

questions.takeaway: Rank by what the finding threatens and how fast. A critical value is an actual, life-threatening problem and it outranks scheduled care, an unassessed patient, and anything short.
questions.strategy: Three options have a defensible rule behind them. Ask which patient could deteriorate while you do the others.

strategies: Ask what each delay would cost

steps.action: Weigh insulin against the laboratory call

elimination.verdict: Call about the potassium.

questions.stem: A nurse is given seven patients including two who returned from surgery within the hour. She believes the assignment is unsafe. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Record the concern through the facility's reporting process
options.rationale: It creates the pattern evidence that changes staffing, and it protects her if something goes wrong.

options.text: Begin caring for the patients while the concern is being worked on
options.rationale: Once she has accepted the patients, walking away is abandonment. Raising the concern and providing care happen at the same time.

options.text: Tell the charge nurse specifically what makes it unsafe and what she needs to make it workable
options.rationale: A named problem with a named remedy can be acted on. This assignment is too heavy cannot.

options.text: Decide privately which patients she will not get to and work through the shift from that
options.rationale: A silent rationing plan nobody else knows about. The patients who get dropped are chosen without anyone able to check the choice.

options.text: Refuse the assignment outright and leave the unit
options.rationale: Leaving patients already in her care is abandonment and a licensure matter, whatever the staffing was.

options.text: Tell the patients the unit is short staffed so they understand the delays
options.rationale: It transfers her problem to people who cannot solve it and undermines their confidence in their own care.

options.text: Escalate to the next level of management if the charge nurse cannot resolve it
options.rationale: The chain of command exists for exactly this, and stopping at the first no is where escalation usually fails.

questions.takeaway: Speak specifically, stay with the patients, document, and escalate. Refusing to care and quietly triaging in your head are the two ways this goes wrong.
questions.strategy: Separate protesting the assignment from abandoning the patients. The first is required and the second is never an option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Specify, stay, document, and escalate.

chapters.title: Ethics, Legal Implications, and Documentation
chapters.subtitle: Ethical principles and dilemmas, standards and statutes, malpractice, informatics, and the health record

sources.title: Legal Implications in Nursing Practice
sources.label: Potter Ch. 23 · Legal Implications in Nursing Practice

questions.scenario: A nurse works on a unit where several difficult situations arise during one week.
questions.stem: For each situation, indicate which ethical principle is most directly at stake.

rows.text: A competent patient refuses a recommended amputation
rows.rationale: His right to decide for himself, even when the team disagrees with the decision.

rows.text: A nurse withholds a medication because the dose would harm the patient
rows.rationale: She is preventing harm, and the action is defined by what she stopped rather than by what she did.

rows.text: A nurse promised to return after her break and does
rows.rationale: Keeping the promises you make, which is what builds trust across a shift.

rows.text: A unit reviews whether two patients with equal need receive equal access to a scarce bed
rows.rationale: This is fairness in how care and scarce resources get distributed between people with equal claims.

rows.text: A nurse arranges additional analgesia so a patient can tolerate physiotherapy
rows.rationale: She is acting to do good rather than just to avoid harm, and that is what separates this from nonmaleficence.

rows.text: A nurse tells a patient she will pass his question to the provider today, and does
rows.rationale: Another promise kept. Fidelity appears twice because it is the principle that runs through ordinary shifts.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy is the patient deciding. Beneficence is doing good. Nonmaleficence is avoiding harm. Justice is fairness between people. Fidelity is keeping promises.
questions.strategy: Beneficence and nonmaleficence are the pair that gets confused. One adds a benefit; the other prevents a harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate doing good from avoiding harm
steps.detail: Adding analgesia, or withholding a dose.

steps.action: Watch for more than one person

elimination.verdict: Autonomy, nonmaleficence, fidelity, justice, beneficence, fidelity.

questions.stem: A patient's family insists that aggressive treatment continue, while he has a valid advance directive declining it. The team is divided. Which type of ethical problem is this?

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: The near-miss. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being unable to do it. Here the right course is contested.

options.text: A legal problem requiring the risk management department
options.rationale: Legal input may follow, and the situation is first an ethical one about whose wishes govern.

options.text: A communication failure between the team and the family
options.rationale: Communication is involved and the conflict would remain even if everyone understood each other perfectly.

options.text: An ethical dilemma
options.rationale: A dilemma exists when there are competing legitimate claims and no option satisfies everyone. Both positions have an ethical basis.

questions.takeaway: An ethical dilemma has competing defensible options. Moral distress is knowing the right action and being prevented from taking it.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is moral distress. Ask whether the right course is unclear, or clear and blocked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the right action is known

steps.detail: That requires a known right action.

steps.action: Cut the legal and communication framings
steps.detail: Both would leave the conflict intact.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an ethical dilemma.

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly assigned to give treatments she believes are prolonging suffering in a dying patient. She has raised it twice and nothing has changed. She dreads her shifts. Which is she experiencing?

options.text: An ethical dilemma
options.rationale: A dilemma is uncertainty between two defensible options. She is not uncertain; she is blocked.

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: She knows what she believes is right and is constrained from acting on it. The repetition and the dread are characteristic.

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Exhaustion from prolonged exposure to suffering. Related, and it does not name the constraint she is describing.

options.text: Burnout from workload
options.rationale: Workload is not what she describes. The distress is about what she is being asked to do, not how much.

questions.takeaway: Moral distress is knowing the ethically right action and being unable to take it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which action is right.
questions.strategy: The pair worth separating is dilemma and distress. Uncertainty against constraint.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is clear about what she believes is right.

elimination.verdict: That leaves moral distress.

questions.stem: Place the steps of processing an ethical problem in the correct order.

options.text: Ask whether this is an ethical problem
options.rationale: First. Not every difficult situation is an ethical one, and some are clinical or communication problems.

options.text: Gather information relevant to the case
options.rationale: Gathering information is the second step, and it draws on the patient, the family, the agency and the wider social context.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine your own values
options.rationale: Third. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinions from values.

options.text: Name the problem in a clear, simple statement
options.rationale: Fourth. Difficult to do well, and it is what makes the final plan effective and the discussion possible.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Identifying possible courses of action is the fifth step. Ask others and be creative about what the options are.

options.text: Create and implement an action plan
options.rationale: Sixth. Gather support, and identify an alternative if the chosen action does not resolve it.

options.text: Evaluate the action plan
options.rationale: Seventh. Decide whether further action is needed, and what transfers to the next situation.

questions.takeaway: Seven steps: is it ethical, gather information, identify elements and examine values, name the problem, identify options, create and implement a plan, evaluate.
questions.strategy: The step people invert is naming the problem. It comes after examining values, not before, because your values shape how you name it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is this even an ethical problem?
A clear problem statement makes the options possible.

elimination.verdict: Ask, gather, identify, name, options, implement, evaluate.

questions.stem: A nurse working through an ethical problem has gathered information from the patient, the family and the agency. Which step comes next?

options.text: Name the problem in a clear statement
options.rationale: Step four, and it comes after the elements have been identified. Naming it first risks naming it wrongly.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Step five. Options generated before the problem is recognized tend to answer the wrong question.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine her own values
options.rationale: Step three. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinion from values.

options.text: Convene the ethics committee
options.rationale: Committees support the process rather than replacing its steps, and this stage is still hers to work through.

questions.takeaway: The seven steps run in order: ask, gather, identify elements and examine values, name, options, implement, evaluate.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are later steps in the same sequence. Ask what has to happen before you can name a problem accurately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Naming and options both come after.

elimination.verdict: That leaves identifying elements and examining values.

questions.stem: A nurse decides to report a near miss that harmed nobody, speaks up about an unsafe assignment, and declines to discuss a patient's diagnosis with a colleague not involved in the care. Which principles from the profession's code of ethics is she acting on? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.rationale: Confidentiality is recognized, and it sits underneath every decision about what gets documented and who gets told.

options.text: Advocacy
options.rationale: Advocacy is recognized, and it places the nurse between the patient and everyone else in the building.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility is recognized, and it concerns what the nurse is obliged to do in the first place.

options.text: Loyalty to the employing institution
options.rationale: The code binds the nurse to the patient. Institutional loyalty is not a principle of it, and it can conflict with advocacy.

options.text: Efficiency in the use of resources
options.rationale: This is a legitimate organizational value, but it is not among the code's key principles.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Accountability is recognized, and it concerns answering for what you did.

questions.takeaway: A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. Its key principles are advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.
questions.strategy: One distractor would put the institution where the patient belongs. That substitution is the reason advocacy is first on the list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse posts on social media that she had 'a rough shift with a difficult 40-year-old motorcycle crash patient' without naming anyone. Which problem does this create?

options.text: It should have been posted to a private group of nurses instead
options.rationale: A private audience is still an audience, and the information is still disclosed.

options.text: None, because no name or medical record number was used
options.rationale: Identifiability is not limited to names. This is the misunderstanding that produces most social media breaches.

options.text: It reflects poorly on the profession but breaches no principle
options.rationale: Professional image is a real concern, but the confidentiality breach is the specific problem here.

options.text: The detail may identify the patient
options.rationale: A specific age, mechanism and timeframe can identify someone in a small community. Removing the name does not anonymize a case.

questions.takeaway: Social media is a recognized contemporary ethical issue. Confidentiality is breached by identifiable detail, not only by names.
questions.strategy: One distractor states the exact reasoning that causes these breaches. Ask whether a reader could work out who this is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a reader could piece together

elimination.verdict: That leaves potential identification.

questions.stem: A nurse strongly disagrees with a competent patient's decision to decline dialysis. Which action reflects her professional obligation?

options.text: Ensure the information is complete, then support the decision
options.rationale: Autonomy means the competent patient decides. Her role is making sure the decision is informed, not making sure it is the one she would choose.

options.text: Arrange for the provider to explain the consequences again
options.rationale: Explaining again is reasonable once. After a settled decision it becomes pressure rather than information.

options.text: Document that the patient is refusing recommended treatment
options.rationale: Documenting is necessary, but it does nothing about whether the decision was informed in the first place.

options.text: Request a consultation from the ethics committee
options.rationale: Committees are for genuine dilemmas. A competent patient declining treatment is not one.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy governs when a competent patient has made an informed decision. The nurse's disagreement is not an ethical problem.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a settled competent decision as a dilemma. Ask whether anything here is contested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves informing and supporting.

questions.stem: A nurse says she thinks it is wrong to lie, and her colleague says the hospital policy requires honest disclosure of errors. Which distinction do these two statements illustrate?

options.text: Ethics are individual beliefs and morals are institutional rules
options.rationale: This reverses both terms. Morals are the personal beliefs; ethics are the shared professional standards.

options.text: Values are personal preferences and morals are professional duties
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship. Values are what a person holds important; morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong.

options.text: Morals are personal beliefs; ethics are shared professional standards
options.rationale: Her first belief is a moral position she holds. The policy expresses an ethical standard the profession and institution accept.

options.text: Both terms describe bioethics as applied to nursing practice
options.rationale: Bioethics concerns ethical questions arising in health care and the life sciences. Neither statement is specifically bioethical.

questions.takeaway: Morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong. Ethics are the standards a group or profession accepts. Values are what a person holds important.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap the two terms. Fix which one is personal before reading the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves morals personal, ethics shared.

questions.stem: A family and the team cannot agree about continuing treatment, and a nurse suggests involving the ethics committee. A colleague says that just hands the decision to someone else. Which statement describes the committee's role?

options.text: It provides a structured forum for discussion and recommendation
options.rationale: Committees support the resolution process, bringing perspectives together and helping the team work through the steps.

options.text: It determines whether the nurse acted within her legal scope
options.rationale: That is a regulatory and legal question. An ethics committee advises on the right thing to do, not on whether a license was breached.

options.text: It replaces the need to work through the ethical steps
options.rationale: The steps are how the case is prepared for and used in the discussion.

options.text: It makes the final decision when the team cannot agree
options.rationale: Committees advise. The decision remains with the patient, the surrogate and the treating team.

questions.takeaway: Ethics committees support the process of resolving ethical problems. They advise rather than decide.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes the committee the decision-maker. Ask who is left holding the decision afterwards.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the scope and replacement options
steps.detail: One is regulatory, one skips the work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a structured forum and recommendation.

questions.stem: At an ethics committee orientation, a nurse describes how to work through an ethical problem on the unit. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Naming the problem clearly makes the final plan more effective."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is stated directly. A clearly named problem produces a better plan.

options.text: "If I feel strongly enough about it, my personal beliefs should guide the plan."
options.rationale: Examining your values is step three, and examining them means recognizing their influence rather than letting them determine the outcome.

options.text: "If the first action does not resolve it, I should have an alternative identified."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Step six includes having an alternative ready if the first action does not resolve it.

options.text: "I should distinguish among facts, opinions and values when I look at the situation."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and separating facts from opinions and values is part of step three.

questions.takeaway: Examine your own values so you know what is influencing you. That is not the same as letting them decide the outcome.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the steps correctly. The fourth turns self-examination into justification.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Personal belief as the deciding factor.

elimination.verdict: That leaves personal beliefs guiding the plan.

questions.stem: A patient in skeletal traction develops pale, cold toes with reduced sensation. The nurse becomes occupied elsewhere and neither documents nor reports it. Two days later his leg requires amputation. Which term describes the nurse's conduct?

options.text: Negligence
options.rationale: Malpractice is a type of negligence. The distinction is that the person held liable is a professional, not that negligence stops applying.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm and include breaches such as confidentiality. This is a failure to meet a standard of care.

options.text: Malpractice
options.rationale: Conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent nurse, by someone acting in a professional role, causing harm.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Intentional torts require intent. Nothing suggests she meant to harm him; she got busy and failed to act.

questions.takeaway: Negligence is conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent person. Malpractice is negligence by a professional.
questions.strategy: One distractor says negligence does not apply to professionals. It does; malpractice is a subtype of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A licensed nurse in her professional role.
Malpractice is a type of negligence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves malpractice.

questions.stem: A nursing expert is asked to testify in a case about a patient harmed on a medical unit. Against what standard will the nurse's conduct be judged?

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do in similar circumstances
options.rationale: The standard of proof, almost word for word. It is not the best possible nurse and it is not this nurse's own opinion.

options.text: What the most experienced nurse on the unit would have done
options.rationale: The standard is reasonably prudent, not exemplary. Holding everyone to the best performer would make the standard unreachable.

options.text: What the hospital's policy manual required at the time
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard and does not define it. A policy can itself fall below the standard.

options.text: What the nurse believed was appropriate at the time
options.rationale: The standard is external to her. What she personally believed was appropriate does not set the bar she is measured against.

questions.takeaway: Standard of proof: what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the geographical area where the alleged breach occurred.
questions.strategy: Two distractors set the bar too high or too low. One substitutes policy for the standard itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same area.
One is evidence, one is internal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reasonably prudent nurse standard.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse assigns work among a registered nurse, a licensed vocational nurse, and a certified nursing assistant.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate the least qualified person who may appropriately perform it.

rows.text: Recording intake and output
rows.rationale: Among the tasks that may go to assistive personnel, alongside vital signs, ambulation, position changes, bathing and feeding.

rows.text: Initial admission assessment of a newly admitted patient
rows.rationale: Assessment belongs to the registered nurse. The licensed vocational nurse may perform secondary assessment and reinforcement.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the registered nurse has already provided to a stable patient
rows.rationale: The vocational nurse takes secondary and reinforcing roles: assessing, teaching and monitoring stable patients, and discharge.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met an outcome
