rows.rationale: Evaluation is a registered nurse function. Judging whether an outcome was met takes nursing judgment.

rows.text: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
rows.rationale: Walking a stable patient is recognized among the assistant's tasks, and stability is what makes it delegable.

rows.text: Caring for a patient whose condition is unstable
rows.rationale: An unstable patient is a registered nurse responsibility. Instability is what pulls the task back up the ladder.

questions.takeaway: RN: unstable patients, assessment, evaluation, teaching. LVN: secondary and reinforcing, stable patients, discharge. CNA: vitals, ambulation, positioning, bathing, eating, intake and output.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about teaching and assessment at different depths. First contact belongs to the registered nurse; reinforcement can go to the vocational nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is
Ask whether it is initial or reinforcing

elimination.verdict: Two CNA, one LVN, three RN.

questions.stem: A patient is scheduled for surgery in an hour and the nurse checks what he was told before he signed the consent form. Which elements must have been covered? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knowledge that he may refuse without losing other supportive care
options.rationale: It removes the fear that refusing one thing costs him everything else.

options.text: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting
options.rationale: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting are required, and this is the element most often skipped in practice.

options.text: A description of serious harm including death, and anticipated pain or discomfort
options.rationale: A description of serious harm is required, and it must include death where death is a real possibility.

options.text: An explanation of alternative therapies and the risks of doing nothing
options.rationale: Alternatives must be explained, and doing nothing is itself an alternative with its own consequences.

options.text: A guarantee that the procedure will achieve the intended result
options.rationale: No procedure can be guaranteed, and promising an outcome would invalidate rather than strengthen the consent.

options.text: The provider's personal success rate with the procedure
options.rationale: Patients often want it and it is not a required element. Required content is the procedure, the personnel, the risks, the alternatives, and the right to refuse.

options.text: An explanation of the procedure
options.rationale: An explanation of the procedure is the first element. He has to know what is being proposed.

questions.takeaway: Informed consent requires explanation of the procedure, who is performing it, serious harm including death, alternatives and the risks of doing nothing, the right to refuse without losing other care, and the right to withdraw even after the procedure has begun.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers a guarantee. Consent describes risk honestly; it never promises a result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Procedure, people, risks, alternatives, right to refuse.
He may refuse even after it has begun.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse stops at the scene of a road collision and provides care within her competence until paramedics arrive. Which law addresses her legal position?

options.text: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
options.rationale: EMTALA governs how hospitals must treat people presenting for emergency care. It does not apply at a roadside.

options.text: Good Samaritan laws
options.rationale: They protect a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act
options.rationale: The practice act defines her scope. Good Samaritan laws address liability for helping outside employment.

options.text: Her employer's malpractice insurance
options.rationale: Employer coverage applies to care given in the course of employment. She stopped at a roadside on her own time.

questions.takeaway: Good Samaritan laws limit liability and offer legal immunity to a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a real emergency statute that governs hospitals rather than roadsides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At a roadside, not at work.

steps.action: Cut the practice act and insurance
steps.detail: One is scope, one is employment coverage.

elimination.verdict: That leaves Good Samaritan laws.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the federal statutes affecting her practice.

The law requiring institutions to give patients written information about their right to refuse treatment and to formulate an advance directive is the [[1]].

The law giving patients rights over their health information and protecting employees is [[2]].

The law requiring insurers to cover mental health and substance use treatment is the [[3]].

The act prohibiting the purchase or sale of organs is the [[4]].

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: The Americans with Disabilities Act protects the rights of people with physical or mental disabilities.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: The Affordable Care Act concerns consumer protections, affordable coverage, access and quality.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires written information about the right to make decisions, refuse treatment, and formulate an advance directive such as a power of attorney or living will.

options.text: Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act
options.rationale: The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act changed the way health care is delivered to older adults.

options.text: EMTALA
options.rationale: EMTALA governs emergency treatment and active labor, not health information.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: HIPAA gives patients rights over their health information and protects employees as well.

options.text: HITECH
options.rationale: The near-miss. HITECH concerns health information technology and requires nurses to ensure protected health information is secured.

options.text: the Mental Health Parity Act
options.rationale: The Mental Health Parity Act concerns insurance coverage for mental health and substance use.

options.text: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
options.rationale: Requires insurers to provide coverage for mental health and substance use disorder treatment.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: The Americans with Disabilities Act concerns discrimination and access rather than insurance coverage.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: HIPAA concerns health information, not what an insurer has to cover.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: The Affordable Care Act is broader coverage and access legislation, not parity specifically.

options.text: Uniform Determination of Death Act
options.rationale: Determines actual death, cardiopulmonary or irreversible cessation of the entire brain and brain stem.

options.text: Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
options.rationale: The near-miss. It provides the foundation for the national organ donation system; the Transplant Act is what prohibits sale.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: The Patient Self-Determination Act concerns advance directives and the right to refuse treatment.

options.text: National Organ Transplant Act
options.rationale: The National Organ Transplant Act prohibits buying or selling organs.

questions.takeaway: Self-Determination is advance directives. HIPAA is information rights. Parity is insurance coverage. Anatomical Gift builds the donation system; Transplant Act prohibits sale.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: HIPAA against HITECH, and the two organ acts. One builds the system, the other prohibits the market.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Self-Determination, HIPAA, Parity, Transplant Act.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication and the vial does not look like the one she usually uses. She is behind on her round. Which action reflects the lessons drawn from the RaDonda Vaught case?

options.text: Give it and document that the appearance was unfamiliar
options.rationale: Documenting a concern is not resolving it, and the patient receives the drug either way.

options.text: Stop, verify with a drug guide or the pharmacist before proceeding
options.rationale: Pause and verify when something does not look right, particularly with high-alert medications, and use resources when in doubt.

options.text: Proceed, since she selected it from the automated cabinet under the correct name
options.rationale: An override and a confirmation error were central to that case. The cabinet is not the verification.

options.text: Ask another nurse to check it while she moves to her next patient
options.rationale: The check belongs to the person giving it. Delegating the verification does not transfer the accountability.

questions.takeaway: Follow all the rights, pause and verify when something looks wrong, use resources, avoid workarounds, and report system failures.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats the automated cabinet as the verification step. That was central to what went wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An override and confirmation error caused the harm.

steps.action: Cut delegating the check and documenting
steps.detail: Neither resolves the doubt before administration.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping to verify.

questions.stem: In a hospital lift where visitors can hear, a nurse discusses a patient's diagnosis. She intended no harm. Which category does this fall into?

options.text: An unintentional tort
options.rationale: The near-miss. Unintentional torts arise when someone is harmed and the person knew or should have known their actions fell below the standard of practice, which describes negligence.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent to cause the harm. She intended to speak, not to harm.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: A quasi-intentional tort is harm caused without intending it, and breach of confidentiality is the classic example.

options.text: A criminal offense under state law
options.rationale: Torts are civil wrongs. Criminal law covers felonies and misdemeanors, which this is not.

questions.takeaway: Torts are civil wrongful acts or omissions. Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known their conduct fell below the standard.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is unintentional tort. Both involve no intent, and they differ in whether a standard of care was breached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One needs intent, one is a different body of law.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a quasi-intentional tort.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to reduce her personal legal risk. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Developing and using clinical judgment to identify patient needs
options.rationale: Sound clinical decisions are what keep practice above the standard.

options.text: Remaining aware of current issues in health care
options.rationale: Staying current is recognized, and standards move. What was defensible five years ago may not be now.

options.text: Documenting thoroughly and accurately
options.rationale: One of the lessons drawn from the Vaught case, and an undocumented action is difficult to defend.

options.text: Carrying personal malpractice insurance instead of relying on the employer's
options.rationale: Insurance covers the cost of a claim. It reduces financial exposure rather than legal risk, and the question asks about the risk itself.

options.text: Declining any assignment outside the nurse's comfort level
options.rationale: Competence is the standard, not comfort. A nurse who is competent but uncomfortable still owes the care, and one who is comfortable but not competent is the actual exposure.

options.text: Becoming involved in professional organizations and committees that define standards
options.rationale: It means she helps set the standard she is judged against.

options.text: Participating in risk management and quality improvement programs
options.rationale: Risk management and quality improvement are recognized, and they find hazards before anyone is harmed by them.

questions.takeaway: Reducing legal risk: clinical judgment, awareness of current issues, professional involvement, risk management and quality improvement, and thorough documentation.
questions.strategy: One distractor reduces what a claim costs rather than the chance of one. Read what the question asks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: At the end of her scheduled hours, with no replacement yet on the unit, a nurse leaves without notifying anyone. Which does this represent?

options.text: Patient abandonment
options.rationale: One of the workforce guidelines. Leaving a scheduled shift without transferring care to someone qualified is abandonment.

options.text: None
options.rationale: The end of her hours does not end her responsibility until care has been transferred.

options.text: A staffing ratio violation by the employer
options.rationale: The ratio problem is real and it belongs to the employer. Her own exposure comes from how she left.

options.text: A breach of her nurse practice act's scope provisions
options.rationale: Scope concerns what she is permitted to do, not how she ends a shift. Leaving without handover is a different problem.

questions.takeaway: Nursing workforce guidelines cover staffing and ratios, assignments, patient abandonment, delegation, and nursing students.
questions.strategy: One distractor points at a genuine employer failing. The question asks what this raises for her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the ratio and scope options
steps.detail: One is the employer's, one is unrelated.

elimination.verdict: That leaves patient abandonment.

questions.stem: At the annual risk management in-service, a nurse summarizes what creates legal exposure in practice. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Malpractice is a type of negligence, and the person held liable must be a professional."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the definition. Malpractice is negligence committed by someone acting as a professional.

options.text: "Risk management programs reduce legal risk by finding hazards before harm occurs."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Risk management reduces exposure by finding hazards before anyone is harmed by them.

options.text: "A nursing expert will testify about the standard of care as applied to the facts."
options.rationale: This is accurate. A nurse expert testifies about the standard of care as it applies to these particular facts.

options.text: "If I follow hospital policy exactly, I cannot be found negligent."
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard, not the standard itself. A policy can fall below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.

questions.takeaway: Policy is evidence of the standard of care, not a defense in itself. The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth treats policy compliance as complete protection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the policy statement.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews four documentation formats used across the organization.
questions.stem: For each note component, indicate which documentation format it belongs to.

rows.text: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
rows.rationale: Four components, and it is the only format separating subjective from objective explicitly.

rows.text: Problem, Intervention, Evaluation
rows.rationale: Problem, intervention, evaluation. The note is organized around the nursing problem rather than the patient's words.

rows.text: Data, Action, Response
rows.rationale: Data, action, response. Focus charting opens with what you found and ends with how the patient responded.

rows.text: Begins with the nursing diagnosis rather than the patient's words
rows.rationale: The P is the nursing problem, which is what makes it a nursing-focused format.

rows.text: Separates what the patient reports from what the nurse measures
rows.rationale: The S and the O are that split.

rows.text: Ends with how the patient responded to the intervention
rows.rationale: The R. PIE ends with the nurse's evaluation; DAR ends with the patient's response.

questions.takeaway: PIE: problem, intervention, evaluation. DAR: data, action, response. SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan.
questions.strategy: PIE and DAR both end with a verdict, and they differ in whose. PIE ends with the nurse's evaluation; DAR ends with the patient's response.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the subjective and objective split

elimination.verdict: SOAP, PIE, DAR, PIE, SOAP, DAR.

questions.stem: A chart audit finds entries on the unit that are vague, written hours late, and full of unapproved abbreviations. Which characteristics should those entries have had? Select all that apply.

options.text: Detailed enough to argue why each decision was made
options.rationale: Slides from recording into arguing. The entry states what was observed and done, and the reasoning belongs in the care plan rather than as justification inside the note.

options.text: Appropriate use of abbreviations
options.rationale: Using only approved abbreviations is a recognized guideline, and unapproved ones are a recognized source of medication error.

options.text: Accurate
options.rationale: Accurate is a recognized guideline, and it means exact measurements rather than words like moderate or a small amount.

options.text: Current
options.rationale: Entries made long after the event lose reliability and may be questioned.

options.text: Factual
options.rationale: Factual is a recognized guideline. Record what you observed and what you did, not what you assumed was going on.

options.text: Persuasive in explaining the nurse's reasoning
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. An entry written to justify rather than to record undermines its value as a legal record.

options.text: Organized
options.rationale: A reader must be able to follow the sequence of events.

questions.takeaway: Quality documentation is factual, accurate, uses appropriate abbreviations, and is current, organized and complete.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a record into an argument. Ask what the entry is for.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factual, accurate, abbreviations, current, organized, complete.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient transfers from a clinic to a hospital. The clinic's system holds only that practice's visits, while the hospital's follows him across every facility in the network. Which distinction does this illustrate?

options.text: An electronic medical record versus an electronic health record
options.rationale: Span is the whole distinction. The medical record covers care within one practice or episode, and the health record follows the patient across facilities over a lifetime.

options.text: A paper record converted into an electronic format
options.rationale: Both of these systems are already electronic. Format is not what separates them.

options.text: A personal health record maintained by the patient
options.rationale: A personal health record is one the patient keeps and controls. Neither system in the stem is that.

options.text: A clinical data warehouse used for quality reporting
options.rationale: A data warehouse aggregates information for reporting and analysis. Neither record described is doing that.

questions.takeaway: The electronic health record is an individual's lifetime computerized record. The electronic medical record is the record for an individual health care visit.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes the difference a matter of who uses it. Ask what each one covers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the paper and interchangeable options

elimination.verdict: That leaves lifetime against single visit.

questions.stem: A provider gives a telephone order for a new analgesic. Which action comes first?

options.text: Read the order back to the provider for verification
options.rationale: Reading it back is the essential second step, and you cannot do it accurately from memory. Write it down first.

options.text: Write the order down as it is given
options.rationale: Writing it first is what makes read-back possible. Memory is where telephone orders go wrong.

options.text: Record that it was received as a telephone order
options.rationale: Labelling it as a telephone order is necessary, and it comes after the order has been written and read back.

options.text: Administer the medication and document it afterwards
options.rationale: This gives the drug before anyone has verified the order. That sequence is what produces the error.

questions.takeaway: Telephone orders: write it down, read it back, record it as a telephone order, administer, and obtain the countersignature within the required window.
questions.strategy: Three options are genuine steps in the sequence. Ask which one has to happen before read-back is possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves writing it down.

questions.stem: On a unit that uses charting by exception, a nurse transferring in finds far fewer entries in each record than she is used to. Which statement about this format is accurate?

options.text: Documentation is completed only when a patient's condition changes
options.rationale: This is close, and it leaves out that the comparison is against a defined norm rather than against the patient's own earlier state.

options.text: Only the most significant findings of the shift are recorded
options.rationale: Significance is a judgment. Charting by exception rests on defined standards rather than on what struck the nurse as important.

options.text: Only findings that deviate from a defined norm are documented
options.rationale: Its efficiency comes from the unit having agreed norms. Anything not recorded is understood to be within them.

options.text: Narrative entries replace flow sheets in this method
options.rationale: Flow sheets are central to it. They record the routine so the notes can record the exceptions.

questions.takeaway: Charting by exception documents findings that deviate from a defined norm. It depends on the norms being explicit and agreed.
questions.strategy: One distractor substitutes the nurse's judgment of significance for a defined standard. That difference is the whole method.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the comparison is against
Cut the change-only and narrative options
steps.detail: One omits the norm, one reverses the tools.

elimination.verdict: That leaves deviation from a defined norm.

questions.stem: Which purposes does the health care record legitimately serve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recording a nurse's concerns about unit staffing levels
options.rationale: A legitimate concern that belongs in an occurrence report or a conversation with the manager, not in a patient's record.

options.text: Facilitating communication among the interprofessional team
options.rationale: Communication is recognized first. The record is how everyone else follows the clinical course without asking you.

options.text: Providing a record the patient is not entitled to read
options.rationale: Factually wrong. Patients have a right of access, and nothing should be written on the assumption that they will not see it.

options.text: Supporting quality and performance improvement
options.rationale: Quality and performance improvement is a recognized purpose, and auditing depends entirely on what was written.

options.text: Providing a legal record of the care given
options.rationale: The legal record is a recognized purpose, and it is the reason the quality guidelines exist at all.

options.text: Justifying billing and reimbursement
options.rationale: Billing is a recognized purpose, and diagnosis-related groups draw directly on what was documented.

options.text: Serving as a resource for education and research
options.rationale: Education and research is the fifth purpose. The record outlives the admission.

questions.takeaway: Five purposes: interprofessional communication, legal record, billing justification, quality improvement, and education and research.
questions.strategy: One distractor puts a workplace concern into a patient's record. Ask whose record it is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: B, D, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient falls while being assisted to the bathroom. The nurse completes an occurrence report. Which statement about that report is accurate?

options.text: A copy should be filed in the patient's medical record
options.rationale: The occurrence report is kept separate from the chart. Filing it in the record defeats the purpose of having it.

options.text: It replaces the need to document the fall in the patient's record
options.rationale: The fall, the assessment and the response all belong in the record. The report is additional.

options.text: The record should state that an occurrence report was completed
options.rationale: The fall and the assessment are documented in the record. That a report was filed is not.

options.text: It is an internal risk management document, not part of the record
options.rationale: Keeping it separate is what allows staff to describe system failures honestly without that account becoming part of the chart.

questions.takeaway: Occurrence reports are internal risk management documents. They are kept separate from the medical record, and the event itself is still documented in the record.
questions.strategy: Two distractors connect the report to the chart in some way. The separation is the point of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the report is for
Cut filing it in the chart

steps.detail: One references it, one replaces documentation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an internal document kept separate.

questions.stem: A charge nurse is told to staff the unit by acuity rather than by the number of patients. Which does the acuity rating system measure?

options.text: The number and type of nursing interventions required daily
options.rationale: The definition. It drives the hours of care and the number of staff needed for a group of patients.

options.text: The patient's risk of clinical deterioration overnight
options.rationale: Early warning scores predict deterioration. Acuity measures the nursing work a patient generates.

options.text: The severity of the patient's primary medical diagnosis
options.rationale: Medical severity and nursing workload are related and not the same. A medically stable patient can require intensive nursing.

options.text: The expected length of the patient's hospital admission
options.rationale: Length of stay is predicted by other measures. Acuity is about how much nursing care is needed per day.

questions.takeaway: An acuity rating system determines hours of care and staffing needed, based on the type and number of nursing interventions a patient requires over 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Three distractors measure something about the patient's condition. Acuity measures the work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what it is used for
Cut deterioration risk and length of stay

elimination.verdict: That leaves nursing interventions required.

questions.stem: In home health care, which data sets are used to document an assessment?

options.text: The Joint Commission and CMS standards
options.rationale: These are regulatory bodies that govern documentation. They are not data sets.

options.text: OASIS and the Omaha system
options.rationale: These are the two data sets used to document clinical assessment and care in home health.

options.text: Diagnosis-related groups and core measures
options.rationale: Diagnosis-related groups classify for reimbursement and core measures are clinical standards. Neither is a home health data set.

options.text: Flow sheets and charting by exception
options.rationale: These are documentation methods used across every setting rather than data sets specific to home health.

questions.takeaway: Home health uses two data sets: OASIS and the Omaha system. Documentation there is both quality control and the justification for reimbursement.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real things from the same chapter that are not data sets.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a data set is
steps.detail: A structured format for recording assessment.
Neither is a home health data set.

elimination.verdict: That leaves OASIS and the Omaha system.

questions.stem: A chart audit team reviews how nurses on the unit document their care. Which practice described by a nurse needs correcting?

options.text: "Findings within the defined norm are not separately recorded on this unit."
options.rationale: This is accurate for charting by exception, which is what her unit uses. Only deviations from the norm get written.

options.text: "I document what I observed and what I did, not what I assumed."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Factual is the first guideline: what you saw and what you did, not what you inferred.

options.text: “If I am busy, I can chart the whole shift at the end.”
options.rationale: Documentation must be current. Charting hours later loses accuracy and creates a record that is difficult to defend.

options.text: “I use only the abbreviations this organization has approved.”
options.rationale: This is accurate. Using only the organization's approved abbreviations is a recognized guideline.

questions.takeaway: Current is one of the six documentation guidelines. Charting at the end of a shift risks both accuracy and credibility.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the guidelines correctly. The fourth trades one guideline for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factual, accurate, abbreviations, current, organized, complete.

elimination.verdict: That leaves charting the whole shift at the end.

questions.nursesNote: 1120: Nurse reviews an entry made by a colleague earlier in the shift. Entry reads: 'Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery. Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much. Family member was rude to staff. Gave pain medication PRN. Will continue to monitor. BP 118/72, HR 84. Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1. Dressing dry and intact.'
questions.stem: Highlight the parts of this entry that do not meet the guidelines for quality documentation.

segments.rationale: Measured values recorded as measured. This is factual and accurate, which is what the guidelines ask for.

segments.text: Dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: An observed finding stated plainly. Nothing is inferred and nothing is vague.

segments.text: Will continue to monitor
segments.rationale: This commits to nothing measurable and records no action taken. It fills space without documenting care.

segments.text: Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1
segments.rationale: Factual, specific about the level of assistance, and useful to the next nurse.

segments.text: Family member was rude to staff
segments.rationale: A judgment about a person rather than a record of what occurred, and it has no place in a patient's record.

segments.text: Gave pain medication PRN
segments.rationale: Not accurate or complete. No drug, dose, route, time, or response to it.

segments.text: Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much
segments.rationale: Appeared is an impression, and refused characterizes him. Record the observed behavior and his actual words.

segments.text: Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery
segments.rationale: Not factual. Seemed and probably are the nurse's inference. Record what he said or what she observed.

questions.takeaway: Factual means observed and done, not inferred. Accurate and complete means the drug, dose, route, time and response.
questions.strategy: Three parts of this entry are exactly right, which is what makes the rest visible. Watch for seemed, probably, appeared, and judgments about people.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No drug, dose, route or response.

elimination.verdict: s3, s5, s6, s7, and s8: empty commitment, inference, incomplete medication, impression, and judgment.

questions.stem: A team disagrees about continuing tube feedings for a patient with advanced dementia and no advance directive. The group has gathered information from the patient's family and the record, and has clarified the values and ethical principles each position rests on. In the ethical decision-making process, which step comes next?

options.text: State the problem in a clear, simple sentence
options.rationale: Naming it comes before solving it. A group that skips this argues past each other, because each member is solving a slightly different problem.

options.text: Identify every possible course of action available
options.rationale: The common skip. Generating options before the problem is recognized produces solutions to different questions.

options.text: Create an action plan and gather support for it
options.rationale: This is two steps early. Nothing has been named clearly and no option has been chosen yet.

options.text: Evaluate whether any further action will be needed
options.rationale: This is the last step, and it judges a plan that does not exist yet.

questions.takeaway: Gather information, clarify the values involved, then name the problem in one sentence before anyone proposes a course of action.
questions.strategy: The step everyone drops is naming the problem. When a question puts it among the options, that is usually why.

strategies: Place the group in the sequence

steps.detail: Options, plan, and evaluation all come after.

elimination.verdict: State the problem.

questions.stem: An hour after charting, a nurse realizes she entered an entire assessment on the wrong patient's paper record. Which action meets the legal guidelines for documentation?

options.text: Obliterate the entry so it cannot be misread later
options.rationale: This looks tidy and comes across as concealment. An unreadable entry in a legal record is worse than a visible correction.

options.text: Draw one line through it, label it, and initial
options.rationale: The entry stays legible, the correction is attributable, and the record shows what happened and who fixed it. That is what a court looks for.

options.text: Ask the charge nurse to remove the page entirely
options.rationale: Removing a page destroys part of the legal record, and involving someone else does not make it permissible.

options.text: Leave the entry and chart a correct note elsewhere
options.rationale: Leaves a false assessment standing in a patient's chart, where the next clinician will act on it.

questions.takeaway: Never erase, white out, or destroy. One line through, a label such as mistaken entry, your initials and the date, and the original stays readable.
questions.strategy: Anything that makes the original unreadable or removes it is wrong, however reasonable the motive sounds.

strategies: Protect the record first

steps.detail: A false entry stays in force.

elimination.verdict: One line, labeled and initialed.

questions.stem: A patient is going home after treatment for cellulitis of her lower leg. Which entry in the discharge documentation best demonstrates that teaching was effective?

options.text: Written and verbal instructions were given to the patient
options.rationale: Documents what the nurse did. It says nothing about what the patient took away.

options.text: The patient verbalized understanding of the discharge instructions
options.rationale: The most-charted phrase in nursing and the weakest. It records agreement, not comprehension, and will not hold up if the patient returns septic.

options.text: The patient described when to call about spreading redness
options.rationale: The patient produced the content back. That is evidence of learning, and it is specific enough that a reader knows exactly what the patient can do.

options.text: Discharge teaching was completed before the patient left
options.rationale: This records a task closed. Completing teaching is not the same as the patient being able to do anything with it.

questions.takeaway: Document what the patient demonstrated, not what you delivered. Verbalized understanding is a task record wearing an outcome's clothes.
questions.strategy: Three options describe nursing activity. Only one describes the patient doing something.

strategies: Ask who is the subject of the sentence

steps.action: Cut entries whose subject is the nurse
Keep the entry showing patient performance

elimination.verdict: The patient described when to call.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a telephone order from a provider to change a medication dose. Which action most directly prevents a transcription error?

options.text: Read the order back and record the provider's name
options.rationale: The read-back catches the error while the provider is still on the line, which is the only moment it can be corrected by the person who gave it.

options.text: Enter the order and ask a second nurse to verify it
options.rationale: A second nurse can confirm what was written and cannot confirm what was said.

options.text: Record it and chart it clearly as a verbal order
options.rationale: Labelling it correctly matters and it happens after the risk has passed. Documentation does not catch a dose you misheard.

options.text: Write the order and have the provider sign it later
options.rationale: Required by policy and too late to help. A countersignature days later ratifies whatever was written down.

questions.takeaway: Read-back is the step that catches the error. Labeling and countersigning are required and neither protects the patient at the moment of risk.
questions.strategy: Several options are things you must do. Only one of them happens before the error can reach the patient.

strategies: Find the step that acts in time

steps.detail: Only read-back is during the call.

steps.action: Keep read-back with the name recorded

elimination.verdict: Read back and record the name.

questions.stem: Using the record's copy-forward function, a new graduate carries yesterday's assessment into today's note and edits the fields that changed. Which risk does this create?

options.text: The entry will not be time-stamped by the system
options.rationale: Systems time-stamp every entry automatically. The time will be right; the content will not.

options.text: Findings will no longer reflect today's actual assessment
options.rationale: Anything she did not notice to change now stands as a finding assessed today. The chart claims an examination that did not happen, and the next clinician cannot tell which lines are real.

options.text: Other disciplines will lose access to the note
options.rationale: Access is unchanged. Everyone can read it, which is part of the problem.

options.text: Billing will be generated at a lower level of service
options.rationale: If anything, cloned notes inflate documented care. Reimbursement is not the patient-safety risk here.

questions.takeaway: Copy-forward carries yesterday's findings in as today's. The record stops being a record of what was assessed and becomes a record of what was not corrected.
questions.strategy: Three options describe system behavior. The risk in a documentation question is almost always what the next reader will believe.

strategies: Ask what the next clinician will act on

steps.detail: Time stamps and access are unaffected.

steps.action: Name what the note now asserts

elimination.verdict: The findings no longer reflect today.

questions.stem: A new graduate is oriented to the electronic health record and asks which informatics competencies the role actually requires. Which expectations belong to a new graduate nurse rather than to an informatics specialist? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enter and retrieve patient data accurately in the record
options.rationale: The floor of the competency. Data the nurse enters becomes the data every other discipline reasons from, and a wrong field is a wrong decision later.

options.text: Use clinical decision support without deferring to it blindly
options.rationale: Alerts and scores support judgment. A competent new graduate weighs the prompt against the patient in front of them and documents the reasoning when the two disagree.

options.text: Audit colleagues' records for documentation compliance
options.rationale: A quality or compliance function. Reviewing peers' charts without that role is both outside scope and a privacy problem.

options.text: Configure the record's alert thresholds for the unit
options.rationale: System configuration belongs to informatics and IT. A nurse who changes thresholds is outside the role.

options.text: Build the unit's documentation templates and flow sheets
options.rationale: This is design work. Nurses give input on templates, and building them belongs to the informatics specialist.

options.text: Protect patient information and use access credentials correctly
options.rationale: Confidentiality is a practice competency, not a technical one. Sharing a password or leaving a session open is a nursing failure regardless of who built the system.

questions.takeaway: A new graduate's informatics competencies are about using the record safely: accurate entry, protected access, and decision support that informs judgment instead of replacing it. Configuring, designing, and auditing the system are different roles.
questions.strategy: Three options describe things done to the system and three describe things done with it. The new graduate works with it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Sort by whose role it is

steps.detail: Configuration, design, and audit are specialist roles.
A nursing obligation, not an IT one.

steps.action: Keep decision support with judgment intact
steps.detail: Weigh the alert against the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery in thirty minutes has a signed consent form in his record and tells the nurse, I am still not sure what they are actually going to do. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Explain the procedure to the patient in plain language
options.rationale: Kind and outside the nurse's scope for this purpose. The nurse reinforces and clarifies; the prescriber discloses. Filling the gap here produces a consent nobody obtained.

options.text: Notify the surgeon that informed consent is not established
options.rationale: A signature on a form is not consent. The patient does not understand the procedure, which means the disclosure failed, and only the person performing it can repair that.

options.text: Document that the patient expressed uncertainty
options.rationale: Charting the problem instead of stopping it. The patient still goes to the operating room.

options.text: Cancel the procedure and arrange a new date
options.rationale: Not the nurse's decision to make. Halting the process until consent is valid is, and that is done by notifying the surgeon.

questions.takeaway: Consent is understanding, not a signature. When the patient cannot say what the procedure is, the nurse stops the process and returns it to the prescriber.
questions.strategy: The tempting option is the helpful one. Ask who is permitted to perform the disclosure.

strategies: Scope of practice
Stop the line

steps.action: Separate the signature from the understanding

steps.detail: Each is outside the role or too passive.

elimination.verdict: Notify the surgeon.

questions.stem: During a chart audit, a nurse finds that a colleague has charted complete head-to-toe assessments on three patients the colleague has not entered the rooms to see. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Report the practice through the chain of command
options.rationale: It must be reported, and reporting does not change the fact that three patients are currently unassessed.

options.text: Speak with the colleague privately and ask them to stop
options.rationale: Addresses the behavior and leaves the patients in the same position. It also puts the nurse between the problem and its resolution.

options.text: Assess the three patients, who have not been assessed
options.rationale: The documentation is false, so the assessments did not happen. Three patients have gone a shift without anyone laying eyes on them, and one of them may be deteriorating right now.

options.text: Complete an incident report describing the entries
options.rationale: This is the record of what happened, and it comes after the three patients have been looked at.

questions.takeaway: Falsified documentation is first a patient-safety problem and second a professional one. Find out how the patients are, then report.
questions.strategy: Three options act on the colleague or the paperwork. The question is who is currently at risk.

strategies: Patient before process

steps.action: Ask what the false entries mean
Cut reporting and the incident report
steps.detail: Both are necessary and neither is first.
It helps nobody in a bed.

elimination.verdict: Assess the three patients.

questions.stem: A nurse has twice raised with the team that continued treatment is prolonging a dying patient's suffering against his valid advance directive. Nothing has changed and she is assigned to him again tonight. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Request an ethics committee consultation
options.rationale: The informal route has been tried twice and failed. The committee exists for exactly this: a structured forum where the directive, the family and the team can be worked through.

options.text: Refuse the assignment on the grounds of conscience
options.rationale: Conscientious objection has a place and it abandons this patient tonight without resolving anything for the next shift.

options.text: Tell the family the team is acting against the patient's wishes
options.rationale: Going to the family outside the team escalates a conflict rather than resolving it, and it puts the nurse between the family and the providers.

options.text: Document her objection in the record and carry out the treatment
options.rationale: Documenting an objection protects the nurse and changes nothing for the patient.

questions.takeaway: When the informal route has failed, the ethics committee is the next step. It is a forum, not a tribunal, and asking for one is within any nurse's role.
questions.strategy: Three options are things nurses do when they feel unheard. Ask which one moves the patient's situation rather than the nurse's position in it.

strategies: Ask what has already been tried

steps.action: Raising it with the team, twice

elimination.verdict: That leaves the ethics consultation.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a medication to the wrong patient. He is unharmed. She tells the charge nurse, completes an occurrence report, and documents the administration and the patient's condition in the record. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The occurrence report should be referenced in the patient's record
options.rationale: The record should not state that a report was completed, because the report is a separate internal document.

options.text: A copy of the occurrence report belongs in the patient's record
options.rationale: It is not part of the record and filing it there makes it discoverable.

options.text: No occurrence report is needed
options.rationale: A near miss is reported precisely because it reached the patient without harming him.

options.text: Her documentation is correct
options.rationale: The record holds what was given and how the patient is. The occurrence report is an internal risk management document.

questions.takeaway: The clinical facts go in the record. The occurrence report is internal risk management and is never referenced in the chart.
questions.strategy: Three distractors link the report to the record in some way. The relationship is that there is none.

strategies: Separate the two documents

steps.detail: What was given, how the patient is.
Internal, never in the chart, never referenced.

steps.action: Cut every option that connects them

elimination.verdict: That leaves her documentation being correct.

questions.stem: A confused patient repeatedly tries to climb out of bed. A nurse applies wrist restraints and plans to call the provider for an order after the shift settles. Which legal risk has she created?

options.text: Negligence
options.rationale: Negligence is a failure to act reasonably. Restraining someone is an act, and an intentional one.

options.text: False imprisonment
options.rationale: Restricting a person's movement without consent or a lawful order is false imprisonment, whatever the intention behind it.

options.text: Battery
options.rationale: Battery is harmful or offensive contact. The confinement, rather than the contact, is what the law reaches here.

options.text: Breach of confidentiality
options.rationale: Confidentiality concerns information, not movement.

questions.takeaway: Restraints need an order and the least restrictive alternative tried first. Restraint without authority is false imprisonment, and good intentions do not change that.
questions.strategy: The urge is to call it negligence because she meant well. Intentional torts are judged by the act, not the motive.

strategies: Ask what the patient lost

steps.detail: This was an act, not an omission.

elimination.verdict: That leaves false imprisonment.

questions.stem: A patient admitted with advanced dementia cannot explain or recall the proposed procedure. His daughter holds an activated durable power of attorney for health care. Who gives consent?

options.text: The patient
options.rationale: Consent requires the capacity to understand this decision, and a formal declaration is not what creates or removes that.

options.text: The provider
options.rationale: A provider does not consent on a patient's behalf outside an emergency.

options.text: Two physicians
options.rationale: Two-physician provisions apply when there is no surrogate, and here there is one.

options.text: The daughter
options.rationale: An activated durable power of attorney for health care names the person who decides when the patient cannot.

questions.takeaway: Capacity is decision-specific. When the patient cannot understand this decision, the person named in an activated durable power of attorney consents.
questions.strategy: One distractor trades on the idea that only a court can remove capacity. Capacity is clinical, competence is legal, and the two are not the same test.

strategies: Ask who can understand this decision

steps.action: Cut the provider and the two-physician route
steps.detail: Both are for when no surrogate exists.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the daughter.

questions.stem: At 2300 a nurse realizes she never documented a dressing change she performed at 1500. Which action is correct?

options.text: Insert the entry in the space left after the 1500 note so the record reads in order
options.rationale: Writing into earlier space is a falsified sequence, whatever the content says.

options.text: Document it now as a late entry, with the time of writing and the time the care was given
options.rationale: A late entry is written at the current time, labeled, and states when the care occurred.

options.text: Leave it undocumented, since the care was given and the patient is fine
options.rationale: Care not documented cannot be shown to have happened.

options.text: Ask the oncoming nurse to chart it at the start of her shift
options.rationale: Nobody documents care they did not perform.

questions.takeaway: A late entry is labeled, written at the time you write it, and names the time the care was given. Nothing is squeezed into earlier space.
questions.strategy: Filling the space after the earlier note looks tidy, and that is the problem: a record that reads in order when it was not written in order is falsified.

strategies: Ask what the record must show

steps.action: When it was written and when it happened

elimination.verdict: That leaves the labeled late entry.

questions.stem: On nights, a nurse discovers that an entry she carried forward with the copy-forward function describes a wound that was debrided yesterday. Which problem has this created?

options.text: A minor charting inefficiency that can be corrected at the end of the shift
options.rationale: The chart currently asserts an assessment that did not happen, which is not minor.

options.text: A breach of confidentiality, since yesterday's note was reused
options.rationale: Reusing one's own entry on the same patient discloses nothing.

options.text: No problem, provided the wound is reassessed before the end of the shift
options.rationale: The false entry exists now and later assessment does not retract it.

options.text: A false record that the wound was assessed and found unchanged today
options.rationale: Carried-forward text reads as a finding from today, so the chart claims an assessment nobody performed.

questions.takeaway: Copy-forward turns yesterday's findings into today's assertions. Anything not changed reads as assessed today.
questions.strategy: The option that promises a later fix is the most tempting. Ask what the chart asserts in the meantime.

strategies: Ask what the chart currently claims

steps.action: Cut the minor and the no problem options

elimination.verdict: That leaves the false record.

questions.stem: A nurse posts in a private online group for nurses that she looked after a 34-year-old motorcyclist from a crash on the bypass last Tuesday. She uses no name and no record number. Which element makes this a breach of confidentiality?

options.text: The combination of age, mechanism, location and date
options.rationale: Identifiability comes from details in combination, and these four identify one person in a small area.

options.text: The absence of the patient's written consent to be discussed
options.rationale: Consent would not make the post appropriate, and the breach does not turn on a missing form.

options.text: The size of the group she posted to
options.rationale: A private audience is still an audience, and the number of members does not decide it.

options.text: Nothing, since no name or record number appeared
options.rationale: Removing the name does not anonymize a case that the remaining details identify.

questions.takeaway: Identifiability comes from the combination. Removing the name does not anonymize a case, and a private audience is still a disclosure.
questions.strategy: The post contains no identifier in the usual sense, which is what makes the option saying no breach occurred tempting. Read the four details together.

strategies: Ask whether the patient could be picked out
elimination.verdict: That leaves the combination of details.

questions.stem: A nurse works through an ethical problem on her unit. Which steps belong to the process? Select all that apply.

options.text: Asking whether this is actually an ethical problem
options.rationale: Step one, and it is skipped more often than any other.

options.text: Gathering information from the patient, family and agency
options.rationale: Step two, and those three perspectives are the relevant sources.

options.text: Distinguishing among facts, opinions and values
options.rationale: Step three, clarifying values and recognizing the principles involved.

options.text: Stating the problem in a clear simple sentence
options.rationale: Step four, and a clear statement is what makes the later discussion possible.

options.text: Determining whether anyone acted outside their legal scope
options.rationale: That is a legal question and it belongs to risk management rather than the ethical process.

options.text: Evaluating the action plan afterwards
options.rationale: Step seven closes the loop and decides whether more is needed.

options.text: Identifying who should be held responsible for the situation
options.rationale: Assigning blame is not one of the steps and it works against the discussion the process requires.

questions.takeaway: Seven steps: is it ethical, gather information, identify elements and examine values, name the problem, identify courses of action, create and implement a plan, evaluate.
questions.strategy: Both distractors sound like accountability. The ethical process is about deciding what to do, not who was at fault.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: None assigns blame or tests legality.

elimination.verdict: The five steps are selected.

questions.stem: A newly admitted patient asks about advance directives. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A living will states what treatment he would want if he could not speak for himself
options.rationale: It records the wishes rather than naming a person.

options.text: A durable power of attorney for health care names a person to decide on his behalf
options.rationale: It names the decision maker, which is a different document from the living will.

options.text: He may change or revoke a directive at any time while he has capacity
options.rationale: Directives are revocable, and that right stands as long as capacity does.

options.text: A do-not-resuscitate order must be written by a provider to be acted on
options.rationale: A wish stated by the patient is not an order until a provider writes it.

options.text: Having a directive means other treatments will be withheld as well
options.rationale: A directive about resuscitation does not limit antibiotics, pain relief, or anything else not addressed in it.

options.text: A directive takes effect only when he can no longer make his own decisions
options.rationale: While he has capacity, his current decision governs, whatever the document says.

options.text: The nurse should complete the form for him so it is on the chart before surgery
options.rationale: Completing it is the patient's act, and rushing it before a procedure undermines the point of it.

questions.takeaway: A living will states wishes, a durable power of attorney names a person, a do-not-resuscitate order is written by a provider, and all of it yields to the patient while he can still decide.
questions.strategy: The most common error in practice is the first wrong option: treating a resuscitation decision as a decision about everything else.

strategies: Sort each statement by what it claims

steps.action: Wishes, agent, revocable, provider order, timing

elimination.verdict: The five accurate statements are selected.

questions.stem: Which actions protect patient privacy under federal privacy rules? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accessing only the records of patients she is caring for
options.rationale: Looking at a record out of curiosity is a violation even when nothing is repeated.

options.text: Logging off the workstation before leaving it
options.rationale: An open session is an open record to whoever sits down next.

options.text: Verifying identity and authorization before releasing information to a caller
options.rationale: A voice on a telephone is not proof of who is asking.

options.text: Sharing only the minimum information needed for the task at hand
options.rationale: The minimum necessary standard applies even between clinicians.

options.text: Discussing a patient in the lift because she uses no name
options.rationale: Enough detail identifies a patient without a name, and a public space makes it a disclosure.

options.text: Photographing a wound on her own phone to show the provider
options.rationale: A personal device takes the image outside the protected record.

options.text: Positioning the screen away from visitors in a shared room
options.rationale: A displayed record is a disclosed record.

questions.takeaway: Privacy is about access, disclosure and the minimum necessary. A name is not what identifies a patient, and a personal device is not part of the record.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options have a reason attached that sounds like care: no name used, and showing the provider. Neither changes what was disclosed.

strategies: Ask whether the information left where it belongs

steps.action: Access limits, logging off, verifying, minimum necessary, screen position

elimination.verdict: The five protective actions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is off duty and shopping when a stranger collapses in the aisle beside her. She walks on. The man survives with a permanent deficit and his family brings a malpractice claim against her. Which element of the claim would be hardest to establish?

options.text: Causation
options.rationale: An argument could be made that the delay worsened the outcome. It never gets examined if there was no duty.

options.text: Breach of the standard of care
options.rationale: The tempting one, because doing nothing looks like the breach. A breach can only exist against a duty that was owed, and without the duty there is no standard to fall below.

options.text: Duty
options.rationale: Malpractice requires a professional relationship that creates an obligation to this person. A nurse off duty in a shop has not accepted that relationship, and most states impose no legal duty to rescue a stranger.

options.text: Damages
options.rationale: A permanent deficit is a clear injury, so this element is the one most obviously present.

questions.takeaway: All four elements have to be present: duty, breach, causation and damages. Duty is the one that fails off duty, and Good Samaritan laws exist to protect the nurse who chooses to help anyway.
questions.strategy: The morally uncomfortable option is not the legally weak one. Test the elements in order and stop where the chain breaks.

strategies: Test the four elements in sequence
elimination.verdict: Duty.

questions.stem: Midway through a shift a nurse notices that a colleague's hands are unsteady, smells alcohol when they speak, and watches her draw up a dose twice before getting it right. The colleague says she had one glass at lunch, asks her not to say anything, and tells her a report would cost her custody of her children. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Watch her closely for the rest of the shift and decide at the end
options.rationale: Assessing before acting is usually right and here the assessment is complete. Waiting adds no information and adds eight hours of exposure.

options.text: Keep it between them and offer to help her arrange treatment
options.rationale: Compassionate and it leaves patients with her for the rest of the shift. Covering is also how a colleague's problem becomes a licensure matter for two nurses instead of one.

options.text: Suggest she report herself sick and go home
options.rationale: It removes the immediate risk and leaves no record, no evaluation and nothing that stops the same shift happening next week.

options.text: Report it to the supervisor now
options.rationale: She has three observations and an admission. Patients are receiving care from an impaired nurse during the hour this is being discussed, and reporting is both a practice act obligation and the route to treatment.

questions.takeaway: Impairment is reported, not managed privately. The consequences the colleague fears are real and they do not transfer the risk away from the patients.
questions.strategy: Three options delay or privatize. Ask who is receiving care while each one plays out.

strategies: Ask what happens to patients during each option
elimination.verdict: Report now.

questions.stem: A patient signed a consent form yesterday. On the table this morning, before anything has begun, he says he has changed his mind and does not want to go ahead. The provider replies that the consent is signed and starts the procedure. Which has occurred?

options.text: Negligence
options.rationale: Negligence is unintentional. This was deliberate and against a stated refusal.

options.text: Battery
options.rationale: Consent can be withdrawn at any point up to and during a procedure. Touching that continues after withdrawal is intentional unconsented contact, whatever the paperwork says.

options.text: False imprisonment
options.rationale: That is unjustified restriction of movement. The wrong here is the touching, not the confinement.

options.text: Assault
options.rationale: The strongest distractor. Assault is placing someone in fear of unwanted contact. Once the contact happens it is battery, and the two are routinely confused in exactly this scenario.

questions.takeaway: A signature records a decision at a moment. The decision belongs to the patient continuously, and proceeding past a withdrawal is battery.
questions.strategy: Assault and battery split on whether contact occurred. Read the stem for whether anything was done.

strategies: Match the act to the definition
elimination.verdict: Battery.

questions.stem: A nurse reads an order for a dose she believes is ten times higher than the usual amount for this drug. She calls the prescriber, who tells her the dose is intended and to give it. What does she do?

options.text: Give it, since the prescriber confirmed the order and the responsibility is his
options.rationale: An order authorizes a drug and transfers nothing. A nurse who gives a dose she believed was wrong is answerable for having given it.

options.text: Ask a colleague to give it instead
options.rationale: It passes a known risk to someone with less information than she has.

options.text: Give it and document that she questioned the dose and was told to proceed by the prescriber she called
options.rationale: The most tempting wrong answer, because documenting feels like protection. Writing down that you knew and did it anyway documents the breach rather than excusing it.

options.text: Hold the dose and take the question to the pharmacist and up the chain of command
options.rationale: A nurse who administers answers for the administration. The order is in dispute, so the dose waits while the question is resolved by people with the information to resolve it.

questions.takeaway: Documenting a concern is not a substitute for acting on it. When an order looks wrong, the dose waits and the question goes up.
questions.strategy: Two options give the drug with a justification attached. Ask whether the justification would help in a review afterward.

strategies: Ask who answers for the administration
elimination.verdict: Hold it and escalate.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to witness a patient's signature on a surgical consent form. Which actions belong to her before she signs? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explain the risks, the benefits and the alternatives to him herself before he signs
options.rationale: That belongs to the person performing the procedure. A nurse who provides the explanation has taken on a duty that is not hers and let the provider skip one that is.

options.text: Confirm the patient can say what the procedure is, why it is being done, and what the main risks are
options.rationale: She is attesting that this is informed consent, and the only way to know is to hear him say it.

options.text: Confirm that a qualified interpreter was used if the conversation was not in his own language
options.rationale: Consent obtained without comprehension is not consent, and the language barrier is the most common place comprehension fails.

options.text: Accept a family member's signature when the patient hesitates about signing
options.rationale: A competent patient's hesitation is information, not a problem to route around. A relative has no authority unless the patient lacks capacity and that relative is the named surrogate.

options.text: Check whether he has received a sedative before signing
options.rationale: A premedicated patient cannot give informed consent, and this is one of the most common reasons a consent is later challenged.

options.text: Verify that the signature is his and that he is signing without pressure
options.rationale: Identity and voluntariness are exactly what a witness attests to.

options.text: Have him sign the form and then let the provider know afterward that he still had some questions before the procedure starts
options.rationale: The order is wrong. Unanswered questions stop the signing, because the signature says the questions were answered.

questions.takeaway: The nurse witnesses, she does not obtain. She attests to identity, voluntariness and comprehension, and she stops the process when any of the three is missing.
questions.strategy: Sort each action into obtaining consent and witnessing consent. Everything in the first pile belongs to the provider.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Comprehension, identity and voluntariness, sedation, and interpreter are selected.

chapters.title: Communication and Patient Education
chapters.subtitle: The communication process, therapeutic techniques and blocks, readiness to learn, teaching strategies, and evaluating learning

questions.stem: While a patient is speaking, the nurse says she is listening but continues to type and does not look up. The room is quiet and there are no interruptions. Which element of the process has broken down?

options.text: Ineffective feedback
options.rationale: Feedback is the response coming back. She did respond, and the problem is that her two responses contradicted each other.

options.text: A channel problem
options.rationale: The channel is the route a message travels. The spoken channel worked and the patient heard her clearly.

options.text: Environmental interference
options.rationale: The environment is everything outside the two of them. The stem rules out noise and interruptions, and her typing comes from her rather than from the room.

options.text: Incongruent communication
options.rationale: Congruence is whether the words and the body say the same thing. The patient got both and believed the behavior.

questions.takeaway: Four different failures: the channel is whether words arrive, feedback is whether a response comes back, the environment is disruption from outside, congruence is whether words and body agree.
questions.strategy: When two options both look true, check which one explains his reaction. Interference stops a message arriving; he received it and withdrew.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He stopped talking rather than repeating himself.
The stem states the room is quiet.
Both worked and carried contradictory content.

elimination.verdict: That leaves incongruent communication.

questions.scenario: A nurse talks with a patient who has just been told the cancer has returned.
questions.stem: For each nurse response, indicate whether it is a therapeutic technique or a communication block.

rows.text: "If I were you, I would start the treatment right away."
rows.rationale: This is unsolicited advice, and it puts her judgment in place of his decision.

rows.text: "Why didn't you come in sooner?"
rows.rationale: Asking why puts him on the defensive and implies he did something wrong.

rows.text: "So what worries you most is what this means for your work."
rows.rationale: This is focusing. It narrows a broad worry down to the part he can work on.

rows.text: "I am here with you. Let me sit down."
rows.rationale: Offering self. It demonstrates presence and reduces the sense of being alone with it.

rows.text: "You don't feel confident that you can manage this."
rows.rationale: This is reflection. It turns his attention back onto his own feelings rather than onto her view of them.

rows.text: "My mother went through this and she was fine."
rows.rationale: This changes the subject to herself, and it carries false reassurance on top of that.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic: clarification, restating, reflection, silence, offering self, giving information. Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing, judging, stereotyping, approving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: Every block here is well-intentioned. Ask whether the response keeps him talking or shuts the conversation down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does he say more, or stop?
It always sounds like an accusation.

elimination.verdict: Three therapeutic, three blocking.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says none of it makes sense and that everyone uses words he does not know. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask what he does understand so far, to find where the gap begins
options.rationale: You cannot pitch an explanation without knowing where to start. Assessing before teaching applies here as it does everywhere else.

options.text: Explain heart failure again using plain language
options.rationale: The right eventual move, and starting there means guessing which part lost him.

options.text: Provide written material he can read at his own pace
options.rationale: Useful once you know his reading level and where the gap is. Handing over paper before assessing repeats the problem in a new format.

options.text: Reassure him that it will make more sense over time
options.rationale: This is false reassurance, and it closes the opening he just gave you. He told you he is lost and you told him to wait.

questions.takeaway: Assess before teaching. Excessive medical jargon is the recognized barrier, and plain language is the remedy once you know where to begin.
questions.strategy: Two distractors deliver the teaching correctly and too early. One closes the conversation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That he is lost, not where.

elimination.verdict: That leaves finding where the gap begins.

questions.stem: A patient is to be told about a difficult diagnosis. Which environmental factors should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient's level of education
options.rationale: A real factor influencing communication, but it is not environmental. The environment is what surrounds the conversation.

options.text: How the nurse and the patient are positioned
options.rationale: Position is recognized, and standing over someone communicates something before either of you speaks.

options.text: The time available for the conversation
options.rationale: A conversation started without time for it is worse than one deferred.

options.text: The patient's preferred language for the conversation
options.rationale: Important and not environmental. The question asks about the setting the nurse controls, and language is a patient factor you plan around rather than adjust.

options.text: Noise in the room and corridor
options.rationale: Noise is recognized, and it makes both of you work harder to be understood during a conversation that is already hard.

options.text: The number of people present
options.rationale: The number of people present is recognized, and an audience changes what a patient is willing to disclose.

options.text: Privacy from other patients and visitors
options.rationale: Privacy decides what the patient is prepared to say out loud.

questions.takeaway: Environment: noise, privacy, lighting, temperature, number of people present, positioning, and time available.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real factor from the otthe list. Environment is what is around the conversation, not what either person brings to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A factor influencing communication, not environmental.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient stops talking and looks out of the window after describing the symptoms. The nurse waits without speaking. Which technique is she using and why?

options.text: Silence
options.rationale: A therapeutic technique. It feels uncomfortable because nurses feel they are supposed to be doing something.

options.text: Clarification
options.rationale: Clarification asks a question when a statement is unclear or incomplete. She has asked nothing.

options.text: Reflection
options.rationale: Reflection names the feeling out loud. Silence makes room for it without naming it.

options.text: Offering self
options.rationale: The near-miss. Offering self involves saying something like I am here with you. Silence is presence without words.

questions.takeaway: Silence gives the patient time to think, allows emotions to surface, and encourages communication. It is a technique rather than an absence of one.
questions.strategy: Three distractors require the nurse to say something. She has said nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves silence.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the communication process with a student.

The response that tells the sender the message was received is the [[1]].

The person who initiates the communication and encodes the message is the [[2]].

Repeating a patient's main idea in different words is [[3]].

The route the message travels, whether spoken, written or electronic, is the [[4]].

options.text: decoding
options.rationale: Decoding is what the receiver does internally to interpret the message. It is not the response you can see.

options.text: feedback
options.rationale: What tells the sender whether the message arrived and how it was understood.

options.text: congruence
options.rationale: Congruence is whether the verbal and nonverbal messages agree. That is a different idea.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: The channel is the route, not the response that comes back along it.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: The channel is the route the message travels. This blank names who starts it.

options.text: context
options.rationale: Context is the environment the exchange happens in, not the person initiating it.

options.text: receiver
options.rationale: The receiver takes the message in, interprets it and decodes it. That is the other end of the exchange.

options.text: sender
options.rationale: The sender starts the communication and encodes the message into words and behavior.

options.text: clarification
options.rationale: Clarification is used when a statement is unclear or incomplete. This blank describes repeating what was said.

options.text: restating
