options.rationale: Repeats the main idea using different words, which demonstrates listening and verifies understanding.

options.text: reflection
options.rationale: The near-miss. Reflection directs attention to feelings and thoughts; restating repeats the idea.

options.text: giving information
options.rationale: Giving information means supplying accurate, usable detail. It is not repeating the patient's own words back.

options.text: feedback
options.rationale: Feedback is the response coming back. This blank is about how the message travels.

options.text: message
options.rationale: The near-miss. The message is the content; the channel is how it travels.

options.text: context
options.rationale: Context is the surrounding environment. This blank is about the route the message travels along.

options.text: channel
options.rationale: Speech, writing, a phone or a screen. The route rather than the content.

questions.takeaway: Six components: sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context. Restating repeats the idea; reflection names the feeling.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: message against channel, and restating against reflection. Content against route, and idea against feeling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: What is said, and how it travels.

elimination.verdict: Sender, channel, feedback, restating.

questions.stem: A patient says, I do not know whether I can manage the insulin at home. Which nurse response is reflection?

options.text: "So you are unsure about the insulin injections specifically."
options.rationale: Restating. It repeats his idea in different words rather than naming the feeling underneath it.

options.text: "Can you tell me more about which part concerns you?"
options.rationale: This is clarification. It asks a question to make an incomplete statement clearer rather than reflecting the feeling back.

options.text: "You are not feeling confident that you can manage this."
options.rationale: Reflection directs his attention back to his own feeling, which is her exact example.

options.text: "Most people find it easier after the first week."
options.rationale: This is false reassurance, which is a block rather than a technique. It also predicts something nobody can promise.

questions.takeaway: Reflection directs attention back to feelings, thoughts and ideas. Restating repeats the content.
questions.strategy: Restating and reflection are the pair that gets confused. One returns the idea, the other returns the feeling.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is returned to him

elimination.verdict: That leaves reflection.

questions.stem: A patient is newly admitted to the unit. Which actions establish a therapeutic relationship with him? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain professional boundaries
options.rationale: Maintaining professional boundaries is recognized, and it is what keeps the relationship therapeutic rather than something else.

options.text: Introduce herself and explain her role
options.rationale: He needs to know who is in the room and why.

options.text: Share a personal experience to build rapport
options.rationale: Moves the focus to the nurse. Changing the subject to yourself is one of the blocks to communication.

options.text: Inviting the patient to use the nurse's first name
options.rationale: This feels like warmth and erodes the boundary the relationship depends on. Therapeutic closeness is not social closeness.

options.text: Address the patient properly
options.rationale: It means asking rather than assuming what he wants to be called.

options.text: Maintain privacy
options.rationale: Privacy is recognized, and it decides how much he is willing to tell you.

options.text: Follow through on commitments
options.rationale: Following through is recognized, and small promises kept are what make the larger assurances believable.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic communication: introduce yourself, explain your role, address the patient properly, maintain privacy, demonstrate respect, maintain boundaries, be present and attentive, follow through.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds warm and moves the conversation to the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who the focus stays on

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a patient's condition has changed but mentions it vaguely to the provider without giving him the specific findings. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is acceptable
options.rationale: Mentioning is not communicating. The specific findings are what allow someone else to act on it.

options.text: This is a safety concern
options.rationale: Professional communication supports safety and clinical decision-making. A provider cannot act on information he did not receive.

options.text: The responsibility passes to the provider once he has been told something
options.rationale: She remains accountable for communicating clearly enough that it can be acted on. Saying something vague does not discharge that.

options.text: The written record makes verbal communication less important
options.rationale: The record documents what happened. It does not alert anybody in time to change the outcome.

questions.takeaway: Professional communication supports continuity, safety, collaboration and clinical decision-making. Miscommunication causes errors.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat partial communication as sufficient. Ask whether the provider can act on what he received.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he can do with it
Cut the acceptable and transfer options

elimination.verdict: That leaves the safety concern.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a frightened preoperative patient not to worry, because the surgeon is excellent. Which block is this?

options.text: Minimizing feelings
options.rationale: The near-miss, and both are present. Minimizing dismisses the feeling as unimportant; false reassurance replaces it with a promise.

options.text: Changing the subject
options.rationale: She stayed on the topic. She answered it with a promise instead of an exploration.

options.text: Defending
options.rationale: Defending protects a person or the institution from criticism. Nobody has been criticized.

options.text: False reassurance
options.rationale: It promises an outcome nobody can guarantee, and it tells him the subject is closed.

questions.takeaway: Blocks: false reassurance, unsolicited advice, asking why, changing the subject, minimizing feelings, judging, stereotyping, approving and disapproving, defending, leading questions.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is minimizing, and both elements are arguably present. The promise about the outcome is the defining feature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves false reassurance.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Nurse enters to discuss discharge medications with a 68-year-old. Television is on at volume. An adult child and two grandchildren are visiting. Patient is due to leave for a scan in ten minutes, reports pain of 7 of 10, and has not had analgesia since 0600. Bilateral hearing aids are worn, both in place. Alert and oriented. The curtain is open and the adjacent bed is occupied. Speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should make the nurse defer or change this conversation.

segments.text: Due to leave for a scan in ten minutes
segments.rationale: Time available is recognized. Starting a discharge medication discussion with ten minutes is worse than deferring it.

segments.text: Alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Cognitive ability is a recognized factor and here it is intact, which removes it as a barrier.

segments.text: Speaks English fluently and reads without difficulty
segments.rationale: Language and literacy are both potential barriers, and both are ruled out by this finding.

segments.text: Pain of 7 of 10, no analgesia since 0600
segments.rationale: Health status, specifically pain, is a recognized factor influencing communication. Nobody learns well at 7 of 10.

segments.text: An adult child and two grandchildren are visiting
segments.rationale: The number of people present is recognized, and young children in the room affect what anyone will raise.

segments.text: The curtain is open and the adjacent bed is occupied
segments.rationale: Privacy is recognized, and a conversation about medication discloses the diagnosis to whoever is in the next bed.

segments.text: Television is on at volume
segments.rationale: Noise is a recognized environmental factor, and it is the easiest of these to fix.

segments.text: Wears bilateral hearing aids, both in place
segments.rationale: A potential barrier that is already managed. Aids in place is the reassuring detail.

questions.takeaway: Factors influencing communication: developmental level, culture, language, health status, emotional state, cognitive ability, environment, previous experience, personal perceptions.
questions.strategy: Three findings are barriers that are already resolved or absent. They are there to be left alone, and each one tells you something useful.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate present barriers from absent ones

elimination.verdict: s1, s4, s5, s6, and s7: four environmental factors and his pain.

questions.stem: Asked whether his pain is worse today, a patient answers yes and says nothing further. Which change would improve the exchange?

options.text: Ask an open-ended question about how the pain has been
options.rationale: An open question invites more than a yes. The closed question produced exactly the answer it asked for.

options.text: Ask whether the pain is sharp or dull
options.rationale: This is another closed question. It narrows the exchange further rather than opening it up.

options.text: Ask why he did not mention it sooner
options.rationale: Asking why is a recognized block and it puts him on the defensive.

options.text: Tell him the analgesia will be due shortly
options.rationale: This moves to a solution before the assessment is finished. You still do not know what the pain is doing.

questions.takeaway: Questions that encourage communication are open-ended. Closed questions have a place and they produce short answers.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is another closed question dressed as a follow-up. Ask which option cannot be answered in one word.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Test each for a one-word answer

elimination.verdict: That leaves the open-ended question.

questions.stem: A nurse is told that a patient from a particular cultural background will avoid eye contact and will want his family present for decisions. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Plan the encounter around the pattern as described
options.rationale: Applies a group generalization to an individual, which is how cultural knowledge becomes stereotyping.

options.text: Avoid eye contact throughout to demonstrate respect
options.rationale: This adopts the assumption as a rule. He may find a nurse who never looks at him disconcerting.

options.text: Treat this as something to ask about, not assume
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about. Not everyone from a background communicates the same way.

options.text: Ask the family what the patient would prefer
options.rationale: This asks about him without asking him. He is the person who knows what he prefers.

questions.takeaway: Not all people from a particular culture communicate the same way. Cultural knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: Two distractors act on the generalization. One asks the wrong person.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the two options acting on the assumption

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking rather than assuming.

questions.stem: A patient reads at a sixth-grade level and is anxious about the side effects of a new medication. Which characteristic should the explanation have?

options.text: Delivered in language free of excessive medical jargon
options.rationale: Plain language is one of effective verbal communication, and jargon is the recognized barrier to it.

options.text: Understandable
options.rationale: Understandable is recognized, and information he cannot use has not really been given to him.

options.text: Accurate
options.rationale: Information that turns out to be wrong damages more than it helped.

options.text: Comprehensive enough to cover every possible side effect
options.rationale: Overloading with information is a recognized thing to avoid, and an exhaustive list is unusable at home.

options.text: Appropriate to the patient's needs
options.rationale: Appropriate to his needs is recognized, and it means relevant to this patient rather than comprehensive.

questions.takeaway: Giving information: accurate, appropriate to the patient's needs, understandable. It decreases uncertainty and supports decision making.
questions.strategy: One distractor mistakes completeness for quality. Overloading is a recognized error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Overloading is recognized as a thing to avoid.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse sits at eye level, does not interrupt, repeats key phrases, and watches the patient's face while he speaks. Which does this describe?

options.text: Therapeutic silence
options.rationale: Silence is waiting without speaking. She is repeating phrases and responding, which is more than silence.

options.text: Clarification
options.rationale: Clarification is one technique inside an exchange. The stem describes the whole approach, not a single move.

options.text: Active listening
options.rationale: Paying attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allowing him to speak, being mindful of interruptions, clarifying, and attending to nonverbal cues.

options.text: Offering self
options.rationale: Offering self means making yourself available: I am here with you. This describes how she listens.

questions.takeaway: Active listening: pay attention, appropriate eye contact and body language, allow the patient to speak, mind interruptions, clarify and repeat phrases, reflect and validate, attend to nonverbal cues.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name a single technique. The stem describes several behaviors together.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position, silence from interruption, repetition, observation.
Each is one part of it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves active listening.

questions.stem: A patient with expressive difficulty after a stroke struggles to find a word and the nurse finishes his sentence. Which problem does this create?

options.text: Interrupting
options.rationale: Being mindful of interruptions is part of active listening. For a patient with expressive difficulty, the time is the intervention.

options.text: Minimizing feelings
options.rationale: Nothing about his feelings is addressed or dismissed. The problem is the time taken from him.

options.text: Giving unsolicited advice
options.rationale: She supplied a word, not advice. The problem is that she took the time he needed to find it himself.

options.text: Asking a leading question
options.rationale: The near-miss. She supplied a word he may or may not have wanted, and the core failure is that she did not let him finish.

questions.takeaway: Be mindful of interruptions. For a patient with expressive difficulty, allowing time is the intervention.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is leading, and supplying a word does steer him. What the technique names is the interruption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The time to find his own word.
Related, and the recognized barrier is interrupting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves interrupting.

questions.stem: A nurse explains a procedure quickly, uses several abbreviations, and asks at the end whether the patient has any questions. He says no. Which error has the nurse made?

options.text: Failing to obtain informed consent for the procedure
options.rationale: Consent is a separate process, and it is not what the stem describes. This is a teaching failure.

options.text: Failing to document the patient's response to the teaching
options.rationale: A real omission, and not the error the stem describes. Documenting a response the nurse never obtained would compound the problem rather than fix it.

options.text: Providing information that was not accurate
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the content was wrong. The problem is whether any of it reached him.

options.text: Assuming understanding rather than confirming what was learned
options.rationale: No questions is not evidence of understanding. Talking too fast, using jargon, overloading and assuming understanding are all the same error in different forms.

questions.takeaway: Avoid excessive medical jargon, talking too fast, overloading with information, and assuming understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real weakness in her closing question. Ask what she concluded from his answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: True, and secondary to the assumption.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assuming understanding.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old admitted with pneumonia has become withdrawn. The patient answers in single words, has not touched any meals, and turns toward the window when staff enter. Oxygen saturation is 95% and pain is 2 of 10. A spouse died three weeks ago. The unit is busy and the nurse has been documenting at the bedside computer while talking.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Reassure him that he will feel better once the pneumonia clears
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it also attributes his withdrawal to the infection when his saturation and pain say otherwise.

options.text: Ask him why he is not eating
options.rationale: Asking why is a named communication block. To someone already withdrawn it sounds like an accusation.

options.text: Sit down at eye level, stop documenting, and give him her full attention
options.rationale: Her own congruence example in reverse. Documenting while talking tells him she is not available, whatever she says.

options.text: Use reflection to name what he may be feeling, then allow silence
options.rationale: Reflection directs him back to his own feelings, and silence gives the time for them to surface.

options.text: Hypoxia contributing to altered behavior
options.rationale: His saturation is 95 percent. The stem rules hypoxia out directly.

options.text: Withdrawal with a recent bereavement, and no one has been fully present with him
options.rationale: His emotional state is a named factor influencing communication, and the nurse's own incongruent behavior is part of why nothing has been said.

options.text: Uncontrolled pain limiting his willingness to talk
options.rationale: His pain is 2 of 10. The stem rules this out as well.

options.text: Cognitive impairment affecting his ability to converse
options.rationale: Nothing suggests impairment. He answers, briefly, and turns away on purpose, which is a choice rather than a deficit.

options.text: Whether he begins to say more than single words
options.rationale: This is the behavior that defined the problem, measured directly. More than single words means something shifted.

options.text: Whether he raises his wife or his situation without being prompted
options.rationale: Measures whether the relationship has become one he can use, which is what the actions aimed at.

options.text: Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%
options.rationale: A real parameter, and it evaluates his pneumonia rather than anything that was changed.

options.text: Whether he finishes his next meal
options.rationale: Intake matters and it is a downstream consequence rather than a measure of whether the communication worked.

questions.takeaway: Emotional state is a factor influencing communication. When the clinical numbers are reassuring, the withdrawal is telling you something the numbers cannot.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors are ruled out by values in the stem. The saturation and the pain score are placed there to eliminate the easy explanations.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Note what changed three weeks ago

elimination.verdict: Sit and be present, reflect and allow silence, for withdrawal after bereavement, evaluated by what he says.

questions.stem: A nurse says to a patient, "You didn't take your medication again, did you?" Which two blocks does this combine?

options.text: Clarification and restating
options.rationale: Both of those are therapeutic techniques, and neither one is present in what she said.

options.text: A leading question and judging
options.rationale: The phrasing directs him to a particular answer, and again carries a verdict about him before he has spoken.

options.text: False reassurance and defending
options.rationale: Nothing is being promised and nobody is being defended. Those are different blocks.

options.text: Changing the subject and stereotyping
options.rationale: The subject has not changed, and no generalization about a group is being made.

questions.takeaway: Blocks include leading questions and judging. A single sentence can carry more than one.
questions.strategy: Two options list therapeutic techniques or blocks that are not present. Read the sentence for what it does to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the techniques and absent blocks

elimination.verdict: That leaves a leading question with judging.

questions.stem: A nurse mentoring a student describes how therapeutic communication works at the bedside. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: “My nonverbal behavior may communicate more than my words do.”
options.rationale: This is accurate. What your face and body do often reaches the patient before your words land.

options.text: “If the patient has no questions, I can chart that the teaching was understood.”
options.rationale: Assuming understanding is a recognized error. No questions may mean he does not know what to ask, or does not want to appear slow.

options.text: "Silence is a technique, not a gap I need to fill."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Nurses find silence uncomfortable because it feels like they should be doing something.

options.text: “Therapeutic communication is purposeful rather than simply being nice.”
options.rationale: This is accurate. Therapeutic communication is purposeful and goal-directed, not the same as being pleasant.

questions.takeaway: Assuming understanding is a recognized error. Silence is a technique. Nonverbal behavior often says more than words.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth treats an absence of questions as proof of comprehension.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves recording that he understood.

questions.stem: A newly diagnosed patient is due to be taught about a new insulin. He reports pain of 8 of 10, his roommate's television is on, and his daughter is due in ten minutes. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach now and repeat the session before discharge
options.rationale: Two ineffective sessions rather than one effective one, and the first may leave him thinking he has already been taught.

options.text: Give written material and review it together later
options.rationale: Written material is a strategy, not a substitute for assessing readiness. He is unlikely to read it at 8 of 10.

options.text: Address the pain and distractions, then teach when ready
options.rationale: Readiness asks whether pain is controlled, whether he is free from distractions, and whether he is interested. Teaching through 8 of 10 pain wastes the session.

options.text: Teach the daughter instead when she arrives
options.rationale: Family involvement is appropriate when he wants it and when they will provide the care. It is not a workaround for his pain.

questions.takeaway: Readiness to learn: is pain controlled, is he free from distractions, is he interested. Assess readiness before teaching.
questions.strategy: Three options proceed in some form. Ask what he is likely to retain at 8 of 10 with a television on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not a substitute for teaching him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves addressing the barriers first.

questions.scenario: A nurse writes learning objectives for a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes.
questions.stem: For each objective, indicate which learning domain it belongs to.

rows.text: The patient will name three signs of hypoglycemia
rows.rationale: Naming three signs is knowledge and recall, which puts it in the cognitive domain.

rows.text: The patient will draw up and inject the correct insulin dose
rows.rationale: Drawing up and injecting a dose is a physical skill performed and watched, which is psychomotor.

rows.text: The patient will express his concerns about injecting himself
rows.rationale: Expressing his concerns is about feelings and attitudes, which is the affective domain.

rows.text: The patient will decide what to do when his glucose reads 58 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Deciding what to do with a reading of 58 is problem solving, which sits in the cognitive domain alongside recall.

rows.text: The patient will demonstrate rotating his injection sites
rows.rationale: Rotating injection sites is another physical skill performed and observed, so it is psychomotor.

rows.text: The patient will state that managing his diabetes is worth the effort
rows.rationale: Saying it is worth the effort is a value and a motivation rather than a fact or a skill.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing. Psychomotor is doing. Affective is valuing. The domain determines how the outcome is evaluated.
questions.strategy: Problem solving sits in cognitive rather than forming a domain of its own. Deciding what to do is still knowing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A fact, a movement, or a feeling.

elimination.verdict: Two cognitive, two psychomotor, two affective.

questions.stem: A nurse writes the objective that a patient will understand his new anticoagulant. Which revision is better?

options.text: The patient will state three foods to limit before discharge
options.rationale: Observable, measurable and time-bound. Understand cannot be observed, and that is exactly the contrast being drawn.

options.text: The nurse will teach the patient about the anticoagulant
options.rationale: This describes what the nurse will do. A learning objective describes what the patient will be able to do.

options.text: The patient will feel confident managing the medication
options.rationale: Confidence is no more observable than understanding. It replaces one unmeasurable verb with another.

options.text: The patient will comprehend the importance of consistent dosing
options.rationale: Comprehend is understand wearing different clothes. Neither one can be observed or scored.

questions.takeaway: Learning objectives describe what the patient will be able to do after teaching, and they must be evaluable.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap one unobservable verb for another. One changes the subject to the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One option is about the nurse.

steps.action: Find the one you could watch
steps.detail: State three foods and two signs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the specific, observable objective.

questions.stem: Which assessments belong to the period before patient teaching begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: What the patient already knows
options.rationale: What he already knows is recognized first. You cannot pitch a session without knowing where to start it.

options.text: The patient's ability to learn
options.rationale: His ability to learn is recognized, and it covers both cognitive capacity and physical ability to do the task.

options.text: Whether any barriers are present
options.rationale: Barriers are recognized, and they include pain, distraction, language and literacy.

options.text: Whether his pain is controlled
options.rationale: Pain control is recognized under readiness. A patient who hurts is not in a state to take anything in.

options.text: Whether the patient can repeat the instructions back
options.rationale: Evaluation, which comes afterward. Two options here describe the period after teaching, and both are out for the same reason.

options.text: Whether the teaching was effective
options.rationale: Evaluation comes after teaching. It cannot be assessed before anything has been taught.

options.text: Whether he is interested
options.rationale: Part of readiness, and a patient who is not interested will not retain it.

questions.takeaway: Before teaching: assess what he knows, what barriers exist, and his ability to learn. Assess readiness: pain controlled, free from distractions, interested.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the end of the process. Place yourself in time before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A visiting daughter is told that her mother has hypertension exacerbated by failure to take her diuretic, that her systolic has been over 160, and that she is NPO after midnight. Which problem does this create?

options.text: The nurse breached confidentiality by discussing the mother's care
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the daughter is not an appropriate person to speak with. The problem is what she was told.

options.text: The jargon means the daughter may not have understood
options.rationale: Documenting that a family was updated records what the nurse said, not what they received. The entry is only true if the information landed.

options.text: The information that was given was clinically inaccurate
options.rationale: The content is accurate. The problem is that it was delivered in a form she cannot use.

options.text: The nurse should have waited for the provider to give this information
options.rationale: Explaining the plan of care is squarely nursing work. The failure is in how it was explained.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Never assume a patient or family understood, and documenting that you updated someone records your action rather than their understanding.
questions.strategy: One distractor questions the accuracy of the content. Ask what the daughter can now do with what she was told.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves jargon making the chart entry doubtful.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse plans education for a patient going home with a new wound.

Watching the patient perform the dressing change unaided is [[1]].

What the nurse does to facilitate learning is [[2]].

The capacity to obtain, understand and use health information is [[3]].

A change in knowledge, behavior, skill or understanding is [[4]].

options.text: hands-on practice
options.rationale: Practice builds the skill. Return demonstration is where you find out whether it worked.

options.text: demonstration
options.rationale: The near-miss. Demonstration is the nurse showing; return demonstration is the patient doing.

options.text: teach-back
options.rationale: Teach-back has the patient explain in his own words. Useful, and it evaluates knowledge rather than a physical skill.

options.text: return demonstration
options.rationale: The patient performs the skill back to you, which evaluates a psychomotor objective directly.

options.text: teaching
options.rationale: This is the definition: what the nurse does to make learning possible.

options.text: learning
options.rationale: The near-miss. Learning is what happens in the patient; teaching is what the nurse does.

options.text: health literacy
options.rationale: Health literacy is the patient's capacity to work with health information, not the nurse's activity.

options.text: evaluation
options.rationale: Evaluation is determining whether learning happened, which comes later.

options.text: the affective domain
options.rationale: The affective domain covers feelings, attitudes and motivation. This blank is about something else.

options.text: health literacy
options.rationale: Affects the ability to obtain, understand and use information, make decisions, and follow instructions.

options.text: readiness to learn
options.rationale: Readiness to learn is whether he can engage right now, not which kind of learning is involved.

options.text: cognitive ability
options.rationale: Closer, and health literacy is specific to health information rather than to general capacity.

options.text: readiness
options.rationale: Readiness is whether the patient is in a state to learn right now. It is a precondition, not the learning itself.

options.text: learning
options.rationale: This is the definition, and learning is measured by a change in the patient rather than by exposure to information.

options.text: teaching
options.rationale: This is the nurse's activity, not the patient's. Teaching can happen without any learning, and that is what evaluation catches.

options.text: reinforcement
options.rationale: Reinforcement is the final step, where what was learned gets repeated and strengthened.

questions.takeaway: Teaching is what the nurse does. Learning is the change in the patient. Demonstration is the nurse showing; return demonstration is the patient doing.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: teaching against learning, and demonstration against return demonstration. In both, the question is who is acting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Health literacy is specific to health information.

elimination.verdict: Teaching, learning, return demonstration, health literacy.

questions.stem: After being taught to use a new inhaler, a patient is asked whether he understood. He nods and says yes. Which action should follow?

options.text: Ask him to use the inhaler while she watches
options.rationale: A psychomotor skill is evaluated by watching it performed. Never assume a patient understands because they nod.

options.text: Provide written instructions to reinforce the teaching
options.rationale: Reinforcement is a legitimate later step, but it does not tell you whether he can use the device.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the inhaler
options.rationale: This is another closed question, and no questions is not evidence of competence. It invites the same nod.

options.text: Document that the patient verbalized understanding
options.rationale: This records the nod as if it were proof. Assuming understanding from a nod is the recognized error.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate learning by the method the objective requires. A physical skill is evaluated by demonstration, not by a nod.
questions.strategy: Three options accept a verbal answer as proof of a physical skill.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what kind of objective it is

elimination.verdict: That leaves watching him use it.

questions.stem: A patient with a new abdominal wound cannot reach the site to change the dressing. He lives with his daughter, who will perform the care. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Teach the patient thoroughly, since the education is for the patient
options.rationale: He cannot physically perform it. Teaching the person who cannot do the task leaves the person who will untrained.

options.text: Provide written instructions for the son to follow
options.rationale: Written material supports a skill. It does not establish that he can perform it.

options.text: Arrange home health so that nobody at home needs to be taught
options.rationale: May be appropriate, but it does not remove the need for someone in the house to recognize problems.

options.text: Teach the son and confirm by return demonstration that he can perform it
options.rationale: Teaching should include the caregiver who will perform the care, and the confirmation is what makes it safe.

questions.takeaway: Ask who will provide care after discharge, who needs to learn the skill, whether the patient wants family involved, and whether the caregiver is an appropriate learner. Confirm by demonstration.
questions.strategy: One distractor keeps the teaching with the patient on principle. Ask who will be holding the dressing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut home health and written material

elimination.verdict: That leaves teaching the son with return demonstration.

questions.stem: After teaching about a new anticoagulant, a patient answers every question correctly but says he will skip it on days he feels well. Which part of the teaching has not succeeded?

options.text: The nurse's impression of how motivated the patient seemed
options.rationale: A judgment rather than an observation. Chart what the patient said and did, not how it struck the nurse.

options.text: The patient's response
options.rationale: His response is a recognized element, and it is the part that separates teaching from learning.

options.text: What was taught
options.rationale: What was taught is recognized first, and it tells the next nurse what ground has already been covered.

options.text: The amount of time the session took
options.rationale: Duration is not one of the elements, and how long you talked says nothing about whether he learned.

options.text: The teaching method used
options.rationale: It matters because a video and a return demonstration are not equivalent.

options.text: The level of understanding demonstrated
options.rationale: The level of understanding demonstrated is what is recognized, and demonstrated is the word that matters.

options.text: Any questions or concerns raised
options.rationale: Questions and concerns raised are recognized, and the unanswered ones are the agenda for the next session.

questions.takeaway: Document what was taught, the method, the patient or caregiver response, level of understanding, demonstrated skills, questions and concerns, and any additional teaching needed.
questions.strategy: One distractor records effort rather than outcome. Ask what the next nurse needs to know.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the next nurse needs

elimination.verdict: B, C, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the same standardized diabetes teaching packet for a 20-year-old university student and a 74-year-old who lives alone. Which principle has she overlooked?

options.text: The younger patient requires less teaching than the older patient
options.rationale: This assumes from age in the opposite direction, which is the same error wearing different clothes.

options.text: Written materials are inappropriate for older adults
options.rationale: Age does not decide whether written material works. Assessing this patient does.

options.text: Diabetes teaching should always be delivered over multiple sessions
options.rationale: The number of sessions is not the principle at stake. The problem is that both patients got the same packet.

options.text: Teaching must be individualized rather than one size fits all
options.rationale: The two patients differ in ability, resources, routine and what they need to manage, so one session cannot serve both.

questions.takeaway: Avoid one size fits all. Assess the individual, identify specific needs, match teaching to ability, use appropriate resources, and adapt the method.
questions.strategy: Two distractors make a new assumption based on age. That is the same error the question is about.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One packet for two different people.

elimination.verdict: That leaves individualization.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Nurse prepares discharge teaching for a 79-year-old going home with a new anticoagulant and a wound requiring daily dressing changes. Patient reports pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen. States the reading glasses were left at home. Says school ended at 14 and that forms are difficult. A spouse, who will do the dressings, is present and attentive. Alert and oriented. The room is quiet. Asks three specific questions about the medication. Has no prior experience of wound care.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should change how the nurse delivers this teaching.

segments.text: Pain of 3 of 10, controlled with acetaminophen
segments.rationale: His pain is controlled, so readiness is satisfied on this count. That is what puts it in the list.

segments.text: Stopped school at 14 and finds forms difficult
segments.rationale: Points to limited health literacy, which affects obtaining, understanding and using the information.

segments.text: A spouse will do the dressings and is present
segments.rationale: That is the person who will perform the skill, so that is who demonstrates it back.

segments.text: The room is quiet
segments.rationale: A quiet room means he is free from distractions, which is one of the readiness criteria already met.

segments.text: Alert and oriented
segments.rationale: Alert and oriented means his cognitive ability is intact, which removes one barrier to learning.

segments.text: No prior experience of wound care
segments.rationale: What he already knows is the first thing you assess, and starting from nothing changes the pace and the method.

segments.text: Asks three specific questions about the medication
segments.rationale: Evidence of interest, and interest is the third readiness criterion. A strength rather than a barrier.

segments.text: Left the reading glasses at home
segments.rationale: A physical barrier to written material, and it is fixable within the session by using verbal and demonstrated methods.

questions.takeaway: Four findings change the method: no glasses, limited literacy, a caregiver who will do the skill, and no prior experience. Four confirm he is ready.
questions.strategy: Every readiness criterion is met here and stated explicitly. The findings that matter are about how to teach, not whether to.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s2, s3, s6, and s8: the four that change how you teach.

questions.stem: Which statement about assigning patient education to assistive personnel during a busy shift is accurate?

options.text: It may be delegated if the assistive personnel is familiar with the content
options.rationale: Familiarity with content does not confer the scope to assess or evaluate learning.

options.text: Patient education is within the nurse's scope and cannot be delegated
options.rationale: This is stated directly. Teaching requires assessment of learning needs and evaluation of learning, neither of which is delegable.

options.text: It may be delegated provided the nurse documents the education afterwards
options.rationale: Documenting something you did not do is a separate problem on top of the delegation error.

options.text: It may be delegated for routine topics such as diet
options.rationale: The topic does not change the scope. Reinforcing a message is different from teaching.

questions.takeaway: Patient education is in the nurse's scope of practice and is not something that can be delegated.
questions.strategy: Three distractors offer conditions under which it becomes acceptable. There are none.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves education being non-delegable.

questions.stem: A patient must learn to use a walker safely before discharge. Which teaching strategy best matches the objective?

options.text: A video showing correct walker technique
options.rationale: A video beats a leaflet and it is still passive. Watching someone use a walker is not using one.

options.text: Written instructions with diagrams for reference at home
options.rationale: Useful as reinforcement. Nobody learns to walk with a device from a page.

options.text: Demonstration followed by hands-on practice and return demonstration
options.rationale: Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills, and practice with return demonstration is how the skill is built and confirmed.

options.text: A discussion about the importance of using the walker correctly
options.rationale: Discussion suits cognitive and affective objectives. It does not build a physical skill.

questions.takeaway: Match the teaching strategy to the learning goal. Demonstration is useful for psychomotor skills.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are strategies that would support the learning without producing it. Ask what the objective requires him to do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves demonstration with practice and return demonstration.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed heart failure says there is no point weighing himself daily, because it will not change anything. Which learning domain should the nurse address first?

options.text: Cognitive
options.rationale: This is reasonable teaching aimed at knowledge he may already have. He never said he did not understand.

options.text: All three at once
options.rationale: Spreads effort across two domains where there is no gap, and misses that his objection is about meaning.

options.text: Affective
options.rationale: He is not lacking the knowledge or the skill. Feelings, attitudes, values and motivation sit in the affective domain.

options.text: Psychomotor
options.rationale: Weighing is not the skill gap. He knows how to stand on a scale.

questions.takeaway: Cognitive is knowing, psychomotor is doing, affective is valuing. Address the domain where the gap is.
questions.strategy: One distractor is correct teaching aimed at a gap he has not shown. Ask what he said.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Effort where there is no gap.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the affective domain.

questions.stem: A patient is going home after surgery. Which topics belong in the discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Activity and diet restrictions
options.rationale: Activity and diet restrictions both count, and they are where patients improvise if nobody tells them.

options.text: The names of the staff who provided his care
options.rationale: Courteous and not part of discharge education. Nothing about it affects his safety at home.

options.text: Warning signs and when and how to seek help
options.rationale: Warning signs and when to seek help are recognized, and this is the topic that prevents the readmission.

options.text: Medications and how to take them
options.rationale: Medications and how to take them are first among the discharge topics.

options.text: A list of the restrictions that no longer apply
options.rationale: This sounds reassuring and teaches nothing he can act on. Discharge teaching covers what to do, watch for and report.

options.text: Follow-up appointments
options.rationale: Confirming them is part of the plan rather than an afterthought.

options.text: Wound care
options.rationale: Wound care is recognized, and it is the topic most likely to need a return demonstration before he leaves.

questions.takeaway: Discharge education: medications, follow-up appointments, activity, diet, wound care, warning signs, when and how to seek help, equipment, and self-management.
questions.strategy: One distractor is pleasant and changes nothing about how he manages at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he needs at home

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse completes a teaching session and moves on to her next patient without checking what the patient took from it. Which error has she made?

options.text: Failing to individualize the teaching
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests the content was generic. The omission is at the end, not the start.

options.text: Teaching without evaluating learning
options.rationale: Teaching and learning are separate things, and only evaluation tells you whether the second happened.

options.text: Failing to identify barriers before teaching
options.rationale: That error happens before teaching starts. Hers happened after, when she never checked what the patient took from it.

options.text: Failing to document the session
options.rationale: Documentation matters and it is a separate step. She could document accurately and still not know whether learning occurred.

questions.takeaway: Avoid teaching without evaluation of learning. Evaluation may be verbal explanation, demonstration, observation, or asking questions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real errors that occur at other points in the process. Place the omission in time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves teaching without evaluation.

questions.stem: Which order does effective patient education follow?

options.text: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce
options.rationale: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce. Assessment opens the sequence and reinforcement closes it.

options.text: Teach, assess, practice, evaluate, communicate, reinforce
options.rationale: Places teaching before assessment, which is the error the whole chapter is built against.

options.text: Assess, teach, evaluate, communicate, practice, reinforce
options.rationale: Places evaluation before practice, so the skill is assessed before it has been built.

options.text: Communicate, teach, assess, reinforce, practice, evaluate
options.rationale: Assessment third and evaluation last with practice after reinforcement. The sequence is scrambled.

questions.takeaway: Assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce. Effective education depends on effective communication.
questions.strategy: Two things anchor the sequence: assessment comes first, and practice comes before evaluation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Build the skill, then assess it.
Each breaks one of those two rules.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assess, communicate, teach, practice, evaluate, reinforce.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a patient to ambulate three times daily, watch for edema, and remain NPO after midnight. Which change would most improve this?

options.text: Replace the clinical terms with words the patient uses
options.rationale: Ambulate, edema and NPO are all on the list of commonly used jargon. None of them means anything to most patients.

options.text: Repeat the instructions a second time before leaving
options.rationale: Repeating words he does not understand produces the same result a second time.

options.text: Provide the instructions in writing as well
options.rationale: This is the same jargon in a different format. Writing NPO down does not explain it.

options.text: Ask whether he has any questions about the instructions
options.rationale: He cannot form a question about terms he did not follow, and no questions would then be recorded as understanding.

questions.takeaway: Avoid medical jargon. Ambulate, edema, NPO, dyspnea, hypertension, PRN, EDD and SBA are all common examples of and commonly misunderstood.
questions.strategy: Three distractors deliver the same words again in a different way. Ask what he did not understand the first time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three clinical terms in one sentence.
He cannot ask about what he missed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves replacing the terms.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her own documentation of a teaching session with a colleague. Which entry requires correction?

options.text: "Patient education is in my scope and I cannot delegate it."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is stated directly. Teaching is in your scope and it does not get delegated.

options.text: "Teaching is what I do; learning is the change in the patient."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and the distinction is the whole reason evaluation exists.

options.text: "A 20-year-old with diabetes needs different teaching from a 74-year-old."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the standard example of why teaching has to be individualized.

options.text: “Patient nodded and stated understanding; learning objectives met.”
options.rationale: Never assume a patient understands because they nod. Learning is a change that has to be evaluated, not inferred.

questions.takeaway: Never assume understanding from a nod. Teaching is what the nurse does; learning is the change that has to be demonstrated.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth treats a nod as evaluation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Inferring learning rather than evaluating it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves recording learning from a nod.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old is readmitted with heart failure three weeks after discharge. The patient was taught about daily weights, fluid restriction and the diuretic before leaving, and can recite the instructions accurately when asked. The diuretic has been taken in the evening because mornings are rushed, and the daily weights have not happened because there are no scales at home. The discharge record documents that the patient verbalized understanding of all topics.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Establish what he can actually do at home, including what equipment he has
options.rationale: Assessment before teaching. Nobody established that he owned scales, and the plan assumed he did.

options.text: Document that he verbalized understanding of the corrected instructions
options.rationale: The same entry that was made last time, and the readmission shows what it was worth.

options.text: Work out a medication timing and monitoring plan that fits his mornings
options.rationale: Individualizing rather than repeating a generic plan. The evening dosing has a reason, and the reason can be worked with.

options.text: Repeat the discharge teaching on all three topics before he leaves
options.rationale: He can recite the instructions. Repeating them addresses a gap the stem rules out.

options.text: Low health literacy affecting his understanding of the instructions
options.rationale: He can state the instructions accurately, which is evidence against a literacy barrier rather than for one.

options.text: Knowledge deficit regarding heart failure self-management
options.rationale: He recites the instructions accurately. The stem rules a knowledge gap out directly.

options.text: Nonadherence with the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: Names the outcome and explains nothing. He has been taking the diuretic, at a time that suits him.

options.text: Teaching was delivered and learning was never evaluated against his actual circumstances
options.rationale: He knows the content and cannot apply it. Nobody checked whether the plan was executable in his house.

options.text: Whether the discharge teaching was documented completely
options.rationale: Evaluates the record rather than the patient. The last record was complete and he came back.

options.text: Whether he is recording daily weights using equipment he now has
options.rationale: Measures whether the practical barrier was actually removed, rather than whether he was told again.

options.text: Whether he can state three signs of fluid overload
options.rationale: This tests knowledge he has already demonstrated twice. It was never the thing that failed.

options.text: Whether he is readmitted within 30 days
options.rationale: The outcome the whole intervention exists to prevent, and the pattern that brought him back.

questions.takeaway: Verbalized understanding is not learning. Evaluate whether the plan can be executed in the patient's actual circumstances.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out knowledge and literacy explicitly by telling you he can recite the instructions. Two evaluation distractors test knowledge or paperwork.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weigh himself, take it in the morning.

elimination.verdict: Assess his circumstances and individualize the plan, for teaching never evaluated against his life, measured by weights and readmission.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a patient to use a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. Which closing action evaluates his learning rather than his satisfaction?

options.text: Ask the patient to demonstrate the technique now
options.rationale: The skill is psychomotor, so the evidence has to be psychomotor. Watching it done is the only way to find the step the patient will get wrong at home.

options.text: Ask the patient whether the explanation was clear
options.rationale: Measures how the teaching felt. Patients say yes, and many say yes without being able to do it.

options.text: Ask the patient to read the instruction sheet aloud
options.rationale: Tests reading, not technique. A patient can read every word and still not coordinate the breath.

options.text: Ask the patient if any questions remain about it
options.rationale: A reasonable courtesy, but not an evaluation. Someone who does not know what they missed has no question to ask.

questions.takeaway: Match the evaluation to the domain. Psychomotor learning is evaluated by return demonstration, never by asking whether the patient understood.
questions.strategy: Three options collect the patient's opinion of the teaching. Only one collects the patient's performance.

strategies: Match evaluation to the learning domain
elimination.verdict: Have the patient demonstrate.

questions.stem: A nurse is behind on the shift and asks assistive personnel to teach a newly admitted patient how to use an incentive spirometer, since the AP sets them up for patients all day. Which consideration applies?

options.text: Delegation is appropriate because the task is routine
options.rationale: Routine describes the device, not the activity. Teaching is not a task even when the equipment is simple.

options.text: Delegation is acceptable with documented AP competency
options.rationale: Competence with the device is real, but it is not the issue. The AP cannot assess readiness, adapt to the patient, or evaluate learning.

options.text: Patient teaching is a nursing responsibility, not delegable
options.rationale: Teaching requires assessing what this patient already knows and evaluating what was learned. Both are nursing judgment, so the activity does not transfer.

options.text: The AP may teach if the nurse evaluates afterward
options.rationale: The cleverest option, and it splits an activity that does not split. Assessment of readiness happens before the teaching, not after it.

questions.takeaway: Teaching is not delegable, because it contains assessment and evaluation. Reinforcing what the nurse already taught is a different thing.
questions.strategy: When an option offers a way to delegate half of a nursing activity, check whether the half it keeps is the half that comes first.

strategies: Ask what the activity contains
elimination.verdict: Teaching is not delegable.

questions.stem: A patient who is deaf and communicates in American Sign Language is admitted for a procedure requiring consent. His son offers to interpret so the discussion is not delayed. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Accept the offer, since the family member knows the patient
options.rationale: Convenient and it puts a relative between the patient and a legal decision. Family interpreters soften, omit, and answer on the patient's behalf, and consent is exactly where that matters.

options.text: Arrange a qualified sign language interpreter
options.rationale: Consent requires the patient to receive the disclosure directly and accurately. A qualified interpreter is the only route that delivers it, and the delay is part of the cost of doing it.

options.text: Write the information down for the patient to read
options.rationale: Assumes written English is an equivalent channel. For many Deaf patients whose first language is sign, it is not.

options.text: Speak slowly while facing the patient for lip reading
options.rationale: Lip reading captures a fraction of speech at best, and it is not a consent discussion.

questions.takeaway: A qualified interpreter is required for consent, and a family member is not one. Convenience and the patient's own suggestion do not change that.
questions.strategy: The family member's offer is in the stem to make the shortcut attractive. Ask what consent requires.

strategies: Patient-centered care
Scope and legal requirement
elimination.verdict: Arrange a qualified interpreter.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a patient to change her new colostomy appliance. She becomes tearful, turns away, and says, I cannot even look at it. Discharge is planned for tomorrow. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the teaching, since discharge is tomorrow
options.rationale: The deadline is real, but the learning will not happen. A patient who cannot look at the stoma is not going to retain a procedure performed on it.

options.text: Reassure the patient that it becomes easier with time
options.rationale: Probably true, but it closes the subject the patient just opened. Reassurance substitutes for presence here.

options.text: Arrange a referral to the ostomy nurse for tomorrow
options.rationale: A correct action at the wrong moment. The patient is crying now, and the referral is a way of handing the feeling to someone else.

options.text: Stop the teaching and stay with the patient
options.rationale: The affective domain is blocking the psychomotor one. Nothing is learned until the distress is addressed, and the teaching restarts from a usable place once it is.

questions.takeaway: Readiness is a precondition, not a formality. When the affective response blocks learning, the teaching stops and the person gets attended to.
questions.strategy: The discharge deadline is in the stem to make pressing on seem responsible. Teaching into distress produces no learning and costs the relationship.

strategies: Assess readiness before teaching
Address the affective domain first

steps.detail: Both move away from the patient.

elimination.verdict: Stop and stay with the patient.

questions.stem: A patient three days after a stroke follows instructions correctly but can produce only single words and becomes frustrated mid-sentence. Which approach fits his deficit?

options.text: Speak slowly in short sentences and confirm he has understood each one
options.rationale: He already understands. Simplifying your input treats a comprehension problem he does not have.

options.text: Write instructions out so he can read rather than listen
options.rationale: Writing helps a patient who cannot process speech. His problem is producing it.

options.text: Ask questions he can answer with a gesture or a yes, and allow time
options.rationale: Comprehension is intact and output is not, so you lower the cost of answering without lowering the content.

options.text: Exaggerate your mouth movements so he can follow the words visually
options.rationale: Exaggerated speech distorts the words and still addresses the wrong side of the deficit.

questions.takeaway: Expressive deficit: comprehension intact, output impaired. Adjust how he answers, not how you speak.
questions.strategy: Three options modify your speech. Ask which side of the exchange is broken.

strategies: Locate the deficit before choosing the adaptation
elimination.verdict: That leaves the yes or no and gesture approach.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a patient to draw up and inject her own insulin. Which evaluation measures learning in the psychomotor domain?

options.text: She lists the steps of the injection in the correct order
options.rationale: Ordering steps is knowledge and she can recite a sequence she cannot perform.

options.text: She names two sites and explains why she rotates them
options.rationale: Explaining is knowledge again, however well reasoned.

options.text: She says she feels ready to manage the injections at home
options.rationale: Feeling ready is attitude and belongs to the affective domain.

options.text: She draws up the ordered dose and injects it while the nurse watches
options.rationale: Psychomotor learning is evaluated by performance, not by description of performance.

questions.takeaway: Psychomotor learning is evaluated by return demonstration. Cognitive by explanation, affective by expressed values and feelings.
questions.strategy: Three options are good teaching evaluation of the wrong domain. Match the evaluation to the domain the question names.

strategies: Sort each option by domain
elimination.verdict: That leaves the return demonstration.

questions.stem: Four patients need discharge teaching this afternoon. Which one is ready to learn?

options.text: A man who asks how he will shower with his new drain in place
options.rationale: A question about managing the problem at home shows he has accepted it and is looking ahead, which is readiness.

options.text: A woman who says she will do whatever the nurse thinks is best
options.rationale: Deferring to the nurse is compliance and shows no engagement with the learning itself.

options.text: A man newly diagnosed with diabetes who says the laboratory must have mixed up his results
options.rationale: He has not accepted the diagnosis, so teaching has nothing to attach to.

options.text: A woman rating her incision pain at 8 of 10 who says she will try to concentrate
options.rationale: Pain at that level occupies attention and teaching will not be retained.

questions.takeaway: Readiness shows as engagement with the problem: asking how, planning, anticipating. Denial, deference and unrelieved pain all block it.
questions.strategy: Willingness is the trap, because it sounds like readiness. Unrelieved pain removes the attention learning requires.

strategies: Ask what each patient is doing with the information

steps.action: Asking how to manage at home

elimination.verdict: That leaves the man asking about the drain.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for surgery tomorrow says quietly that she keeps thinking about not waking up. Which response encourages her to say more?

options.text: Why does that thought keep coming back?
options.rationale: A why question asks her to justify a feeling and tends to close the conversation.

options.text: You are thinking about not waking up from the surgery.
options.rationale: Restating what she said hands it back to her and invites her to continue without steering her.

options.text: I felt the same way before my own surgery.
options.rationale: Self disclosure moves the focus to the nurse at the moment she was ready to speak.

options.text: Your surgeon has done hundreds of these operations.
options.rationale: Reassurance answers a fear she has not finished expressing and signals the subject is closed.

questions.takeaway: Restating keeps the patient talking and adds nothing of your own. Why questions, self disclosure and reassurance all redirect her.
questions.strategy: All four sound kind. Ask which one leaves her holding the conversation.

strategies: Ask where each response puts the focus
elimination.verdict: That leaves the restatement.

questions.stem: A patient nods at every instruction, agrees he understands, and asks the nurse to leave the booklet so he can read it at home when he has his glasses. Which action is best?

options.text: Provide a large print version of the booklet
options.rationale: The glasses may not be the obstacle and a bigger font does not test understanding.

options.text: Ask a family member to review the material with him later
options.rationale: This moves responsibility to someone who was not taught either, and nobody has checked whether they can read it.

options.text: Document that written material was provided and he verbalized understanding
options.rationale: Verbalized understanding here is a nod, and documenting it records something that was never checked.

options.text: Teach in plain language and have him tell you his plan
options.rationale: Agreeing without questions and deferring to reading later both suggest limited literacy. Plain language and teach-back check understanding without asking him to admit anything.

questions.takeaway: Nodding along, no questions, and taking the material home to read later are signals of limited health literacy. Verify with teach-back, not with a bigger booklet.
questions.strategy: He never says he cannot read, and the question is whether you recognize the pattern without being told.

strategies: Ask what has been confirmed

steps.action: Cut print size and the daughter

elimination.verdict: That leaves plain language and teach-back.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with age-related hearing loss struggles to follow the nurse in a busy room. Which adjustment helps most?

options.text: Face him, lower the pitch of your voice, and reduce the background noise
options.rationale: High frequencies are lost first, so a lower pitch carries. Facing him adds the visual cues and the noise competes directly with speech.

options.text: Raise your volume and repeat the same words until he responds
options.rationale: Volume distorts speech and repeating unchanged words gives him nothing new to work with.

options.text: Speak into his better ear from the side so the sound is closer
options.rationale: Speaking from the side removes his view of your face, which is where the remaining cues are.

options.text: Write out everything so hearing is not required
options.rationale: Writing is a fallback and abandons speech he can still use with the right conditions.

questions.takeaway: Age-related loss hits high frequencies first. Lower pitch, face the patient, cut the noise.
questions.strategy: Louder is the instinct and it is wrong, because the problem is frequency rather than loudness.

strategies: Ask what is lost and what remains
elimination.verdict: That leaves pitch, position and noise.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for a mastectomy says she is fine and ready while her jaw is tight and she will not look at the nurse. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept her statement and let her raise the subject when she is ready
options.rationale: Accepting the words alone ignores what the rest of her is saying.

options.text: Tell her it is normal to be frightened before this operation
options.rationale: Naming the feeling for her assumes a diagnosis of her emotion and may be wrong.

options.text: Name the difference between what she says and what you see, and ask about it
options.rationale: Naming the gap between the words and the behavior without interpreting it lets her decide what to do with it.

options.text: Ask whether she would like the chaplain to visit before the surgery
options.rationale: Referral hands the conversation to someone else before you have found out what is wrong.

questions.takeaway: When words and behavior disagree, say what you observe and let the patient resolve it. Do not choose for her which one is true.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a single move away from correct: it tells her what she feels instead of asking.

strategies: Ask who names the feeling
elimination.verdict: That leaves naming the discrepancy.

questions.stem: A nurse is in the orientation phase of a relationship with a newly admitted patient. Which activities belong to this phase? Select all that apply.

options.text: Agreeing with the patient on what the two of you will work on
options.rationale: Setting goals together is orientation work and it defines everything that follows.

options.text: Explaining what the patient can expect from you and over what period
options.rationale: Clarifying roles and the limits of the relationship belongs here.

options.text: Reviewing the chart and speaking with the previous shift before the first meeting
options.rationale: Gathering data before meeting the patient is preinteraction, which happens before orientation.

options.text: Assessing the patient's health status, strengths and concerns
options.rationale: Assessment in the first meetings is orientation.

options.text: Helping the patient express feelings about the diagnosis and work through them
options.rationale: Working through feelings and problems is the working phase.

options.text: Setting the tone by showing warmth and competence at the first meeting
options.rationale: Trust is established here and the rest of the relationship rests on it.

options.text: Summarizing what was accomplished and preparing the patient for discharge
options.rationale: Summarizing accomplishments and preparing for discharge is termination, which comes after the work is done.

questions.takeaway: Preinteraction is before you meet. Orientation sets tone, clarifies roles, assesses and sets goals. Working does the work. Termination summarizes and separates.
questions.strategy: The three wrong options are all real nursing activities from the phase before and the phases after. Place each one on the timeline.

strategies: Place each activity on the timeline
elimination.verdict: The four orientation activities are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to teach a patient who had a laryngectomy and writes his responses on a pad. Which nursing actions support the exchange? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allowing extra time for him to write out answers
options.rationale: Written answers take far longer than speech and rushing him ends the exchange.

options.text: Asking one question at a time
options.rationale: Stacked questions cannot be answered on a pad and he will answer only the last.

options.text: Watching his face and hands while he writes
options.rationale: Nonverbal communication carries more of the message when speech is unavailable.

options.text: Phrasing everything so it can be answered yes or no
options.rationale: Closed questions make it faster for the nurse and strip him of the ability to say anything you did not anticipate.

options.text: Speaking at a normal volume and rate
options.rationale: His hearing is unaffected and raising your voice is a common and pointless reflex.

options.text: Finishing his sentences when his meaning is clear
options.rationale: Completing his words saves time and takes the exchange away from him.

questions.takeaway: Output is impaired and input is not. Give him time, keep questions single, read his nonverbal signals, and let him finish.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options make the conversation faster for the nurse. Speed is not the goal.

strategies: Ask who each action serves

steps.action: Time, single questions, normal volume, watching
Yes or no phrasing and finishing sentences

elimination.verdict: The four supporting actions are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure is to be discharged on a new diuretic and a daily weight log. Which findings suggest teaching will not succeed as planned? Select all that apply.

options.text: He says his late wife always handled the medicines
options.rationale: He is telling you he has never managed a regimen and the plan assumes he can.

options.text: He has no scale at home
options.rationale: A daily weight log without a scale cannot be carried out, however well he understands it.

options.text: He asks whether the new pill will make him get up at night
options.rationale: A specific practical question about living with the drug is engagement. It is the finding that most looks like a problem and is not.

options.text: He repeats the instructions back word for word from the handout
options.rationale: Verbatim repetition shows memory of the words rather than understanding, and it hides a gap.

options.text: He says he will start the weights once he feels stronger
options.rationale: Deferring the behavior signals he has not accepted that it is part of his treatment now.

options.text: He wears reading glasses to look at the handout
options.rationale: Corrected vision is not a barrier.

questions.takeaway: Teaching fails on ability, resources and acceptance. A practical question about the drug is engagement, and verbatim repetition hides a gap.
questions.strategy: One option is engagement dressed as a problem and one is a problem already solved. Separate what blocks learning from what only looks awkward.

strategies: Ask whether each finding blocks the plan

steps.action: The nocturia question and the reading glasses

elimination.verdict: The four blocking findings are selected.

questions.stem: Four days after a stroke a patient speaks in long fluent sentences that do not answer what was asked. He does not follow a one-step instruction and seems untroubled that the conversation is not working. How does the nurse adapt?

options.text: Write the questions down so he can read them at his own pace
options.rationale: Reading comprehension is usually affected alongside listening comprehension, so this changes the channel and not the barrier.

options.text: Use gestures and demonstration, give one idea at a time, and judge whether he understood by what he does rather than what he says
options.rationale: Comprehension is the impaired side here. Speech output is fluent and empty, so his words cannot be used to check whether the message arrived.

options.text: Give him extra time to find his words and ask him questions that he is able to answer with a yes or a no
options.rationale: These are the right adaptations for the opposite problem. A patient who cannot understand the question gains nothing from being given longer to answer it, and a yes means nothing.

options.text: Speak more loudly and more slowly
options.rationale: Volume treats a hearing problem. His hearing is intact and the words are arriving without meaning.

questions.takeaway: Work out which side is broken before adapting. Impaired output needs time and yes-or-no questions. Impaired comprehension needs gestures, demonstration and evidence from behavior.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides it is that he is not frustrated. A patient who knows what he wants to say and cannot say it is frustrated.

strategies: Identify which half of communication failed
elimination.verdict: Gestures, one idea, check by behavior.

questions.stem: A man admitted with complications of cirrhosis tells the nurse he has had the lecture about drinking from three doctors and his sister, and does not need it from her. Which response best fits a motivational approach?

options.text: It sounds like you are not ready to discuss this. I will come back later
options.rationale: The closest wrong answer. It respects his autonomy and abandons the conversation, and not ready is a conclusion he did not state.

options.text: I understand, and your liver numbers are worse than they were last admission and you should know what that means for the next year
