questions.takeaway: Sleep hygiene: consistent times including weekends, avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals near bedtime, limit screens and reserve the bed for sleep, daytime exercise not within 1 to 2 hours of bed, relaxation techniques.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds restful and contradicts reserving the bed for sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contradicts reserving the bed for sleep.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to improve sleep for patients on a busy medical unit. Which intervention addresses the most common modifiable cause of nighttime awakening in hospital?

options.text: Dim the lights throughout the evening hours
options.rationale: Useful, supporting melatonin release. It does not stop anyone entering the room.

options.text: Close doors and lower the alarm volumes
options.rationale: Noise control is recognized and it addresses a different disruption. The commonest cause is being woken on purpose.

options.text: Position patients for comfort and airway safety
options.rationale: Positioning is recognized, and it addresses comfort rather than the number of times he is woken.

options.text: Cluster nursing care to reduce nighttime interruptions
options.rationale: Clustering care is the first thing to change in the hospital environment, because interruptions are the cause nursing controls most directly.

questions.takeaway: Hospital sleep interventions: cluster care, dim lights in the evening, control noise, and position for comfort and airway safety.
questions.strategy: All four belong on the list. The question asks which addresses the most common modifiable cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both real and neither stops entries.

elimination.verdict: That leaves clustering care.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man in intensive care has been sleeping poorly and is becoming confused at night. Which evidence-based intervention should the nurse consider?

options.text: A benzodiazepine at bedtime to establish a sleep pattern
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines carry a risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and confusion is already present.

options.text: Moving him to a single room away from the nursing station
options.rationale: May reduce noise and it distances him from observation in a unit where he needs it, and it is not the intervention with the evidence behind it.

options.text: A sleep bundle including earplugs, eye masks and lavender aromatherapy
options.rationale: Sleep bundles have shown measurable benefit in intensive care, reducing delirium and improving perceived sleep quality.

options.text: Allowing him to sleep during the day to make up the deficit
options.rationale: Daytime sleep reduces the drive to sleep at night and worsens the circadian disruption.

questions.takeaway: Sleep bundles in intensive care use earplugs, eye masks and aromatherapy. They reduce delirium and improve perceived sleep quality.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats confusion with a drug that causes confusion. Ask what the evidence supports in this setting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Causes the problem it is meant to treat.

steps.action: Cut daytime sleep and the room move
steps.detail: One worsens the rhythm, one reduces observation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the sleep bundle.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient is 71, admitted three days ago with a chest infection. Reports sleeping poorly since admission. Furosemide scheduled at 2000. Chest discomfort rated 6 of 10 overnight, no analgesia given since 2200. Overhead light switched on each time staff enter. Vital signs taken separately by three different staff members between 2300 and 0500. Drinks one cup of coffee at breakfast. Has a history of hypertension managed with medication. Slept well at home before admission. Room is shared with one other patient.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings contributing to his poor sleep that nursing can modify.

segments.text: Overhead light switched on each time staff enter
segments.rationale: Dimming lights during evening hours supports melatonin release. Using a task light is a nursing decision.

segments.text: Drinks one cup of coffee at breakfast
segments.rationale: Caffeine matters close to bedtime. One cup at breakfast is not what is waking him at 0300.

segments.text: Furosemide scheduled at 2000
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia. The nurse cannot change the order alone and raising it with the provider is squarely nursing work.

segments.text: Room is shared with one other patient
segments.rationale: A real source of disruption and not something nursing can modify on a full unit. Noise control is addressed differently.

segments.text: Chest discomfort 6 of 10 overnight with no analgesia since 2200
segments.rationale: Pain is a recognized cause of disrupted sleep in older adults, and this is uncontrolled and within nursing control.

segments.text: History of hypertension managed with medication
segments.rationale: Hypertension managed on medication is a stable condition, and nothing about it is waking him at night.

segments.text: Slept well at home before admission
segments.rationale: The finding that tells you this is situational rather than a chronic sleep disorder. Useful, and not a modifiable cause.

segments.text: Vital signs taken separately by three staff members between 2300 and 0500
segments.rationale: Clustering care is the first named hospital intervention, and three separate entries is the clearest example of what it prevents.

questions.takeaway: Cluster care, control light and noise, treat pain, and review medication timing. Those are the four levers nursing holds.
questions.strategy: One finding tells you the problem is situational rather than chronic, and that is why it is in the list. One is real and outside nursing's control.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One cup at breakfast is not the cause.

elimination.verdict: s1, s3, s5, and s8: the four modifiable causes.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a sleep history. Which source of information is primary?

options.text: The overnight nurse's observations of when he appeared asleep
options.rationale: Useful supporting data, and appearing asleep is not the same as sleeping. Only he knows what the night was like.

options.text: The number of hours recorded on the flow sheet
options.rationale: A flow sheet counts observed time. It misses the awakenings and says nothing about quality.

options.text: His partner's account of his sleep pattern
options.rationale: Valuable for witnessed events such as apnea or movement, and it is a supplementary source rather than the primary one.

options.text: The patient's own report of the sleep pattern
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective and the patient is the primary source. Perceived quality matters as much as the hours.

questions.takeaway: Sleep is subjective. The patient is the primary source: bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are useful supporting sources. The question asks which is primary.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supplementary, and essential for witnessed apnea.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the patient's own report.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with insomnia asks for something to help her sleep. She has already tried a consistent bedtime and reduced her evening caffeine. Which is the most appropriate first pharmacological option to discuss?

options.text: Trazodone
options.rationale: A safer alternative for older or depressed patients, and it sits behind melatonin rather than ahead of it.

options.text: Melatonin
options.rationale: Treated as generally safe and specifically useful in older adults whose own melatonin production has fallen.

options.text: A benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Short-term use only, with risk of falls, confusion and respiratory depression in older adults.

options.text: Diphenhydramine
options.rationale: Anticholinergic, and it causes confusion and falls in older adults. Availability is not safety.

questions.takeaway: Non-drug strategies come first. Melatonin is generally safe, benzodiazepines are short-term only, and trazodone is a safer alternative for older or depressed patients.
questions.strategy: The stem says non-drug strategies have already been tried, which is the only reason a medication is on the table. Rank the options by risk in an older adult.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Anticholinergic, and dangerous in older adults.

elimination.verdict: That leaves melatonin.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's medications as part of a sleep assessment. Which are recognized as affecting sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Opiates
options.rationale: Opiates are recognized alongside antidepressants and anticonvulsants, and they worsen sleep-disordered breathing too.

options.text: Benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Carries risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and it is intended for short-term use only.

options.text: Acetaminophen taken for mild pain
options.rationale: Not a sleep-affecting drug, and treating pain usually improves sleep. The trap is selecting every medication that appears on a list.

options.text: Inhaled bronchodilators taken in the morning
options.rationale: Not one of the agents in question, and morning dosing does not disrupt sleep. Diuretic timing is the recognized problem here, not bronchodilators.

options.text: Anticonvulsants
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants are recognized, and the daytime drowsiness they cause often gets mistaken for a bad night.

options.text: Antidepressants
options.rationale: Antidepressants are recognized among the agents that suppress REM and leave daytime drowsiness behind.

options.text: Caffeine, nicotine and alcohol
options.rationale: These are recognized as common but underreported disruptors, and patients rarely count tea, soda or a nightcap.

questions.takeaway: Medications and sleep: caffeine, nicotine and alcohol; benzodiazepines; antidepressants, opiates and anticonvulsants suppressing REM; diuretic timing.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a drug class not on the list, taken at a time that would not affect sleep anyway.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Substances, benzodiazepines, REM suppressors, diuretic timing.
Not named, and timed away from sleep.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient's family says they co-sleep with their toddler and asks whether the nurse disapproves. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that co-sleeping is unsafe and should be discontinued
options.rationale: Delivers a verdict rather than a conversation, and it is likely to end the discussion of safety entirely.

options.text: Acknowledge the practice and discuss safety considerations without judgment
options.rationale: Respect the practice and talk about safety without judgment. That keeps the conversation open and still covers the risk.

options.text: Tell them the practice is entirely a family matter
options.rationale: This avoids the safety discussion the nurse is well placed to have. Respecting a practice does not mean saying nothing.

options.text: Refer them to the pediatrician for advice about sleeping arrangements
options.rationale: Passes on a conversation within nursing scope, and it implies the topic is too difficult to discuss.

questions.takeaway: Respect cultural sleep practices such as co-sleeping, and discuss safety without judgment.
questions.strategy: One distractor avoids the safety topic and one delivers it as a verdict. The instruction is to do both things at once.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves acknowledging it and discussing safety.

questions.stem: A patient has taken a benzodiazepine nightly for three weeks. The nurse stops it abruptly at discharge at his request. Which does the nurse monitor for?

options.text: Increased REM sleep resolving his daytime drowsiness
options.rationale: REM does rebound, and the presentation is disrupted sleep rather than resolution of drowsiness.

options.text: Immediate improvement in sleep quality
options.rationale: This is not what follows stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly after three weeks of nightly use.

options.text: Rebound insomnia, with sleep worse than before the drug was started
options.rationale: Part of the nursing role: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.

options.text: No change, since three weeks is too short for dependence
options.rationale: Three weeks of nightly use is long enough for rebound insomnia, and that is the reason short-term use is specified.

questions.takeaway: Nursing role with sleep medications: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats three weeks as too brief to matter. Short-term use is specified because this is what happens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves rebound insomnia.

questions.stem: A patient on bedrest for five days reports feeling exhausted despite lying still most of the day. Which understanding guides the nurse's response?

options.text: Rest is mental and physical calm, not simply inactivity
options.rationale: the standard wording. Rest is not the absence of activity, and it is not a substitute for sleep.

options.text: Rest is any period when the patient is not moving
options.rationale: This equates rest with inactivity, and the two are deliberately separate. He has been still for five days and is exhausted.

options.text: Rest requires that the patient first be free of pain
options.rationale: Pain makes rest harder and it does not make rest impossible. His pain is not the issue here.

options.text: Rest and sleep meet the body's needs interchangeably
options.rationale: Both are basic needs and they are not the same. Sleep does things rest cannot.

questions.takeaway: Sleep and rest are as essential as nutrition and exercise. Rest is a state of mental, physical and spiritual calm rather than inactivity.
questions.strategy: One distractor collapses rest and sleep into the same thing. The two are deliberately kept separate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut interchangeable and the pain condition

elimination.verdict: That leaves rest as a state of calm.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 82-year-old woman has slept four hours a night for three nights. Which safety concern should the nurse prioritize?

options.text: Delayed wound healing from reduced growth hormone
options.rationale: A real consequence of poor sleep, but it is not the immediate safety concern.

options.text: Impaired immune function raising infection risk
options.rationale: This is real, but it develops over a longer period than the next few hours. The fall could happen tonight.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance requiring more analgesia
options.rationale: This is real, and it concerns comfort and pain management rather than immediate safety.

options.text: Increased fall risk from confusion and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation produces confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk, and excessive daytime sleepiness raises it further in older adults.

questions.takeaway: Sleep deprivation causes confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk. Sleep disturbances affect patient safety directly.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuine consequences of poor sleep. The question asks specifically about safety.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves fall risk.

questions.stem: A nurse teaching a sleep hygiene class describes sleep in older adults. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Older adults need less sleep, so fragmented sleep is not a concern."
options.rationale: Their pattern changes and their need does not. Around 30 to 40% report sleep problems, and treating fragmentation as expected means it goes unassessed.

options.text: “The patient is the primary source of information about their own sleep.”
options.rationale: This is accurate, because sleep is subjective. What he reports outranks what you observed.

options.text: "Non-drug strategies come first and sedatives are a last resort."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the stated order. Non-drug strategies first, sedatives last.

options.text: "Sleep deprivation raises fall risk through confusion and slowed reflexes."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is why sleep belongs on the safety list rather than the comfort list.

questions.takeaway: Older adults sleep less and their sleep is fragmented. That is a change in pattern, not a reduced need, and problems still require assessment.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth uses an expected pattern to dismiss a problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drug order, primary source, fall risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reduced-need statement.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has slept in a chair for four nights because lying flat leaves him breathless. He asks the nurse to get him something to help him sleep. He is using his inhalers correctly, his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air, and his pain is 1 of 10. He says he is exhausted and cannot think straight.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and support him with pillows so he can sleep in bed
options.rationale: Positioning for comfort and airway safety is a named hospital intervention. A chair gives him neither proper rest nor proper positioning.

options.text: Cluster overnight care and reduce light and noise during the night
options.rationale: The environmental interventions named first for the hospital setting, and four nights of poor sleep needs every lever pulled.

options.text: Reassure him that sleeping in a chair is adequate rest
options.rationale: A chair rarely allows the deep sleep that repairs tissue, and four nights of it is already showing in his thinking.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so he can settle
options.rationale: Sedatives depress respiration, which is the opposite of what a patient breathless on lying flat can afford. Non-drug strategies come first.

options.text: Sleep disrupted by a positioning need arising from his respiratory disease
options.rationale: Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning needs and breathlessness. The cause is mechanical and it is solvable.

options.text: Insomnia requiring pharmacological management
options.rationale: Names the symptom and reaches for a drug. He is not failing to fall asleep; he cannot lie down.

options.text: Uncontrolled pain preventing sleep
options.rationale: His pain is 1 of 10. The stem rules this out directly.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea causing fragmented sleep
options.rationale: No snoring or witnessed pauses are described, and his difficulty is with lying flat rather than with obstruction during sleep.

options.text: The number of hours recorded as asleep on the flow sheet
options.rationale: A flow sheet records observed time rather than experienced sleep, and it misses every awakening.

options.text: Whether he is able to sleep in bed rather than the chair
options.rationale: This measures whether the positioning change actually solved the mechanical problem keeping him in the chair.

options.text: Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%
options.rationale: This is a real respiratory parameter, and it was already 93 percent before anything changed.

options.text: His own report of sleep quality the following morning
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective, so the patient's perception is the measure. Compare it with his report from the previous nights.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning and breathlessness. Fix the position before reaching for a drug, and evaluate sleep by what the patient reports.
questions.strategy: He asks for a sedative, which is the pull. His pain and saturation are given to rule out the two obvious alternatives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Depresses respiration in a patient who cannot spare it.

elimination.verdict: Reposition and cluster care, for a positioning problem, evaluated by where he sleeps and what he reports.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old says she wakes four or five times a night and is up for good by five. Her daughter is worried something is wrong. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Sleep need drops with age, so six hours is enough for her now
options.rationale: The amount of sleep needed stays about the same. What changes is the ability to get it in one block.

options.text: More awakenings and an earlier wake time are expected with age, and her total sleep still matters
options.rationale: Older adults spend more time in light sleep and less in deep sleep, so they wake more easily. The requirement itself does not fall.

options.text: Frequent awakening at her age points to an underlying sleep disorder
options.rationale: Awakening is expected, and treating a normal change as pathology leads to unnecessary sedatives.

options.text: She should stay in bed longer in the morning to make up the lost hours
options.rationale: Extending time in bed fragments sleep further and weakens the association between bed and sleeping.

questions.takeaway: Age changes sleep architecture, not sleep requirement. More light sleep, more awakenings, earlier rising, same need.
questions.strategy: The idea that older adults need less sleep is the most common belief about aging, and it is false.

strategies: Separate architecture from requirement

steps.action: Cut less sleep needed and the disorder

elimination.verdict: That leaves the accurate explanation.

questions.stem: A man says he has insomnia and cannot stay asleep. He falls asleep in the waiting room, and his wife reports loud snoring with pauses in his breathing. His blood pressure is 158/94. Which problem does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Insomnia, since he describes difficulty maintaining sleep
options.rationale: Insomnia is his description of the result. The question is what is waking him.

options.text: Circadian rhythm disruption from his schedule
options.rationale: Nothing here points to a shifted schedule.

options.text: Restless legs syndrome causing repeated arousals
options.rationale: Restless legs produces an urge to move the legs, which is not reported.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Witnessed apneic pauses, loud snoring, daytime sleepiness and hypertension make the pattern.

questions.takeaway: A patient reports the symptom and the partner reports the cause. Snoring with witnessed pauses plus daytime sleepiness is apnea until proven otherwise.
questions.strategy: He hands you a diagnosis in his first sentence. The wife's report is what reframes it.

strategies: Separate the complaint from the findings
elimination.verdict: That leaves obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.stem: A patient says a few drinks before bed are the only thing that gets him to sleep. Which explanation should the nurse give?

options.text: Alcohol speeds sleep onset and then fragments the second half of the night
options.rationale: It is sedating at first and the sleep that follows is disrupted, with awakening in the early morning hours.

options.text: Alcohol has no effect on sleep quality as long as the amount is modest
options.rationale: Even modest amounts alter sleep architecture.

options.text: Alcohol increases deep sleep, which is why he feels he sleeps better
options.rationale: Deep sleep is not increased by it in a sustained way and the overall quality falls.

options.text: Alcohol is an acceptable sleep aid if he avoids prescription hypnotics
options.rationale: Substituting one depressant for another is not the point and the sleep is still disrupted.

questions.takeaway: Alcohol gets you to sleep faster and keeps you asleep worse. The second half of the night is where it shows.
questions.strategy: He is reporting a real effect, so do not deny it. Explain what happens after it.

strategies: Separate onset from maintenance

steps.action: Cut no effect and increased deep sleep

elimination.verdict: That leaves the onset and fragmentation explanation.

questions.stem: A patient on a medical unit has had no uninterrupted stretch longer than forty minutes for two nights. Which action helps most?

options.text: Offer the ordered sleep medication at bedtime
options.rationale: Medication does not stop the interruptions and sedation plus repeated waking is worse than either alone.

options.text: Close his door and turn off the overhead light
options.rationale: Useful, but it does not address what is waking him.

options.text: Cluster night care so he gets blocks of at least ninety minutes
options.rationale: A full sleep cycle runs about ninety minutes, and clustering care protects whole cycles rather than minutes.

options.text: Move him to a room farther from the nurses' station
options.rationale: Reasonable, but it does nothing about the staff entering the room.

questions.takeaway: Sleep restores in cycles of about ninety minutes. Cluster care to protect whole cycles rather than trimming noise around the edges.
questions.strategy: The other three are all genuine sleep hygiene measures for a problem he does not have. Ask what has been waking him.

strategies: Name the cause of the awakenings
elimination.verdict: That leaves grouping the care.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old is started on a hypnotic for insomnia during a hospital stay. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Teach her the medication is intended for short-term use only
options.rationale: True, but it does not address what could happen tonight.

options.text: Assess her for next-day drowsiness and put fall precautions in place
options.rationale: Sedatives in older adults carry residual sedation, confusion and falls, and the fall is the harm that arrives first.

options.text: Instruct her to take the dose at the same time each night
options.rationale: Timing matters and it is not the priority.

options.text: Monitor for tolerance developing over the course of the admission
options.rationale: Tolerance is a longer-term concern.

questions.takeaway: Hypnotics in older adults mean residual sedation, confusion and falls. Safety precautions come before teaching about the drug.
questions.strategy: Three options are correct teaching. Ask which one prevents harm tonight.

strategies: Ask what harm comes first
elimination.verdict: That leaves the fall precautions.

questions.stem: A patient with insomnia reviews what he has learned. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: I will get up and go to another room if I am still awake after about twenty minutes
options.rationale: Getting up after about twenty minutes is right, because lying awake teaches the bed to mean wakefulness.

options.text: I will get up at the same time every morning even after a bad night
options.rationale: A fixed rise time is right, because it is what anchors the rhythm.

options.text: I will have my coffee before two in the afternoon and not after
options.rationale: Limiting caffeine by early afternoon is right, since its half-life is long enough to matter in the evening.

options.text: I will stay in bed and keep trying to fall asleep so I at least get the rest
options.rationale: Lying in bed awake strengthens the association between the bed and being awake, which makes the insomnia worse.

questions.takeaway: The bed is for sleeping. Awake longer than about twenty minutes means getting up, and the rise time stays fixed regardless of the night before.
questions.strategy: Staying in bed sounds like the restful choice, and it is the one behavior that maintains insomnia.

strategies: Ask what each statement conditions the bed to mean

steps.action: Getting up, fixed rise, caffeine limit

elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement about staying in bed.

questions.stem: A young man is newly diagnosed with narcolepsy after falling asleep mid-conversation and having his knees buckle when he laughs. Which instruction is the priority?

options.text: Do not drive until your provider clears you
options.rationale: Sudden sleep attacks and loss of muscle tone behind the wheel are lethal, and safety comes before everything else in the plan.

options.text: Take short scheduled naps during the day
options.rationale: Helpful, but it is not what prevents a death.

options.text: Avoid heavy meals and alcohol, which worsen sleepiness
options.rationale: Avoiding heavy meals and alcohol reduces daytime sleepiness, and it prevents nothing fatal.

options.text: Tell your employer so accommodations can be arranged
options.rationale: Telling the employer allows accommodations and it is not urgent tonight.

questions.takeaway: Narcolepsy brings sudden sleep attacks and loss of muscle tone with emotion. Driving restriction comes first.
questions.strategy: Three options are correct management. Rank by what is lethal.

strategies: Rank by consequence
elimination.verdict: That leaves the driving restriction.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient who has slept poorly for two weeks. Which findings are consistent with sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Difficulty concentrating and slowed responses
options.rationale: Cognitive slowing is among the earliest effects.

options.text: Irritability out of proportion to the situation
options.rationale: Emotional regulation falls off quickly with lost sleep.

options.text: Increased sensitivity to pain
options.rationale: Deprivation lowers the pain threshold, which matters in any patient reporting worse pain.

options.text: Hand tremor and poor fine motor control
options.rationale: Fine motor control degrades with deprivation.

options.text: A rise in core body temperature above 38 degrees Celsius
options.rationale: Fever is not a feature of sleep loss and points elsewhere.

options.text: Falling asleep briefly without intending to
options.rationale: Brief involuntary sleep episodes appear as deprivation accumulates.

options.text: Blurred vision
options.rationale: Visual disturbance is reported with ongoing deprivation.

options.text: Pupils that are unequal in size
options.rationale: Unequal pupils are a neurological finding and have nothing to do with lost sleep.

questions.takeaway: Sleep deprivation shows as cognitive slowing, irritability, lower pain threshold, motor and visual disturbance, and intrusion of sleep into waking.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options are findings that would send you looking somewhere else: one at infection, one at the nervous system.

strategies: Treat each finding as true or false
elimination.verdict: Everything but the fever is selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans sleep promotion for an adult admitted to a medical unit. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the usual bedtime routine the patient follows at home
options.rationale: Familiar rituals cue sleep and the hospital removes almost all of them.

options.text: Offer a light carbohydrate snack if the patient wants one
options.rationale: A light snack is appropriate and a heavy meal is not.

options.text: Dim the lights and reduce corridor noise during the night
options.rationale: Light and noise are the two most cited hospital disruptors.

options.text: Encourage a daytime nap of two to three hours to catch up
options.rationale: A long daytime nap reduces the drive to sleep at night and worsens the pattern.

options.text: Have the patient empty the bladder before settling
options.rationale: Removing a predictable reason to wake protects the first cycle.

options.text: Position the call light within reach and explain when you will return
options.rationale: Knowing when the next interruption comes reduces the vigilance that keeps patients awake.

options.text: Provide caffeinated tea if the patient normally drinks it in the evening
options.rationale: Keeping a routine does not extend to a stimulant before bed.

questions.takeaway: Protect the home routine, reduce light and noise, remove reasons to wake, and tell the patient when you will be back.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options are dressed as respecting the patient's habits. Routine does not override physiology.

strategies: Ask whether each action protects or shortens sleep

steps.action: Routine, snack, dark, voiding, call light

elimination.verdict: The five protective interventions are selected.

questions.stem: Which patients are at increased risk for disturbed sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: A woman on a corticosteroid taper for an asthma exacerbation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids disrupt sleep and the effect is dose related.

options.text: A man who works rotating twelve-hour shifts
options.rationale: Shifting schedules keep the circadian rhythm from settling.

options.text: A patient receiving a diuretic at eight in the evening
options.rationale: Evening dosing produces nocturia and repeated awakenings.

options.text: A man with chronic pain rated at 6 of 10 most nights
options.rationale: Pain both delays onset and fragments maintenance.

options.text: A woman taking a daily multivitamin with breakfast
options.rationale: A morning multivitamin has no effect on sleep.

options.text: A patient with heart failure who becomes short of breath when lying flat
options.rationale: Orthopnea prevents the position sleep requires.

options.text: A man newly widowed three weeks ago
options.rationale: Grief and anxiety are among the most common causes of disrupted sleep.

options.text: A man who drinks one cup of coffee with breakfast
options.rationale: Caffeine in the morning clears long before bedtime.

questions.takeaway: Sleep is disrupted by drugs, by schedules, by symptoms that will not let the body settle, and by distress.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options involve a substance, which is enough to make them look like risks. Ask whether it is still acting at bedtime.

strategies: Ask what each risk acts through
elimination.verdict: Everything but the multivitamin is selected.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she is asleep within about ten minutes of lying down, then wakes around 0200 most nights and lies there for two hours before drifting off again. Which intervention fits the problem she described?

options.text: Nap in the early afternoon to make up some of the hours she is losing overnight
options.rationale: Napping lowers the pressure to sleep at night and makes the 0200 waking longer.

options.text: Add a warm bath and a wind-down routine in the hour before bed, with the lights kept low so her body learns the hour means sleep
options.rationale: A good intervention for the opposite problem. She already falls asleep in ten minutes, so nothing about the approach to sleep needs fixing.

options.text: Get out of bed after twenty minutes awake, do something quiet in low light, and return when sleepy, with the rise time fixed
options.rationale: Her trouble is staying asleep, and lying awake for two hours teaches the bed to mean wakefulness. Leaving and returning breaks that, and a fixed rise time protects the drive to sleep the next night.

options.text: Request a hypnotic to take at bedtime
options.rationale: Behavioral measures come first, and a drug taken at bedtime does little for a wakening five hours later except leave residual sedation in the morning.

questions.takeaway: Insomnia has two shapes and they need different interventions. Trouble falling asleep is treated at the start of the night. Trouble staying asleep is treated with stimulus control and a fixed rise time.
questions.strategy: Read which half of the night is broken before choosing. Two of these options treat the half that is working.

strategies: Locate the problem in the night
elimination.verdict: Stimulus control with a fixed rise time.

questions.stem: A woman says that on most evenings, once she sits down, her legs build up a feeling that she has to move them. Getting up and walking relieves it within seconds and the feeling returns when she sits again. It is worst between about 2100 and midnight. She describes no pain and no cramping. Which does this fit?

options.text: Restless legs syndrome
options.rationale: An urge to move, worse at rest, worse in the evening, and relieved immediately by movement. Those four features together belong to this and to nothing else.

options.text: Nocturnal leg cramps
options.rationale: Cramps are sudden, painful and involve a palpably contracted muscle. She reports no pain at all.

options.text: Periodic limb movement disorder
options.rationale: The other strong option. Those movements happen during sleep, are usually reported by a bed partner, and the patient is unaware of them. Hers happen while she is awake and sitting.

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy
options.rationale: A real contender, since neuropathic symptoms are often worse at night. Neuropathy does not produce an urge to move and is not relieved by walking.

questions.takeaway: The urge to move and relief by movement are what separate this from everything else that bothers legs at night. Pain points elsewhere.
questions.strategy: Three options are real conditions affecting legs at night. Find the two features the stem gives that only one of them has.

strategies: Match the feature set, not the body part
elimination.verdict: Restless legs syndrome.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man's wife reports that over the past few months he has started shouting and swinging his arms while asleep, and last week caught her across the face. When she wakes him he is immediately alert and describes a dream that matches what he was doing. Which does the nurse plan around?

options.text: Nocturnal seizures, with a neurology referral as the first step
options.rationale: Worth excluding and the picture does not fit. Seizure activity is stereotyped and followed by a period of confusion rather than immediate clear recall.

options.text: Sleepwalking, with bedroom safety as the first intervention
options.rationale: The safety intervention is identical, which is what makes this tempting. Sleepwalking happens early in the night out of deep non-dreaming sleep, the person is confused when woken, and there is no dream to report.

options.text: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, with bedroom safety as the first intervention
options.rationale: Acting out a dream that the patient can recall on waking is the defining feature, and it appears in later life. The muscle paralysis that normally accompanies dreaming has failed.

options.text: Night terrors, with reassurance for his wife as the first step
options.rationale: These bring a scream, a surge of heart rate and sweating, and no memory of anything afterward. They belong mostly to childhood.

questions.takeaway: Dream recall on waking is the finding that separates this from the parasomnias that arise from deep sleep. Safety for the bed partner comes before anything else.
questions.strategy: Two options lead to the same first action. The question is still asking you to name it, and one detail in the stem does that.

strategies: Find the detail that distinguishes dreaming sleep
elimination.verdict: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder.

questions.stem: A man with a long history of loud snoring and pauses witnessed by his wife, never investigated, is one night after abdominal surgery. He has patient-controlled analgesia with an opioid and oxygen by nasal cannula. He is asleep and his oxygen saturation reads 94 percent. What concerns the nurse most?

options.text: A saturation of 94 percent in a sleeping postoperative patient shows hypoventilation and calls for immediate intervention, with oxygen already running at the prescribed flow
options.rationale: Taken on its own that value is unremarkable. Treating the number as the finding is how the real risk gets missed in both directions.

options.text: The patient-controlled analgesia should be discontinued until he is fully awake
options.rationale: Pain after abdominal surgery has to be treated and worsens breathing if it is not. The answer is monitoring and settings, not removing analgesia.

options.text: He should be repositioned supine so that the airway is brought into line
options.rationale: Supine is the worst position for an obstructing airway. Side-lying or head of bed raised is what helps.

options.text: Supplemental oxygen can hold the saturation in range while carbon dioxide climbs, so the monitor will not show the problem developing
options.rationale: Oxygen treats the desaturation and not the hypoventilation. With untreated sleep apnea and an opioid on board, the thing to watch is respiratory rate and depth of sedation, not the pulse oximeter.

questions.takeaway: In untreated sleep apnea with opioids, oxygen masks the warning. Monitor respiratory rate and sedation level, because saturation falls last.
questions.strategy: Two options are built on the saturation reading. Ask what that number can and cannot tell you in a patient receiving oxygen.

strategies: Ask what the monitor measures
elimination.verdict: Saturation will not show the carbon dioxide rising.

questions.stem: Which findings should lead the nurse to recommend evaluation in a sleep clinic? Select all that apply.

options.text: Feeling sleepy on the drive home after a run of night shifts
options.rationale: An expected consequence of the schedule. It is worth planning around and it is not a disorder of sleep itself.

options.text: Waking twice nightly to pass urine in a 70-year-old who takes a diuretic at suppertime
options.rationale: Move the dose to the morning and see what is left. Fix the obvious cause before referring.

options.text: Morning headaches with daytime sleepiness in a man with a thick neck and untreated hypertension
options.rationale: Morning headache suggests overnight carbon dioxide retention, and the rest of the picture fits the same diagnosis.

options.text: Falling asleep while stopped at traffic lights
options.rationale: Sleepiness that intrudes during an activity like driving is both a diagnostic red flag and an immediate safety problem.

options.text: Acting out dreams, with a bed partner injured
options.rationale: Dream enactment needs evaluation, and the injury makes it urgent.

options.text: One broken night after a difficult day at work
options.rationale: A single night is not a sleep disorder.

options.text: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing that a partner has watched
options.rationale: A witnessed pause is the single most useful piece of history for obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.takeaway: Refer for what is persistent, dangerous, or unexplained. A single bad night, an obvious schedule effect, and a problem a medication change would solve are not referrals.
questions.strategy: Two distractors have a cause sitting in the stem. Ask whether anything simpler would fix it first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Witnessed pauses, sleeping at the wheel, the morning headache picture, and dream enactment are selected.

chapters.title: The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus
chapters.subtitle: Glands and hormones, feedback mechanisms, endocrine dysfunction, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, hypo- and hyperglycemia, DKA and HHS, insulin safety, and patient education

sources.title: The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus
sources.label: Iggy Ch. 56 · The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus

questions.scenario: A nurse assesses four patients in an endocrine clinic.
questions.stem: For each set of findings, indicate whether it suggests an overactive or underactive gland.

rows.text: Tingling around the mouth, muscle spasm, and a positive Chvostek sign
rows.rationale: Too little parathyroid hormone drops the calcium, and low calcium makes nerves and muscles irritable.

rows.text: Muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones with a raised serum calcium
rows.rationale: Too much parathyroid hormone pulls calcium out of bone, and the high calcium produces weakness, confusion and stones.

rows.text: Weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, pulse 118
rows.rationale: Hyperthyroidism. Too much hormone speeds metabolism up, so everything runs fast and hot.

rows.text: Fatigue, weight gain on a normal intake, cold intolerance, constipation, pulse 52
rows.rationale: Metabolism has slowed, so everything runs slow and cold. That is an underactive thyroid.

questions.takeaway: Thyroid: hyper runs fast and hot, hypo runs slow and cold. Parathyroid: hyper raises calcium and weakens, hypo lowers calcium and irritates.
questions.strategy: The parathyroid pair inverts the pattern. High calcium sedates nerve and muscle; low calcium excites them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Sort the thyroid pair by speed
steps.detail: Fast and hot, or slow and cold.

steps.action: Sort the parathyroid pair by calcium

steps.detail: A sign of low calcium, not high.

elimination.verdict: Two overactive, two underactive.

questions.stem: A patient asks why her insulin lowers her blood glucose but does nothing to her hair or her bones, when it travels everywhere in her blood. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Only cells carrying insulin receptors respond to the hormone
options.rationale: Receptor specificity determines which tissues are affected. The hormone circulates everywhere and acts only where it can bind.

options.text: Each tissue produces its own insulin according to its needs
options.rationale: Insulin is produced by the pancreas. Local production is not how the endocrine system works.

options.text: Insulin is broken down before reaching tissues without receptors
options.rationale: Nothing selectively destroys it en route. It has no effect where there is nothing to bind.

options.text: Insulin is delivered selectively to tissues that need glucose
options.rationale: Hormones travel through the bloodstream to the whole body. Selectivity comes from the receptor, not from the delivery.

questions.takeaway: Hormones travel through the blood to the whole body. Only cells with matching receptors respond, so the same hormone produces different effects in different tissues.
questions.strategy: Three distractors invent a delivery mechanism. The selectivity happens at the receiving end.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves receptor specificity.

questions.stem: A patient's blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, cells take up glucose, the glucose falls, and insulin secretion decreases. Which mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Positive feedback
options.rationale: Positive feedback would drive the glucose higher still. Here the response opposes the rise and shuts itself off.

options.text: Negative feedback
options.rationale: The body detects the change, the gland adjusts secretion to oppose it, balance is restored, and the stimulus stops.

options.text: Receptor specificity
options.rationale: A real concept, but it explains which tissues act, not how secretion is regulated.

options.text: Homeostatic failure
options.rationale: A rise after a meal is normal. Homeostasis is maintaining balance through change, not preventing it.

questions.takeaway: Negative feedback: the body detects a change, glands adjust secretion to counteract it, balance is restored, and signaling stops. Diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats any fluctuation as failure. Homeostasis is the correction, not the absence of change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves negative feedback.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient with fatigue and unexplained weight change. Which findings would support an endocrine cause? Select all that apply.

options.text: Intolerance of heat or cold
options.rationale: Temperature tolerance is recognized, and it is one of the most specific pointers toward a thyroid cause.

options.text: Changes in fluid balance and urine output
options.rationale: Fluid balance and urine output are recognized, and both pituitary and adrenal disorders disturb them.

options.text: A family history of appendicitis
options.rationale: Not an endocrine pointer. Family history matters for some endocrine conditions and this is not one of them.

options.text: Changes in heart rate or blood pressure
options.rationale: Heart rate and blood pressure are recognized, and both thyroid and adrenal disorders move them.

options.text: Changes in skin texture or hair
options.rationale: Skin texture and hair are recognized, and both change noticeably with thyroid dysfunction in either direction.

options.text: Joint pain in the hands lasting several months
options.rationale: Points toward a rheumatologic cause. The endocrine picture is temperature intolerance, cardiovascular change, skin and hair change, mood shift, and fluid balance.

options.text: Mood or mental status shifts
options.rationale: Mood and mental status shifts are recognized, and they are the findings most easily blamed on something else.

questions.takeaway: Endocrine signs: weight, energy and appetite changes; temperature tolerance; heart rate and blood pressure changes; skin, hair, mood and mental status; fluid balance and urine output; blood glucose.
questions.strategy: One distractor names an unrelated family history. Endocrine dysfunction presents subtly, so the list of things to ask about is broad.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, temperature, cardiovascular, skin, mental status, fluid.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with known hypothyroidism is admitted with a temperature of 34.8 C, a pulse of 44, and a decreasing level of consciousness. He stopped his levothyroxine two months ago. Which does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Expected worsening of his hypothyroidism
options.rationale: Fatigue and constipation worsening is expected. Hypothermia with a pulse of 44 and falling consciousness is an emergency.

options.text: Thyroid storm
options.rationale: Thyroid storm is the hyperthyroid emergency, with fever and tachycardia. Every finding here is the opposite.

options.text: Myxedema coma
options.rationale: Rare and life-threatening. The hypothermia, bradycardia and falling consciousness together are the picture.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Worth checking in any patient with altered mental status, and it would not explain the temperature and the bradycardia.

questions.takeaway: Myxedema coma is the rare, life-threatening complication of severe untreated hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine adherence matters for exactly this reason.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is thyroid storm, and every number in the stem points the opposite way. Check the direction before choosing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hot and fast is the other emergency.

elimination.verdict: That leaves myxedema coma.

questions.stem: A patient asks why he is urinating so much now that his glucose is high. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Increased thirst leads to increased fluid intake and therefore more urine
options.rationale: This reverses the sequence. The urinating comes first, driven by glucose pulling water out, and the thirst follows it.

options.text: Glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis. Once glucose appears in the urine it pulls water out with it, which is what produces the polyuria and then the dehydration.

options.text: High glucose irritates the bladder and increases the urge to void
options.rationale: The mechanism is osmotic rather than irritative, and the volume is increased.

options.text: The kidneys increase urine output to lower the blood glucose deliberately
options.rationale: Glucose loss in urine is a consequence of exceeding the kidney's capacity to reabsorb it, not a regulatory strategy.

questions.takeaway: Osmotic diuresis: high glucose spills into urine, glucose in urine draws water with it, producing polyuria and then dehydration and electrolyte loss.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses cause and effect between thirst and urination. Ask which came first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves osmotic diuresis.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews glucose regulation with a student.

The hormone that moves glucose from the bloodstream into cells is [[1]].

The hormone that signals the liver to release stored glucose is [[2]].

Diabetes in which beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process is [[3]].

Diabetes in which cells respond poorly to insulin that is still being produced is [[4]].

options.text: glucagon
options.rationale: Glucagon gets glucose out into the bloodstream and raises the level. This blank needs the opposite.

options.text: cortisol
options.rationale: Influences glucose metabolism as part of the stress response rather than moving glucose into cells.

options.text: insulin
options.rationale: Insulin puts glucose into cells, which is what lowers the level in the blood.

options.text: aldosterone
options.rationale: Aldosterone controls sodium and water retention to maintain blood pressure. It does nothing to glucose.

options.text: insulin
options.rationale: Insulin does the opposite, moving glucose out of the bloodstream and into cells.

options.text: glucagon
options.rationale: Glucagon raises blood glucose by telling the liver to release what it has stored.

options.text: calcitonin
options.rationale: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium. It has nothing to do with glucose.

options.text: growth hormone
options.rationale: Growth hormone comes from the pituitary and concerns growth and development.

options.text: diabetes insipidus
options.rationale: A pituitary disorder of water balance producing dilute urine and thirst. Unrelated to glucose.

options.text: type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Type 2 is insulin resistance, with insulin still present but insufficient or ineffective.

options.text: type 1 diabetes
options.rationale: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells, little or no insulin, and insulin replacement required for survival.

options.text: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: This is an acute complication rather than a type of diabetes.

options.text: gestational diabetes
options.rationale: Gestational diabetes is not among the recognized types here.

options.text: type 1 diabetes
options.rationale: In type 1 there is little or no insulin produced at all, which is a different mechanism.

options.text: type 2 diabetes
options.rationale: Cells respond poorly to insulin. The pancreas compensates at first and eventually cannot keep up.

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Ketoacidosis is an acute complication of severe insulin deficiency, not a type of diabetes.

questions.takeaway: Insulin puts glucose IN. Glucagon gets glucose OUT. Type 1 is beta cell destruction; type 2 is insulin resistance.
questions.strategy: Diabetes insipidus appears as a distractor because the name misleads. It is a pituitary water problem with no connection to glucose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Insulin, glucagon, type 1, type 2.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department. His blood glucose is 486 mg/dL, pH 7.21, bicarbonate 11, ketones present in urine, with deep rapid respirations and a fruity odor on his breath. Which does this represent?

options.text: Hypoglycemia with altered mental status
options.rationale: His glucose is 486. Hypoglycemia is the opposite problem.

options.text: Uncomplicated hyperglycemia requiring a correction dose
options.rationale: A pH of 7.21 with ketones is not uncomplicated. This is an emergency requiring intravenous fluids and insulin per protocol.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS has severe hyperglycemia without significant ketones and without acidosis. The pH of 7.21 and the ketones rule it out.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Severe insulin deficiency drives fat breakdown, ketones accumulate, and metabolic acidosis follows. The Kussmaul respirations are the body blowing off acid.

questions.takeaway: DKA: insulin deficiency, fat breakdown, ketones, metabolic acidosis, rapid onset over hours, more common in type 1. Fruity breath and Kussmaul respirations are the signature.
questions.strategy: Three values decide this: the pH, the bicarbonate, and the ketones. Any one of them separates DKA from HHS.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One has no ketones, one has low glucose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is admitted after three days of increasing confusion. Her blood glucose is 742 mg/dL, serum osmolality 340, pH 7.38, no ketones in urine, with dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor. Which does this represent?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Severe hyperglycemia with profound dehydration, no significant ketones, gradual onset over days, and altered mental status prominent.

options.text: Myxedema coma
options.rationale: A hypothyroid emergency with hypothermia and bradycardia. Nothing here points to the thyroid.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: DKA has ketones and acidosis. The pH here is normal and there are no ketones.

options.text: Dehydration from an unrelated cause
options.rationale: The dehydration is real and it is produced by the osmotic diuresis. Treating it as unrelated misses the emergency driving it.

questions.takeaway: HHS: severe hyperglycemia without significant ketones, profound dehydration, hyperosmolarity, altered mental status, gradual onset over days, more common in type 2.
questions.strategy: The pH and the absence of ketones are what separate this from DKA. A normal pH with a glucose of 742 is the signature.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews causes of hypoglycemia with a patient starting insulin. Which should be included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Taking more insulin than was intended
options.rationale: Taking more insulin than intended is recognized first, and it is the most direct cause of a low.

options.text: A missed dose of insulin at breakfast
options.rationale: Produces hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia. Read too fast, any insulin error looks like a hypoglycemia cause, and this one is the opposite.

options.text: Missing or delaying a meal
options.rationale: It is why mealtime insulin is held when the tray has not arrived.

options.text: Drinking alcohol without food
options.rationale: Alcohol without food is recognized, and alcohol stops the liver releasing its stored glucose when it is needed.

options.text: Developing an acute infection or fever
options.rationale: Illness and infection are recognized as causes of hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia. Stress hormones raise glucose.

options.text: Inadequate carbohydrate intake at meals
options.rationale: Too little carbohydrate is recognized, and eating something is not the same as eating enough to cover the dose.

options.text: Increased physical activity without adjustment
options.rationale: Extra activity without adjustment is recognized, and exercise pulls glucose into muscle independently of insulin.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia causes: excess insulin or medication, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate, increased activity without adjustment, alcohol without food.
questions.strategy: One distractor appears on the hyperglycemia list. Illness raises glucose rather than lowering it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Excess drug, missed meal, low carbohydrate, activity, alcohol.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a patient with type 1 diabetes drowsy, confused and unable to follow instructions. His blood glucose is 44 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give intravenous dextrose or glucagon rather than anything by mouth
options.rationale: Never give oral intake if swallowing is unsafe. A drowsy, confused patient cannot protect his airway.

options.text: Give a complex carbohydrate with protein to sustain the correction
options.rationale: Protein and complex carbohydrate follow the initial correction. Neither is given first, and neither is given orally to this patient.

options.text: Recheck the glucose before treating, to confirm the reading
options.rationale: The reading and the symptoms agree. Delaying treatment to reconfirm risks seizure and loss of consciousness.

options.text: Give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate by mouth and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The correct treatment for a patient who can swallow safely. This one cannot, which is the line the question tests.

questions.takeaway: Treat hypoglycemia with the 15-15 rule when swallowing is safe. When it is not, use intravenous dextrose or glucagon.
questions.strategy: The 15-15 rule is the right answer to a different question. The words drowsy and confused are what change the route.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves intravenous dextrose or glucagon.

questions.nursesNote: 1130: Patient is 62 with type 2 diabetes, admitted two days ago with cellulitis of the left leg. Reports the leg feels numb and that the original wound went unnoticed. Blood glucose this morning 268 mg/dL. Says the feet get checked 'when I remember'. Wears open sandals on the unit. Reports blurred vision that has worsened over six months, with no optometrist visit in four years. Blood pressure 148/88. Takes metformin as prescribed. Ate 100% of breakfast. Temperature 37.2 C.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate diabetes complications or gaps in self-management.

segments.text: Wears open sandals on the unit
segments.rationale: Protective footwear at all times is a recognized teaching point, and open sandals on an insensate foot invite the next wound.

segments.text: Leg feels numb and the original wound went unnoticed
segments.rationale: Peripheral neuropathy. Decreased sensation means injuries go unnoticed, which is exactly how this admission started.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2 C
segments.rationale: A temperature of 37.2 is within normal limits, which is reassuring given the cellulitis.

segments.text: Ate 100% of breakfast
segments.rationale: Adequate intake, and it is reassuring in a patient at risk of hypoglycemia.

segments.text: Blood glucose 268 mg/dL
segments.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia, which is what drives every complication on this list and impairs healing now.

segments.text: Blurred vision worsening over six months, no optometrist in four years
segments.rationale: Possible retinopathy going unmonitored. Eyes are one of the recognized sites of microvascular damage.

segments.text: Takes metformin as prescribed
segments.rationale: Taking the metformin as prescribed is adherence. This is a strength rather than a gap.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/88
segments.rationale: Raised blood pressure compounds the cardiovascular and kidney risk that diabetes already carries.

segments.text: Checks the feet 'when I remember'
segments.rationale: Daily inspection is the teaching priority, and in a patient with reduced sensation it is the only way an injury is found.

questions.takeaway: Long-term complications affect eyes, kidneys, nerves, cardiovascular system, skin and feet. Decreased sensation plus unprotected feet is how ulcers begin.
questions.strategy: Three findings are strengths or normal values. One of them, taking metformin as prescribed, is there to stop you assuming nonadherence explains everything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1, s2, s5, s6, s8, and s9: footwear, nerves, glucose, eyes, pressure, and feet.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches foot care to a patient with diabetic neuropathy. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear proper footwear at all times
options.rationale: Proper footwear is recognized, and at all times includes indoors. Most injuries happen barefoot at home.

options.text: Report any sores, cuts or changes promptly
options.rationale: Reporting promptly is recognized, and with delayed healing a small break becomes an infection fast.

options.text: Test water temperature with the hand before bathing the feet
options.rationale: Follows directly from decreased sensation. A foot that cannot feel heat cannot warn him.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet to improve circulation
options.rationale: Dangerous on an insensate foot. He will not feel a burn, and poor circulation impairs healing of one.

options.text: Attend regular follow-up appointments
options.rationale: It is how changes are caught before he can feel them.

options.text: Soak the feet daily to keep the skin soft
options.rationale: Common advice and wrong for a neuropathic foot. Soaking macerates the skin and raises the risk of a wound that the patient cannot feel.

options.text: Inspect the feet daily for wounds, redness or swelling
options.rationale: The first teaching priority, and the only way an injury is found on an insensate foot.

questions.takeaway: Foot care matters because decreased sensation means injuries go unnoticed, healing is delayed, circulation is poor, and ulcers lead to serious complications.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies heat to a foot that cannot feel it. Every foot care rule follows from the lost sensation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He cannot feel injury or heat.
He would not feel a burn.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to administer insulin. Which step reflects its status as a high-alert medication?

options.text: Confirm the patient's identity using a single identifier
options.rationale: Two identifiers are standard, and identity verification is not what makes insulin high-alert specifically.

options.text: Document the dose immediately after it is administered
options.rationale: Documenting is necessary, and it happens after the dose is already in the patient.

options.text: Perform an independent double-check of type, dose and timing
options.rationale: High-alert medications require strict safety practices, and the double-check is the one never to skip.

options.text: Administer it promptly so the dose is not delayed
options.rationale: Timing matters and speed is not the safety practice. Rushing is how the wrong type gets drawn.

questions.takeaway: Insulin is a high-alert medication. Verify patient identity, insulin type, dose and timing. Never skip double-checks, and consider meal timing.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are reasonable practice that happen at the wrong moment or apply to every medication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the independent double-check.

questions.stem: A nursing student says a patient must have type 1 diabetes because he uses insulin. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The distinction between the two types is determined by the patient's age
options.rationale: Type 2 onset is gradual and not determined by age or weight alone.

options.text: Some patients with type 2 diabetes require insulin without poor control
options.rationale: This is stated directly. Type 2 may require lifestyle change, oral medication, insulin, or a combination.

options.text: Insulin use always indicates that oral medications have failed
options.rationale: Calling it a failure is what makes patients resist it. Insulin may be needed because the pancreas can no longer keep up.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes is managed with oral medication and lifestyle change only
options.rationale: This is wrong: insulin therapy is one of the options in type 2.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 always requires insulin. Type 2 may require it over time, and using insulin does not mean poor control or a failure.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat insulin in type 2 as a failure or exclude it entirely. One falls back on age.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lifestyle, oral agents, insulin, or a combination.

steps.action: Cut the option that calls it a failure

steps.detail: Onset is not determined by age alone.

elimination.verdict: That leaves insulin being appropriate in type 2.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a diabetes medication to a newly admitted patient. Which assessment should she complete first?

options.text: The patient's understanding of the medication
options.rationale: Patient understanding is essential for discharge teaching, and it is not the safety check that comes before a dose.

options.text: The patient's most recent A1C
options.rationale: Useful for evaluating control over time, but it does not determine whether this dose is safe now.

options.text: Renal and hepatic function
options.rationale: Always assess renal and hepatic function before administering diabetes medications. Some agents require dose adjustment or are contraindicated in organ impairment.

options.text: The patient's usual home dose
options.rationale: Part of medication reconciliation, and it does not establish whether the drug is safe with current organ function.

questions.takeaway: Assess renal and hepatic function before administering diabetes medications. Some require dose adjustment or are contraindicated in organ impairment.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are useful. The question asks what must be established before the dose goes in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Whether the organs can handle it.

steps.action: Cut the A1C and home dose
steps.detail: Both inform management rather than safety.

elimination.verdict: That leaves renal and hepatic function.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes is found confused and irritable, and his heart rate is 112. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the blood glucose
options.rationale: Always check blood glucose when neurological changes occur. Mental status changes may indicate hypoglycemia, which progresses rapidly.

options.text: Review his medication record for recent doses
options.rationale: Informative once you know what you are dealing with. The glucose reading takes seconds.

options.text: Reorient the patient and ensure the environment is safe
options.rationale: Worth doing alongside, and it manages the confusion without finding out what is causing it.

options.text: Assess for signs of infection as a cause of the confusion
options.rationale: Infection is a real cause of both confusion and hyperglycemia. It takes longer to establish and hypoglycemia can seize within minutes.

questions.takeaway: Always check blood glucose when neurological changes occur in a patient with diabetes. Confusion, irritability or unresponsiveness may be hypoglycemia.
questions.strategy: Three options are reasonable and slower. Ask which possible cause could kill him in the next fifteen minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All take longer than a glucose check.

elimination.verdict: That leaves checking the glucose.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes who normally walks 20 minutes daily plans to hike for four hours at the weekend. Which teaching is most important?

options.text: Exercise has no predictable effect on blood glucose
options.rationale: It lowers glucose substantially and fairly predictably, so it shows up on the list of hypoglycemia causes.

options.text: The patient should avoid prolonged exercise because of diabetes
options.rationale: Activity is part of managing diabetes. The answer is adjusting the plan rather than avoiding the hike.

options.text: The insulin dose should be increased to cover the exertion
options.rationale: This is backwards. Exercise lowers glucose, so more insulin on top of it compounds the risk.

options.text: Increased activity raises hypoglycemia risk and the plan needs adjusting
options.rationale: Increased physical activity without adjustment is a recognized cause of hypoglycemia. Exercise increases glucose uptake independently of insulin.

questions.takeaway: Increased physical activity without adjustment causes hypoglycemia. Exercise increases glucose uptake, so the plan is adjusted rather than the activity avoided.
questions.strategy: One distractor increases insulin before exercise, which is the dangerous inversion. Ask which direction exercise moves the glucose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what exercise does to glucose

steps.detail: One restricts, one denies the effect.

elimination.verdict: That leaves adjusting for the hypoglycemia risk.

questions.stem: A nurse orienting to an endocrine unit describes insulin safety and diabetes care. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Insulin is a high-alert medication and I never skip the double-check."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Insulin is high-alert and the independent double-check is not optional.

options.text: "DKA involves ketones and acidosis; HHS has severe hyperglycemia without significant ketones."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the distinction between the two emergencies: ketones and acidosis, or neither.

options.text: "I check the glucose whenever a patient with diabetes becomes confused."
options.rationale: This is accurate. New confusion in a patient with diabetes gets a glucose check first.

options.text: “A patient with type 2 diabetes who needs insulin has failed to manage it.”
options.rationale: Some type 2 patients require insulin as the pancreas becomes unable to keep up. It does not indicate poor control.

questions.takeaway: Type 2 may require insulin over time. Needing insulin is not evidence of failure.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth attaches a judgment to a treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what insulin in type 2 means
steps.detail: The pancreas can no longer keep up.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the failure statement.

questions.scenario: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with influenza. The patient tells the nurse that insulin was stopped two days ago because nothing would stay down, and that insulin without food seemed dangerous. Blood glucose is 412 mg/dL, urinary ketones are moderate, and respirations are deep and rapid at 28. Blood pressure is 96/58 and the mucous membranes are dry.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Withhold insulin until she is able to tolerate food
options.rationale: The belief that brought her in. Insulin need usually rises during illness, and stopping it is what produced the ketones.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and reassess in two hours
options.rationale: She cannot keep anything down, and a two-hour delay in a patient with moderate ketones and Kussmaul respirations is not safe.

options.text: Administer intravenous fluids and insulin per protocol
options.rationale: Both are needed. The fluids address the dehydration from osmotic diuresis and the insulin stops the fat breakdown producing the ketones.

options.text: Monitor blood glucose, ketones, pH and electrolytes closely
options.rationale: Named among DKA nursing priorities, and the treatment response has to be tracked rather than assumed.

options.text: Dehydration from influenza and poor oral intake
options.rationale: The dehydration is real and it is a component rather than the diagnosis. It does not explain the ketones.

options.text: Hypoglycemia from inadequate food intake
options.rationale: Her glucose is 412. The absence of food did not produce a low because there was no insulin either.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin omission during illness
options.rationale: Ketones, Kussmaul respirations, hyperglycemia and dehydration, with a clear precipitant she has told you herself.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS has no significant ketones and develops over days in type 2. She has moderate ketones and type 1.

options.text: Blood glucose trend and clearance of ketones
options.rationale: The two findings that defined the emergency, measured as the treatment takes effect.

options.text: Whether she can state the sick-day rules
options.rationale: Essential teaching before discharge, and it evaluates knowledge rather than whether she is recovering now.

options.text: Respiratory rate and level of consciousness
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations should settle as the acidosis corrects, and mental status is the fastest bedside indicator of the response.

options.text: Her temperature over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Her temperature tracks the influenza rather than the ketoacidosis the actions were aimed at.

questions.takeaway: Insulin need rises during illness. Stopping it because food is not being kept down is the most dangerous sick-day error and it is what produces DKA.
questions.strategy: She tells you the precipitant herself. One action distractor repeats the belief that caused the admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read the ketones and the breathing

elimination.verdict: Fluids and insulin with close monitoring, for DKA from insulin omission, evaluated by glucose, ketones, respirations and consciousness.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes calls the clinic reporting that he has vomited twice and has had no appetite since morning. He has taken no insulin today, reasoning that he has not eaten. His glucose an hour ago was 248 mg/dL. Applying sick-day rules, which instruction takes priority?

options.text: Hold insulin until eating resumes, then resume the usual dose
options.rationale: This is the patient's own reasoning, and that is what makes it the trap. Type 1 patients make no insulin at all, so holding it during illness is how ketoacidosis starts.

options.text: Take half the usual dose and recheck in the morning
options.rationale: Halving the dose during illness moves in the wrong direction, and waiting until morning gives ketosis a full night.

options.text: Continue insulin, check glucose and ketones, sip fluids
options.rationale: Illness raises counterregulatory hormones, so insulin need goes up while intake goes down. Insulin continues, monitoring goes to every two to four hours, ketones get checked, and fluids go in by sips.

options.text: Come to the clinic now for intravenous fluid replacement
