options.rationale: Premature. The glucose is 248 mg/dL and the patient is talking on the phone, so sick-day management comes first and the criteria for coming in get taught alongside it.

questions.takeaway: Sick-day rule: never stop insulin in type 1 diabetes. Illness raises insulin requirements even when intake stops, and ketones are what you check.
questions.strategy: When a patient explains their reasoning in the stem, that reasoning is usually one of the options and usually wrong.

strategies: Ask what illness does to insulin need

steps.action: Recall that stress hormones raise glucose

steps.detail: Not yet indicated by these findings.

elimination.verdict: Continue insulin, check ketones, sip fluids.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes who also takes a beta blocker becomes confused and diaphoretic at 1500. Which statement explains the presentation?

options.text: The beta blocker has caused the low glucose and should be withheld
options.rationale: Beta blockers do not lower glucose and withholding one is not a nursing decision here.

options.text: Confusion without tremor or palpitations means the cause is unlikely to be hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Absent tremor is expected on a beta blocker and absence of it rules nothing out.

options.text: The beta blocker blunts the warning signs, so she can go lower unnoticed
options.rationale: Beta blockade suppresses the adrenergic symptoms. Sweating persists and the neurological signs still appear, so confusion can be the first thing seen.

options.text: The diaphoresis is unrelated, since beta blockers suppress sweating
options.rationale: Diaphoresis is the adrenergic sign that survives beta blockade and it is the one to rely on.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the shaking and pounding heart of hypoglycemia. Sweating persists and neuroglycopenic signs still arrive, so the first sign may be confusion.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses the missing symptoms as evidence against the diagnosis. Her medication removed those symptoms.

strategies: Ask what the beta blocker removes

steps.action: Cut the two options built on absent symptoms

elimination.verdict: That leaves the blunted warning explanation.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to give rapid-acting insulin before breakfast and learns the meal trays will be forty minutes late. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the insulin now and ask dietary to prioritize the tray
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin begins working within about fifteen minutes and she would be hypoglycemic before the food arrives.

options.text: Hold the dose and give it when the tray is at the bedside
options.rationale: The dose is matched to a meal, so it is timed to the meal and not to the clock.

options.text: Give half the dose now and the remainder with the meal
options.rationale: Splitting a mealtime dose is not within nursing practice and it still delivers insulin with no food.

options.text: Give the insulin now and provide juice to cover the delay
options.rationale: Juice treats a low that has not happened and adds unmeasured carbohydrate to the plan.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin follows the meal. Rapid-acting is given when the food is in front of the patient.
questions.strategy: Three options find a way to give it anyway. Ask what the dose was calculated against.

strategies: Ask what the dose covers

steps.action: Cut giving it now in any form
Keep holding until the tray arrives

elimination.verdict: That leaves holding the dose.

questions.stem: A patient takes NPH insulin at 0700 each morning. At which time is the risk of hypoglycemia greatest?

options.text: Within thirty minutes of the dose
options.rationale: That is the onset window for rapid-acting insulin, not an intermediate-acting one.

options.text: Around mid-morning, two to three hours after the dose
options.rationale: This is the peak of a short-acting insulin.

options.text: Mid to late afternoon
options.rationale: Intermediate-acting insulin peaks roughly six to twelve hours after the dose, which places the risk in the afternoon.

options.text: Overnight, about twenty hours after the dose
options.rationale: Beyond the usual duration of this insulin, where a long-acting agent would still be working.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia follows the peak. Rapid-acting peaks in about an hour, short-acting in two to three, intermediate in six to twelve, and long-acting has no pronounced peak.
questions.strategy: The question is never when the insulin was given. It is when that particular insulin peaks.

strategies: Match the insulin to its peak

steps.detail: They belong to other insulin types.

elimination.verdict: That leaves mid to late afternoon.

questions.stem: A man with type 1 diabetes plans to begin running in the late afternoon. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Check glucose before you run, carry fast carbohydrate, and expect a delayed low
options.rationale: Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and uptake, and the delayed drop hours later is what patients are least prepared for.

options.text: Increase your evening insulin on the days you run
options.rationale: Exercise lowers glucose, so increasing the dose moves in the wrong direction.

options.text: Eat a large meal immediately before running so you do not go low
options.rationale: A large meal before exercise causes discomfort and overshoots.

options.text: Avoid running on days when your morning glucose is below 150 mg/dL
options.rationale: Arbitrary thresholds that discourage exercise are not the teaching, and the plan is to prepare rather than to cancel.

questions.takeaway: Exercise lowers glucose during the activity and for hours afterwards. Check before, carry carbohydrate, and expect the delayed drop.
questions.strategy: The delayed hypoglycemia is the part that gets left out, and it is where the question lives.

strategies: Ask which direction exercise moves glucose

steps.action: Cut the large meal and the avoidance rule

elimination.verdict: That leaves checking, carrying carbohydrate and watching afterwards.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes of thirty years says he no longer feels his lows and has twice been found sweating and confused by his wife. Which instruction is most important?

options.text: Check your glucose more often, including before every drive, and do not rely on symptoms
options.rationale: Once the warning symptoms are gone, measurement is the only remaining warning, and driving is where the consequence is lethal.

options.text: Carry a fast-acting carbohydrate at all times
options.rationale: Necessary, but it does nothing to tell him when to use it.

options.text: Ask your wife to watch for sweating and confusion
options.rationale: It makes his safety depend on someone being present.

options.text: Eat on a fixed schedule so your glucose stays stable
options.rationale: Helpful, but it does not restore a warning he has lost.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia unawareness removes the body's alarm. The replacement is measurement, and the first place it matters is behind the wheel.
questions.strategy: Three options are reasonable diabetes advice. Only one replaces the specific thing he has lost.

strategies: Ask what he has lost

steps.action: Cut carbohydrate, his wife, meal timing

elimination.verdict: That leaves checking more often, including before driving.

questions.stem: A patient taking evening intermediate-acting insulin has fasting glucose readings near 240 mg/dL. A 0300 reading is 52 mg/dL. Which change should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Increasing the evening insulin dose to bring the morning value down
options.rationale: That lowers the overnight glucose further and deepens the rebound.

options.text: Decreasing the evening insulin dose
options.rationale: The overnight low triggers counterregulatory hormones that drive the morning rise, so the correction is less insulin rather than more.

options.text: Moving the evening dose later in the night
options.rationale: Moving the peak later does not address a dose that is already too large.

options.text: Adding a rapid-acting dose at bedtime
options.rationale: Adding insulin at bedtime makes the nocturnal low worse.

questions.takeaway: A low at 0300 with a high fasting value is rebound. The morning number is produced by the overnight low, so the dose comes down.
questions.strategy: The high morning glucose argues for more insulin and the 0300 value reverses that. Always ask for the overnight reading before adjusting.

strategies: Start from the 0300 value

steps.action: Cut every option that adds or delays insulin

steps.detail: Treats the cause of the rebound.

elimination.verdict: That leaves decreasing the evening dose.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic neuropathy reviews foot care. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: I check the bottoms of my feet with a mirror every day
options.rationale: Daily inspection is right, because it finds what neuropathy prevents him from feeling.

options.text: I dry carefully between my toes after washing
options.rationale: Drying between the toes is right, since trapped moisture macerates skin and invites infection.

options.text: I wear shoes in the house as well as outdoors
options.rationale: Shoes indoors is right, because a bare foot with reduced sensation finds hazards by injury.

options.text: I soak my feet in hot water each night because it helps the circulation
options.rationale: Soaking softens and macerates the skin, and reduced sensation means he cannot judge the temperature, so burns happen at temperatures he never registers.

questions.takeaway: Neuropathic feet are washed and dried, never soaked, and water temperature is tested by hand or thermometer rather than by the foot.
questions.strategy: Soaking sounds like care and comfort. The deficit is sensation, which is what makes hot water dangerous.

strategies: Ask what the neuropathy removes

steps.detail: He cannot feel heat or injury.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the soaking statement.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes is found drowsy and difficult to rouse. A fingerstick reads 44 mg/dL. He can swallow and follow simple direction. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give 15 grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: Fifteen grams is the starting treatment for a conscious patient who can swallow.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck interval is part of the rule and skipping it is the usual error.

options.text: Repeat the carbohydrate if the glucose is still below 70 mg/dL
options.rationale: The sequence repeats until the value comes up.

options.text: Follow with a protein and carbohydrate snack if a meal is not due soon
options.rationale: A longer-acting source prevents the glucose from falling again.

options.text: Give his scheduled rapid-acting insulin to prevent a rebound high
options.rationale: Giving insulin to a hypoglycemic patient is the most dangerous action on the list.

options.text: Treat with a carbohydrate that also contains fat, such as chocolate
options.rationale: Fat slows absorption and delays the correction.

options.text: Stay with him until the glucose and his mental status have returned to normal
options.rationale: He can deteriorate, so he is not left alone.

questions.takeaway: Fifteen grams, recheck in fifteen minutes, repeat if still low, then a longer-acting snack. No fat, no insulin, and do not leave him.
questions.strategy: The chocolate option is the quiet one, because it is carbohydrate and the fat in it is what makes it wrong.

strategies: Work through the rule

steps.action: Fifteen and fifteen, repeat, snack, stay

elimination.verdict: The five correct actions are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares insulin for a patient. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Roll an intermediate-acting suspension between the palms before drawing it up
options.rationale: Gentle rolling resuspends it, and shaking introduces bubbles that make the dose inaccurate.

options.text: Draw up the clear short-acting insulin before the cloudy suspension when mixing in one syringe
options.rationale: Clear before cloudy, so the suspension does not contaminate the vial of clear insulin.

options.text: Have a second nurse verify the dose before administration
options.rationale: Insulin is a high-alert medication and independent double check is standard.

options.text: Massage the site after a subcutaneous injection to speed absorption
options.rationale: Massage alters the absorption rate and is not done with insulin.

options.text: Rotate within one anatomical area rather than moving between the abdomen and the thigh each dose
options.rationale: Absorption differs by site, so rotating within an area keeps it predictable.

options.text: Store the vial in current use at room temperature for the period stated on the label
options.rationale: The in-use vial is kept at room temperature, and cold insulin stings.

options.text: Discard the dose and start over if an air bubble is seen in the syringe
options.rationale: The bubble is expelled rather than the dose discarded.

questions.takeaway: Roll do not shake, clear before cloudy, double check, rotate within one area, no massage, in-use vial at room temperature.
questions.strategy: Both wrong options sound careful. One changes absorption and one wastes a dose for a problem with a simple fix.

strategies: Treat each action as correct or not

steps.action: Rolling, clear before cloudy, double check, rotation, storage

elimination.verdict: The five correct actions are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes comes for a routine visit. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: A hemoglobin A1C of 9.4 percent
options.rationale: Well above target and it means months of elevated glucose.

options.text: A small area of redness and warmth on the plantar surface of the left foot
options.rationale: An early foot infection in a patient with diabetes escalates quickly and is reported the day it is found.

options.text: Fasting glucose values between 95 and 120 mg/dL over the past two weeks
options.rationale: These are at or near target and nothing here requires reporting.

options.text: New numbness and tingling in both feet
options.rationale: New neuropathic symptoms change the risk profile and the foot care plan.

options.text: Three episodes of glucose below 60 mg/dL in the past week
options.rationale: Recurrent hypoglycemia is as reportable as hyperglycemia and it suggests the regimen needs adjustment.

options.text: Weight loss of 12 pounds over two months without trying
options.rationale: Unintentional loss in diabetes suggests poor control or another process.

options.text: Blood pressure of 118/72
options.rationale: Within target and it does not need reporting.

questions.takeaway: Report what changes management: values far off target, new neuropathy, recurrent lows, unexplained weight loss, and any foot lesion.
questions.strategy: Two options are normal findings placed among abnormal ones. The lows are the ones most often left unreported.

strategies: Sort each finding against target

steps.action: A1C, foot lesion, neuropathy, lows, weight loss

elimination.verdict: The five reportable findings are selected.

questions.stem: A patient on an evening dose of intermediate-acting insulin has fasting glucose values between 180 and 210 mg/dL every morning. At the nurse's request he checks at 0300 on three nights and records 118, 126 and 132 mg/dL. Nothing about the evening dose has changed. What do these values indicate?

options.text: Insufficient coverage during the day that is carrying over into the morning values
options.rationale: Daytime dosing would show in the daytime values, and the 0300 readings sit in range.

options.text: A meter that reads inaccurately in the small hours
options.rationale: Three consistent values in a plausible range, taken on three separate nights, do not suggest equipment failure.

options.text: Rebound hyperglycemia after an overnight low that nobody caught, which would call for reducing the evening dose rather than raising it
options.rationale: The reason the 0300 checks were ordered. A rebound requires a low at 0300 and there is none. Reducing the evening dose here would make the fasting values worse.

options.text: A rise driven by the early morning release of counterregulatory hormones, which may call for increasing the evening dose or moving it later
options.rationale: The overnight values are in range, so nothing dropped and nothing rebounded. The glucose climbs between 0300 and waking, which is the hormone surge before dawn.

questions.takeaway: A high fasting glucose has two explanations with opposite treatments. The 0300 value is what separates them, and you do not change the evening dose until you have it.
questions.strategy: Two options describe real causes of a high morning value, and the actions they lead to are opposite. The overnight number decides it.

strategies: Use the 0300 value as the pivot
elimination.verdict: A dawn rise, not a rebound.

questions.stem: A patient's hemoglobin A1C returns at 6.4 percent. His home log over the same period shows readings ranging from 48 to 290 mg/dL, including four values under 60. He received two units of packed red cells six weeks ago for a gastrointestinal bleed. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: His medications can be increased, since the result sits below the usual target for most patients
options.rationale: Increasing therapy in a patient who is already dropping below 60 would make the lows more frequent.

options.text: The A1C is not a reliable picture here, and the log and the low values are what the team acts on
options.rationale: An average sits between a 48 and a 290 and describes neither. Recent transfusion also distorts the result, because the transfused cells carry the donor's exposure rather than his.

options.text: His control is good and the home readings most likely reflect poor technique or an inaccurate meter, which are a common source of error at home
options.rationale: The comfortable reading, and it discards the data that shows he is having repeated lows. Four values under 60 are the most dangerous thing in the record.

options.text: The A1C should be repeated today to confirm it
options.rationale: It measures the preceding two to three months, so repeating it the same week returns the same distorted value.

questions.takeaway: A1C is an average over months and it hides swings. Transfusion, bleeding and anemia distort it, and a reassuring number beside repeated lows is a warning rather than a result.
questions.strategy: Two options accept the A1C at face value. Ask what an average does to a patient who is going from 48 to 290.

strategies: Ask what the test can and cannot see

steps.action: Weigh the number against the log

elimination.verdict: Act on the log, not the A1C.

questions.stem: Six hours after a thyroidectomy a patient reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. She is anxious and her voice is slightly hoarse. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Check for facial twitching and carpal spasm, notify the provider, and confirm that calcium and airway equipment are at hand
options.rationale: Tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips after this surgery is low calcium from parathyroid injury until proven otherwise, and the progression runs to tetany and laryngospasm.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and give the analgesic that has been ordered
options.rationale: Comfort measures applied to a finding that needs a cause.

options.text: Inspect the dressing and slide a hand behind her neck to check for swelling or firmness, which is the standard check after this operation
options.rationale: The other emergency after this operation, and it has to be checked. The symptom pattern she describes points at calcium rather than at a hematoma, and she has no respiratory distress or sensation of pressure.

options.text: Reassure her that tingling and hoarseness are both expected after surgery on the neck
options.rationale: Hoarseness alone is common. Hoarseness with perioral and fingertip tingling is a specific pattern that is never dismissed.

questions.takeaway: After thyroid surgery two emergencies share the first hours: bleeding into the neck and low calcium from parathyroid injury. Perioral and fingertip tingling names the second one.
questions.strategy: Two options respond to a real postoperative emergency. Match the symptom pattern to the one it belongs to.

strategies: Match symptoms to the specific complication
elimination.verdict: Assess for tetany and get calcium available.

questions.stem: A man who has taken an oral corticosteroid daily for two years stopped it four days ago because he felt well. He now has profound weakness, nausea, vague abdominal pain, and a blood pressure of 86/52 mm Hg lying flat. What does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: A delayed adverse effect of the corticosteroid he had been taking
options.rationale: Excess corticosteroid raises blood pressure and glucose. These findings are what happens when there is not enough.

options.text: Gastroenteritis with dehydration
options.rationale: It accounts for the nausea and the low pressure and not for the timing. Four days after stopping a two-year course is the detail that decides this.

options.text: Acute adrenal insufficiency from abrupt withdrawal, needing intravenous fluid and corticosteroid replacement
options.rationale: Long-term therapy suppresses the body's own production, and the glands cannot restart in four days. Weakness, gastrointestinal symptoms and hypotension together are the crisis presentation.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: It can occur alongside and it does not explain the hypotension or the abdominal pain, and he is not taking a glucose-lowering drug.

questions.takeaway: Long-term corticosteroids are never stopped abruptly. The adrenal glands have been idle and need weeks of tapering, and the crisis that follows a sudden stop is life-threatening.
questions.strategy: The deciding fact is not a symptom. It is what he stopped and when.

strategies: Look for the timing in the history
elimination.verdict: Adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A patient is being monitored after pituitary surgery. Which findings point toward diabetes insipidus rather than the opposite complication? Select all that apply.

options.text: Intense thirst
options.rationale: The thirst mechanism responds to the rising concentration, and it is what keeps an alert patient alive until the deficit is treated.

options.text: A serum sodium of 124 mmol/L
options.rationale: A low sodium from retained water belongs to the opposite complication.

options.text: Urine output of about 400 mL per hour for four hours
options.rationale: Large volumes that do not slow down are the first sign, and the sustained rate is what separates it from an expected postoperative diuresis.

options.text: A urine specific gravity of 1.030
options.rationale: That is concentrated urine, which is what you see when too much of the hormone is being released rather than too little.

options.text: Weight gain of 2 kg since yesterday morning
options.rationale: Retaining water is the opposite problem. Here the patient is losing it.

options.text: A serum sodium that is climbing
options.rationale: Water is leaving and sodium is staying, so the concentration rises.

options.text: Urine that is pale and watery
options.rationale: Without the hormone the kidney cannot concentrate, so the volume is high and the urine is dilute.

questions.takeaway: Too little antidiuretic hormone means water pouring out: high volume, dilute urine, rising sodium, thirst. Too much means water held back: low output, concentrated urine, falling sodium, weight gain.
questions.strategy: Pick one anchor, such as where the water is going, and read every option against it. The two sets are mirror images.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: High output, dilute urine, rising sodium, and thirst are selected.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old being discharged on six medications explains his plan to the nurse, including an enteric-coated tablet, a topical ointment, and eye drops. He lives alone and will manage the regimen himself. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will keep the head of my bed raised for an hour after my tube feed medication."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Keeping the head up at least 30 degrees for an hour afterwards reduces the risk of aspiration.

options.text: "I will clean the skin before applying the next dose of my ointment."
options.rationale: This is accurate. A new dose is never applied on top of the previous one, because the amount absorbed becomes unpredictable.

options.text: "If a tablet is hard to swallow I will crush it and mix it with applesauce."
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, because the coating protects the stomach lining from the medication. A different form is requested from the prescriber or pharmacist instead.

options.text: "Temporary blurring after my eye drops is expected rather than a reaction."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Brief burning or blurring after eye drops is expected rather than a sign of a reaction.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated tablet. Change the form, not the technique.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is what a patient with swallowing difficulty would reasonably do. It destroys the coating that protects the stomach.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Topical, tube feed positioning, and eye drops are correct.

elimination.verdict: The statement needing correction: request a different form rather than crushing.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with assistive personnel and reviews which parts of medication administration may be assigned and what the AP must be told. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assistive personnel may give oral medications if the nurse observes
options.rationale: Watching does not change scope. Administration stays with the nurse whether or not she is standing there.

options.text: Administering medications through an enteral feeding tube cannot be delegated
options.rationale: Tube medications cannot be delegated, and the aspiration risk is the reason. Placement has to be verified first.

options.text: Assistive personnel may crush tablets if the nurse has checked they are crushable
options.rationale: Preparing a medication is part of administering it, and preparation stays with the nurse.

options.text: Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel
options.rationale: Giving oral medications stays with the nurse. The skill itself is not delegable to assistive personnel.

options.text: Ophthalmic and otic medications may be delegated if the AP has been shown the technique
options.rationale: Neither may be delegated. Being shown a technique does not change the scope.

options.text: The AP reports coughing, choking, gagging, or drooling of liquid to the nurse immediately
options.rationale: The AP is told what to watch for and what to report, which is what makes the instruction complete.

questions.takeaway: The administration itself stays with the nurse. What is delegated is observation, positioning, and reporting. The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.
questions.strategy: Topical is the single exception where agency policy may allow trained AP, and being shown a technique never expands scope on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the skill from the support
steps.detail: Administration stays; positioning and reporting go.
Some topical agents, by agency policy.
Technique training does not change scope.

elimination.verdict: B, D, and F are selected.

questions.concept: The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has been prescribed a pressurized metered-dose inhaler but cannot reliably coordinate pressing the canister with inhaling. His technique has been assessed twice with the same result. Which options should the nurse discuss with the provider?

options.text: A spacer device or a breath-actuated inhaler
options.rationale: Both remove the need to coordinate actuation with the breathing cycle, which is the specific problem.

options.text: Having the AP administer the inhaler for him
options.rationale: Administering an inhaled medication cannot be delegated to assistive personnel, so this is not an option to raise.

options.text: Increasing the number of puffs to compensate for poor delivery
options.rationale: Delivers more of a dose that is not reaching the airways, and it risks adverse effects.

options.text: Switching to an oral tablet because inhalers are unsuitable
options.rationale: Abandons the inhaled route without trying the adaptations that exist for this problem.

questions.takeaway: A pMDI requires coordination during the breathing cycle. Poor coordination calls for a spacer or a breath-actuated inhaler. A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the patient's inspiratory effort.
questions.strategy: The three inhaler types differ in what they ask of the patient: a pMDI needs coordination, a BAI triggers on inhalation, and a DPI needs inspiratory effort but no propellant and no spacer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More puffs of an undelivered dose.
One abandons the route, one exceeds AP scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: remove the coordination requirement.

questions.concept: A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the patient's inspiratory effort.

questions.stem: A newly prescribed oral medication is due for a patient admitted this morning. She wants to be sure she has gathered what safe administration requires before she goes into the room. Which actions are part of safe medication preparation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check that a second nurse is available to witness
options.rationale: A second check applies to high-alert medications rather than to every oral dose.

options.text: Check the expiration date
options.rationale: An expired medication may have lost potency or changed chemically, and that applies to every route.

options.text: Administer the dose if the calculation looks approximately correct
options.rationale: Calculations get double-checked, and a dose that looks wrong does not get given on the strength of looking approximately right.

options.text: Determine the purpose, usual dose and route, common side effects, onset and peak, and contraindications
options.rationale: This is what you find out about any drug before giving it: purpose, usual dose and route, side effects, onset and peak, and contraindications.

options.text: Confirm the patient has not eaten within the past hour
options.rationale: Food timing matters for specific medications rather than as a universal preparation step.

options.text: Assess the patient for drug allergies
options.rationale: Always assessed before administration, and a documented allergy changes whether the drug is given at all.

questions.takeaway: Allergies, drug information, interactions, expiry, and the patient's sensory and physical capacity.
questions.strategy: The wrong option lowers the standard on a calculation. If a dose appears incorrect it is not given, and approximately correct is not a standard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five actions occur before the drug reaches the patient.
Approximately correct is not a safety standard.

elimination.verdict: B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: The next scheduled dose of a prescribed ointment is due for a patient's forearm. The previous application from twelve hours ago is still visible on the skin, and the area is intact with no redness. Which action is correct?

options.text: Apply the new dose over the existing layer to avoid disturbing the skin
options.rationale: Layering a new dose over the old one makes the amount absorbed unpredictable. Two doses may be on the skin at once.

options.text: Apply the new dose to an adjacent area of skin instead
options.rationale: This changes the prescribed site rather than preparing it. The site was specified for a reason.

options.text: Withhold the dose until the previous application has worn off
options.rationale: This delays a prescribed dose when cleaning the skin solves the problem in under a minute.

options.text: Clean the skin thoroughly to remove the previous application, then apply the new dose
options.rationale: New medication is never applied over a previous application, and the skin or wound is cleaned before each new dose.

questions.takeaway: Never apply new medication over a previous application. Clean the skin or wound thoroughly before each new dose. Topical medications are applied to skin, mucous membranes, or tissues. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin.
questions.strategy: Topical doses look forgiving and are not. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin, so the amount matters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One moves the site, one delays the dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: clean first, then apply.

questions.concept: Topical medications are applied to skin, mucous membranes, or tissues. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin.

questions.stem: Medications are due through a newly inserted small-bore nasogastric tube. The medications are in liquid form and the correct connector is attached. The tube was placed 20 minutes ago. Which action must she take before administering?

options.text: Flush the tube with 200 mL of water to confirm patency
options.rationale: A 200 mL flush before placement is confirmed risks delivering all of it into the lungs.

options.text: Verify correct placement of the tube
options.rationale: Placement is verified before medications are given, because a displaced tube delivers the dose into the airway.

options.text: Position the patient flat to ease instillation
options.rationale: The head of the bed is elevated, not lowered, and flat positioning increases aspiration risk.

options.text: Crush the medications finely before mixing
options.rationale: They are already in liquid form, and crushing requires pharmacist consultation in any case.

questions.takeaway: Verify tube placement before giving anything through it. A newly inserted tube requires x-ray confirmation. Medications given through a feeding tube should be in liquid form, and a pharmacist is consulted before crushing or dissolving any tablet. The correct enteral access connector is used and tube placement is verified before administration.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option here delivers something into a tube whose position has not been confirmed. Placement comes before patency, positioning, and preparation.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm placement first.

questions.concept: Medications given through a feeding tube should be in liquid form, and a pharmacist is consulted before crushing or dissolving any tablet. The correct enteral access connector is used and tube placement is verified before administration.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the precautions for administering eye and ear medications with a student before a shift on a unit where two patients receive both. The student asks what differs between the two routes. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm ear drops in hot water immediately before instillation
options.rationale: Drops go in at room temperature. Warming them in hot water risks burning the canal.

options.text: Temporary burning or blurring of vision may follow eye medication
options.rationale: Expected, and the AP is told about it so it is not mistaken for an adverse reaction.

options.text: Occlude the ear canal with the dropper to prevent leakage
options.rationale: Occluding the canal with the dropper creates pressure as the drops go in. Leave the canal open.

options.text: Sterile drops and solutions are used in case the eardrum is ruptured
options.rationale: Sterile solution is used in case the eardrum is perforated, because then the solution reaches the middle ear.

options.text: Eye ointments are instilled directly onto the cornea
options.rationale: Medication is placed in the conjunctival sac. The cornea is sensitive and direct instillation causes pain and injury.

options.text: Ear medications are administered at room temperature
options.rationale: Room temperature is the rule, because cold solution in the ear canal causes dizziness and discomfort.

questions.takeaway: Ear drops at room temperature, sterile, without occluding the canal. Eye medication into the conjunctival sac, never onto the cornea. Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.
questions.strategy: The wrong option names a target that sounds plausible and is not. The cornea is richly supplied and highly sensitive, so drops absorb fast from the membranes and the cornea itself is avoided.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The conjunctival sac is the target.

elimination.verdict: B, D, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.

questions.stem: During medication administration through a feeding tube the patient begins coughing, his respiratory rate rises from 18 to 30, and his saturation falls from 96% to 89%. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: Necessary, and another staff member makes the call while the nurse stays with the patient.

options.text: Stop all medications and fluids going through the tube
options.rationale: Stopping the instillation halts what is entering the airway, and it is the first step before positioning or assessment.

options.text: Continue the medication slowly to avoid wasting the dose
options.rationale: This keeps delivering fluid into a patient who is already showing signs of aspiration.

options.text: Assess vital signs and breath sounds

options.text: Once at the cabinet and twice at the bedside

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after receiving a newly prescribed oral antibiotic, a patient develops a raised itchy rash, reports his nose is running, and has audible wheezing. Which nursing actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Withhold further doses of the medication
options.rationale: Further doses would add to a reaction that is already underway. Stop before anything else is decided.

options.text: Assess the patient's vital signs
options.rationale: Establishes how far the reaction has progressed and whether the airway is threatened.

options.text: Enter the allergy in the patient's medical record
options.rationale: Recording the allergy is what stops the next person giving it to him again.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose and observe whether the reaction repeats
options.rationale: This deliberately re-exposes a patient to a drug he is reacting to right now.

options.text: Document the findings and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Wheezing means the airway is involved, and that cannot wait until the end of the shift.

options.text: Notify the health care provider and pharmacy immediately
options.rationale: Both the provider and pharmacy are notified, and emergency medications may be needed within minutes.

questions.takeaway: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold, notify provider and pharmacy, assess vital signs, and record the allergy. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.
questions.strategy: Wheezing is what raises this from a rash to an airway problem, so observing or deferring are both wrong.

strategies: Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Wheezing cannot wait until the end of the shift.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.

questions.stem: A patient with difficulty swallowing is prescribed an enteric-coated tablet. The nurse considers how to give it, since the patient manages liquids and crushed tablets well but gags on whole tablets. Which action is correct?

options.text: Contact the provider or pharmacist to request an alternative form of the medication
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, so the form has to change rather than the technique.

options.text: Have the patient swallow it with a large volume of water
options.rationale: Does not address the gagging and risks aspiration in a patient with swallowing difficulty.

options.text: Crush the tablet and mix it with applesauce
options.rationale: Destroys the coating that protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication.

options.text: Split the tablet in half so it is easier to swallow
options.rationale: Splitting breaks the enteric coating exactly as crushing does. Half a tablet is still a broken coating.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated medication. The coating protects the stomach lining from the drug. Enteric coating protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication, so an enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split. Liquids are absorbed faster than tablets or capsules and are usually absorbed in the stomach.
questions.strategy: When a form cannot be altered and the patient cannot take it as supplied, the answer is always to change the form through the prescriber or pharmacist rather than to work around it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does not solve the swallowing problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: change the form, not the technique.

questions.concept: Enteric coating protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication, so an enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split. Liquids are absorbed faster than tablets or capsules and are usually absorbed in the stomach.

questions.stem: Four medications are to be given through a gastrostomy tube. Which action requires correction?

options.text: Crushing an extended-release tablet and mixing it with water
options.rationale: Crushing an extended-release form delivers the whole dose at once, so the provider is called for a different formulation.

options.text: Giving each medication separately and flushing between them
options.rationale: Separate doses with flushes between is right, because mixing them causes clumping and tube occlusion.

options.text: Checking tube placement before any medication is given
options.rationale: Checking placement first is right, and it is the step that prevents instilling medication into a lung.

options.text: Holding the head of the bed at 30 degrees or higher during and after the dose
options.rationale: Keeping the head elevated is right, because it reduces aspiration risk.

questions.takeaway: Never crush extended-release or enteric-coated forms. Give medications one at a time with flushes between, verify placement, keep the head up.
questions.strategy: The crushing option is the only one that changes the drug itself. The other three are technique.

strategies: Ask which action alters the medication

steps.action: Separate doses, placement check, head elevation

elimination.verdict: That leaves the crushed extended-release tablet.

questions.stem: Eye drops are prescribed for a patient with glaucoma. Which instillation technique is correct?

options.text: Dropping the medication directly onto the cornea so it spreads evenly
options.rationale: The cornea is sensitive and a drop placed there triggers blinking that expels the medication.

options.text: Pulling down the lower lid and placing the drop in the conjunctival sac, then applying gentle pressure at the inner canthus
options.rationale: The sac holds the drop and pressure at the inner canthus limits systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct.

options.text: Asking the patient to squeeze the eyes shut firmly after the drop
options.rationale: Squeezing pushes the medication out.

options.text: Touching the dropper to the lid margin to steady it
options.rationale: Touching the dropper to the lid contaminates it, and the next drop carries that contamination into the eye.

questions.takeaway: Drop into the conjunctival sac, not onto the cornea. Press the inner canthus to keep the drug in the eye and out of the circulation.
questions.strategy: The punctal pressure step is the one students drop, and it is what keeps a glaucoma drop from producing systemic effects.

strategies: Ask where the drop goes and what happens next

steps.action: Cut squeezing and touching the lid

elimination.verdict: That leaves the conjunctival sac technique.

questions.stem: A patient with dysphagia on a thickened liquid diet has oral medications due. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Position the patient upright at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Upright positioning is the first protection against aspiration.

options.text: Check whether a liquid or dispersible form of the drug is available
options.rationale: A formulation the patient can manage is better than altering a tablet.

options.text: Mix crushed medication into a spoonful of thickened liquid if crushing is permitted
options.rationale: A thickened vehicle matches the ordered consistency.

options.text: Give the medication with thin water to help it go down
options.rationale: Thin liquids are what this patient cannot safely swallow.

options.text: Confirm the patient has swallowed before offering the next medication
options.rationale: One at a time, with confirmation, prevents a pocketed tablet.

options.text: Have suction available at the bedside
options.rationale: Suction is set up before, not retrieved during, an aspiration event.

options.text: Lay the patient flat immediately afterwards for comfort
options.rationale: Remaining upright for a period after the dose is part of the protection.

questions.takeaway: Upright before and after, right formulation, one at a time with confirmation, suction ready, nothing thin.
questions.strategy: The thin water option is the reflex from every other patient, and it is the one thing this patient cannot have.

strategies: Ask what each action does to aspiration risk

steps.action: Upright, formulation, thickened vehicle, one at a time, suction

elimination.verdict: The five protective actions are selected.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receives 18 units of Humulin N subcutaneously at 0800. He eats breakfast at 0830 and lunch at 1230. The nurse plans when to monitor most closely for hypoglycemia from this dose. Which window is correct?

options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.

questions.takeaway: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. That wide peak is why NPH catches people off guard. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.
questions.strategy: The NPH peak is broad rather than sharp, so the risk is spread across a whole shift rather than concentrated in an hour.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.

questions.concept: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.

questions.stem: A nurse is orienting a student who will be checking insulin doses with her. She asks the student to identify each vial by appearance before reading the label, as a first check rather than a substitute for one. Which insulins are clear? Select all that apply.

options.text: Novolin R
options.rationale: Novolin R is regular insulin. Regular insulin is short-acting and clear, and the R in the name is the clue.

options.text: Humulin N
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension, so it is cloudy by design and has to be rolled to mix it evenly before drawing.

options.text: Humulin R
options.rationale: Humulin R is regular insulin. Regular insulin is short-acting and clear, and the R in the name is the clue.

options.text: NovoLog
options.rationale: Aspart is rapid-acting and clear. Clear insulins do not need resuspending before you draw them up.

options.text: Novolin N
options.rationale: Novolin N is NPH, so it is cloudy. The cloudiness is the suspension itself, not spoilage.

options.text: Humalog
options.rationale: Lispro is rapid-acting and comes as a clear solution, so cloudiness in this vial would mean something is wrong.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting and regular insulins are clear. NPH is the cloudy one. Rapid-acting insulins (Humalog, NovoLog) and regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) are clear. NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) is cloudy. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.
questions.strategy: Appearance narrows the field and never replaces reading the label. Two different insulins can look identical and act over completely different time courses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulins (Humalog, NovoLog) and regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) are clear. NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) is cloudy. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old newly started on insulin is preparing for discharge and demonstrates his technique to the nurse while explaining what he plans to do at home. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will not inject into my thigh right before I go for a walk."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Exercise speeds absorption from the limb that was injected, so the walk would drop his glucose faster.

options.text: "I will roll the cloudy vial gently rather than shaking it."
options.rationale: This is accurate. NPH is a suspension, and shaking it froths the vial so an accurate dose is hard to draw.

options.text: "I will rotate between my abdomen, arm, and thigh so I never use the same area twice."
options.rationale: Anatomical site rotation is no longer recommended, because absorption differs by site and rotating between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate. One anatomical site is selected and rotation occurs within that region.

options.text: "If my glucose is under 70 and I can swallow, I take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and the glucose gets rechecked 15 minutes later to see whether it worked.

questions.takeaway: One anatomical site, rotate within that region. Between-region rotation varies absorption dose to dose.
questions.strategy: This guidance changed, so the wrong statement is what patients were taught for years.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rolling, rule of 15, and exercise are correct.

elimination.verdict: The statement needing correction: rotate within one region, not between regions.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's insulin orders before the morning round and must identify which doses are timed to meals and which are not. The patient is prescribed four different insulin products. Which insulins are given in relation to a meal? Select all that apply.

options.text: NovoLog, just before or with the meal
options.rationale: NovoLog is rapid-acting, with onset in 10 to 30 minutes, so it goes in right at the meal.

options.text: Humalog, just before or with the meal
options.rationale: Humalog is rapid-acting, with onset in 10 to 30 minutes, so it goes in right at the meal.

options.text: Levemir, with the largest meal of the day
options.rationale: Levemir is long-acting basal insulin. It covers the whole day rather than matching what he eats.

options.text: Novolin R, about 30 minutes before the meal
options.rationale: Novolin R is short-acting, with onset in 30 to 60 minutes, so it needs that half-hour head start.

options.text: Lantus, 30 minutes before the evening meal
options.rationale: Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak. Its timing is not tied to food.

options.text: Humulin R, about 30 minutes before the meal
options.rationale: Humulin R is short-acting, with onset in 30 to 60 minutes, so it needs that half-hour head start.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting goes with the meal. Regular goes 30 minutes before. Long-acting basal is not timed to food at all. Rapid-acting insulin is given just before or with the meal. Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before. Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A vial labeled Humulin N holds a uniformly cloudy solution. The vial is within date and has been refrigerated. Which action is correct?

options.text: Return the vial to the pharmacy
options.rationale: Cloudiness is the normal appearance of NPH. There is nothing wrong with the vial.

options.text: Draw the dose without mixing
options.rationale: An unmixed suspension has the particles settled at the bottom, so the dose drawn is unpredictable.

options.text: Roll the vial gently between the palms
options.rationale: NPH is an intermediate-acting suspension and is expected to be cloudy. Rolling redistributes it before the dose is drawn.

options.text: Shake the vial until the particles dissolve
options.rationale: Shaking froths the suspension, and froth makes an accurate dose hard to draw. Gentle rolling mixes it without the bubbles.

questions.takeaway: The N in Humulin N and Novolin N stands for NPH. Intermediate-acting, cloudy, gently rolled before use. Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH, intermediate-acting insulin. Onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. Cloudy in appearance and gently rolled before use.
questions.strategy: Cloudy identifies exactly one class. If a vial is cloudy it is NPH, and any other insulin here is clear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cloudiness is the normal appearance of this product.
Shaking froths the suspension and makes an accurate dose difficult to draw.
An unmixed suspension delivers an unpredictable dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: NPH is an intermediate-acting suspension and is expected to be cloudy.

questions.concept: Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH, intermediate-acting insulin. Onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. Cloudy in appearance and gently rolled before use. The N stands for NPH.

questions.stem: An order reads Humulin R 8 units subcutaneously before meals. The nurse removes a vial labeled Humulin N from the cabinet and notices the discrepancy before drawing up the dose. Which action is correct?

options.text: Return it and obtain Humulin R
options.rationale: The two differ in onset, peak, and duration. NPH given in place of regular would peak hours after the meal it was meant to cover.

options.text: Give the Humulin N as drawn
options.rationale: These two share a brand name and differ by class. The N is NPH, not regular insulin.

options.text: Give half the Humulin N dose
options.rationale: Halving the dose still gives the wrong insulin, now at an improvised dose.

options.text: Give both at the next meal
options.rationale: This administers an insulin that was never ordered, just later in the day.

questions.takeaway: Humulin R is regular and short-acting. Humulin R is regular and short-acting; Humulin N is NPH and intermediate-acting. The shared brand name is the trap. A shared brand name does not mean a shared class, and look-alike insulin names are a recognized cause of medication error.
questions.strategy: Look-alike names are a causes of insulin error. The brand tells you the manufacturer; the letter after it tells you what the drug does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The brand is shared and the class is not.
Improvises a dose of the wrong insulin.
Administers an insulin that was never ordered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the two differ in onset, peak, and duration.

questions.concept: Humulin R is regular and short-acting; Humulin N is NPH and intermediate-acting. A shared brand name does not mean a shared class, and look-alike insulin names are a recognized cause of medication error.

questions.stem: A nurse is called to a patient who seems unwell an hour after receiving mealtime insulin. She considers whether the presentation fits a falling blood glucose before checking. Which findings are consistent with hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia
options.rationale: Tachycardia is part of the same adrenergic response that produces the shakiness and sweating.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with a fruity odor
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations, meaning deep rapid breathing that blows off acid, and ketotic breath indicate ketoacidosis.

options.text: Shakiness and diaphoresis
options.rationale: Shakiness and sweating are sympathetic responses, and they are usually the earliest warning you get.

options.text: Irritability or anxiety
options.rationale: Irritability or anxiety is a real sign, and it often gets mistaken for a behavioral issue.

options.text: Warm, dry, flushed skin
options.rationale: Warm, dry, flushed skin points to hyperglycemia. Hypoglycemia produces the opposite: cool, clammy skin from the adrenergic response.

options.text: Polyuria developing over the past two days
options.rationale: The picture of hyperglycemia, driven by osmotic diuresis, meaning sugar in the urine drags water out with it. It builds over days rather than minutes.

questions.takeaway: Shaky, sweaty, tachycardic, hungry, irritable, confused. Hypoglycemia comes on fast; hyperglycemia builds over days. Hypoglycemia presents as shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hunger, irritability or anxiety, confusion, and altered level of consciousness.
questions.strategy: Onset separates them as reliably as the symptoms do. Anything developing over minutes after insulin points at a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polyuria and polydipsia are hyperglycemia over days.

elimination.verdict: A, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Hypoglycemia presents as shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hunger, irritability or anxiety, confusion, and altered level of consciousness.

questions.stem: An order reads Novolin R 8 units subcutaneously before lunch. Meal trays arrive on the unit at 1200. The patient is eating normally and his 0700 glucose was 142 mg/dL. At what time should the dose be given?

options.rationale: Giving it after the tray arrives leaves the insulin working after the food has already been absorbed.
Giving it right at the meal is the timing for rapid-acting insulin, not regular.
Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so a dose half an hour ahead matches its action to the meal.
Two hours ahead brings the insulin to its peak well before any carbohydrate arrives.

questions.takeaway: The R in Humulin R and Novolin R stands for Regular. Short-acting, given about 30 minutes before meals. Humulin R and Novolin R are regular, short-acting insulin. Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: Two hours ahead brings the insulin to its peak well before any carbohydrate arrives.
That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Leaves the insulin acting after the food has been absorbed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so a dose half an hour ahead matches its action to the meal.

questions.concept: Humulin R and Novolin R are regular, short-acting insulin. Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. Given about 30 minutes before meals. The R stands for Regular.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to give a scheduled dose of insulin to a patient admitted two days ago. Insulin is a high-alert medication and she works through her checks before drawing it up. Which checks does she complete before administering? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine whether the patient is eating and whether the timing fits the meal
options.rationale: A dose that was correct for a normal meal becomes too much when the meal is skipped or delayed, and that is a frequent cause of inpatient lows.

options.text: Administer the dose before checking the glucose so the timing is not delayed
options.rationale: Reverses the order and removes the check that decides whether the dose is safe.

options.text: Review the insulin ordered, the dose, and any hold or notify parameters
options.rationale: You check the insulin, the dose, and any hold or notify parameters. Those parameters exist so the dose is not given automatically.

options.text: Establish the current blood glucose and whether it is safe to give insulin now
options.rationale: You get a current glucose first, because the value decides whether the dose goes ahead at all.

options.text: Confirm the patient has a working intravenous line
options.rationale: This insulin is subcutaneous, so an intravenous line has nothing to do with it.

options.text: Confirm the expiry date on the vial
options.rationale: Checking expiry applies to any medication and is not one of the specific checks before an insulin dose.

questions.takeaway: Patient, glucose, order, food, safety, then reassess. Incorrect type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Before insulin, check patient, glucose, order, food, safety, and reassessment plan.
questions.strategy: Each of the four causes of inpatient hypoglycemia is caught by one of these checks. That is what the order of the list is built around.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Giving before checking removes the deciding check.

elimination.verdict: A, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Before insulin, check patient, glucose, order, food, safety, and reassessment plan. Incorrect type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A patient receives 10 units of Humulin R subcutaneously at 0730 and eats breakfast at 0800. At which time is he at greatest risk of hypoglycemia from this dose?

options.rationale: Beyond the peak, and approaching the end of the 5 to 8 hour duration.
Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is barely working.
Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which places the risk window mid-morning.
Twelve hours out is well past the duration of regular insulin, so this dose is finished by then.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R): onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. The peak is when you watch. The peak is the window for hypoglycemia.
questions.strategy: Peak is the single most useful number in the table. Onset tells you when to give it; peak tells you when a low is most likely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular insulin peaks at 2 to 4 hours.
Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is barely working.
Beyond the peak, and approaching the end of the 5 to 8 hour duration.
Twelve hours out, well past the duration of this dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose, which places the risk window mid-morning.

questions.concept: Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R): onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. The peak is the window for hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: An order reads insulin lispro 6 units subcutaneously three times daily with meals. The patient has just been made nothing by mouth for an endoscopy later this morning. His fingerstick glucose is 134 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider that the patient is nothing by mouth
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is matched to carbohydrate. With the meal cancelled, the dose is held and the prescriber decides what the patient needs.

options.text: Give the dose now, since it is ordered for this time
options.rationale: Mealtime insulin with no meal coming produces hypoglycemia within the hour.

options.text: Give half the dose to cover the basal requirement
options.rationale: This insulin is not a basal insulin, and splitting a dose is not a nursing decision.

options.text: Give the dose and provide intravenous dextrose to cover it
options.rationale: Covering an unnecessary dose with dextrose adds two interventions where none was needed.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin covers a meal. No meal means no mealtime dose, and the prescriber is told so the plan for the procedure can be set.
questions.strategy: The order exists and the glucose is normal, which makes giving it feel safe. Ask what the dose was there to cover.

strategies: Ask what the dose covers

steps.detail: Not basal, not a nursing decision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves holding and notifying.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a student to sort the unit's insulin supply into classes before the morning medication round, since several products share a brand name and differ only by a letter. Which statements pair the product with its class correctly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lantus is rapid-acting because it is clear
options.rationale: Appearance does not tell you the class. Lantus is clear and it is long-acting.

options.text: Humulin R and Novolin R are short-acting regular insulin
options.rationale: The R in both names stands for Regular, which is short-acting. Both are the same drug under two brand names.

options.text: Humalog and NovoLog are rapid-acting
options.rationale: Lispro and aspart both start working within about 15 minutes, so they go in with the food already in front of the patient.

options.text: Humulin R and Humulin N are the same class because they share a brand name
options.rationale: The brand identifies the manufacturer's family. The letter after it identifies the class, and R and N behave completely differently.

options.text: Lantus and Levemir are long-acting basal insulin
options.rationale: Glargine and detemir release steadily over roughly 24 hours with no pronounced peak, which is what makes them basal insulin.

options.text: Humulin N and Novolin N are intermediate-acting NPH
options.rationale: The N in both names stands for NPH, which is intermediate-acting. Both are the same drug under two brand names.

questions.takeaway: Four classes: Humalog and NovoLog rapid, Humulin R and Novolin R short, Humulin N and Novolin N intermediate, Lantus and Levemir long. Four classes by name: Humalog and NovoLog are rapid-acting; Humulin R and Novolin R are short-acting regular; Humulin N and Novolin N are intermediate-acting NPH; Lantus and Levemir are long-acting basal.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options use a shortcut that fails: the brand name and the appearance. The letter after the brand carries the class, and clear covers three of the four.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

questions.stem: Fasting glucose results at 0630 for four patients are 48 mg/dL, 96 mg/dL, 164 mg/dL and 212 mg/dL. All four are alert. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: 212 mg/dL
options.rationale: Hyperglycemia requiring assessment and orders, and not the immediate emergency a low is.

options.text: 164 mg/dL
options.rationale: A glucose of 164 is within the common inpatient target range, so nothing is needed right now.

options.text: 96 mg/dL
options.rationale: A glucose of 96 is within the common inpatient target of 70 to 180.

options.text: 48 mg/dL
options.rationale: Below 70, and within ADA level 2 hypoglycemia at under 54. It is an immediate safety concern.

questions.takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range. Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia requiring assessment and review of orders. ADA levels: level 1 is 54 to 69 mg/dL, level 2 is under 54 mg/dL.
questions.strategy: A high glucose needs attention and a low glucose needs it now. When a stem offers both, the low wins on urgency every time.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: One below 70, two in range, one above 180.
Within the common inpatient target range of 70 to 180.
Hyperglycemia requiring assessment and orders, and not the immediate emergency a low is.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: below 70, and within ADA level 2 hypoglycemia at under 54.
