questions.stem: A patient is prescribed Lantus 20 units at bedtime and NovoLog 5 units with meals. He asks why the bedtime dose does not have to be timed to food. Which response is accurate?

options.text: It is used only when he is fasting
options.rationale: Basal insulin keeps working whether or not he eats. It covers the glucose his liver releases between meals and overnight.

options.text: It has no pronounced peak
options.rationale: Glargine covers the background need over 20 to 24 hours or more, so its timing is not tied to carbohydrate.

options.text: It acts the same way but lasts longer
options.rationale: NovoLog is rapid-acting with a defined peak. The two classes differ in more than duration.

options.text: It peaks overnight while he sleeps
options.rationale: There is no pronounced peak, and that is why it is used for basal coverage.

questions.takeaway: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak, lasting 20 to 24 hours or more.
questions.strategy: No pronounced peak is the defining feature. It explains why basal insulin is not timed to meals and why it is not the insulin that causes a mealtime low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: There is no pronounced peak, and that is why it is used for basal coverage.
Basal insulin continues regardless of intake.
NovoLog is rapid-acting with a defined peak.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: glargine provides background coverage over 20 to 24 hours or more, so its timing is not tied to carbohydrate.

questions.concept: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with an onset of 1 to 2 hours, no pronounced peak, and a duration of 20 to 24 hours or more. Never mixed with other insulin types.

questions.stem: A point-of-care glucose is due on a patient whose hands are cold and who has been resting under a blanket. The meter and strips are at the bedside and the patient has just woken. Which actions reflect correct technique? Select all that apply.

options.text: Squeeze the finger firmly to obtain an adequate sample quickly
options.rationale: Excessive squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid and produces an inaccurate result.

options.text: Puncture the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Less painful and yields a better sample than the pad, which has more nerve endings.

options.text: Wash and dry hands thoroughly before testing
options.rationale: Hands get washed and dried before testing, and the drying matters because leftover water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Warm the finger under hot running water to improve flow
options.rationale: Hot water is unnecessary and risks a burn. Warming gently or lowering the hand is sufficient.

options.text: Verify the patient's identity before testing
options.rationale: Identity gets verified before a fingerstick the same as before any other procedure, because the result goes in someone's chart.

options.text: Wipe away the first drop and use the second
options.rationale: Applies to some devices by manufacturer instruction rather than as a universal rule.

questions.takeaway: Identify, wash and dry, check the meter and strips, use the side of the fingertip, and never squeeze hard. Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is the shortcut everyone takes when blood is slow to come. It changes the number you are about to act on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid.

elimination.verdict: B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A patient injects his insulin into his thigh at 0700 and goes for a brisk 30-minute walk at 0730. His glucose has dropped during the walk on three consecutive mornings. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The thigh absorbs faster than the abdomen
options.rationale: This has the two sites backwards. The abdomen absorbs faster than the thigh.

options.text: Absorption differs by site
options.rationale: The abdomen is fastest and the thigh slower, and exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.

options.text: Site choice affects comfort only
options.rationale: Comfort does matter, but absorption rate is the clinical reason the site is chosen.

options.text: Absorption is the same at every site
options.rationale: Absorption differs by site, and that is why the site gets chosen deliberately.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas and rotate sites per policy. Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip.
questions.strategy: Site choice interacts with activity. Exercise speeds absorption from the limb you injected, so a thigh dose before a walk behaves differently from the same dose before sitting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It differs by site, so the site is chosen deliberately.
Comfort matters and absorption is the clinical reason.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the abdomen is fastest and the thigh slower, and exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas and rotate sites per policy.

questions.stem: A student is preparing to give her first subcutaneous insulin injection and describes her plan to the nurse before approaching the patient. She has practiced in the skills laboratory and wants her technique checked. Which elements of her description are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Massage the site after withdrawing the needle
options.rationale: Massaging the site changes how fast the insulin absorbs, so it is avoided after an insulin injection.

options.text: Pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat as appropriate for the site and needle length
options.rationale: Pinching makes sure the dose lands in subcutaneous tissue rather than muscle, and whether you pinch depends on the site and needle length.

options.text: Aspirate before injecting to check for blood return
options.rationale: Aspiration is not part of a subcutaneous insulin injection. It belongs to some intramuscular injections, not this one.

options.text: Withdraw the needle at the same angle used for insertion
options.rationale: Pulling straight back out along the track you made avoids dragging the needle sideways through tissue.

options.text: Aspirate before injecting to confirm placement
options.rationale: Aspiration is not part of a subcutaneous insulin injection, and it does not confirm anything about placement here.

options.text: Insert the needle at a 90 degree angle
options.rationale: The typical angle for subcutaneous insulin, adjusted for the site and needle length.

questions.takeaway: Pinch, insert at 90 degrees, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold briefly, withdraw at the same angle, dispose immediately. Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle, and dispose in a sharps container immediately.
questions.strategy: Aspiration is the step students import from intramuscular technique. It is not part of subcutaneous insulin administration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pinch, insert, inject, hold, withdraw, dispose.
Aspiration belongs to a different route.

elimination.verdict: B, D, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle, and dispose in a sharps container immediately.

questions.stem: An order reads regular insulin 6 units subcutaneously before breakfast. The tray is expected in 30 minutes. The patient is alert, eating normally, and his fingerstick glucose is 156 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the dose now
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

options.text: Hold the dose until bedtime
options.rationale: Holding a mealtime insulin until bedtime separates it from the meal it was written to cover.

options.text: Give the dose when the tray arrives
options.rationale: Giving it when the tray arrives is the timing for rapid-acting insulin, not regular.

options.text: Give the dose after he has eaten half the meal
options.rationale: Giving it mid-meal leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate is already absorbed.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting goes just before or with the meal. Regular goes about 30 minutes before, because its onset is slower. Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.
questions.strategy: Match the onset to the food. The number to remember is not the duration but when the insulin starts working relative to when carbohydrate arrives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.
Separates a mealtime insulin from the meal it covers.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.

questions.stem: A patient is alert and swallowing safely. His fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. His rapid-acting insulin is due now and his breakfast tray has not arrived. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the scheduled insulin
options.rationale: Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. It would drive the glucose lower.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: A glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck comes after treatment. It does not take the place of treating a glucose of 58.

options.text: Wait for the breakfast tray
options.rationale: Waiting on the tray delays treatment while the glucose keeps falling. A glucose of 58 gets treated now.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then work out why it happened. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low.
questions.strategy: The scheduled insulin and the missing tray are both deliberate pressure. Neither changes the rule that a glucose under 70 is treated now.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.
The recheck follows treatment rather than replacing it.
Delays treatment while the glucose continues to fall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: During her morning insulin round a nurse is told the breakfast trays are delayed by an hour. Two of her patients are due rapid-acting insulin and one is due long-acting basal insulin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give a double dose of Humalog once the tray arrives to make up the delay
options.rationale: Doubling a mealtime dose has no basis and creates a serious hypoglycemia risk.

options.text: Give the patient's Lantus as scheduled
options.rationale: Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not timed to food, so a delayed tray does not change it.

options.text: Notify the provider if the delay affects the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: The provider gets notified, because the regimen was written around a meal schedule that has now changed.

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose if there is any further delay
options.rationale: The glucose gets rechecked if the delay goes on, because delayed intake is a common cause of inpatient hypoglycemia.

options.text: Give the Humalog now so the round stays on time
options.rationale: Prioritizes the schedule over the patient and produces the exact mismatch that causes hypoglycemia.

options.text: Hold the rapid-acting Humalog until the tray is actually in front of the patient
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin begins working in 10 to 30 minutes, so giving it an hour before food creates a low.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin waits for the meal. Basal insulin does not, because it is not matched to food. Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.
questions.strategy: This single scenario separates the two classes. If a delayed tray changes whether you give it, it is a mealtime insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime; Lantus is basal.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.

questions.stem: Six units of regular insulin and 14 units of NPH are to be drawn into one syringe. The NPH vial has been rolled and air has been drawn up. Which step comes next?

options.text: Inject air into the NPH vial without withdrawing insulin
options.rationale: Air is injected into the cloudy vial first, without drawing any insulin, so the clear vial is never contaminated with suspension.

options.text: Inject air into the regular vial and withdraw the regular insulin
options.rationale: The regular insulin is drawn later. Injecting air into the cloudy vial comes first.

options.text: Withdraw the NPH first since it is the larger dose
options.rationale: Dose size does not set the order. Clear is always drawn before cloudy.

options.text: Withdraw both doses into separate syringes and combine them
options.rationale: Transferring insulin between syringes adds a chance for error and breaks the closed system for no reason.

questions.takeaway: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, draw cloudy. The clear vial must stay uncontaminated.
questions.strategy: The order protects the clear vial. If suspension enters it, every later dose drawn from that vial is altered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Air into cloudy first, without drawing.
Regular is drawn after the air step is complete.
Dose size is irrelevant, and combining syringes adds error.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: air into the NPH vial first.

questions.concept: NPH is intermediate-acting with an onset of 1 to 2 hours, a peak at 4 to 12 hours, and a duration of 14 to 24 hours. It is cloudy and is gently rolled before use. Rapid-acting and regular insulins are clear.

questions.stem: A patient taking glyburide is also prescribed metoprolol for hypertension. Which concern does the nurse identify?

options.text: The beta blocker will raise the blood glucose
options.rationale: Beta blockers have a modest and unpredictable effect on glucose. Losing the warning signs is the danger.

options.text: The beta blocker reduces absorption of the glyburide
options.rationale: There is no meaningful absorption interaction between these two drugs. The problem is what the beta blocker hides, not what it absorbs.

options.text: The combination increases the risk of lactic acidosis
options.rationale: Lactic acidosis is a metformin concern. Glyburide is a sulfonylurea and works differently.

options.text: The beta blocker may mask the early warning signs of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The shakiness, sweating, and racing heart that warn of a low are adrenergic. A beta blocker blunts them, so the first sign may be confusion instead.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia. Sweating usually persists; shakiness and palpitations do not.
questions.strategy: Ask what the patient would normally feel first during a low, and what a beta blocker does to that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a beta blocker blocks

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the warning signs are masked.

questions.stem: A patient who takes acarbose with each meal becomes hypoglycemic. Which does the nurse administer?

options.text: Table sugar dissolved in water
options.rationale: Sucrose has to be split into glucose and fructose first, and acarbose is blocking exactly that step. This is the trap.

options.text: A slice of bread
options.rationale: Bread is a complex carbohydrate that has to be digested first, so it works too slowly here.

options.text: A glass of milk
options.rationale: Lactose also requires breakdown, and milk raises glucose too slowly for an acute low.

options.text: Glucose tablets
options.rationale: Acarbose blocks the enzyme that breaks table sugar into absorbable glucose, so sucrose will not work. Glucose tablets need no digestion.

questions.takeaway: On acarbose or miglitol, treat hypoglycemia with glucose specifically. Sucrose and starch will not be absorbed.
questions.strategy: This is the one hypoglycemia scenario where the usual juice-or-sugar answer is wrong. The drug name in the stem is what tells you.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breakdown of complex sugars in the gut.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: glucose tablets.

questions.stem: A patient is starting empagliflozin. Which teaching does the nurse include?

options.text: Expect increased urination, and report burning or genital itching
options.rationale: SGLT-2 inhibitors work by dumping glucose into the urine. Sugar in the urine raises the risk of urinary and genital yeast infections.

options.text: This is a form of insulin taken by mouth
options.rationale: There is no oral insulin. Insulin taken by mouth is destroyed in the stomach.

options.text: Your urine should stay free of glucose on this medication
options.rationale: This has it backwards. Putting glucose into the urine is how the drug works, not a complication.

options.text: Take it only when the glucose reads above 200
options.rationale: This drug is taken on a schedule, not in response to a glucose reading.

questions.takeaway: SGLT-2 inhibitors lower glucose by excreting it in the urine, which brings polyuria and a risk of urinary and yeast infections.
questions.strategy: Work out the mechanism from the drug class and the side effects follow from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose is excreted in the urine.
More urine, and sugar feeding organisms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: more urination, and report infection signs.

questions.stem: A patient on metformin is scheduled for a computed tomography scan with iodinated contrast. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give half the usual dose
options.rationale: Not a recognized approach. The decision is to hold or not, and it is the provider's.

options.text: Confirm with the provider that the metformin is held around the study
options.rationale: Contrast can impair kidney function, and metformin cleared by the kidneys accumulates. The build-up risks lactic acidosis.

options.text: Give the metformin with a full glass of water before the scan
options.rationale: Water does not protect the kidneys from the contrast or clear the drug faster.

options.text: No action, since metformin does not interact with contrast
options.rationale: Metformin and contrast do interact, and this is one of the most heavily tested drug and procedure pairings.

questions.takeaway: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast because contrast-related kidney impairment lets it accumulate and cause lactic acidosis.
questions.strategy: Ask what clears the drug and what the contrast does to that organ.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm the hold with the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the oral diabetes medications for four patients and needs to know which ones require teaching about hypoglycemia even when taken alone. Select all that apply.

options.text: Acarbose
options.rationale: Slows carbohydrate absorption rather than adding insulin. Low risk alone, though it changes how a low must be treated.

options.text: Metformin
options.rationale: Reduces liver glucose output and improves sensitivity. It does not force insulin release, so alone it rarely causes a low.

options.text: Glimepiride
options.rationale: Glimepiride is the third of the commonly used sulfonylureas, and it carries the same risk.

options.text: Glyburide
options.rationale: Glyburide is also a sulfonylurea, so it pushes insulin out of the pancreas whether or not the patient has eaten.

options.text: Sitagliptin
options.rationale: A DPP-4 inhibitor. It acts through incretins, which work only when glucose is rising, so the risk is low.

options.text: Glipizide
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea. It pushes the pancreas to release insulin whether or not glucose is high, so a low can follow.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia because they force insulin release regardless of the glucose level. Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors and acarbose do not.
questions.strategy: Sort by mechanism. Anything that pushes insulin out regardless of glucose can cause a low; anything that is glucose-dependent cannot.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: Force insulin, or work only when glucose rises.

elimination.verdict: C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: Which observation about a patient's insulin supply requires follow-up?

options.text: The regular insulin appears clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is a clear solution, so this is exactly what it should look like.

options.text: The NPH insulin appears cloudy
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension and is cloudy by design. It is rolled to mix it before drawing.

options.text: The insulin lispro appears clear
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is clear, so this is exactly what the vial should look like.

options.text: The insulin glargine appears cloudy
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation, and the vial must not be used.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH should look cloudy. Every other insulin is clear, and cloudiness in a clear insulin means discard it.
questions.strategy: One insulin is meant to be cloudy. Any other cloudy vial is the finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH cloudy, regular and lispro clear.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: cloudy glargine.

questions.stem: A patient wakes with a glucose of 240 mg/dL. Overnight readings show a fall to 48 mg/dL at 0300 followed by a rise. Which does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Somogyi phenomenon
options.rationale: An overnight low triggers counter-regulatory hormones, which drive the glucose up by morning. The high reading is the rebound from the low.

options.text: Insufficient evening basal insulin
options.rationale: That would produce a steady overnight rise, not a fall to 48 first.

options.text: An inaccurate morning meter reading
options.rationale: The overnight trend explains the morning value. Dismissing it as error loses the pattern.

options.text: Dawn phenomenon
options.rationale: Dawn is a morning rise from overnight growth hormone and cortisol, with no preceding low. The 0300 reading of 48 is what separates them.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi has an overnight low that rebounds. Dawn rises without a low. The 0200 to 0300 check is what distinguishes them.
questions.strategy: Both produce a high morning glucose, and the overnight reading is the only thing that separates them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One predicts a steady rise, one dismisses real data.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: Somogyi phenomenon.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes has influenza and is vomiting. Which sick-day instructions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the insulin until eating normally again
options.rationale: This is the most dangerous sick-day error there is. Insulin need usually goes up during illness, not down.

options.text: Take small sips of fluid frequently
options.rationale: Vomiting plus a rising glucose dehydrates quickly, and dehydration accelerates the whole process.

options.text: Wait until the fever settles before contacting the provider
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting, ketones, or a glucose that will not come down need reporting rather than waiting.

options.text: Keep taking the insulin, even when not eating normally
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose through stress hormones. Stopping insulin during illness is how patients arrive in ketoacidosis.

options.text: Test for ketones when the glucose stays above 240
options.rationale: Ketones signal that fat is being broken down for fuel and that ketoacidosis may be developing.

options.text: Check the glucose every three to four hours
options.rationale: The glucose gets checked more often than usual, because illness makes it unpredictable.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: never stop insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, test ketones above 240, and keep fluids going.
questions.strategy: Two options tell the patient to wait or to stop. Ask what illness does to the insulin requirement.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: The need goes up, not down.
Vomiting with ketones is what needs reporting.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A patient using an insulin pump reports the glucose has risen from 140 to 310 mg/dL over four hours and ketones are now present. Which does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: A faulty glucose meter
options.rationale: The ketones corroborate the reading. Two findings agreeing is not a meter fault.

options.text: The pump is delivering too much basal insulin
options.rationale: Too much would lower the glucose, not raise it, and would not produce ketones.

options.text: An expected rise after a high-carbohydrate meal
options.rationale: A meal does not produce ketones, and the rise would not continue over four hours.

options.text: An interruption in insulin delivery at the site or in the tubing
options.rationale: A pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin, with no long-acting reserve. An occlusion or dislodged cannula leaves the patient with no insulin at all within hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump patients have no long-acting insulin on board. An interruption produces hyperglycemia and ketones within hours.
questions.strategy: Ask what a pump does and does not deliver. The ketones are the finding that rules out a simple meal-related rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: They indicate no insulin is reaching the patient.

steps.action: Cut the meal and meter options

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an interruption in delivery.

questions.stem: A patient's fingerstick reads 268 mg/dL, which is far above his usual range. He was eating sliced peaches and wiped his hands on a napkin before the test. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the value and hold the next meal
options.rationale: Acting on a value that may be contaminated commits the team to a wrong number.

options.text: Have him wash his hands with soap and water and repeat the test
options.rationale: Sugar residue on the skin raises the reading, and washing with soap and water is what removes it.

options.text: Give the ordered correction insulin for that range
options.rationale: Giving insulin for a false high can produce hypoglycemia.

options.text: Wipe the finger with alcohol and repeat using the same drop of blood
options.rationale: Alcohol does not reliably remove sugar residue and the residual alcohol itself affects the reading.

questions.takeaway: A value that does not fit the patient gets verified before it is acted on. Soap and water, then repeat.
questions.strategy: The high number invites treatment. Ask what else could have produced it before you treat it.

strategies: Ask whether the number is believable

steps.detail: Both act on an unverified value.

elimination.verdict: That leaves washing and repeating.

questions.stem: A patient is learning to use an insulin pen. Which instruction is essential to an accurate dose?

options.text: Hold the needle in the skin for about ten seconds after pushing the button all the way in
options.rationale: The dose leaves the pen over several seconds, and withdrawing early leaves part of it on the skin.

options.text: Massage the site for thirty seconds after withdrawing the needle
options.rationale: Massage changes the absorption rate and is not done.

options.text: Store the pen in the freezer between doses
options.rationale: Freezing destroys insulin, and a frozen pen is discarded rather than thawed.

options.text: Reuse the same needle for a full day to reduce cost
options.rationale: Reused needles dull, hurt and raise infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Count to ten before withdrawing a pen needle. The dose is still being delivered after the button bottoms out.
questions.strategy: Three options are things patients do. The ten-second count is the step that decides whether the dose arrives.

strategies: Ask what affects the dose delivered
elimination.verdict: That leaves holding for ten seconds.

questions.stem: Which situations can produce an inaccurate capillary glucose result? Select all that apply.

options.text: Squeezing the finger hard to get enough blood
options.rationale: Milking dilutes the sample with tissue fluid and lowers the reading.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the major endocrine glands with a student before a shift on a medical unit where three patients have endocrine disorders. She asks the student to pair each gland with what it regulates, since the symptoms follow from the function. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thymus: regulates blood glucose
options.rationale: The pancreas regulates blood glucose. The thymus is lymphatic tissue and has no role in it.

options.text: Thyroid: controls metabolism, energy, and body temperature
options.rationale: The thyroid sets metabolism, energy and temperature, so its symptoms cluster around rate and warmth.

options.text: Pituitary: the master gland that regulates other endocrine glands
options.rationale: The pituitary directs the other glands, and it also controls growth hormone and water balance through ADH.

options.text: Adrenal glands: produce insulin and glucagon
options.rationale: The pancreas produces insulin and glucagon. The adrenals manage stress response and fluid balance.

options.text: Hypothalamus: produces reproductive hormones
options.rationale: The ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

options.text: Parathyroids: regulate calcium and phosphate in blood and bone
options.rationale: The parathyroids run calcium and phosphate, and calcium is what nerves, muscle and cardiac rhythm depend on.

questions.takeaway: Hypothalamus links the systems, pituitary directs, thyroid sets the pace, parathyroids manage calcium, adrenals handle stress and fluid, pancreas handles glucose. Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.
questions.strategy: Disorders affect the whole body, not just the gland. Once you know what a gland regulates, its dysfunction predicts which systems will show symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reproductive hormones come from the ovaries and testes.

elimination.verdict: B, C, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old is admitted with symptoms her provider suspects are thyroid-related. She reports feeling constantly warm, has lost weight over three months despite eating well, and her hands are visibly tremulous. Which findings are consistent with hyperthyroidism? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cold intolerance and dry skin
options.rationale: Cold intolerance and dry skin come from a slowed metabolism, which is the opposite problem.

options.text: Restlessness, anxiety, and tremors
options.rationale: Everything speeds up, including the nervous system, which is where the restlessness and tremor come from.

options.text: Constipation and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Constipation and slow reflexes also point to an underactive thyroid, where everything runs slower.

options.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: A faster heart and higher pressure follow directly, and they are why cardiovascular monitoring is the nursing priority.

options.text: Heat intolerance and excessive sweating
options.rationale: The thyroid sets temperature regulation, so an overactive one leaves her warm and sweating.

options.text: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone drives metabolism, so an excess burns through calories faster than she can eat them.

questions.takeaway: Hyper speeds everything up: weight loss, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia. Hypo slows everything down. Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.
questions.strategy: You do not need to memorize two lists. Decide whether metabolism is fast or slow, then predict what each system does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, temperature, mood, and heart rate all speed up.
Cold intolerance and constipation are the slow picture.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.concept: Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with adrenal dysfunction has an unstable blood pressure, a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L, and reports profound fatigue. Which hormone's action best explains the blood pressure and sodium findings?

options.text: Aldosterone
options.rationale: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium, and disruption produces both the electrolyte abnormality and the unstable pressure.

options.text: Insulin
options.rationale: Insulin is a pancreatic hormone affecting glucose. It does nothing to sodium or blood pressure.

options.text: Antidiuretic hormone
options.rationale: ADH does affect water balance and can dilute sodium, but it is released by the pituitary. The stem points at the adrenal glands.

options.text: Parathyroid hormone
options.rationale: Parathyroid hormone regulates calcium. It explains neither the sodium nor the pressure.

questions.takeaway: The adrenal glands manage stress response, blood pressure through aldosterone, fluid and electrolyte balance, and glucose metabolism through cortisol. The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.
questions.strategy: Adrenal dysfunction shows up as unstable blood pressure, electrolyte imbalance, fatigue, and an impaired stress response. Those four together are the pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves A: aldosterone.

questions.concept: The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.

questions.stem: A patient with a pituitary disorder has a urine output of 4,200 mL over eight hours with a specific gravity of 1.002, and reports constant thirst. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Serum calcium and phosphate
options.rationale: Calcium and phosphate are parathyroid concerns. Nothing here points at the parathyroids.

options.text: Serum sodium and fluid balance
options.rationale: Pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

options.text: Blood glucose and serum ketones
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces urine loaded with glucose. Urine this dilute points elsewhere.

options.text: Thyroid function and temperature tolerance
options.rationale: This fits a thyroid disorder, and it does not explain 4,200 mL of very dilute urine.

questions.takeaway: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Monitor urine output, fluid balance, and serum sodium.
questions.strategy: Diabetes insipidus and diabetes mellitus both cause polyuria and thirst. The urine tells you which: very dilute points at ADH, glucose-laden points at osmotic diuresis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fits a thyroid disorder and does not explain dilute polyuria.
Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces glucose-laden urine, not urine this dilute.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

questions.concept: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Nursing focus includes monitoring urine output and fluid balance, assessing serum sodium, and recognizing diabetes insipidus, which presents with excess dilute urine and thirst.

questions.stem: A patient's serum calcium is 7.4 mg/dL on the first day after a thyroidectomy. She reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Which nursing actions are indicated? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage a high-phosphate diet
options.rationale: Phosphate and calcium move in opposite directions. Raising the phosphate would push her calcium lower still.

options.text: Restrict dietary calcium
options.rationale: Her calcium is already low at 7.4. Restricting it makes the problem worse.

options.text: Assess for Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs
options.rationale: Trousseau's and Chvostek's are the neuromuscular signs of low calcium, and they are what you check at the bedside.

options.text: Watch for muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones
options.rationale: This is the picture of high calcium, which is the opposite imbalance to the one she has.

options.text: Monitor cardiac rhythm
options.rationale: Calcium is essential to cardiac rhythm, and an imbalance in either direction produces arrhythmias.

options.text: Implement fall prevention measures
options.rationale: Low calcium makes muscles irritable and unreliable, so fall prevention belongs in the plan.

questions.takeaway: Hypocalcemia produces tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones. PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs.
questions.strategy: PTH raises calcium when it drops; calcitonin lowers it when it is high. Knowing which hormone is missing predicts which direction the calcium moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weakness and kidney stones describe hypercalcemia.

elimination.verdict: C, E, and F are selected.

questions.concept: PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones.

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews endocrine physiology with a student before a clinical shift, asking her to explain how hormones reach their targets and what happens when regulation fails. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "A hormone only reaches the tissues it is meant to affect."
options.rationale: Hormones are released into the bloodstream and reach every tissue. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, so the same hormone does different things in different places.

options.text: "Hypocalcemia causes tetany and seizures; hypercalcemia causes weakness and confusion."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Which direction the calcium has moved decides the whole presentation.

options.text: "Negative feedback counteracts a change and then switches off."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and diabetes is that same loop broken at the glucose step.

options.text: "Hyperthyroidism speeds everything up, so I would expect weight loss and heat intolerance."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Setting the direction first lets you predict what each system will do.

questions.takeaway: Hormones reach every tissue. Receptors decide which ones respond.

Feedback, thyroid direction, and calcium are correct.

questions.stem: A student asks why insulin circulates through the entire body but does not affect every tissue in the same way. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Hormones are broken down before reaching most tissues
options.rationale: Hormones do reach nearly every tissue. Whether a tissue responds depends on whether it has receptors for that hormone.

options.text: Every cell reached responds equally
options.rationale: If every cell responded equally, targeted hormonal regulation would be impossible.

options.text: Only cells with matching receptors respond
options.rationale: Receptor specificity decides which tissues are affected, so the same hormone produces different responses in different places.

options.text: Hormones reach only the organ that produced them

Hormones are released into the bloodstream and travel to distant targets.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four patients with endocrine disorders at the start of a shift and must decide what to assess first on each. Two have laboratory results pending and one has been increasingly drowsy overnight. Which questions guide her priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine how long the endocrine diagnosis has been present
options.rationale: Duration of a diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

options.text: Are vital signs within a safe range, including blood pressure and temperature extremes?
options.rationale: Endocrine disorders produce hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia and temperature extremes, so the vital signs come early.

options.text: Are the ABCs affected, with a patent airway, adequate breathing, and stable circulation?
options.rationale: The ABCs are the first priority-setting question in any acute situation, endocrine or not.

options.text: Has the patient's gland disorder been present for more than a year?
options.rationale: Duration of the diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

options.text: Is there altered mental status, confusion, or decreased level of consciousness?
options.rationale: A specified priority, and mental status change is often the first sign of a critical glucose or electrolyte value.

options.text: Confirm the patient has a follow-up appointment booked
options.rationale: A discharge consideration rather than a question that sets priority at the bedside.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old newly prescribed levothyroxine for hypothyroidism tells the nurse he plans to take it only on the days he feels sluggish, since he does not want to take medication he does not need. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Document that he is non-adherent with his prescribed regimen and notify the provider of his intent
options.rationale: This labels a misunderstanding as non-adherence before anyone has taught him anything.

options.text: Explain that consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications
options.rationale: Consistent daily dosing is what controls the symptoms. Taking it only on bad days leaves the deficiency untreated.

options.text: Tell him to take a double dose on the days he feels sluggish to compensate for the missed doses
options.rationale: This improvises a dose and risks overtreatment. Doubling up does not compensate for a missed day.

options.text: Agree with his plan, since the dose can reasonably be adjusted according to how he feels each day
options.rationale: Self-titrating a hormone replacement by how he feels leaves the level permanently unstable.

questions.stem: A patient's laboratory results show a low thyroid-stimulating hormone level with an elevated free T4. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The pituitary is failing to stimulate the thyroid
options.rationale: A failing pituitary would produce low stimulating hormone with a low T4.

options.text: The thyroid is producing hormone independently of pituitary control
options.rationale: High circulating hormone has suppressed the pituitary signal, which is negative feedback working correctly against a gland that is overproducing.

options.text: The results are inconsistent and the sample should be redrawn
options.rationale: The pattern is internally consistent and it is exactly what feedback predicts.

options.text: The patient is receiving too little thyroid replacement
options.rationale: Too little replacement raises the stimulating hormone and lowers T4.

questions.takeaway: Read the pair, not either value alone. A suppressed stimulating hormone with a high target hormone means the target gland is the source.

questions.stem: A patient has been taking a high-dose corticosteroid for four months and asks whether she can stop it now that she feels well. Which response is correct?

options.text: You can stop once your symptoms have been gone for a full week
options.rationale: Symptom resolution has nothing to do with the adrenal suppression the drug has produced.

options.text: You can stop if you taper over two or three days
options.rationale: A taper of days is far too short to let suppressed glands resume output.

options.text: The dose has to be reduced gradually, because your own adrenal production has been suppressed while you took it
options.rationale: Exogenous steroid suppresses the body's own production through feedback, and stopping abruptly leaves the patient without either source.

options.text: Stopping suddenly is safe as long as you resume if symptoms return
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal crisis before any symptom returns.

questions.takeaway: Exogenous hormone suppresses endogenous production. Any sustained course comes off by taper so the gland can restart.

questions.stem: A patient has been on long-term corticosteroid therapy. Which findings are consistent with excess glucocorticoid effect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fasting glucose of 182 mg/dL in a patient without diabetes
options.rationale: Glucocorticoids raise glucose and this is among the earliest findings.

options.text: Fat deposition in the trunk and face with thin extremities
options.rationale: Central fat redistribution is characteristic.

options.text: Thin skin that bruises with minimal contact
options.rationale: Protein breakdown thins skin and weakens capillary support.

options.text: Blood pressure of 158/96
options.rationale: Sodium and water retention raise pressure.

options.text: Hyperpigmentation of the skin creases
options.rationale: Darkened creases come from excess pituitary stimulating hormone in adrenal insufficiency, not from steroid excess.

options.text: A wound that has not closed after three weeks
options.rationale: Impaired healing follows from the protein catabolism and immune suppression.

options.text: Serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid activity holds sodium and wastes potassium, so a low potassium fits steroid excess.

questions.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a patient on contact and droplet precautions. She is wearing a gown, gloves, a surgical mask, and a face shield. Which item does she remove FIRST?

options.text: The gown

questions.stem: A 71-year-old is admitted with a surgical wound colonized with MRSA and is placed on contact precautions. The nurse will be changing the dressing, which has been draining moderately. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Surfaces and equipment matter as much as the contact with the patient does.

questions.stem: A nurse orients a student to infection prevention on a medical unit where several patients have no confirmed diagnosis yet. options.text: Gloves, gown, or mask are added depending on the anticipated interaction

questions.stem: A nurse has donned her gown, mask, and eye protection and is putting on gloves before entering an isolation room. The gown cuffs sit at her wrists and the gloves are the correct size. Which action is correct?
