questions.takeaway: A cuff that is too small reads falsely high. A blood pressure cuff that is too small produces a falsely high reading; a cuff that is too large produces a falsely low reading.
questions.strategy: Before acting on an abnormal blood pressure, ask whether the equipment could have produced it. A repeat with the right cuff costs a minute and may change the number entirely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cuff size is one of the commonest sources of measurement error.
A smaller cuff would make the falsely high reading worse.
Reporting a value you have reason to doubt sends the team a number that may not be real.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: A cuff that is too small requires more pressure to compress the artery, so the recorded value exceeds the true pressure.

questions.concept: A blood pressure cuff that is too small produces a falsely high reading; a cuff that is too large produces a falsely low reading.

questions.stem: A nurse selects a temperature measurement site for four patients: an unconscious adult, an infant, a confused older adult who will not stay still, and a patient who has just finished a hot drink. Which statements about the sites are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The oral route is contraindicated in an unconscious patient and after recent hot or cold intake
options.rationale: Oral is out for an unconscious patient, after hot or cold intake, and for anyone mouth breathing.

options.text: The axillary route is the most accurate and is preferred for adults
options.rationale: This is backwards. Axillary is the least accurate route and it is used mainly for infants.

options.text: The rectal route gives the most accurate core temperature
options.rationale: And it is contraindicated after rectal surgery and with a low platelet count.

options.text: The temporal artery route is noninvasive and useful for an uncooperative patient
options.rationale: Sweeping across the forehead needs no cooperation from the patient, which suits a confused or distressed one.

options.text: The tympanic route is fast but affected by cerumen and the angle of the ear canal
options.rationale: It gives a reading in seconds, and wax or a poorly aimed probe will make that reading wrong.

questions.takeaway: Rectal is most accurate, axillary is least. Oral is convenient and contraindicated with unconsciousness, mouth breathing, or recent hot or cold intake. Tympanic is fast and affected by cerumen and canal angle. Temporal artery is noninvasive and useful for uncooperative patients. Rectal is the most accurate core temperature and is contraindicated after rectal surgery or with low platelets. Axillary is the least accurate and is used for infants.
questions.strategy: Accuracy and accessibility pull in opposite directions here. The most accurate site is the most invasive, and the easiest is the least reliable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reverses the accuracy and the population.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Oral is convenient and contraindicated with unconsciousness, mouth breathing, or recent hot or cold intake. Tympanic is fast and affected by cerumen and canal angle. Temporal artery is noninvasive and useful for uncooperative patients. Rectal is the most accurate core temperature and is contraindicated after rectal surgery or with low platelets. Axillary is the least accurate and is used for infants.

questions.stem: An order reads digoxin 0.125 mg orally daily, hold for apical rate below 60. The patient has atrial fibrillation with an irregular rhythm. Which site does the nurse use to count the rate?

options.text: Dorsalis pedis
options.rationale: This site reflects perfusion to the limb rather than giving a reliable rate.

options.text: Apical
options.rationale: The fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line, used for infants, irregular rhythms, and before certain cardiac medications.

options.text: Brachial
options.rationale: The brachial is also a peripheral site, so it carries the same problem as the radial in atrial fibrillation.

options.text: Radial
options.rationale: A peripheral pulse may not reflect every ventricular contraction when the rhythm is irregular.

questions.takeaway: The apical pulse is taken at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line and is used for infants, irregular rhythms, and before certain cardiac medications. Pulse character includes rate, rhythm, strength on a 0 to 4+ scale, and equality.
questions.strategy: This stem gives you two of the three indications at once. An irregular rhythm and a cardiac medication both point to the same site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irregular rhythm and a cardiac medication.
A peripheral pulse may not reflect every ventricular contraction when the rhythm is irregular.
Also peripheral, carrying the same limitation.
A perfusion site rather than a rate site for this purpose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line, used for infants, irregular rhythms, and before certain cardiac medications.

questions.concept: The apical pulse is taken at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line and is used for infants, irregular rhythms, and before certain cardiac medications. Pulse character includes rate, rhythm, strength on a 0 to 4+ scale, and equality.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed oxygen at 3 L/min by nasal cannula. A student asks what percentage of oxygen the patient is receiving. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Exactly 32%, calculated at 4% for each litre above room air
options.rationale: The rule of thumb gives an estimate, not a delivered concentration. Oxygen flow is not the same thing as FiO2.

options.text: The delivered concentration varies with the breathing pattern and airway
options.rationale: Flow rate is not the same as FiO2. On a low-flow device the patient draws room air around the prongs, so how fast and how deeply the patient breathes changes what the patient receives.

options.text: The same concentration as any device set to 3 L/min
options.rationale: Different devices deliver very different concentrations at the same flow, so the device is prescribed alongside the rate.

options.text: It cannot be estimated without an arterial blood gas
options.rationale: An approximate range is known for each device. A blood gas measures what reached the blood, not what the device delivered.

questions.takeaway: Oxygen flow does not equal FiO2. On low-flow devices the delivered concentration depends on the patient's respiratory pattern, airway, and device fit.
questions.strategy: Two options treat flow and concentration as the same thing. Ask what else is entering the airway besides the prescribed oxygen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the delivered concentration varies with the patient.

questions.stem: A nurse applies a simple face mask and sets the flow at 3 L/min so the patient feels less overwhelmed by the airflow. Which problem does this create?

options.text: The oxygen concentration falls below room air
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen does not deliver less than the 21% already in the room. The hazard is the carbon dioxide, not a lack of oxygen.

options.text: The reservoir bag fails to inflate
options.rationale: A simple face mask has no reservoir bag. That belongs to the non-rebreather.

options.text: Exhaled carbon dioxide collects in the mask and is rebreathed
options.rationale: The mask holds a volume of exhaled gas. It takes at least 5 L/min to flush that volume out between breaths, and below that the patient breathes the own carbon dioxide back in.

options.text: The mask seal is lost at low flow rates
options.rationale: The seal depends on how the mask fits and how tight the strap is, not on the flow rate.

questions.takeaway: A simple face mask runs at 5 L/min minimum. Below that, exhaled carbon dioxide is not flushed from the mask and gets rebreathed.
questions.strategy: The instinct that lower flow is gentler is what this question punishes. Ask what has to be cleared from the mask between breaths.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the flow is clearing
steps.detail: Exhaled carbon dioxide sitting in the mask.
A simple mask has no bag.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: carbon dioxide rebreathing.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to place a non-rebreather mask on a patient with a saturation of 84%. Which action does she take before putting the mask on the face?

options.text: Inflate the reservoir bag
options.rationale: The bag is the oxygen supply for the next breath. Placing the mask on an empty bag means the first breaths draw against nothing.

options.text: Remove the one-way valves to allow easier exhalation
options.rationale: The valves are what keep room air out and make the high concentration possible. Removing them defeats the device.

options.text: Attach a humidifier to the oxygen source
options.rationale: Humidification belongs with high-flow nasal cannula. It is not a step before applying a non-rebreather.

options.text: Set the flow to 5 L/min and increase it once the mask is on
options.rationale: A non-rebreather runs at 10 to 15 L/min. Starting low leaves the bag unable to fill.

questions.takeaway: Inflate the reservoir before the mask goes on the face. The bag holds the oxygen for the next breath.
questions.strategy: Three options interfere with the thing that makes a non-rebreather work. Ask what the bag is for.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Holds the oxygen the patient is about to inhale.
The bag cannot fill at 5 L/min.
One belongs to HFNC, one disables the device.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: inflate the reservoir first.

questions.stem: A patient on 6 L/min by nasal cannula has a saturation of 87% and is using accessory muscles. The provider asks the nurse to anticipate the next device. Which is most appropriate?

options.text: A nasal cannula increased to 8 L/min
options.rationale: Above 6 L/min the cannula dries and irritates the nares without adding useful concentration. The device has run out of range.

options.text: A non-rebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min
options.rationale: The patient is already at the ceiling of what a nasal cannula can safely deliver and still failing. A non-rebreather gives roughly 60 to 90%.

options.text: A simple face mask at 5 L/min
options.rationale: A step sideways rather than up. At 5 L/min a simple mask delivers around 40%, which is close to what is already being delivered.

options.text: Room air with upright positioning and coached breathing
options.rationale: This takes the oxygen away from a patient who is already hypoxemic on 6 L/min.

questions.takeaway: A nasal cannula tops out at 6 L/min and 44%. When that is not enough, the next step up is a device with a reservoir.
questions.strategy: One option increases a device past its range, one moves sideways, one removes oxygen entirely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read where the patient already is
steps.detail: 6 L/min, the top of the cannula range, and still hypoxemic.
Beyond what the device can usefully deliver.

steps.action: Cut the simple mask and room air
steps.detail: One is a sideways move, one takes oxygen away.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a non-rebreather.

questions.stem: A patient is placed on high-flow nasal cannula. Which feature distinguishes it from a standard nasal cannula?

options.text: It seals against the face to prevent room air entering
options.rationale: It uses prongs in the nares, not a seal. The high flow rate is what limits room air dilution.

options.text: It delivers oxygen only during inspiration to conserve supply
options.rationale: That describes the oxymizer, which uses a reservoir to deliver a bolus on inspiration.

options.text: The gas is heated and humidified and the FiO2 can be set precisely
options.rationale: Heating and humidifying is what makes flows up to 60 L/min tolerable, and the high flow is what allows the delivered concentration to be set rather than estimated.

options.text: It requires no humidification because the flow is warmed
options.rationale: Both heating and humidification are part of it. Dry gas at those flows would damage the airway.

questions.takeaway: High-flow nasal cannula: heated, humidified, with a set FiO2, up to about 60 L/min, and it can provide some positive airway pressure.
questions.strategy: One distractor describes the oxymizer. Ask what makes 60 L/min through the nose bearable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what limits ordinary high flow
steps.detail: Cold dry gas injures the airway.

steps.action: Cut the seal and no-humidification options
steps.detail: It uses prongs, and humidification is essential.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: heated, humidified, and precisely set.

questions.stem: A patient needs more oxygen than a standard nasal cannula provides, but the team wants to avoid a mask so eating and speaking can continue. Which device fits?

options.text: An oxymizer reservoir cannula
options.rationale: It stores oxygen between breaths and delivers a bolus on inspiration, which makes it more efficient than a standard cannula while staying out of the way of the mouth.

options.text: A simple face mask at 5 L/min
options.rationale: It covers the mouth, which is what the team wants to avoid, and interference with eating and drinking is a real consideration.

options.text: A second nasal cannula at a higher flow
options.rationale: Not a device. A cannula above 6 L/min dries the nares without adding useful concentration.

options.text: A non-rebreather at 10 L/min
options.rationale: A non-rebreather is also a mask, and it is a higher concentration than this situation calls for.

questions.takeaway: An oxymizer is a reservoir cannula. It conserves oxygen and delivers more than a standard cannula without a mask.
questions.strategy: The constraint in the stem is that the mouth must stay free. Two options put a mask on the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the oxymizer.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to apply oxygen to a newly admitted patient. Which actions belong to the assessment before the device goes on? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the oxygen saturation
options.rationale: The saturation is the number the prescribed target is written against, so you need it before you start.

options.text: Document the patient's response to the oxygen
options.rationale: That comes after the device is applied and the patient has been reassessed.

options.text: Compare the new saturation with the baseline
options.rationale: There is no new saturation yet. Comparing to baseline belongs to the reassessment after the oxygen is on.

options.text: Verify the prescribed device and setting
options.rationale: Oxygen is a medication. The device and the flow are both part of the order.

options.text: Listen to the lung sounds
options.rationale: Part of the respiratory assessment and it may change which device is appropriate.

options.text: Assess respiratory rate, depth, and effort
options.rationale: The baseline you will compare against afterwards. Without it you cannot tell whether the oxygen helped.

questions.takeaway: Assess, apply, reassess. The assessment is rate, depth, effort, lung sounds, saturation, and the order itself.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things that can only happen after the oxygen is on.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: The device is not on yet.
Nothing has happened to respond to.
There is only a baseline so far.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A patient has been on a simple face mask for six hours. Which findings require nursing attention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness over the bridge of the nose
options.rationale: This is a pressure point under the mask, and the skin around the nose, mouth and ears is an assessment area.

options.text: The patient says the mask makes the patient feel closed in
options.rationale: Anxiety and claustrophobia are listed considerations, and a patient who pulls the mask off receives nothing.

options.text: The patient is sitting upright in bed
options.rationale: Sitting upright is the position you want him in, so there is nothing to address here.

options.text: The patient has eaten almost nothing from the lunch tray
options.rationale: The mask interferes with eating and drinking, so intake needs addressing rather than being recorded and left.

options.text: The flow meter reads 7 L/min
options.rationale: Seven liters sits inside the 5 to 10 L/min range a simple mask runs at.

questions.takeaway: Simple mask considerations: skin over nose, mouth and ears, claustrophobia, and interference with eating and drinking.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things that are correct as they stand. Check the flow against the device range before assuming it is wrong.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.action: Check the flow against the range

steps.detail: Skin, anxiety, and intake are all named considerations.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse applies oxygen at the prescribed rate and leaves the room to chart. Which step has she omitted?

options.text: Obtaining a repeat provider order for the device
options.rationale: The order already exists. Applying it does not call for a second order.

options.text: Placing a humidifier on the flow meter
options.rationale: Humidification is not required at low flows and is not a step in the sequence.

options.text: Waiting thirty minutes before documenting
options.rationale: No such waiting period. Reassessment happens when the patient can be expected to have responded.

options.text: Reassessing the patient's response to the oxygen
options.rationale: The sequence is assess, apply, reassess. Without the third step nobody knows whether the device worked.

questions.takeaway: Assess, apply, reassess. The last step is what closes the loop and it is the one most often dropped.
questions.strategy: Ask what the third step of her own sequence is. Two distractors invent a requirement that does not exist.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No repeat order, no waiting period.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: she did not reassess.

questions.stem: A student says that a patient on 15 L/min must be receiving more oxygen than a patient on 6 L/min. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Only an arterial blood gas can answer the question
options.rationale: A blood gas measures the patient's oxygenation, not what the device is delivering.

options.text: Yes, because flow rate and delivered concentration rise together
options.rationale: They rise together within one device. Across devices the relationship breaks down entirely.

options.text: No, because all devices deliver the same concentration above 10 L/min
options.rationale: Concentrations differ widely between devices at every flow rate, including above 10 L/min.

options.text: The device matters as much as the number, so the two cannot be compared directly
options.rationale: 15 L/min through a non-rebreather gives roughly 60 to 90%, while 6 L/min by nasal cannula gives about 44%. But 15 L/min on a high-flow cannula could be set anywhere from 21 to 100%.

questions.takeaway: Compare flow rates only within the same device. Across devices, the device sets the range and the flow positions you inside it.
questions.strategy: The student's error is comparing numbers without naming the devices. Ask what is missing from her question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The relationship holds only within one device.
It measures the patient, not the device.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the device matters as much as the number.

questions.stem: A nurse applies a simple mask to a patient whose saturation was 86% and is now 93%. Which elements belong in her entry? Select all that apply.

options.text: The device used
options.rationale: Anyone reading later needs to know what was on the face, not just a flow rate.

options.text: The name of the nurse who verified the order
options.rationale: Verifying the order is expected practice and does not need a name attached to it in the entry.

options.text: The patient's response
options.rationale: Whether the oxygen worked is the point of recording any of this, so the response belongs in the entry.

options.text: The flow rate or FiO2 setting
options.rationale: The flow rate or FiO2 is part of the order, so it belongs in the record.

options.text: The saturation compared with the baseline
options.rationale: A single saturation means little on its own. The comparison with baseline is what shows the direction.

options.text: The brand of the flow meter
options.rationale: The brand of the flow meter is equipment detail with no bearing on the care given.

questions.takeaway: Document the device, the flow or FiO2, and the patient's response measured against the baseline.
questions.strategy: Two options record equipment or process detail rather than anything about the patient.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.action: Ask what the next nurse needs
steps.detail: Device, setting, and how the patient responded.
Expected practice rather than a finding.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient on a non-rebreather has a reservoir bag that collapses completely each time the patient breathes in. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Increase the flow rate so the bag stays partially inflated
options.rationale: A bag that empties means the patient is drawing more volume than the flow is supplying, so the next breaths pull room air through the valves and the concentration falls.

options.text: Change the patient to a simple face mask
options.rationale: Steps the patient down to a lower concentration when the finding suggests more is needed, not less.

options.text: Remove the mask and reassess on room air
options.rationale: This takes oxygen away from a patient already on the highest-concentration mask available.

options.text: Reassure the patient that full collapse on inspiration is expected
options.rationale: Partial deflation is expected. Complete collapse means the supply is not keeping up.

questions.takeaway: The reservoir should stay partially inflated through inspiration. Full collapse means the flow is too low for the demand.
questions.strategy: Ask what an empty bag tells you about supply against demand. Two options reduce the oxygen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The bag empties completely on each breath.
Partial deflation is normal; total collapse is not.
Both reduce a concentration the patient evidently needs.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: increase the flow.

questions.stem: A patient needs an intravenous catheter placed for a planned transfusion of packed red blood cells. Which gauge does the nurse select?

options.text: 14 gauge
options.rationale: Reserved for trauma, major surgery and rapid resuscitation. Larger than a planned transfusion needs, and harder on the vein.

options.text: 20 gauge
options.rationale: The standard adult infusion size, and it appears at the small end of the acceptable transfusion range. For gauge selection specifically, 18 is the size named for blood products. This is the near-miss.

options.text: 22 gauge
options.rationale: For pediatric patients, older adults and fragile veins. Too narrow for red cells.

options.text: 18 gauge
options.rationale: Specified for blood products and contrast. Red cells are viscous, and a narrower lumen shears them and slows delivery past the four-hour limit.

questions.takeaway: Gauge selection: 14 to 16 for trauma and rapid resuscitation, 18 for blood products and contrast, 20 for standard adult infusions, 22 to 24 for pediatric, older adult and fragile veins.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is 20 gauge, which appears in the acceptable transfusion range elsewhere. The question asks what to select, and 18 is the gauge named for blood.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One is resuscitation, one is fragile veins.

steps.action: Ask what is named for blood

elimination.verdict: That leaves 18 gauge.

questions.note: Her gauge-selection slide names 18 gauge for blood products; her transfusion slide gives 18 to 20 gauge. Both appear, and they do not contradict: 18 is the gauge to select, and 20 is the smallest that is acceptable. If a question asks what to choose, answer 18. If it asks whether a 20 gauge already in place can be used, it can.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews intravenous solutions ordered for five patients.
questions.stem: For each solution, indicate how water moves relative to the cells.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Hypertonic means more concentrated than the cell. Ask the same question: solute is denser outside, so water leaves the cell and the cell shrinks. This is why it is used for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Isotonic means the same particle concentration as the cell, so there is no gradient to drive water either way. Ask: where is solute denser, inside or outside? Neither. It expands the vascular space without shifting water across the membrane.

rows.text: D10W
rows.rationale: Hypertonic, used for hypoglycemia and to expand volume. The dextrose load makes the solution denser than the cell.

rows.text: Lactated Ringer's
rows.rationale: Isotonic, used for volume expansion and fluid replacement. It stays in the vascular and interstitial space rather than entering cells.

rows.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Hypotonic means less concentrated than the cell. Solute is denser inside, so water enters and the cell swells. Swelling brain cells is why it is contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic produces no net shift. Hypertonic pulls water out of cells and they shrink. Hypotonic pushes water into cells and they swell.
questions.strategy: Water follows the higher particle concentration. Name which side is denser and the direction follows without memorizing each solution.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: In the vessel, or in the cell.
It moves toward the denser side.

elimination.verdict: Two no shift, two out of cells, one into cells.

questions.note: Two different osmolarity ranges are in circulation. One slide puts isotonic at 275 to 295 mOsm/L and hypertonic above 295; another puts isotonic at 250 to 375 and hypertonic above 375. The wider range is the one that makes her own examples work: normal saline is 308 and Lactated Ringer's is 273, and both are taught as isotonic. Classify by the named solution, not by arithmetic against a range. If she gives a number on the exam, use 250 to 375.

questions.stem: During an intravenous insertion attempt the patient reports burning, shooting pain radiating down the arm and numbness in the fingers. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Withdraw slightly and redirect the catheter toward the vein
options.rationale: This keeps the needle moving through tissue where it has already touched a nerve.

options.text: Stop immediately, remove the catheter, and perform a neurological assessment
options.rationale: Burning, shooting pain with numbness points to nerve contact. Continuing risks permanent injury, so you stop at once rather than reposition.

options.text: Complete the insertion quickly to shorten the discomfort
options.rationale: Treats nerve pain as ordinary discomfort to be endured. It is a stop signal, not a tolerance question.

options.text: Reassure the patient that some discomfort is expected during insertion
options.rationale: Some discomfort is expected. Burning, shooting pain with numbness is not, and dismissing it is how a temporary injury becomes a permanent one.

questions.takeaway: Nerve injury: burning or shooting pain, numbness or tingling. Stop immediately, remove, assess neurologically, document.
questions.strategy: Two distractors continue the insertion. One normalizes a specific warning sign as ordinary discomfort.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping immediately.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares the skin before inserting a peripheral intravenous catheter in an adult. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Apply the antiseptic in a widening circular motion and blot dry with sterile gauze
options.rationale: The described technique is back and forth with friction, and blotting removes the antiseptic before it has had time to work.

options.text: Scrub for 30 seconds and fan the site to speed drying
options.rationale: Fanning is one of the things not to do. Moving unfiltered air across a prepared site recontaminates it.

options.text: Scrub the site, let it dry, then palpate the vein once more to confirm the location
options.rationale: Do not re-palpate after preparation. Touching the site contaminates exactly where the needle will enter.

options.text: Scrub back and forth with friction for at least 30 seconds and allow the site to air dry
options.rationale: Friction is what lifts organisms off the skin, and the drying time is when the antiseptic kills them. Chlorhexidine is preferred above 2 months of age.

questions.takeaway: Chlorhexidine above 2 months of age, back-and-forth scrub with friction for at least 30 seconds, air dry completely, and do not re-palpate.
questions.strategy: Each distractor breaks one rule: blotting, fanning, or re-palpating. All three feel efficient, and that is why they are the ones people do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chlorhexidine, friction, air dry, no re-palpation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves friction for 30 seconds and air drying.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to administer a unit of packed red blood cells. Which requirements must be met before the infusion begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: A completed type and crossmatch
options.rationale: Type and crossmatch means the patient's blood is tested against the donor unit for compatibility. Without it there is nothing establishing the unit is safe to give.

options.text: Two-nurse verification of the unit label against the identification band, ABO and Rh, unit number and expiration, with both nurses signing
options.rationale: An incompatible transfusion is a sentinel event, meaning a serious preventable harm. Two people checking independently is what catches a mismatch.

options.text: A baseline set of vital signs before the unit is started
options.rationale: The 15-minute and completion readings mean nothing without a value to compare them against.

options.text: Premedication with an antipyretic for every transfusion
options.rationale: An antipyretic means a fever-reducing drug. Ask: is this ordered for every patient or for selected ones? Selected, usually those with a history of febrile reactions. It is not a universal requirement.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride as the only compatible solution
options.rationale: Dextrose solutions cause hemolysis and Lactated Ringer's contains calcium, which promotes clotting in the line.

options.text: A second intravenous site reserved for emergency medications
options.rationale: Not a requirement. Ask: is this needed before every unit, or only when a patient's situation calls for it? Only when ordered. One compatible line meets the requirement.

options.text: An 18 to 20 gauge intravenous catheter
options.rationale: A narrower lumen shears red cells, which is called hemolysis, and slows delivery past the four-hour limit.

questions.takeaway: Every blood product requires two-nurse identification verification, a type and crossmatch, an 18 to 20 gauge catheter, 0.9% sodium chloride only, and baseline vital signs.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a selective practice into a universal one. Ask which items apply to every unit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A transfusion of packed red blood cells begins at 0900. After the baseline, when does the nurse obtain the next set of vital signs?

options.rationale: The every 30 to 60 minute interval begins after the 15-minute check rather than replacing it.
An hour in is far too late to catch an acute reaction, which is the whole purpose of the early check.
Baseline, then 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes, then at completion. The first 15 minutes is when an acute hemolytic reaction declares itself.

options.text: At completion of the unit
options.rationale: A set is taken at completion, and it is the last rather than the next.

questions.takeaway: Vital signs: baseline, at 15 minutes, every 30 to 60 minutes after that, and at completion. Each unit infuses within four hours.
questions.strategy: The 15-minute check exists because that is when a severe reaction appears. Everything after it is routine surveillance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves 0915.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews vascular access devices with a student.

A catheter inserted in the basilic vein whose tip sits at the cavoatrial junction is a [[1]].

A catheter 3 to 8 inches long whose tip sits below the axilla is a [[2]].

The device with the lowest infection risk, accessed with a non-coring needle, is an [[3]].

The single most effective measure for preventing catheter-related bloodstream infection is [[4]].

options.text: nontunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: Central, and inserted into the subclavian, internal jugular or femoral vein rather than the basilic.

options.text: midline, which is a peripheral line
options.rationale: Both go in peripherally in the arm, and that is what makes this the near-miss. Ask where the tip ends up and only the PICC reaches a central vein.

options.text: peripheral intravenous catheter
options.rationale: A short peripheral catheter is roughly an inch long and never approaches the chest.

options.text: PICC, which is a central line
options.rationale: The cavoatrial junction is where the superior vena cava meets the right atrium. Ask: where does the tip sit? That, not the insertion site, is what makes a line central. An X-ray confirms placement before use.

options.text: midline
options.rationale: The axilla is the armpit, so a tip below it is still in a peripheral vein. That limits it to non-vesicants and solutions under 600 mOsm/L, with a dwell of up to 4 weeks.

options.text: PICC
options.rationale: A PICC tip reaches the lower superior vena cava, which makes it central rather than midline.

options.text: tunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: Anchored under the skin with a Dacron cuff and used for months to years.

options.text: implanted port
options.rationale: An implanted port sits entirely under the skin and is accessed through it, so this is not the device described.

options.text: tunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: The cuff lowers its risk, and the catheter still exits through the skin continuously.

options.text: implanted port
options.rationale: Non-coring means the needle parts the septum rather than cutting a hole in it, so the port reseals. Ask whether anything crosses the skin between uses. Nothing does, so the infection risk is the lowest of the group and swimming and bathing are allowed. Flushed monthly when not in use.

options.text: nontunneled central venous catheter
options.rationale: A nontunneled central venous catheter carries the highest infection risk of the central devices.

options.text: hemodialysis catheter
options.rationale: Large bore, for dialysis only, and never used for routine access or blood draws.

options.text: daily review of whether the line is still needed
options.rationale: The bundle element that removes the risk entirely by removing the line, and still not the one named most effective.

options.text: chlorhexidine skin preparation
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine skin preparation is in the bundle too, specifically 0.5% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol.

options.text: hand hygiene
options.rationale: Named as the single most effective measure, because it interrupts transmission before anything touches the patient or the line.

options.text: maximal barrier precautions
options.rationale: Part of the bundle: sterile gloves, gown, mask, cap and full-body drape. Effective, and not the single most effective.

questions.takeaway: The catheter tip location defines peripheral against central, not the insertion site. A PICC is a central line despite being inserted in the arm.
questions.strategy: PICC and midline are both inserted peripherally and look identical on the arm. Only the tip position separates them, and it decides what may be infused.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cavoatrial junction, or below the axilla.

steps.action: Ask what sits under intact skin

steps.detail: Hand hygiene is recognized most effective.

elimination.verdict: PICC, midline, implanted port, hand hygiene.

questions.stem: A patient has a midline catheter in place and the provider orders total parenteral nutrition. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Begin the infusion through the midline at a reduced rate
options.rationale: The problem is the osmolarity reaching a peripheral vein, not how fast it arrives. A slower rate does not change the solution.

options.text: Begin the infusion and assess the site hourly for infiltration
options.rationale: Monitoring for a complication you have deliberately created is not the same as preventing it.

options.text: Flush the midline and confirm blood return before starting
options.rationale: Patency means the line works. It does not make a peripheral device appropriate for a hyperosmolar solution.

options.text: Notify the provider that a midline cannot be used for parenteral nutrition
options.rationale: A midline tip sits below the axilla, which makes it peripheral, and a midline is limited to solutions under 600 mOsm/L. Parenteral nutrition is far above that and requires a central device.

questions.takeaway: Midline: non-vesicants only and osmolarity under 600 mOsm/L. Not for vesicants, parenteral nutrition, or continuous vasopressors.
questions.strategy: Three distractors proceed with the infusion in some modified form. The device is wrong, not the technique.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: None of them changes the tip location.

elimination.verdict: That leaves notifying the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse must place a peripheral intravenous catheter in an adult who has had a left mastectomy with lymph node dissection and has an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Use the right antecubital fossa, staying away from the fistula itself
options.rationale: The entire fistula arm is avoided, not only the fistula. The antecubital fossa is also a site to avoid for short peripheral catheters.

options.text: Consult the provider, because both arms carry a contraindication
options.rationale: The mastectomy side and the fistula arm are both on the avoid list. With both arms excluded the decision needs escalating rather than improvising a site.

options.text: Use a vein in the left forearm, distal to the surgical site
options.rationale: The mastectomy side is avoided because lymph node dissection impairs drainage in the whole limb, not only near the incision.

options.text: Use a vein in the lower leg, choosing the most distal site available
options.rationale: Legs are specifically sites to avoid in adults, because of the clot risk.

questions.takeaway: Avoid: the mastectomy-side arm, the arteriovenous fistula arm, a paralyzed limb, sites distal to previous infiltration or phlebitis, the antecubital fossa for short catheters, and legs in adults.
questions.strategy: Every distractor finds a site, and each one is on the avoid list. The answer is that no acceptable site exists here.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both arms, and legs in adults.

elimination.verdict: That leaves consulting the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an intravenous site and finds cool, pale skin, edema, a slowed drip rate and no blood return. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the infusion
options.rationale: The first action, because every further milliliter adds to the fluid already in the tissue.

options.text: Document the findings and the grade
options.rationale: Infiltration is graded 0 to 4, and the grade is what determines follow-up and reporting.

options.text: Elevate the affected limb
options.rationale: Elevating the limb uses gravity to drain the fluid the infiltration pushed into the tissue.

options.text: Remove the catheter
options.rationale: The catheter is no longer in the vein, so it has nothing left to do.

options.text: Restart the infusion at a slower rate through the same catheter
options.rationale: The catheter is no longer in the vein, which is what the absent blood return established. A slower rate still delivers fluid into the tissue.

options.text: Apply a warm or cool compress according to the solution that was infusing
options.rationale: Which one you use depends on what infiltrated, so the solution has to be identified first.

options.text: Flush the catheter to determine whether it is still patent
options.rationale: Patent means open and flowing. Ask: has that already been answered? The absent blood return answered it, and flushing drives more fluid into the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration: cool, pale skin, edema, slowed drip, no blood return. Stop, remove, elevate, compress according to the solution, document and grade.
questions.strategy: One distractor tests for something the findings have already established, and the test itself causes harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool, pale, edematous, no blood return.
It worsens the injury it claims to be testing for.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with a head injury and raised intracranial pressure has an order for 0.45% sodium chloride. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Begin the infusion at a reduced rate and monitor neurological status
options.rationale: A slower rate of the wrong tonicity is still the wrong tonicity. The contraindication is to the solution, not to the speed.

options.text: Begin the infusion and watch for signs of circulatory overload
options.rationale: Overload is the hypertonic concern. The danger here is cerebral edema, which means fluid accumulating in brain tissue.

options.text: Hold the infusion and clarify the order with the provider
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution moves water into cells, and swelling brain cells is exactly what raised intracranial pressure cannot tolerate. Increased intracranial pressure and head trauma both count contraindications.

options.text: Substitute 0.9% sodium chloride and document the change
options.rationale: Changing the prescribed solution is prescribing, even when the substitute is safer. The nurse clarifies rather than substitutes.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic solutions are contraindicated with increased intracranial pressure, head trauma, hypotension, third-spacing, and any risk of cerebral edema.
questions.strategy: One distractor slows the infusion as though rate were the problem. One substitutes a different solution, which is prescribing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypotonic, so water moves into cells.

steps.action: Ask what the injured brain cannot tolerate
Cut the rate change and the substitution
steps.detail: One misses the mechanism, one prescribes.

elimination.verdict: That leaves holding and clarifying.

questions.stem: A patient receiving an intravenous infusion suddenly reports dyspnea and chest pain. The nurse hears a churning murmur over the heart and the blood pressure is falling. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Place the patient upright and administer oxygen
options.rationale: Upright is correct for most respiratory distress and wrong here, because it moves air toward the pulmonary circulation rather than away from it.

options.text: Slow the infusion and obtain a full set of vital signs
options.rationale: Slowing allows air to keep entering. This needs the line clamped, not throttled.

options.text: Prepare for blood cultures and begin antibiotics
options.rationale: That is the response to a catheter-related bloodstream infection, which presents with fever and chills rather than a sudden murmur.

options.text: Clamp the tubing and place the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg
options.rationale: This is an air embolism, meaning air has entered the circulation. Clamping stops more air entering, and left lateral Trendelenburg traps the air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: sudden dyspnea, chest pain, a mill-wheel or churning murmur, hypotension. Clamp the tubing, left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response, 100% oxygen.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses the position that is right for almost every other respiratory emergency. The murmur is what identifies this one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A churning murmur with sudden dyspnea.

steps.action: Cut slowing and the infection response
steps.detail: One lets air continue, one treats something else.

elimination.verdict: That leaves clamping and left lateral Trendelenburg.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: A 78-year-old is receiving intravenous ceftriaxone through a 22 gauge catheter in the left forearm, inserted three days ago. The patient reports the arm feels sore. The site is red along the line of the vein with a palpable cord and feels warm. Temperature 37.0 C. The infusion is running at the prescribed rate. The transparent dressing is intact and dated three days ago. Blood return is present. There is no swelling of the hand or fingers. Blood pressure 132/78. The patient has been drinking well and eating most meals.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate a complication requiring the catheter to be removed.

segments.text: Red along the line of the vein with a palpable cord
segments.rationale: Phlebitis means inflammation of the vein. A cord means the vein has hardened and can be felt as a firm line. Ask: does the redness follow the vein rather than spread around the site? Yes, and the cord is the most specific finding.

segments.text: Temperature 37.0 C
segments.rationale: Normal, and it argues against a bloodstream infection as opposed to local inflammation.

segments.text: Transparent dressing intact and dated three days ago
segments.rationale: Transparent dressings are changed every 7 days, so at three days this is correct.

segments.text: Site feels warm
segments.rationale: Warmth completes the picture alongside the pain, the redness, and the palpable cord.

segments.text: Drinking well and eating most meals
segments.rationale: Eating and drinking well is reassuring and has nothing to do with the site.

segments.text: Blood pressure 132/78
segments.rationale: A blood pressure of 132/78 is acceptable and gives you nothing to act on.

segments.text: No swelling of the hand or fingers
segments.rationale: Argues against infiltration, where fluid enters the tissue and the limb swells. Phlebitis inflames the vein wall instead.

segments.text: Blood return is present
segments.rationale: The catheter is still in the vein. This is what separates phlebitis from infiltration, where blood return is absent.

segments.text: Reports the arm feels sore
segments.rationale: Pain is the first of the phlebitis findings and often the only one the patient volunteers.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a red streak and a palpable cord. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify and document the grade.
questions.strategy: Three findings are placed to rule out the other complications. Blood return present and no swelling together exclude infiltration, and a normal temperature argues against a bloodstream infection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1, s4, and s9: the phlebitis findings.

questions.stem: Shortly after a medication is given rapidly through an intravenous line, the patient becomes flushed and reports a headache and chest tightness. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock means a systemic reaction to a drug entering the circulation faster than the body can distribute it. Flushing, headache, chest tightness and shock, immediately after a rapid administration.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Presents with fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other source. The timing here points to the rate rather than to an organism.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a churning murmur. Flushing and headache are not part of that picture.

options.text: Thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis gives you a swollen, painful limb with reduced flow. That is local, and this is systemic.

questions.takeaway: Speed shock: flushing, headache, chest tightness, shock. Use a pump, verify the rate, and never bolus concentrated medications.
questions.strategy: The timing is the discriminator. These findings began immediately after a rapid administration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One is respiratory, one is local.

elimination.verdict: That leaves speed shock.

questions.stem: A charge nurse plans assignments on a unit with ongoing intravenous therapy. Which activities must be performed by the registered nurse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insertion of peripheral and central catheters
options.rationale: Inserting peripheral and central catheters is reserved to the registered nurse and does not move.

options.text: Initiating blood products
options.rationale: The two-nurse verification and the first 15 minutes both sit with the registered nurse.

options.text: Recording the hourly volume of intravenous fluid infused
options.rationale: Ask: does this require interpreting the finding, or recording it? Recording, which assistive personnel may do. The registered nurse interprets what the totals mean.

options.text: The initial vascular access assessment and site selection
options.rationale: Requires judgment about the therapy, the device and the condition of the veins, which is assessment rather than a task.

options.text: Interpreting the patient's response and exercising clinical judgment
options.rationale: Interpretation and clinical judgment are never delegable, no matter who gathered the data.

options.text: Administering high-alert intravenous medications
options.rationale: High-alert means an error carries heightened risk of significant harm, so the administration is not delegated.

options.text: Flushing an established peripheral line on a stable patient
options.rationale: Ask whether this takes judgment or follows a standing routine. It is a routine, so it may go to a licensed practical nurse where state regulation allows, along with routine site monitoring and hanging non-high-alert fluids.

questions.takeaway: Registered nurse only: initial access assessment and site selection, catheter insertion, initiating blood products, high-alert intravenous medications, interpretation and clinical judgment, education, and updating the plan of care.
questions.strategy: One distractor is specifically delegable. Scope turns on whether judgment is required, not on how technical the task feels.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Delegable to a licensed practical nurse per state rules.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an older adult before an intravenous insertion. Which modification is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a larger gauge to compensate for slower flow through fragile veins
options.rationale: A larger catheter in a fragile vein causes the very injury the modification is meant to prevent.

options.text: Select a dorsal hand vein
options.rationale: One of the sites to avoid in older adults. The skin there is thinnest and those veins are the most mobile.

options.text: Apply a warm compress and increase the infusion rate to maintain patency
options.rationale: The warm compress is correct. Increasing the rate works against reduced renal reserve and less total body water, so the option fails on its second half.

options.text: Use a 22 to 24 gauge catheter and avoid over-tightening the tourniquet
options.rationale: Fragile, mobile veins and thin skin raise the risk of hematoma and infiltration. A narrower catheter and gentler pressure address both at once.

questions.takeaway: Older adults: 22 to 24 gauge, gentle traction, no over-tightened tourniquet, lower infusion rates, avoid dorsal hand veins, warm compress, and document the skin before and after.
questions.strategy: One distractor pairs a correct intervention with a wrong one. Check both halves of an option before selecting it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fragile, mobile, thin skin over them.

steps.action: Cut the larger gauge and the dorsal hand
Check both halves of the warm compress option
steps.detail: Warm compress yes, faster rate no.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the narrower gauge with gentle technique.

questions.stem: A frail older adult in palliative care has mild dehydration and no usable venous access after several attempts. Which alternative route is most appropriate?

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
options.rationale: Intraosseous means into the bone marrow space. Reserved for emergencies when intravenous access fails, and limited to 24 hours. This is neither an emergency nor a 24-hour problem.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion, also called hypodermoclysis
options.rationale: Hypodermoclysis means fluid given into the subcutaneous tissue, where it is absorbed gradually. Indicated for mild to moderate dehydration in older and palliative patients, into the abdomen, thighs or scapular area, at a maximum of about 1 mL per minute.

options.text: Intra-arterial infusion placed by interventional radiology
options.rationale: Delivers chemotherapy or thrombolytics directly to a tumor or clot. Not a hydration route.

options.text: Intraspinal infusion through an epidural catheter
options.rationale: An epidural is for analgesics and anesthetics with continuous neurological monitoring. It is not a hydration route.

questions.takeaway: Hypodermoclysis: mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative patients, abdomen, thighs or scapular area, maximum about 1 mL per minute, hyaluronidase aids absorption. Avoid in severe dehydration or shock.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are real routes used for entirely different purposes. Ask which one delivers fluid for hydration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves subcutaneous infusion.

questions.stem: A nurse hangs a secondary intravenous antibiotic. Which action reflects correct practice?

options.text: Change the primary administration set every 24 hours
options.rationale: Tubing is changed every 96 hours or per policy. The 24-hour limit belongs to the container once it is spiked, not to the tubing.

options.text: Leave a spiked container hanging up to 96 hours
options.rationale: The reverse of the rule. Containers hang no longer than 24 hours once spiked; 96 hours belongs to the tubing.

options.text: Scrub the needleless connector for at least 15 seconds before accessing it
options.rationale: The connector sits open to the environment between uses. Friction for the full time is what makes the scrub effective rather than symbolic.

options.text: Use a macro-drip set, which delivers 60 drops per milliliter
options.rationale: Reverses the two drip factors. Macro-drip is 10 to 20 drops per milliliter and micro-drip is 60.

questions.takeaway: Scrub the hub for at least 15 seconds. Tubing every 96 hours or per policy. Containers hang no longer than 24 hours once spiked. Macro-drip 10 to 20 gtt/mL, micro-drip 60 gtt/mL.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap the 24-hour and 96-hour limits between the container and the tubing. One swaps the drip factors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves scrubbing the hub for 15 seconds.

questions.scenario: A 64-year-old had a nontunneled central venous catheter placed in the femoral vein six days ago for antibiotics. Today the temperature is 38.9 C with rigors, blood pressure is 92/54, and there is new confusion. The catheter site is clean and dry with no redness or drainage. The chest is clear, the urine is clear, and a surgical wound from two weeks ago is healed. No other source of infection has been identified.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Prepare for catheter removal and discuss whether access is still needed
options.rationale: A femoral nontunneled catheter carries the highest infection risk of the central devices, it is six days old, and reviewing daily whether the line is still needed is part of the prevention bundle.

options.text: Obtain two sets of blood cultures and notify the provider
options.rationale: Two sets drawn from different places is what separates a true line infection from a contaminated sample, and they have to be drawn before antibiotics change the result.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the catheter site
options.rationale: The treatment for phlebitis, which is local inflammation of a vein. The site here is clean and dry, so there is nothing local to treat.

options.text: Document the fever and reassess in four hours
options.rationale: A temperature of 38.9 C with rigors, hypotension and new confusion will not wait four hours. Rigors means violent shaking chills, which signals bacteria entering the bloodstream.

options.text: Speed shock from a rapid infusion
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a rapid administration with flushing, headache and chest tightness. Ask: does the stem describe a rate problem? No.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A bloodstream infection originating from the catheter. Ask: are there systemic signs of infection with no other source found? Fever, rigors, hypotension and confusion, and three other sources ruled out. A clean site does not exclude it, because the organisms are on the intravascular portion.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a churning murmur. Fever and rigors are not that picture.

options.text: Phlebitis at the catheter site
options.rationale: Phlebitis is local: pain, redness, warmth, a palpable cord. Ask: is there anything at the site? Clean and dry.

options.text: Temperature, blood pressure and mental status
options.rationale: These are the three findings that defined the problem, remeasured to see whether treatment is working.

options.text: Whether the insertion site develops redness
options.rationale: Local signs are absent and may never appear. Waiting for them delays recognition rather than confirming anything.

options.text: Whether the patient can state the signs of infection
options.rationale: Tests teaching in a patient who is currently confused, and it evaluates nothing the actions changed.

options.text: Blood culture results and whether the catheter was removed
options.rationale: Shows whether the suspected source was confirmed and whether it was actually dealt with.

questions.takeaway: A catheter-related bloodstream infection presents systemically with no other source. A clean, dry site does not rule it out.
questions.strategy: The clean site is the trap. Three other sources are excluded in the stem, which is what leaves the line as the explanation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing, which does not exclude the line.

elimination.verdict: Cultures and removal, for a catheter-related bloodstream infection, evaluated by the systemic findings and the cultures.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss infusion therapy. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "D5W is isotonic in the bag and becomes hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is why D5W behaves differently from the other isotonic solutions once it is in.

options.text: "A hemodialysis catheter is never used for routine intravenous access or blood draws."
options.rationale: This is accurate. A hemodialysis catheter is reserved for dialysis, not for routine access or blood draws.

options.text: "An X-ray confirming tip placement is required before a PICC is used."
options.rationale: This is accurate, because the tip position is the whole point of a PICC and nothing else confirms it.

options.text: "A PICC is a peripheral line because it is inserted in the arm."
options.rationale: The tip location defines peripheral against central, not the insertion site. A PICC tip sits at the cavoatrial junction, which makes it a central line.

questions.takeaway: The catheter tip location defines peripheral against central. A PICC is a central line despite peripheral insertion.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the material correctly. One reasons from the insertion site instead of the tip.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Insertion site used as the definition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the PICC statement.

chart.text: 67-year-old man with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, readmitted nine days after a five-day admission for the same problem. Lives with his wife, who works nights. No car. The bus to the cardiology clinic takes ninety minutes with two changes.

Discharged on furosemide 40 mg twice daily, increased from 20 mg daily. Metoprolol and lisinopril continued. Instructed to weigh daily and telephone for a gain of 2 kg over two days. Cardiology follow-up arranged for 0800 in two weeks. Home scale: not confirmed. Teaching documented as patient verbalized understanding.

Says he never received the new strength of the water pill. The pharmacy had it on back order, he left a message, and nobody called him back, so he kept taking the old dose. Has no scale at home. Says he was told to weigh himself but not what to do with the number. Did not attend the cardiology appointment because the bus does not get him there by 0800. Has been sleeping propped on two pillows for four days. Wife works nights and sleeps during the day.
Blood pressure 148/88. Heart rate 98. Respirations 24. Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air. Weight 84 kg, from 80 kg at discharge.

items.nursesNote: 1100: Says he never received the new strength of the water pill. The pharmacy had it on back order, he left a message, and nobody called him back, so he kept taking the old dose. Has no scale at home. Says he was told to weigh himself but not what to do with the number. Did not attend the cardiology appointment because the bus does not get him there by 0800. Has been sleeping propped on two pillows for four days. Wife works nights and sleeps during the day. Weight 84 kg, from 80 kg at discharge. Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that show the discharge plan failed.

segments.text: Weight 84 kg, from 80 kg at discharge
segments.rationale: This is the consequence, the thing the plan was supposed to prevent. It tells you the plan failed without telling you where.

segments.text: nobody called him back
segments.rationale: He did what a patient is supposed to do. The system had no one assigned to close that loop.

segments.text: Wife works nights and sleeps during the day
segments.rationale: A fact about his support that was true before the last admission. It shapes the plan and is not itself a failure of it.

segments.text: the bus does not get him there by 0800
segments.rationale: An appointment was made at a time his transport cannot reach. That is a coordination failure, not a missed appointment.

segments.text: Has no scale at home
segments.rationale: He was discharged on a plan that requires daily weights, and nobody confirmed he owned the one piece of equipment it depends on.

segments.text: he never received the new strength of the water pill
segments.rationale: The single change the admission was built around never reached him. Writing a prescription and the patient having the drug are two different events, and nobody checked the second one.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air
segments.rationale: A current clinical finding that needs acting on now. It belongs to his treatment rather than to the audit of the discharge.

segments.text: he was told to weigh himself but not what to do with the number
segments.rationale: Teaching that stops before the action is information, not education. Verbalized understanding was charted and nothing was evidenced.

items.takeaway: A readmission is usually a chain of small handoffs that nobody owned. Look for the point where somebody arranged something and nobody verified it happened.
items.strategy: Two of the strongest findings are consequences rather than failures. Ask of each one whether it is the breakdown or the result of the breakdown.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: The five places the plan was arranged and never verified.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate which part of the system broke down.

rows.text: The increased dose was on back order and he kept taking the old one
rows.rationale: The prescription was correct and the drug did not reach him. Availability is a separate failure from prescribing.

rows.text: Mild ankle swelling that settles overnight in a patient on a stable dose
rows.rationale: Not every finding in heart failure is a failure. Some of it is the disease behaving the way the disease behaves.

rows.text: He left a message at the pharmacy and nobody returned it
rows.rationale: Nobody was responsible for the space between the pharmacy, the clinic and the patient.

rows.text: Teaching was charted as patient verbalized understanding
rows.rationale: A phrase that records that teaching happened and nothing about whether learning did.

rows.text: Nobody confirmed whether he owned a scale
rows.rationale: The plan depended on equipment and no one checked the equipment existed.

rows.text: He has no supply of the higher dose at home
rows.rationale: Same root as the back order. The plan assumed a supply that was never in his hands.

rows.text: The follow-up was booked at a time his transport cannot reach
rows.rationale: An appointment that cannot be attended is not follow-up. Nobody asked how he would get there.

rows.text: He can state that he should weigh daily but not what weight gain means
rows.rationale: He retained the instruction and not the decision. Teaching that is not tied to an action produces exactly this.

items.takeaway: Sorting a readmission into categories is what turns one patient's bad outcome into a change the unit can make. A problem nobody has named belongs to nobody.
items.strategy: The education rows and the coordination rows are easy to blur. Education is about what he knows. Coordination is about what nobody arranged or checked.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find what he does not know

elimination.verdict: Two access, two education, three coordination, one expected.

items.stem: Which statement best names the problem the nurse brings to the team?

options.text: His heart failure has progressed and he now needs a higher level of care than before
options.rationale: Nothing shows progression. He never received the therapy that was meant to be tested, so nobody knows whether it would have worked.

options.text: He has inadequate social support at home to manage a regimen of this complexity
options.rationale: Partly true and too vague to act on. It drifts toward blaming his wife for working nights, and it would not have been fixed by more support.

options.text: He is nonadherent to his heart failure regimen
options.rationale: The label most often written, and here it is factually wrong. He took the dose he had, called when he could not get the new one, and went to no appointment that his transport could reach.

options.text: A discharge plan that depended on a drug, a scale and an appointment nobody confirmed
options.rationale: It names what happened, in terms that point at something fixable, and it puts the problem where it occurred rather than on the patient.

items.takeaway: Name the problem so that the next sentence can be an action. A label that describes the patient's character ends the inquiry; one that describes a process starts a fix.
items.strategy: Three options describe the patient. One describes what was done to him. Ask which naming leads anywhere.

strategies: Ask what each name leads to
elimination.verdict: The unverified discharge plan.

items.stem: Which actions belong in this admission's plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Advise him to find a relative who can drive him to appointments
options.rationale: It moves the problem onto him and his family and leaves the plan depending on something nobody has verified, which is how this admission started.

options.text: Reteach daily weights using teach-back, including the exact gain that triggers a call and the number he calls
options.rationale: Teaching tied to a decision and verified in his own words. The gap last time was not the weighing, it was what the number meant.

options.text: Give him the heart failure booklet at discharge so he has the information in writing
options.rationale: Printed material on its own changes nothing, and a man who was not taught what the number means will not get that from a leaflet.

options.text: Document that he was nonadherent so the next team is aware
options.rationale: It passes an inaccurate judgment forward, and every clinician who reads it will treat him differently on the strength of it.

options.text: Arrange the follow-up at a time and place his transport can reach, and confirm the transport
options.rationale: An appointment is only arranged once somebody has checked he can physically get to it.

options.text: Begin discharge planning today rather than on the day he leaves
options.rationale: Discharge planning starts at admission. Everything that failed last time failed because it was arranged in the final hour.

options.text: Involve the pharmacist in confirming the dose is obtainable and covered before he goes
options.rationale: The back order is the first link in the chain. Confirming supply and coverage is a specific, assignable task.

items.takeaway: Every element of a discharge plan needs a person attached to it and a check that it happened. Arranged is not the same as in place.
items.strategy: Two distractors hand the work back to the patient and one documents a judgment. None of the three changes a single thing that broke.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Start now, pharmacist, teach-back, reachable follow-up.

items.stem: It is 1115 and he is sitting upright at 90 percent on room air with respirations of 24. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the head of the bed further, apply oxygen as prescribed, and reassess his respiratory status
options.rationale: A saturation of 90 percent with respirations of 24 is the problem in front of her. Positioning and oxygen come before every system fix on the list.

options.text: Begin the teach-back session on daily weights while he is alert and his wife is present
options.rationale: Teaching a breathless patient wastes the session. He cannot attend to learning while he is working to breathe.

options.text: Document the discharge failures in an occurrence report while the detail is fresh
options.rationale: It should be done and it is not clinical care. The report will be just as accurate in an hour.

options.text: Call the pharmacist about the back order so the supply problem is solved before he leaves
options.rationale: The right action at the wrong hour. It belongs in today's plan and not in the next five minutes, while he is hypoxic.

items.takeaway: A systems problem does not suspend the ABCs. Fix the breathing, then fix the process that got him here.
items.strategy: The whole case has been about the system, which makes the clinical answer easy to skip. Read the vital signs in the stem.

strategies: Check the physiology before the process
elimination.verdict: Position, oxygen, reassess.

chartUpdate.text: Furosemide 40 mg twice daily dispensed to the bedside by pharmacy and confirmed covered. Home scale ordered through durable medical equipment and delivery confirmed for tomorrow. Patient states he will call the heart failure nurse at the number on the magnet if he gains 2 kg over two days, and points to the number. Follow-up moved to a 1400 appointment at the clinic two bus stops from his home, transport plan reviewed with his wife. Weight 79 kg. Oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. He says he still does not know which foods are high in salt.

items.stem: For each outcome, indicate how the nurse evaluates it.

rows.text: He can identify foods high in sodium
rows.rationale: He says so himself. Dietary teaching was never part of the first plan and it is still not done.

rows.text: He has the prescribed dose in hand and it is covered
rows.rationale: Confirmed rather than arranged, which is the difference from last time.

rows.text: A scale is in his home
rows.rationale: Delivery is confirmed for tomorrow, which is an arrangement rather than a fact. This is the identical gap that failed last time, and it stays open until somebody verifies it arrived.

rows.text: Follow-up is scheduled at a time and place he can reach
rows.rationale: The time, the location and the transport were all checked with the person who has to make the journey.

rows.text: His fluid status has returned toward his dry weight
rows.rationale: 79 kg against 84 on admission and 80 at the last discharge, with the saturation back to 95 percent.

rows.text: He can state the weight gain that triggers a call and who he calls
rows.rationale: He produced the trigger and the number himself. That is learning evidenced rather than verbalized understanding.

items.takeaway: Evaluate against what is true, not what is scheduled. A confirmed delivery for tomorrow is the same kind of promise that produced this readmission.
items.strategy: The scale row is written to look met, because somebody did the work and documented it. Ask whether the thing itself exists yet.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four met, two not.

case-study.title: Three days of heat, alone upstairs

chart.text: 88-year-old woman who lives alone on the second floor of a building with no air conditioning. Hypertension, osteoarthritis of both knees, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL. Medications: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, acetaminophen 650 mg as needed. Uses a cane indoors. Her daughter visits once a week and does her shopping.

Brought to the emergency department by her daughter after three days of outdoor temperatures above 38 C. Daughter reports she has not been herself since yesterday, dozing through the afternoon and getting the days of the week wrong. Patient says she has not felt thirsty and has been having a cup of tea in the morning and another in the evening. No bowel movement for four days. Describes her urine as dark and scanty. Skin over the forearm tents when pinched. Oral mucosa dry, tongue furrowed. Weight 54 kg, recorded as 57 kg at a clinic visit one month ago. States her own name and her children's names. Cannot say the month or name the building she is in.
Temperature 37.1 C oral. Heart rate 104 and regular. Blood pressure 104/62 lying, 82/54 after one minute sitting upright. Respirations 20. Oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air.

Sodium 152 mmol/L. Potassium 3.1 mmol/L. Chloride 114 mmol/L. Blood urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. Glucose 118 mg/dL. Hematocrit 48 percent. Urine specific gravity 1.032. Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leukocyte esterase.

items.nursesNote: 1400: Brought to the emergency department by her daughter after three days of outdoor temperatures above 38 C. Daughter reports she has not been herself since yesterday, dozing through the afternoon and getting the days of the week wrong. Patient says she has not felt thirsty and has been having a cup of tea in the morning and another in the evening. No bowel movement for four days. Describes her urine as dark and scanty. Skin over the forearm tents when pinched. Oral mucosa dry, tongue furrowed. Weight 54 kg, recorded as 57 kg one month ago. Uses a cane indoors. Daughter visits once a week. Heart rate 104. Blood pressure 104/62 lying and 82/54 sitting. Oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: No bowel movement for four days
segments.rationale: Real and worth addressing, and it is a consequence of the dehydration rather than a threat in the next hour.

segments.text: Weight 54 kg, recorded as 57 kg one month ago
segments.rationale: Three kilograms is about three litres of water. Weight is the most reliable measure of fluid loss there is.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air
segments.rationale: A normal value, and the one measurement in the note that is reassuring.

segments.text: Blood pressure 104/62 lying and 82/54 sitting
segments.rationale: A fall of 22 mm Hg systolic on sitting means there is not enough circulating volume to maintain pressure against gravity.

segments.text: Heart rate 104
segments.rationale: The compensation for the low volume, and in an 88-year-old on an antihypertensive a rate this high is a late sign rather than an early one.

segments.text: she has not felt thirsty
segments.rationale: Thirst sensation declines with age. It explains why she could not correct this herself and it is a background condition, not a new finding.

segments.text: has been having a cup of tea in the morning and another in the evening
segments.rationale: Roughly 400 mL across three days of extreme heat. This is the cause of everything else in the note.

segments.text: Uses a cane indoors
segments.rationale: Her baseline mobility, known before today.

segments.text: she has not been herself since yesterday, dozing through the afternoon and getting the days of the week wrong
segments.rationale: A sudden change in orientation in a woman who knows her children's names is acute. It is the finding that turns a hot week into an emergency.

items.takeaway: In an older adult, the findings that matter are the ones that changed. Separate the new from the baseline before you separate the urgent from the rest.
