items.strategy: Two findings are tempting because they are abnormal: the constipation and the absent thirst. Both are explained by the dehydration rather than driving it.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is new since yesterday

elimination.verdict: Confusion, intake, weight loss, the orthostatic drop, and the tachycardia.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate what it reflects.

rows.text: Sodium 152 mmol/L
rows.rationale: She lost water faster than she lost sodium, so the sodium left behind is concentrated. This is a water problem, not a salt problem.

rows.text: Reduced sensation of thirst
rows.rationale: Thirst is blunted with age, so an older adult can become severely dry without ever feeling it.

rows.text: Blood pressure falling from 104/62 to 82/54 on sitting
rows.rationale: Not enough circulating volume to fill the vessels once gravity is added. This is the bedside test for it.

rows.text: Urine output 15 mL per hour over the last two hours
rows.rationale: Below about 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour is oliguria, and it is how the injury is measured in real time.

rows.text: A smaller proportion of body water than a younger adult
rows.rationale: Total body water falls with age as lean mass falls, so the same litre lost costs an older adult more.

rows.text: Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL against a baseline of 1.1
rows.rationale: A rise above her own baseline is the definition of an acute injury, and her baseline is what makes it visible.

rows.text: Urine specific gravity 1.032
rows.rationale: The kidney is concentrating hard to hold onto water, which it only does when water is short.

rows.text: Blood urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL with a ratio to creatinine above 20 to 1
rows.rationale: Urea rises faster than creatinine when the problem is perfusion rather than the kidney tissue itself. The ratio is what tells you the cause is upstream.

items.takeaway: Two age changes set this up, blunted thirst and less total body water. Everything else is either the volume loss or the kidney injury it caused.
items.strategy: The urea and the creatinine look like one finding. The ratio between them is what separates a perfusion problem from damaged kidney tissue.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four volume, two kidney, two aging.

items.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
items.sentence:
The patient is most likely experiencing [[1]].

The finding that most supports this is [[2]].

The complication the nurse watches for while it is being corrected is [[3]].

options.text: new-onset dementia
options.rationale: Dementia develops over months to years. She was oriented last week.

options.text: a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: The reflex answer for a confused older adult, and the urinalysis is negative for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. The chart rules it out.

options.text: progression of her chronic kidney disease
options.rationale: Her creatinine has risen above her own baseline over days, which is acute. Chronic progression does not happen in a weekend.

options.text: hypovolemia with hypernatremia
options.rationale: Water lost faster than sodium, over three days, in a woman on a diuretic who does not feel thirsty. It accounts for the sodium, the pressures, the urine and the confusion together.

options.text: the orthostatic drop together with a sodium of 152 mmol/L
options.rationale: One finding shows the volume is gone and the other shows it was water that left. Together they name the problem and nothing else explains both.

options.text: the temperature of 37.1 C
options.rationale: A normal temperature. It helps rule infection out rather than ruling anything in.

options.text: the dark, scanty urine
options.rationale: Consistent and not specific. Concentrated urine appears in several conditions and does not pin the diagnosis.

options.text: the four days without a bowel movement
options.rationale: A downstream effect of being dry, and it would be present in many other situations too.

options.text: a further rise in creatinine once fluid is given
options.rationale: Restoring perfusion is what brings a prerenal creatinine back down.

options.text: fluid overload from any intravenous fluid at her age
options.rationale: A real consideration with her kidney disease and not the specific danger here. She is three litres down and the risk is in the speed of correction, not the fact of it.

options.text: cerebral edema from correcting the sodium too quickly
options.rationale: Brain cells have adapted to a high sodium over three days. Bring it down faster than about 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and water rushes in. The treatment is what harms her, so the rate of correction is prescribed and monitored.

options.text: hyperkalemia as the kidney recovers
options.rationale: Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and the diuretic has been taking it. The problem runs the other way.

items.takeaway: Hypernatremic dehydration is corrected slowly, because the brain has already adapted to the high sodium. Roughly 10 mmol/L in 24 hours is the ceiling.
items.strategy: The third blank is where this question lives. Ask what the treatment itself could do, not just what the disease could do.

strategies: Work the blanks in order

steps.action: Pick the finding that does two jobs

elimination.verdict: Hypovolemia with hypernatremia, the orthostatic drop with the sodium, cerebral edema.

items.stem: Which interventions does the nurse anticipate for this patient? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter so she does not have to get up
options.rationale: Convenience is not an indication. A catheter adds an infection risk and takes away the reason to stand up, in a woman already at risk of losing her mobility here.

options.text: Replace potassium once urine output is adequate
options.rationale: She is at 3.1 mmol/L from the diuretic, and replacement waits until the kidney is clearing enough to excrete any excess.

options.text: Hold the hydrochlorothiazide and the lisinopril and discuss both with the provider
options.rationale: One is still making her lose water and the other blunts the kidney's response to low perfusion. Continuing them works against the fluid going in.

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake because she has chronic kidney disease
options.rationale: Her kidney injury was caused by too little fluid. Restriction treats the opposite problem.

options.text: Establish intravenous access and begin the prescribed isotonic fluid
options.rationale: Restoring circulating volume comes before anything else, and it is what brings the creatinine and the blood pressure back.

options.text: Correct the sodium rapidly over the first four hours to clear the confusion
options.rationale: This is the intervention that causes the harm. Her brain has adapted over three days and a fast correction drives water into the cells.

options.text: Measure and record urine output hourly
options.rationale: Output is how the kidney reports back. It is the earliest sign the fluid is reaching where it needs to.

items.takeaway: Fluid in, the drugs that are working against you out, and output measured. Then replace potassium once the kidney can handle it.
items.strategy: Two distractors sound cautious: restricting fluid and correcting the sodium quickly. Caution aimed at the wrong problem is the trap in this case.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Fluid, hold the two drugs, hourly output, potassium when output allows.

chartUpdate.text: Thirty minutes into the intravenous fluid. Patient now pulling at the intravenous line, trying to get a leg over the side rail, and calling for her daughter, who has gone to move the car. Does not respond to redirection.

items.stem: What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the daughter to sit with her when she gets back from the car, so the medication pass can continue
options.rationale: Family presence helps and it is not a plan for the next five minutes, because the daughter is not in the building and the nurse would be leaving her at the rail.

options.text: Stay with her, lower the bed, and check the infusion rate, her oxygen saturation and her glucose
options.rationale: Agitation in this patient is a symptom with a cause: the sodium correcting, pain, a full bladder, hypoxia, low glucose, or the fact that her daughter has disappeared. Staying is the intervention and assessing is what finds the cause.

options.text: Apply a soft wrist restraint until she settles, so the intravenous line stays in and she cannot get over the rail
options.rationale: A restraint on an agitated delirious patient usually raises the agitation, and it is applied before anyone has asked why she is agitated. The least restrictive option has not been tried.

options.text: Request a dose of haloperidol for the agitation
options.rationale: Medication is a chemical restraint when it is given instead of finding the cause. It also makes the next hour of neurological assessment uninterpretable.

items.takeaway: New agitation is a cue, not a behavior to suppress. Stay, look for the cause, and use the least restrictive measure that keeps her safe while you find it.
items.strategy: Two options manage the behavior and two look for its cause. Assessment comes before intervention even when the patient has a leg over the rail.

strategies: Ask what has not been assessed yet

steps.action: Keep eyes on her and look

elimination.verdict: Stay and assess.

chartUpdate.text: Twelve hours after admission. Sodium 146 mmol/L. Potassium 3.6 mmol/L. Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Urine output 40 mL per hour for the last four hours. Heart rate 88. Blood pressure 118/70 lying and 112/68 sitting. States the month correctly and names the hospital. Weight 55.6 kg. Has not been out of bed. A 1 cm area of nonblanchable redness noted over the sacrum. Discharge planning note: lives alone, second floor, no air conditioning, daughter visits weekly.

items.stem: For each finding at twelve hours, indicate how the nurse evaluates it.

rows.text: Urine output 40 mL per hour
rows.rationale: Up from 15 mL per hour and now above 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour. The kidney is working.

rows.text: Blood pressure 118/70 lying and 112/68 sitting
rows.rationale: The orthostatic drop has gone, which is the clearest sign the volume is back.

rows.text: A 1 cm area of nonblanchable redness over the sacrum
rows.rationale: This was not there on admission. Twelve hours flat in bed on a dry, thin, 88-year-old woman produced a stage 1 pressure injury, and it is a harm the admission caused.

rows.text: Sodium 146 mmol/L
rows.rationale: Down 6 mmol/L in twelve hours, which is inside the safe rate. Both the direction and the speed are right.

rows.text: Her ability to manage fluid intake at home in hot weather
rows.rationale: Nothing about the apartment, the absent thirst, the diuretic or the weekly visits has changed. She will be discharged into the conditions that brought her in.

rows.text: Able to state the month and name the hospital
rows.rationale: The confusion was a symptom of the fluid state, and it has cleared with it. This is what confirms it was delirium rather than dementia.

rows.text: Her risk of falling
rows.rationale: She is twelve hours more deconditioned, still 88, still on an antihypertensive, and has not been out of bed. Correcting the sodium did nothing for this.

rows.text: Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Falling toward her baseline of 1.1, which is what a prerenal injury does once perfusion returns.

items.takeaway: The numbers can all improve while the patient gets worse. Evaluate function and the discharge environment alongside the laboratory values, or she is back next week.
items.strategy: Five rows are laboratory and vital sign values and they all improved. The three that did not are the ones about her body and her life, which is where the exam question lives.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Five improved, one worsened, two unchanged.

chart.text: 41-year-old transgender woman admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has taken estradiol and spironolactone for six years. The registration record carries her legal name, which she has not changed, and a male sex marker. She goes by Marisol. No surgical history. Lives with a partner of eight years.

Wristband and door card print the legal name. Assigned to a two-bed room with a male patient. Hormone medications not on the admission list and no order written. Night nurse documented the patient as he throughout the shift. Patient was talkative on admission and now answers in single words and faces the window. Declined the 0600 vital signs and has not used the call light since 0400. Breakfast untouched. When the nurse asks how the breathing is, she says it is fine. Oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, respirations 24, with an audible cough.
Ceftriaxone and azithromycin as prescribed. Acetaminophen as needed. No estradiol. No spironolactone.

items.nursesNote: 0800: Wristband and door card print the legal name. Assigned to a two-bed room with a male patient. Hormone medications not on the admission list and no order written. Night nurse documented the patient as he throughout the shift. Patient was talkative on admission and now answers in single words and faces the window. Declined the 0600 vital signs and has not used the call light since 0400. Breakfast untouched. When the nurse asks how the breathing is, she says it is fine. Oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, respirations 24, with an audible cough.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that show her care is being affected.

segments.text: Wristband and door card print the legal name
segments.rationale: The legal name has to appear where identity is verified, which is a safety requirement rather than a failure. What is missing is her name recorded alongside it and used by staff.

segments.text: answers in single words and faces the window
segments.rationale: She has stopped engaging since admission. Withdrawal is how a patient manages a setting that is costing her something to be in.

segments.text: Declined the 0600 vital signs
segments.rationale: A refusal that fits the withdrawal rather than adding to it, and on its own it is a patient declining one set of observations.

segments.text: Hormone medications not on the admission list and no order written
segments.rationale: Six years of therapy stopped without a decision being made by anyone. Abrupt withdrawal has physical and psychological effects and she was not part of the choice.

segments.text: Breakfast untouched
segments.rationale: Worth noting and common in pneumonia. On its own it says little about how she is being treated.

segments.text: Night nurse documented the patient as he throughout the shift
segments.rationale: Repeated through a whole shift, in a document every clinician after that will read and copy. One slip is a slip; a shift of it is the record teaching the next person to get it wrong.

segments.text: Assigned to a two-bed room with a male patient
segments.rationale: Placement made from the sex marker rather than from a conversation with her. It is a privacy and a safety matter and she was never asked.

segments.text: she says it is fine
segments.rationale: Said by a woman at 91 percent with respirations of 24. She has stopped reporting, and that is the point where the environment becomes a clinical risk.

items.takeaway: The clinical risk is that she has stopped reporting symptoms. Everything upstream of that, the pronouns, the room, the stopped medication, is why.
items.strategy: The legal name on the wristband is the segment most students select. Identity verification needs it; the failure is that nothing else records who she is.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.detail: Down to saying it is fine.

elimination.verdict: Pronouns, stopped hormones, room, withdrawal, and the underreporting.

items.stem: For each nursing action, indicate its effect.

rows.text: Asking her what name and pronouns she wants used, and recording both where staff will see them
rows.rationale: Asking takes ten seconds and recording it is what stops the next six people repeating the error.

rows.text: Verifying identity against the legal name and date of birth before giving a medication
rows.rationale: Identification uses the legal identifiers. Doing that correctly and addressing her as Marisol are not in conflict.

rows.text: Explaining to the other patient in the room why she is there
rows.rationale: Disclosing her status to another patient. Her identity is hers to share and nobody else's to explain.

rows.text: Telling her the staff did not mean anything by it and she should not take it personally
rows.rationale: It asks her to manage the staff's comfort and tells her the subject is closed.

rows.text: Mentioning to the oncoming nurse in the hallway that she is transgender so there is no awkwardness
rows.rationale: A hallway is not a handoff, and framing her as a source of awkwardness is itself the problem. Clinically relevant information goes in the handoff, in private.

rows.text: Raising the stopped hormone therapy with the provider and asking that she be part of the decision
rows.rationale: It puts an unmade decision in front of someone who can make it, with her in the room.

rows.text: Asking her about her surgical history because the nurse is curious how far she has gone
rows.rationale: Curiosity is not assessment. Ask about anatomy when it changes the care in front of you and leave the rest.

rows.text: Asking her where she would feel safest placed and arranging it
rows.rationale: The person who knows the answer is the one being placed. It is also the quickest route to a room that works.

items.takeaway: Ask, record, and act on what the answer tells you. The barriers are curiosity, reassurance that closes a subject, and telling people who do not need to know.
items.strategy: Two rows involve the legal name or a disclosure and look similar. Ask who needs the information and what it is for.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four support, four create barriers.

items.stem: Which problem does the nurse act on first?

options.text: Staff are using the wrong name and pronouns
options.rationale: This is the cause of the withdrawal and the thing to fix for the rest of the admission. Naming it as the first problem skips the hypoxia it produced.

options.text: Her hormone therapy has been stopped without a decision or a discussion
options.rationale: A real harm and it needs raising today. It is not what will deteriorate in the next few hours.

options.text: She has been placed in a room that does not fit her identity
options.rationale: It needs changing and it is part of the same cause. The room is not what is dropping her saturation.

options.text: She has stopped reporting symptoms, and she is hypoxic
options.rationale: A woman at 91 percent with respirations of 24 who says her breathing is fine has withdrawn from the one channel the team relies on. The environment has become a clinical problem.

items.takeaway: A patient who stops talking to you is a clinical finding. Affirming care matters here because the alternative is a hypoxic woman telling you she is fine.
items.strategy: Three options name genuine harms, all of which feed the fourth. Ask which one could kill her today.

strategies: Separate the causes from the consequence
elimination.verdict: The underreporting with the hypoxia.

items.stem: Which actions belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the night nurse privately that she got the pronouns wrong and to be careful
options.rationale: It handles one person and leaves the record as it stands. The correction belongs in the chart, where the next six people will look.

options.text: Raise the stopped hormone therapy with the provider today, with her in the conversation
options.rationale: Six years of therapy was stopped by omission. The decision gets made rather than drifting, and she is part of it.

options.text: Document in the record that she appeared upset about the pronoun use
options.rationale: It makes her reaction the finding. What belongs in the record is her name and pronouns, so the error stops.

options.text: Move her to a private room without discussing it, so she is not asked an awkward question
options.rationale: A private room may well be right and deciding it for her repeats the original error. Ask.

options.text: Ask her where she would feel safest and arrange placement accordingly
options.rationale: Same action as the distractor with the one step that matters added.

options.text: Assess her respiratory status fully and tell her plainly what the numbers are
options.rationale: It treats the immediate problem and it gives her back a reason to engage, because she can see the information is being shared with her.

options.text: Ask her name and pronouns, record them where staff see them, and use them
options.rationale: The fix is recording it rather than remembering it. A field nobody reads produces the same shift again tomorrow.

items.takeaway: Treat the hypoxia, record her name and pronouns where staff will see them, get the hormone decision made with her, and ask about placement.
items.strategy: Two distractors do the right thing without asking her. The asking is not a formality; it is the whole difference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Assess and tell her, record name and pronouns, raise the hormones, ask about the room.

chartUpdate.text: A member of staff enters to collect the breakfast tray and says to the nurse, in the patient's hearing, that he has not eaten anything. The patient looks at the nurse and says nothing.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Apologize to the patient on the colleague's behalf after they leave
options.rationale: An apology for something that was not corrected. It asks her to accept the error as the price of being there.

options.text: Correct it at once, briefly, in front of the patient, and carry on with what she was doing
options.rationale: A short correction in the room shows the patient that it is not hers to manage and that someone in the building will say it. Keeping it brief avoids turning her into the subject of a scene.

options.text: Say nothing now and speak to the colleague outside so the patient is not embarrassed
options.rationale: The strongest distractor. Silence in the room is what the patient experiences, and she has no way of knowing anything was said afterward. It protects the colleague's comfort rather than hers.

options.text: Ask the patient whether she would like the nurse to say something
options.rationale: It hands her the work of deciding whether her own name is worth a conversation, in front of the person who got it wrong.

items.takeaway: Correct the pronoun in the room, briefly, and move on. Handling it in the hallway is invisible to the person it happened to.
items.strategy: Three options are considerate and all three leave the correction out of her hearing. Ask what she experiences in the next ten seconds.

strategies: Ask what the patient sees happen
elimination.verdict: Correct it briefly, in the room.

chartUpdate.text: Name and pronouns recorded in the banner of the record and on the care board. Three staff heard using them correctly; one error at 2200, corrected in the room by the charge nurse. Moved to a private room after she was asked and said she would prefer one. Estradiol and spironolactone restarted after a conversation with her and the provider. She used the call light four times overnight and reported increasing cough at 0300. Oxygen saturation 95 percent on 2 litres, respirations 18. She says she still has not been asked what she wants her partner told when he telephones.

items.stem: For each outcome, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: Her respiratory status is improving
rows.rationale: Saturation 95 percent and respirations down to 18, with the cough now being reported rather than hidden.

rows.text: She reports symptoms as they occur
rows.rationale: Four call light uses and a volunteered report at 0300. This is the outcome that mattered clinically and it has turned around.

rows.text: Her long-term therapy continues unless there is a reason to stop it
rows.rationale: Restarted after a conversation that included her, so a decision now exists where an omission was.

rows.text: Placement reflects where she feels safest
rows.rationale: She was asked and the answer was acted on, which is what makes this different from the private room being decided for her.

rows.text: She controls what is shared about her, and with whom
rows.rationale: Nobody has asked what she wants said to her partner on the telephone. The team fixed the disclosures it got wrong and never set up the one she will need every day of the admission.

rows.text: Staff use her name and pronouns consistently
rows.rationale: One error in a day, corrected in the room by the person who heard it. Consistency means a system that catches errors, not a day without any.

items.takeaway: Fixing the errors that happened is not the same as setting up the decisions that have not come up yet. Ask what she wants shared before the telephone rings.
items.strategy: Five rows are clearly met, which makes the sixth easy to wave through. Read it for what has been arranged rather than what has been repaired.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find what was never set up

elimination.verdict: Five met, one not.

chart.text: 34-year-old woman seen at a community health fair. Two children aged six and three. Works two part-time jobs, neither of which offers health insurance. No regular provider. Last cervical screening nine years ago. Her mother had breast cancer diagnosed at 46. No current contraception, and she describes herself and her partner as not trying and not preventing.
Blood pressure 118/74. Body mass index 27. Random glucose 96 mg/dL. No tetanus booster since school. Both children up to date with immunizations through the school clinic.

Says she knows she should get the smear thing done but it costs money and she cannot take unpaid time off. Says her mother's cancer frightens her so much that she would rather not know. Asks whether anywhere does it free. Says she gets the children seen but never herself. Says a friend was diagnosed last year at 38 and that is partly why she stopped at the stand today.

items.nursesNote: Says she knows she should get the smear thing done but it costs money and she cannot take unpaid time off. Says her mother's cancer frightens her so much that she would rather not know. Asks whether anywhere does it free. Says she gets the children seen but never herself. Says a friend was diagnosed last year at 38 and that is partly why she stopped at the stand today. Last cervical screening nine years ago. Her mother had breast cancer diagnosed at 46. Blood pressure 118/74. Both children up to date with immunizations through the school clinic.
items.stem: Highlight the findings the nurse acts on at this visit.

segments.text: her mother's cancer frightens her so much that she would rather not know
segments.rationale: A fear strong enough to prevent screening. It is the barrier that will survive a free clinic and an appointment outside work hours.

segments.text: Last cervical screening nine years ago
segments.rationale: Nine years is far outside any interval. This is the single most actionable finding in front of her today.

segments.text: Her mother had breast cancer diagnosed at 46
segments.rationale: A first-degree relative under 50 changes what screening she should be offered and when. It is not something to leave to a provider she does not have.

segments.text: Asks whether anywhere does it free
segments.rationale: A direct request for information. A woman asking where to go is the easiest thing all day to act on.

segments.text: Blood pressure 118/74
segments.rationale: Normal. Worth telling her, and it needs nothing done about it.

segments.text: Both children up to date with immunizations through the school clinic
segments.rationale: This is going well, and it shows she can navigate a system when the appointment is made for her.

segments.text: a friend was diagnosed last year at 38
segments.rationale: This is the reason she is standing here. It is the thing that brought her in rather than a problem to solve.

segments.text: it costs money and she cannot take unpaid time off
segments.rationale: Two specific, nameable barriers. They are solvable by information she does not have, which is what makes them worth acting on rather than noting.

items.takeaway: The actionable findings are the overdue screening, the two practical barriers, the fear, and the family history. The friend's diagnosis is what got her here, and that is worth naming to her rather than acting on.
items.strategy: Two distractors are things going well, which are easy to select once you are looking for problems. One is the reason she came.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.action: Keep the gap and its barriers

elimination.verdict: The screening gap, the cost and time, the fear, the family history, and her question.

items.stem: For each statement she makes, indicate which belief it reflects.

rows.text: She thinks of screening as something for women older than she is
rows.rationale: A belief that it will not happen to her yet. It is why people with no barriers at all still do not go.

rows.text: Her mother had it at 46 and she worries the same thing is coming for her
rows.rationale: Belief about her own chance of developing it. Family history usually raises this without any teaching from anyone.

rows.text: She says getting it done would stop her worrying every time she reads something
rows.rationale: A benefit she expects from acting, and one that is about relief rather than detection.

rows.text: It costs money and she cannot take unpaid time off
rows.rationale: The cost of acting, as she experiences it. Barriers are usually the strongest single predictor of whether a person follows through.

rows.text: She received a text message from the clinic about a free screening evening
rows.rationale: An external prompt. Reminders work because they supply the cue, not because they change any belief.

rows.text: A friend was diagnosed last year at 38 and that is partly why she stopped at the stand
rows.rationale: An event that prompted her to do something. Cues are what convert a belief into a visit.

rows.text: She knows the screening finds things early when they can be treated
rows.rationale: Belief that the action would do some good. She has this one, and that is what makes the barriers decisive.

rows.text: She would rather not know
rows.rationale: The least obvious barrier and often the strongest. Fear of the result is a cost of acting just as much as the bus fare is.

items.takeaway: People act when they believe it could happen to them, that it would be serious, that acting helps, and that the cost is bearable. A cue then triggers it. Fear of the result is a barrier, not low susceptibility.
items.strategy: Would rather not know is the row that splits a class. It sounds like denial of risk and it is the opposite: she believes the risk so strongly that knowing is the thing she cannot face.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Two susceptibility, two barriers, two benefits, two cues.

items.stem: Which barrier does the nurse work on first?

options.text: She does not understand her risk given her mother's diagnosis
options.rationale: She understands it well enough to be frightened by it. More information about risk would add to the fear rather than move her.

options.text: She puts her children's health before her own
options.rationale: A real pattern, and it is a description of her life rather than something the nurse can change in ten minutes at a stand.

options.text: Her fear of what the result might show
options.rationale: The strongest distractor and probably the barrier that matters most in the end. It is not something to open and leave at a health fair stand, and it will be easier to approach once a concrete plan exists.

options.text: She does not know where to get screening she can afford
options.rationale: She asked the question out loud, it has a concrete answer, and answering it is the only thing in this conversation that can be finished today. Solving one barrier also makes the harder one easier to raise.

items.takeaway: Start with the barrier the person named and that you can remove today. A solved practical barrier is also what earns you the conversation about the frightening one.
items.strategy: Two options are genuine barriers and one of them is deeper. Ask which one can be finished before she walks away.

strategies: Ask what can be completed today
elimination.verdict: Where to get it affordably.

items.stem: Which actions does the nurse take at this visit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Advise her to ask her employer about paid time off for medical appointments she cannot otherwise attend
options.rationale: It hands the problem back to a woman with two part-time jobs and no leverage, and it does not solve it.

options.text: Tell her that her mother's diagnosis under 50 means she should discuss earlier breast screening, and write it down for her
options.rationale: It is information she does not have, it changes what she should be offered, and writing it down is what survives the walk to the car.

options.text: Tell her that at 34 her risk is low and she should not worry too much
options.rationale: Untrue given her family history, and reassurance aimed at a fear she has not yet described.

options.text: Explain in detail how cervical cancer develops over time so that she understands why the screening interval matters
options.rationale: She already believes it matters. A lecture on mechanism treats a knowledge gap she does not have.

options.text: Raise contraception, since she describes herself as not preventing and has not discussed it with anyone
options.rationale: She has no provider and no plan, and a woman who sees nobody about her own health will not raise it elsewhere.

options.text: Give her the name, address and opening hours of a clinic that screens at no cost outside working hours
options.rationale: It answers the question she asked and removes both practical barriers in one piece of information.

options.text: Say that many women put off screening because of what it might find, and ask what worries her most
options.rationale: It normalizes the fear without dismissing it, and the open question is what lets her say the part she has not said.

items.takeaway: Remove the barrier she named, open the one she did not, give her the information her family history changes, and use the one visit she makes for herself.
items.strategy: Two distractors are kind or educational and neither matches what is missing. Check each one against the barrier it would remove.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: The clinic details, opening the fear, the family history, and contraception.

chartUpdate.text: Given the clinic details, she says she will probably go, then adds that if they find something she could not take time off for treatment either, and that her children need her working.

items.stem: What does the nurse say?

options.text: Acknowledge the worry is about what comes after the test, and ask what treatment would mean for her and the children
options.rationale: She has just named the real obstacle, which is not the test. Following her there is the only way to find out what she would really need.

options.text: Say that her children need her well, and that is the reason to go
options.rationale: True and it turns her children into an argument. She already puts them first and that is the pattern keeping her away.

options.text: Explain that treatment for something found early is usually shorter and much less disruptive than treatment found late
options.rationale: Accurate, and it answers a question about statistics when she has asked one about her life.

options.text: Reassure her that most results come back normal and that she is worrying a long way ahead of herself here
options.rationale: It argues with a fear instead of hearing it, and most results being normal is no comfort to a woman whose mother's was not.

items.takeaway: When someone moves the objection, follow it. She was never frightened of the smear; she is frightened of what happens to her children if the result is bad.
items.strategy: Three options answer the objection she raised first. Only one answers the one she has just moved to.

strategies: Ask what she just said
elimination.verdict: Follow her to what comes after.

chartUpdate.text: She attended the free evening clinic eight weeks after the fair and the cervical screening was normal. She has registered with a primary care practice. Referred for earlier breast screening on the basis of her mother's history and has an appointment next month. Started a contraceptive method she chose after a discussion. Has not had the tetanus booster. Says she is still frightened about the breast appointment and has told nobody about it. Her children remain up to date.

items.stem: For each outcome at six months, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: Her immunizations are up to date
rows.rationale: Still no tetanus booster. It was the smallest item at the fair and it fell off the list, which is what happens to items nobody attaches to a visit.

rows.text: She attends cervical screening
rows.rationale: Attended and the result was normal. Nine years became eight weeks once the barrier was removed.

rows.text: She has a contraceptive method she chose
rows.rationale: Chosen after a discussion rather than assigned, which is what makes it likely to continue.

rows.text: Her family history is reflected in what she is offered
rows.rationale: Referred and booked. The information she was given at the stand produced a referral she would not otherwise have had.

rows.text: The fear that was keeping her away has been addressed
rows.rationale: She got through the first test and is frightened about the next one and telling nobody. The behavior changed and the fear did not, which means it will be back at the next appointment.

rows.text: She has a usual source of care
rows.rationale: Registered with a practice, which turns one health fair into ongoing access.

items.takeaway: Removing a practical barrier changes behavior fast. The fear underneath it needs its own work, and the smallest item on the list is the one that gets dropped.
items.strategy: Four clear successes make the last two easy to round up. Check the fear against her behavior, not against the result.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four met, one partially, one not.

chart.text: Patient is 69, admitted eleven days ago with a stroke affecting the brainstem. Ventilated since admission. A family meeting yesterday concluded that recovery is not expected and that comfort-focused care should begin. His wife of forty-four years has been at the bedside every day. Two adult children live out of state and arrive tomorrow.

Wife present since 0700. Stands rather than sits, does not take the chair when offered. Asks the nurse twice what the numbers on the monitor mean. Says the meeting yesterday had eight people in it and she cannot remember what was decided, only that someone said there was nothing more to do. Has not eaten since arriving. Asks whether he can hear her. Three staff have entered in the past hour to complete tasks; each left within two minutes. She apologizes for being in the way when the nurse moves to the pump.

Comfort measures. Turn and reposition two-hourly. Oral care four-hourly. Analgesia and anxiolytic by continuous infusion, titrated. Chaplain referral placed yesterday, not yet seen. No restriction on visiting hours.

items.nursesNote: 1500: Wife present since 0700. Stands rather than sits, does not take the chair when offered. Asks the nurse twice what the numbers on the monitor mean. Says the meeting yesterday had eight people in it and she cannot remember what was decided, only that someone said there was nothing more to do. Has not eaten since arriving. Asks whether he can hear her. Three staff have entered in the past hour to complete tasks; each left within two minutes. She apologizes for being in the way when the nurse moves to the pump.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that show an unmet need for presence and support.

segments.text: Has not eaten since arriving
segments.rationale: Worth attending to and it is a need for food rather than for presence. Name it for what it is and bring her something.

segments.text: each left within two minutes
segments.rationale: Three people in an hour and no one stayed. Every task was completed and nobody was present.

segments.text: She apologizes for being in the way
segments.rationale: She has concluded she is an obstacle in her husband's room. That belief came from somewhere in the last eleven days.

segments.text: Asks the nurse twice what the numbers on the monitor mean
segments.rationale: Asked twice, so it was not answered the first time. She is watching a screen she cannot read for information nobody is giving her.

segments.text: Stands rather than sits, does not take the chair when offered
segments.rationale: A cue that something is wrong and not a need in itself. It is how the apologizing shows up in her body.

segments.text: Asks whether he can hear her
segments.rationale: The real question under the others. What she wants to know is whether the last eleven days of talking to him reached anyone.

segments.text: she cannot remember what was decided, only that someone said there was nothing more to do
segments.rationale: A meeting happened and she left it without the information it was for. That sentence is also the cruellest possible summary of a comfort care decision.

segments.text: Wife present since 0700
segments.rationale: A fact about her commitment rather than an unmet need.

items.takeaway: Presence is not the same as attendance. Three staff were in the room within the hour and the measure of presence is whether anyone stayed.
items.strategy: Two segments are real needs of a different kind. The question asks specifically about presence and support, so sort by what each finding is asking for.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: The forgotten meeting, the monitor, whether he can hear, the two-minute visits, and the apology.

items.stem: For each nurse behavior, indicate what it conveys.

rows.text: Silences the pump alarm, checks the line, and leaves without speaking
rows.rationale: The task was done correctly and nothing passed between two people. This is most of what has happened in that room today.

rows.text: Completes the oral care thoroughly and documents it accurately
rows.rationale: Necessary, skilled, and it is care of the body rather than of the two people in the room.

rows.text: Says she will come back in ten minutes to talk, and does
rows.rationale: Presence survives leaving if the return happens. The promise kept is what makes it count.

rows.text: Says she will come back to talk, and does not
rows.rationale: Worse than never offering. It teaches her that what staff say in that room does not hold.

rows.text: Explains the two-hourly turn while doing it, and invites her to help with his hands
rows.rationale: It turns a task she was apologizing around into something she is part of.

rows.text: Answers what the monitor numbers mean, then asks what she is most worried about
rows.rationale: It answers the question she asked and opens the one she has not.

rows.text: Tells her she should go home and get some rest, she will be no use exhausted
rows.rationale: Framed as concern and received as an instruction to leave. It also treats her usefulness as the point of her being there.

rows.text: Sits down, at eye level, and says nothing for a moment before speaking
rows.rationale: Sitting signals that the next few minutes belong to her. The silence is what gives her room to start.

items.takeaway: Competence is the floor and it is not caring on its own. Presence costs minutes rather than skill, and a promise not kept costs more than never offering.
items.strategy: Two rows describe excellent technical care. Competent is not the same as uncaring and it is not the same as present either.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four presence, two competent only, two eroding.

items.stem: Which need does the nurse address first?

options.text: The chaplain referral has not been actioned
options.rationale: It should be chased today and spiritual support lands differently once she knows what is happening.

options.text: She does not know what was decided yesterday or what is happening to her husband now
options.rationale: Everything else follows from it. She cannot grieve, decide, or use the time she has left while she does not know what is going on, and the chaplain and the children all arrive into that gap.

options.text: She believes she is in the way at her husband's bedside
options.rationale: This needs fixing and it is the symptom. It came from eleven days of two-minute visits and no conversation.

options.text: She has not eaten in eight hours and is at risk of becoming unwell herself
options.rationale: Real, and a sandwich can arrive while something else is happening. It is not what is costing her most in this room.

items.takeaway: The first thing a family needs is to know what is happening. Comfort, food and chaplaincy all land better on the other side of that conversation.
items.strategy: All four are genuine needs. Ask which one the other three are waiting on.

strategies: Find the need the others depend on
elimination.verdict: She does not know what is happening.

items.stem: Which actions belong in the plan for this family? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chase the chaplain referral placed yesterday without asking whether she wants to be seen
options.rationale: The referral was placed and whether she wants it is still her call. Spiritual care arranged over someone's head is another thing happening to her.

options.text: Answer whether he can hear her, honestly, including what is not known
options.rationale: She asked. The honest answer is that hearing is often the last sense to go and nobody can be certain, and that is more use to her than a comfortable yes.

options.text: Sit down with her, find out what she understood from the meeting, and fill the gaps in plain words
options.rationale: It starts from what she has rather than repeating the meeting at her, and sitting is what makes it a conversation.

options.text: Offer to be present when she speaks to her children tomorrow, and ask whether she wants that
options.rationale: Tomorrow is the next hard thing and offering in advance gives her something to hold today.

options.text: Reassure her that she did the right thing in agreeing to comfort care for her husband
options.rationale: It assumes she agreed, assumes she is looking for absolution, and closes a subject she has not yet been able to open.

options.text: Suggest she go home and sleep tonight so that she is rested before her children arrive tomorrow morning
options.rationale: A decision about her own time that is hers to make. Offered as advice it reads as being asked to leave.

options.text: Bring her a chair where she wants it and something to drink, and tell her she is not in the way
options.rationale: It answers the apology directly and changes the room from somewhere she is tolerated into somewhere she belongs.

items.takeaway: Sit, answer what she asked, make the room hers, and offer to be there for the next hard part. Caring here is minutes and honesty rather than any procedure.
items.strategy: Three distractors do something for her without asking her. Each one is the same error the last eleven days have been made of.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Sit and explain, answer honestly, make her welcome, offer tomorrow.

chartUpdate.text: During the conversation the wife begins to cry and says: I keep thinking I should have made him go to the doctor in March. The nurse's next patient is due analgesia in ten minutes and the assistive personnel is available.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Offer a tissue and say that many families feel this way
options.rationale: Normalizing moves her from a specific thought to a general category. The specific thought is where the work is.

options.text: Excuse herself to give the analgesia and return afterward, explaining why
options.rationale: The strongest distractor, because the other patient's analgesia is real. The dose can be given by arrangement and this moment cannot be rescheduled.

options.text: Stay, say nothing for a moment, and then ask her what she has been thinking about March
options.rationale: She has arrived at the thing she has been carrying for eleven days. Silence and an open question are what let her say it, and a nurse who leaves now teaches her not to start again.

options.text: Tell her the stroke was not caused by anything she did or did not do in March
options.rationale: True, and it answers a question she did not ask. Guilt is not resolved by being told it is unfounded.

items.takeaway: When someone finally says the thing, stay. Reassurance, normalizing and stepping out all close a door that took eleven days to open.
items.strategy: Two options are kind and one is operationally sensible. Ask which of them keeps her talking.

strategies: Ask what happens to the conversation
elimination.verdict: Stay and open it.

chartUpdate.text: Wife sitting in a chair she positioned at the head of the bed, holding his hand. Ate a meal brought by staff yesterday evening and breakfast this morning. States she now understands that comfort care means his symptoms are treated and nothing will be done to prolong the dying, and can say this in her own words. Asked the nurse to be present when her children arrive at 1400 and the nurse has arranged cover. Chaplain seen after she said she would like it. Still asks several times a day whether he is in any pain. Says she has not told her sister and does not know how to.

items.stem: For each outcome, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: She is confident her husband is not in pain
rows.rationale: She is asking several times a day, which means the reassurance is not holding between askings. It needs a different approach rather than more of the same answer.

rows.text: She can state what comfort care means for her husband
rows.rationale: In her own words, which is the difference between being told and understanding.

rows.text: She has been offered bereavement support for after his death
rows.rationale: Nothing in the record offers her anything beyond the admission. The support she will need most begins on the day the team stops seeing her.

rows.text: She has support in place for the hard conversations ahead
rows.rationale: Today at 1400 is arranged and her sister is not. The need she has named most recently has no plan attached to it.

rows.text: Her spiritual needs have been addressed on her terms
rows.rationale: The chaplain was seen after she said she wanted it, which is what makes it hers rather than something arranged over her head.

rows.text: She experiences the bedside as a place she belongs
rows.rationale: She positioned her own chair and is holding his hand. The apologizing has stopped.

rows.text: Her own physical needs are being met
rows.rationale: Two meals since yesterday evening, brought to her rather than suggested.

items.takeaway: A repeated question is an outcome that is not holding. Asking several times a day whether he is in pain means the answer is not reaching the fear underneath it.
items.strategy: The pain row looks met because the team is answering her every time. Ask why she keeps needing to ask.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.detail: The chair, the meals, the words.

steps.action: Find the conversation with no plan

elimination.verdict: Four met, two partially met, one not met.

chart.text: 44-year-old woman, teaching assistant at a primary school, with rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed six years ago. Takes methotrexate weekly with folic acid, and prednisone during flares. Also has hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. Divorced, two teenage children at home. Attends the clinic for review after a flare.

Says the joint pain is manageable most days but the fatigue takes the whole day. Reduced her hours from five days to three and told her employer it was a transport problem. Says people keep telling her she looks well. Has missed the last two methotrexate doses because the monitoring blood test is only offered on a working morning. Stopped going to her sister's on Sundays because she cannot predict how she will be and does not want to cancel on the day. Has not told her children how bad it gets. Asks whether there is any point doing the hand exercises when she is this tired. Grip strength reduced bilaterally, no new joint swelling.
Inflammatory markers lower than at the flare. Full blood count and liver function within range at the last test, taken ten weeks ago. Next monitoring test overdue.

items.nursesNote: 1000: Says the joint pain is manageable most days but the fatigue takes the whole day. Reduced her hours from five days to three and told her employer it was a transport problem. Says people keep telling her she looks well. Has missed the last two methotrexate doses because the monitoring blood test is only offered on a working morning. Stopped going to her sister's on Sundays because she cannot predict how she will be and does not want to cancel on the day. Has not told her children how bad it gets. Asks whether there is any point doing the hand exercises when she is this tired. Grip strength reduced bilaterally, no new joint swelling.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that need to be addressed in this review.

segments.text: people keep telling her she looks well
segments.rationale: A real and wearing experience of an invisible illness. Worth acknowledging and not itself something to act on.

segments.text: Stopped going to her sister's on Sundays
segments.rationale: Loss of the support she has, driven by unpredictability rather than by severity. This is how chronic illness shrinks a life quietly.

segments.text: Asks whether there is any point doing the hand exercises when she is this tired
segments.rationale: A direct question and a drop in self-efficacy. Left unanswered it becomes the reason she stops.

segments.text: told her employer it was a transport problem
segments.rationale: She is concealing the diagnosis at work, which blocks every adjustment that could keep her in a job she has already cut by two days.

segments.text: Grip strength reduced bilaterally
segments.rationale: Expected in established disease and consistent with her history. It is monitored rather than acted on today.

segments.text: Has missed the last two methotrexate doses because the monitoring blood test is only offered on a working morning
segments.rationale: A clinical risk with an administrative cause. The system's appointment schedule is what stopped her treatment.

segments.text: the fatigue takes the whole day
segments.rationale: She has named the symptom that is costing her the most, and it is the one least likely to be asked about in a review built around joints.

segments.text: no new joint swelling
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding and evidence the flare has settled.

items.takeaway: The review was booked about her joints and the joints are the part going well. What needs addressing is fatigue, concealment, a missed drug, lost support, and a question about whether any of it is worth it.
items.strategy: Two of the distractors are objective findings, which is what makes them feel like the real content of a review. Ask which findings would change her week.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: The fatigue, the concealment, the missed doses, the lost Sundays, and her question.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate what it belongs to.

rows.text: Telling her employer the problem is transport
rows.rationale: How she lives with being ill among other people. The disease did not require this; the way illness is received at work did.

rows.text: Giving up Sundays at her sister's because she cannot predict the day
rows.rationale: A life narrowing around unpredictability. No joint stopped her going; the uncertainty did.

rows.text: The monitoring blood test is only offered on a working morning
rows.rationale: A cost the treatment imposes, and here it is large enough to have stopped the treatment.

rows.text: Inflammatory markers lower than at the flare
rows.rationale: A biological measure of the condition's activity.

rows.text: People telling her she looks well
rows.rationale: The particular burden of a condition nobody can see, and a reason people stop describing how they are.

rows.text: Fatigue that is unrelated to how much she has done
rows.rationale: Inflammatory fatigue is a feature of the condition rather than a consequence of effort, which is exactly why rest does not fix it.

rows.text: A weekly drug, a daily tablet, and a blood test she must attend
rows.rationale: The work the regimen demands of her, separate from the symptoms it treats.

rows.text: Reduced grip strength in both hands
rows.rationale: A measurable physical effect of the condition on her joints.

items.takeaway: The disease is what the condition does to the body. Illness is what living with it does to the person. Treatment burden is the work the plan demands. The second and third are what she came in with.
items.strategy: Fatigue is written to look like illness experience because of how she describes it. Inflammatory fatigue is a feature of the disease itself.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find the work of the regimen
Find what it costs her life

elimination.verdict: Three disease, three illness, two burden.

items.stem: Which problem does the nurse take up first?

options.text: The fatigue, since it is the symptom costing her the most
options.rationale: The right thing to take seriously and the thing she came to talk about. It is managed over months, and it will be worse if the treatment stays stopped.

options.text: She has missed two doses of methotrexate because the monitoring appointment conflicts with her work
options.rationale: An untreated inflammatory disease has consequences that do not reverse, and the cause is an appointment time. It is both the most urgent and the most quickly solved thing on the list.

options.text: She is concealing the diagnosis at work and losing income as a result
options.rationale: A significant problem with real consequences for her job, and it is not what damages joints this month.

options.text: She is withdrawing from the support she has
options.rationale: Important for the long run and not what the nurse has to solve today.

items.takeaway: In chronic illness, go first for the problem with an irreversible consequence and a solvable cause. An appointment time stopping a disease-modifying drug is both.
items.strategy: Three options are about how she is living and one is about whether she is being treated. Ask which one leaves permanent damage.

strategies: Ask which consequence does not reverse

steps.detail: Work, Sundays, fatigue all can wait.

elimination.verdict: The missed methotrexate.

items.stem: Which actions belong in her plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Suggest she give up the Sunday visits to her sister for now, so as to conserve her energy
options.rationale: It endorses the withdrawal that is isolating her. The problem is the unpredictability, which can be planned around.

options.text: Answer her question about the exercises directly, and agree a version small enough to do on a bad day
options.rationale: She asked whether there was any point. A plan she can complete when she is tired rebuilds the belief that her effort changes anything.

options.text: Arrange monitoring bloods at a time that fits three working days and confirm it before she leaves
options.rationale: It removes the specific obstacle, and confirming it here is what distinguishes this from the arrangement that failed.

options.text: Ask what she would want her children to know, and offer help with how to say it
options.rationale: She raised it, and not telling them is costing her support in her own house. The offer leaves the decision with her.

options.text: Reteach the importance of taking the methotrexate consistently every week without a gap
options.rationale: She knows. She missed the doses because the blood test was on a working morning, and teaching treats a gap that is not there.

options.text: Advise her to rest more during the week and to plan a nap each afternoon when she is home
options.rationale: Inflammatory fatigue does not respond to rest the way ordinary tiredness does, and the advice implies she has not tried.

options.text: Explore what she thinks would happen if her employer knew, and what adjustments exist
options.rationale: The concealment is costing her two days of income a week. Working with the belief behind it is what opens the possibility of adjustments.

items.takeaway: Fix the appointment, make the exercise doable on a bad day, work on the concealment, and help her tell her children. Do not reteach what she knows or prescribe rest for inflammatory fatigue.
items.strategy: Two distractors sound like sensible energy management. Both treat inflammatory fatigue as ordinary tiredness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: The appointment, the smaller exercise, the employer, and her children.

chartUpdate.text: She says she will do the exercises if they are worth it, and asks the nurse to tell her honestly whether she is going to end up like her aunt, who used a wheelchair by her fifties.

items.stem: How does the nurse respond?

options.text: Redirect to the exercise plan, since that is what she can control today
options.rationale: It skips the question to get to the task, and the question is why the task felt pointless.

options.text: Explain that outcomes vary and that it is not possible to predict any individual case
options.rationale: Accurate and it is a way of not answering. She asked an honest question and deserves what is known.

options.text: Reassure her that treatment has changed a great deal since her aunt's time and that she will not end up that way
options.rationale: Half of it is true and the promise is not hers to make. A guarantee she may later find was wrong costs her trust in everything else said today.

options.text: Ask what she has seen of her aunt's illness, then say honestly what treatment changes and what nobody can promise
options.rationale: Finding out what she is picturing comes first, because the fear is shaped by a specific person. Then she gets the truth in both directions, which is what makes the encouraging half believable.

items.takeaway: Ask what she is picturing before you answer. Honest encouragement includes what cannot be promised, and that is what makes the rest of it credible.
items.strategy: Two options are honest in opposite directions: one overpromises and one declines to answer. The third does both halves.

strategies: Ask whether the question gets answered
elimination.verdict: Ask what she pictures, then answer honestly.

chartUpdate.text: Monitoring bloods moved to a Saturday clinic and no doses missed since. Does a three-minute hand routine most mornings and says it is the one thing she has not dropped. Told her children, who now cook on her worst evenings. Has not spoken to her employer and still describes the reduced hours as a transport issue. Fatigue unchanged and she says it is the thing she would most want fixed. Has been to her sister's twice, having agreed she can leave early without explaining. Asks whether there is anything at all for the fatigue.

items.stem: For each outcome at three months, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: Her fatigue is managed
rows.rationale: Unchanged, and she is still asking. The symptom she named as the worst is the one nothing in the plan has reached, which is the commonest pattern in invisible illness.

rows.text: She receives her methotrexate as prescribed
rows.rationale: No doses missed since the appointment moved. The fix held because it changed the system rather than her effort.

rows.text: She maintains contact with her wider support network
rows.rationale: Twice in three months, with permission to leave early built in. Better than stopped and not yet what she had.

rows.text: Her work situation reflects her actual needs
rows.rationale: Still concealed and still two days of income down. This was the hardest item and it has not moved at all.

rows.text: She has an exercise routine she can sustain
rows.rationale: Three minutes most mornings, and she describes it as the thing she has not dropped. A plan sized for a bad day survives the bad days.

rows.text: She has support at home
rows.rationale: She told her children and they changed what they do. The support was in the house the whole time.

items.takeaway: The items that moved were the ones with a concrete change behind them. What she named as worst is untouched, and a plan that never reaches the patient's own priority will not hold for long.
items.strategy: Three clean successes make the last three easy to round up. Compare each one against what she said she wanted at the first visit.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Three met, one partially, two not.

chart.text: Patient is 78, admitted for investigation of weight loss and a cough. Biopsy results returned this morning and show a malignancy. He emigrated forty years ago and speaks limited English. His eldest son has attended every appointment and has answered most questions on his behalf. The family has asked that the patient not be told the diagnosis, saying that in their family bad news is carried by the family and that telling him would take away his will to live.

Eldest son met the nurse in the corridor and asked that the results be given to him and not to his father. States his father would want it this way and that he has always made the decisions for the family. Patient, through a telephone interpreter, asks the nurse what the test showed and says he has been waiting three days. Also says he has been taking a preparation his wife makes from a plant, every morning, alongside his tablets, and asks the nurse not to tell the doctor because the last one was angry about it. No capacity concerns documented. No interpreter was present when consent for the biopsy was taken.
No advance directive. No health care proxy. Biopsy consent form signed, interpreter field blank.

items.nursesNote: 1100: Eldest son met the nurse in the corridor and asked that the results be given to him and not to his father. States his father would want it this way and that he has always made the decisions for the family. Patient, through a telephone interpreter, asks the nurse what the test showed and says he has been waiting three days. Also says he has been taking a preparation his wife makes from a plant, every morning, alongside his tablets, and asks the nurse not to tell the doctor because the last one was angry about it. No capacity concerns documented. No interpreter was present when consent for the biopsy was taken.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that require the nurse's action.

segments.text: asks the nurse not to tell the doctor because the last one was angry about it
segments.rationale: He is telling you why clinicians stop hearing about this. The request cannot be granted and how it is handled decides whether he ever mentions anything again.

segments.text: a preparation his wife makes from a plant, every morning, alongside his tablets
segments.rationale: An unidentified preparation taken daily with prescribed drugs. Nobody knows what is in it or what it interacts with.

segments.text: No capacity concerns documented
segments.rationale: This is the finding that settles who decides rather than a problem to act on. Capacity is presumed and nothing contradicts it.

segments.text: asked that the results be given to him and not to his father
segments.rationale: A request to withhold information from the person it belongs to. It needs handling rather than agreeing to or refusing in a corridor.

segments.text: Patient, through a telephone interpreter
segments.rationale: An interpreter is being used, which is the standard being met rather than a problem to act on.

segments.text: he has always made the decisions for the family
segments.rationale: A description of how this family has worked for decades. It is context for the conversation, not something the nurse acts on.

segments.text: asks the nurse what the test showed and says he has been waiting three days
segments.rationale: He has asked directly. Whatever the family prefers, a patient who asks has told you what he wants to know.

segments.text: No interpreter was present when consent for the biopsy was taken
segments.rationale: A procedure was performed on consent obtained across a language barrier with no interpreter. That is a consent problem on the record now.

items.takeaway: Four problems arrived in one conversation: a direct question, a request to withhold, an undisclosed remedy, and a consent taken without an interpreter.
items.strategy: Two segments describe the family's structure. Describing how a family operates is context, and the action lies in what is being asked of you now.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.action: Keep the four asks and the consent

elimination.verdict: His question, the withholding request, the preparation, his request for secrecy, and the consent.

items.stem: For each request or practice, indicate how the nurse responds to it.

rows.text: The son interprets for his father during clinical conversations
rows.rationale: A family member is not a qualified interpreter, and this one has a stated interest in what gets said. He can be present and he cannot be the channel.

rows.text: A female relative stays overnight because the family does not leave an elder alone
rows.rationale: It costs the unit nothing and it is good for the patient. Accommodate practices that do no harm without making them into a negotiation.

rows.text: The family prefers conversations to begin with the son before the patient
rows.rationale: A real preference that can partly be met, as long as it does not become the route by which the patient is bypassed. Ask him what he wants.

rows.text: The results are given to the son and withheld from a patient who has asked for them
rows.rationale: He asked. Withholding from a capable patient who wants to know is not a cultural accommodation, it is a decision taken out of his hands.

rows.text: The daily plant preparation continues alongside his prescribed medication
rows.rationale: It matters to him and it may interact with what he is given. Find out what it is, say what the risk is, and build a plan he will keep to.

rows.text: Nobody tells the medical team about the preparation
rows.rationale: Hiding a daily ingested substance from the prescribers is unsafe. How it is passed on is negotiable; whether it is passed on is not.

rows.text: The son attends every conversation and helps his father think things through
rows.rationale: A patient may involve whoever he wants. Family-centered decision making is a legitimate preference, not a problem to correct.

rows.text: The family would like to be present when the diagnosis is discussed
rows.rationale: Easy to arrange, and it usually makes a hard conversation go better. He decides who is in the room.

items.takeaway: Most cultural requests cost nothing and are accommodated as asked. A few need negotiating. The ones you cannot accommodate are those that take a capable patient's decisions or his safety away from him.
items.strategy: Two rows are about the son's involvement and they split. Being present is always fine; being the channel or the substitute is not.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.detail: The preparation, the order of conversations.

elimination.verdict: Three accommodate, two negotiate, three cannot.

items.stem: Which statement best frames what the nurse brings to the team?

options.text: The son is attempting to exercise an authority over his father that he does not legally have
options.rationale: Legally close and it treats a frightened son as an adversary. He is doing what his family has always done and nobody has talked to him.

options.text: The patient needs a formal capacity evaluation before anything at all is disclosed to him
options.rationale: Nothing suggests impaired capacity, and ordering an evaluation because the family prefers a different answer makes the assessment a tool for the disagreement.

options.text: The patient has asked what his results show, and nobody has established from him how much he wants to know
options.rationale: It keeps the decision with him, and it names the step that was skipped. He may well choose to have his son told everything, and that is a choice he gets to make.

options.text: The family's cultural beliefs about disclosure are in direct conflict with the team's duty to inform the patient
options.rationale: It states the clash accurately and leaves out the only person who can resolve it. Framed this way it becomes a contest between two groups with the patient as the prize.

items.takeaway: Ask the patient how much he wants to know and who he wants told. Nondisclosure can be his informed choice, and it cannot be someone else's choice for him.
items.strategy: Three options are framed as a conflict between two parties. The one that resolves it puts the question to the person whose results they are.

strategies: Ask who has not been consulted

steps.detail: He is left out of both.

steps.action: Find the option that asks him

elimination.verdict: Establish from him what he wants to know.

items.stem: Which actions belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report the missing interpreter on the biopsy consent through the appropriate process
options.rationale: A procedure was done on a consent that cannot be shown to have been informed. It has to be recorded whatever happens next.

options.text: Agree not to mention the preparation, so he keeps being honest with the nurse
options.rationale: A promise that cannot be kept, bought with his safety. The trust is worth having and not at that price.

options.text: Ask the patient what is in the preparation, how much he takes, and tell him it has to be shared with the prescribers
options.rationale: It gets the information, states the limit honestly, and does it without the reaction that made him stop telling people.

options.text: With a qualified interpreter, ask the patient how much he wants to be told and who else he wants in the conversation
options.rationale: It settles the whole question and takes five minutes. Whatever he answers becomes the plan, including an answer that gives it all to his son.

options.text: Sit with the son, find out what he is afraid will happen, and explain what will be asked of his father
options.rationale: He has a belief that the news will kill his father's will to live. That belief is where the pressure is coming from and it can be worked with.

options.text: Tell the son the nurse cannot withhold results from a capable patient and that his father will be told today
options.rationale: Legally defensible and it ends the relationship with the family. It also pre-empts the patient, who has not yet said what he wants.

options.text: Ask the son to interpret the conversation about disclosure himself, since he knows his father better than anyone
options.rationale: Using the person who wants the information withheld as the channel through which it is offered.

items.takeaway: Ask the patient, work with the family's fear rather than against it, be honest about what you cannot keep secret, and report the consent.
items.strategy: Two distractors buy something at the cost of a promise or a confrontation. Ask what each action makes impossible later.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Ask him, sit with the son, get the preparation details, report the consent.

chartUpdate.text: With a qualified interpreter, the patient says he wants to know everything and wants his son in the room when he is told. The son, told this, says his father only said that because the interpreter was present and that he will change his mind. He asks the nurse to delay until he has spoken to him alone.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Delay briefly and let the son speak with his father alone first
options.rationale: It hands the son a private opportunity to change an answer the team has already heard. A delay for that purpose is the withholding carried out by another route.

options.text: Ask the provider to speak with the son privately before anything further is said to the patient
options.rationale: It routes the decision back through the family once more, with a different clinician.

options.text: Tell the son his father has decided and that the matter is closed
options.rationale: The decision is right and the delivery shuts out a man who is about to hear that his father is dying. He is in the room by his father's request.

options.text: Record what he said, tell the team he has asked to be told with his son present, and arrange it
options.rationale: He answered the question with a qualified interpreter and asked for his son to be there. The plan he described is the plan, and documenting it protects it from being revisited by other people.

options.text: Ask the patient the same question again later without the interpreter present, to see whether his answer changes
options.rationale: It tests his answer by removing the thing that made it reliable, and it treats the son's prediction as a reason to doubt him.

items.takeaway: Once a capable patient has said what he wants, that answer stands. Document it, because a stated preference that is not recorded gets relitigated by whoever comes next.
items.strategy: Three options revisit a question that has already been answered. Ask whether anything new has come from the patient.

strategies: Ask whether the patient has changed his mind
elimination.verdict: Record it and arrange the conversation he asked for.

chartUpdate.text: Diagnosis given with a qualified interpreter and the son present. Patient asked three questions and said he wanted to know about treatment options next week. Preparation identified from a photograph and reviewed by pharmacy, no interaction with his current drugs, and he has agreed it goes on the medication list. Son met with the nurse for twenty minutes and said he had been afraid his father would stop eating. Occurrence report filed about the biopsy consent. Interpreter used for every clinical conversation since. Patient says he still does not know what the plan is for his cough, which is the thing that has been bothering him most.

items.stem: For each outcome, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: His own priority concern has been addressed
