rows.rationale: The team disclosed the diagnosis and nobody answered the question he came in with. The symptom that is bothering him most is still unexplained, and that is a common cost of a conversation organized around what clinicians think is the headline.

rows.text: The family's concerns have been heard
rows.rationale: Twenty minutes with the son, and the specific fear came out. That is what stops the pressure returning next week.

rows.text: The complementary preparation is known to the team and assessed for safety
rows.rationale: Identified, reviewed by pharmacy, and on the list with his agreement. It stayed in the plan rather than going underground.

rows.text: The patient received the information he asked for, in the way he asked for it
rows.rationale: Interpreter present, son present, and he asked three questions of his own. Participation is the evidence it worked.

rows.text: The consent problem has been addressed
rows.rationale: Reported through the right process, where it can be examined rather than absorbed.

rows.text: Language access is in place for clinical conversations
rows.rationale: Used for every conversation since, which is the standard rather than the exception.

items.takeaway: Ask what matters most to the patient, not only what matters most clinically. A diagnosis conversation that never reaches his cough has answered the team's question.
items.strategy: Five rows close cleanly, which is what makes the sixth easy to miss. Go back to what he said he wanted at the start.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Five met, one not.

chart.text: 58-year-old woman, third day after a total knee replacement on the right. History of osteoarthritis and obesity. The surgical plan requires 90 degrees of knee flexion before discharge and she is at 40 degrees. Physical therapy twice daily. She teaches primary school and intends to return in six weeks.

Declined the morning physical therapy session. Says the exercises hurt too much and she would rather wait until the pain settles. Last analgesia 0400. Reports pain 8 of 10 at rest and worse on movement. Has not asked for anything since. Says she does not want to get hooked on the tablets, and that her brother had a problem with them. Dressing dry and intact. Right calf soft and nontender. Sits out of bed for meals when helped. Sleeps poorly, waking several times.

Oxycodone 5 mg every four hours as needed for severe pain. Acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours scheduled. Last oxycodone 0400, one dose in the last twenty-four hours. Acetaminophen doses given as scheduled.

items.nursesNote: 0900: Declined the morning physical therapy session. Says the exercises hurt too much and she would rather wait until the pain settles. Last analgesia 0400. Reports pain 8 of 10 at rest and worse on movement. Has not asked for anything since. Says she does not want to get hooked on the tablets, and that her brother had a problem with them. Dressing dry and intact. Right calf soft and nontender. Sits out of bed for meals when helped. Sleeps poorly, waking several times.
items.stem: Highlight the cues relevant to why she is not meeting the mobility goal.

segments.text: Dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: An expected finding and a reassuring one. It bears on infection, not on mobility.

segments.text: she does not want to get hooked on the tablets, and that her brother had a problem with them
segments.rationale: The reason she is not asking. Without this cue the plan would be to offer the drug more often, which would change nothing.

segments.text: Sleeps poorly, waking several times
segments.rationale: Poor sleep lowers pain tolerance and the energy for therapy, and here it is almost certainly the pain waking her.

segments.text: Reports pain 8 of 10 at rest
segments.rationale: Uncontrolled pain at rest means movement is going to be worse. Nothing about range of motion improves until this does.

segments.text: Sits out of bed for meals when helped
segments.rationale: This is going well. It shows she will move when the movement does not hurt.

segments.text: Has not asked for anything since
segments.rationale: Available analgesia going unused is the gap between what she has been prescribed and what she is receiving.

segments.text: Declined the morning physical therapy session
segments.rationale: The behavior the goal depends on. Two refused sessions a day is the whole shortfall.

segments.text: Right calf soft and nontender
segments.rationale: Relevant to screening for a clot and not to why she will not bend the knee.

items.takeaway: A relevant cue is one that would change the plan. Normal findings and findings about a different problem are data without being cues for this one.
items.strategy: Two segments are reassuring findings, which makes them easy to select because they are specific and clinical. Ask whether each one bears on the mobility goal.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: The refusal, the pain, the unused analgesia, the fear, and the sleep.

items.stem: For each statement, indicate which step of the nursing process it belongs to.

rows.text: Impaired physical mobility related to acute postoperative pain and fear of opioid dependence
rows.rationale: A human response, with related factors the nurse can act on. Both the pain and the fear are treatable by nursing.

rows.text: Reviews how many doses she has taken in twenty-four hours against what is prescribed
rows.rationale: Gathering data from the record. It is the finding that showed the prescription was not the problem.

rows.text: She will achieve 70 degrees of flexion by the end of tomorrow
rows.rationale: A measurable outcome with a time attached. Writing the outcome is the planning step.

rows.text: Gives the analgesia forty minutes before the therapy session
rows.rationale: Carrying out the intervention, timed so the drug is working when the knee has to bend.

rows.text: Measures flexion after the afternoon session and compares it with the morning
rows.rationale: Judging the response against the stated outcome, which is what evaluation means.

rows.text: Decides the outcome was partly met and extends the target to the end of the week
rows.rationale: Judging the result and revising, which belongs to evaluation rather than to planning the first time around.

rows.text: Explains the difference between dependence, tolerance and addiction
rows.rationale: Teaching is an intervention being carried out, aimed at the second related factor in the diagnosis.

rows.text: Asks her what she is afraid will happen if she takes the oxycodone
rows.rationale: Collecting the data that explains the refusal. You cannot plan around a fear you have not heard her describe.

items.takeaway: The step is decided by what the nurse is doing with the information: collecting it, naming it, setting a target, acting, or judging the result.
items.strategy: The last row is written to look like planning because it sets a new date. Revising after a judgment is still evaluation.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Two assessment, one diagnosis, one planning, two implementation, two evaluation.

items.stem: Complete the diagnostic statement by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Impaired physical mobility
options.rationale: A human response the nurse can treat, and it is the one the discharge criterion is written against.

options.text: Acute pain
options.rationale: Real and present, and here it is the cause rather than the problem. Naming it as the problem loses the reason she is not going home.

options.text: Noncompliance with the therapy regimen
options.rationale: A judgment about her rather than a response. It is also wrong here, since she has a specific and reasonable fear.

options.text: Knee flexion contracture
options.rationale: A medical diagnosis. Nursing does not treat it and cannot write it as the problem.

options.text: acute postoperative pain and fear of opioid dependence
options.rationale: Two factors, both treatable by nursing, and the second is the one that makes the first persist. Treating the pain alone would not have worked.

options.text: refusal of physical therapy
options.rationale: This is a behavior rather than a cause, and it comes close to restating the problem. It would also leave the plan with nothing to aim at.

options.text: total knee replacement
options.rationale: The surgery is a medical diagnosis and nursing cannot change it. Related factors have to be things that can be acted on.

options.text: obesity and deconditioning
options.rationale: Both are real and neither is what happened over the past twelve hours. Nothing in the note points to them as the barrier.

options.text: a report of pain 8 of 10
options.rationale: Evidence of the pain rather than of the impaired mobility. The evidence has to demonstrate the problem you named.

options.text: one dose of oxycodone in twenty-four hours
options.rationale: A real and important finding, and it evidences the undertreated pain rather than the mobility itself.

options.text: 40 degrees of flexion against a goal of 90, and two therapy sessions declined
options.rationale: Observable, measurable, and specific to this patient. Anyone reading it can see the gap and will know when it has closed.

options.text: reduced mobility after surgery
options.rationale: This restates the problem in different words and measures nothing.

items.takeaway: The problem is the human response, the related factor is something nursing can change, and the evidence is observable and measurable. Pain is usually the related factor, not the problem.
items.strategy: Each blank has one option that is the same idea in other words. Circular statements are the commonest fault in a written diagnosis.

strategies: Build the statement one part at a time
elimination.verdict: Impaired physical mobility, pain and fear of dependence, 40 degrees with sessions declined.

items.stem: Which interventions address the related factors in that diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document that she declined therapy and notify the surgeon
options.rationale: It records the problem and does nothing about either cause.

options.text: Add scheduled nonopioid analgesia and ice around the therapy sessions
options.rationale: It lowers the pain without the drug she is frightened of, which gives her a route she will accept.

options.text: Agree a plan with her where she takes a dose before therapy and the nurse reviews the total each day
options.rationale: It gives her the control and the oversight that make the dose acceptable to someone afraid of dependence.

options.text: Explore what she believes will happen if she takes the oxycodone, and address dependence, tolerance and addiction specifically
options.rationale: The fear is the second related factor and it has a name and a family history behind it. Nothing else on the list touches it.

options.text: Tell her the therapy is required before she can be discharged
options.rationale: Pressure applied to a frightened patient. It addresses neither related factor and gives her a reason to say she is fine when she is not.

options.text: Schedule the analgesia so it peaks about forty minutes before each therapy session
options.rationale: Timing the drug to the activity treats the pain at the point where it blocks the goal.

options.text: Request a change to an as-needed schedule so she is in charge of when she takes it
options.rationale: She is already on an as-needed schedule and has taken one dose in a day, so more autonomy is not the gap.

items.takeaway: Interventions are aimed at the related factors, not at the problem. Two factors means the plan has to have something for each.
items.strategy: Check each intervention against the words after related to. If it does not touch the pain or the fear, it will not move the flexion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Time the dose, address the fear, add a nonopioid, agree a plan with her.

chartUpdate.text: Analgesia given at 1230 after a conversation about her brother. Physical therapy due at 1310. She now reports pain 3 of 10 at rest, is sitting on the edge of the bed, and says she is willing to try. Asks the nurse to stay in the room during the session.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that the therapist will be with her throughout and go to the next patient
options.rationale: Accurate and it declines the request she made. The therapist being present is not the same as the person she has just told about her brother being present.

options.text: Stay for the session, since her asking is part of what makes this attempt possible
options.rationale: She has named what she needs to go through with it, and it costs twenty minutes. Presence here is the intervention that converts a willing patient into a completed session.

options.text: Use the time instead to complete the teaching about dependence and tolerance while she is receptive
options.rationale: That conversation has already happened and is the reason she took the dose. Repeating it now spends the window the analgesia opened.

options.text: Suggest she wait for the later session so she is not rushed into it
options.rationale: The analgesia is working now. Waiting lets the window close and tells her that hesitation is the expected response.

items.takeaway: When the window opens, use it. A patient who has just said what she needs has given you the intervention.
items.strategy: Three options are defensible uses of twenty minutes. Only one does the thing she asked for at the moment it matters.

strategies: Ask what she requested

steps.action: Compare the therapist with the nurse

elimination.verdict: Stay for the session.

chartUpdate.text: Flexion 62 degrees after four completed sessions. Goal was 70 degrees by the end of day 3. Pain 3 of 10 at rest and 5 of 10 during therapy. Four oxycodone doses in twenty-four hours, with the total reviewed with her each morning as agreed. She says she understands that needing it now is not the same as addiction. Slept six hours uninterrupted. Discharge criterion of 90 degrees not yet reached.

items.stem: For each outcome, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: She will attend both scheduled therapy sessions daily
rows.rationale: Four completed sessions. The behavior the whole plan was built to produce is now happening.

rows.text: She will use the prescribed analgesia when she needs it
rows.rationale: Four doses against one, taken as part of a plan she agreed to. The behavior changed because the fear was addressed.

rows.text: She will state the difference between needing a drug now and being addicted to it
rows.rationale: She said it herself, unprompted. That is the second related factor resolved.

rows.text: She will achieve 70 degrees of flexion by the end of day 3
rows.rationale: 62 of 70 by day 4. Real progress against a target that was missed, which calls for revising the target rather than abandoning the plan.

rows.text: She will report pain of 4 of 10 or less at rest
rows.rationale: 3 of 10 at rest, down from 8. The intervention that mattered most has worked.

rows.text: She will reach 90 degrees of flexion before discharge
rows.rationale: The discharge criterion, and she is 28 degrees short of it. Nothing about the progress so far changes the fact that she is not ready to go.

items.takeaway: A partially met outcome means the plan is working and the timeframe was wrong. Revise the target. A not met outcome on a discharge criterion means she is not going home.
items.strategy: Most rows improved, so the pull is to mark everything met. Hold each one against the number that was written in the outcome.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find the one short of target

elimination.verdict: Four met, one partially met, one not met.

chart.text:
Room 1: 72-year-old, second day after bowel resection. Reports pain 7 of 10. Scheduled analgesia and a dressing change due.
Room 2: 58-year-old, twenty minutes into the second unit of packed red cells. Reports feeling warm and itchy.
Room 3: 45-year-old admitted at 0300 with cellulitis of the lower leg. Intravenous antibiotic due at 0800. Not yet assessed this shift.
Room 4: 81-year-old for discharge at 1000. Her daughter is at the desk asking for the teaching to be done now.
Room 5: 34-year-old with a tracheostomy placed four days ago. Oxygen saturation 95 percent. Asking to be suctioned.
One licensed practical nurse covering medications for ten patients on the unit. One assistive personnel assigned to these five patients. The charge nurse is in a meeting until 0730.

items.stem: Which items from the handoff require the nurse's own assessment before anything else is arranged? Select all that apply.

options.text: The scheduled dressing change on an uncomplicated wound on the second postoperative day
options.rationale: Routine care on a wound nobody has flagged. It is work to be done, not a finding to be evaluated.

options.text: The patient twenty minutes into a transfusion who feels warm and itchy
options.rationale: Blood is still running into him and those are the first two symptoms of a reaction. Nothing on the list can deteriorate faster.

options.text: The daughter's request at the desk to move the discharge teaching to earlier in the morning
options.rationale: A scheduling matter. It needs an answer and a time, and it does not need an assessment.

options.text: The patient admitted at 0300 who has not been assessed this shift
options.rationale: Four hours into an admission with no assessment on record. He is an unknown, and an antibiotic is due at 0800 on a patient nobody has laid eyes on.

options.text: The patient with a tracheostomy asking to be suctioned
options.rationale: A patient asking for suction is reporting that he cannot clear his own airway. Why he needs it is an assessment, and the trachea was opened four days ago.

options.text: Pain of 7 of 10 on the second day after a bowel resection
options.rationale: Pain at that level the day after bowel surgery is either undertreated pain or the first report of a complication, and you cannot tell which from the handoff.

items.takeaway: An assessment is owed wherever the handoff gives you a symptom rather than a task. Symptoms belong to the nurse; tasks can be arranged.
items.strategy: Sort each line into finding and chore. Two of the six are chores, and everything else is somebody telling you something is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: The transfusion, the airway, the unassessed admission, and the pain.

items.stem: For each task, indicate who may carry it out.

rows.text: Evaluating whether the analgesia relieved the pain
rows.rationale: Evaluation is a step of the nursing process. Someone else can ask the number; deciding what it means about the plan cannot be handed over.

rows.text: Stopping the transfusion and assessing the patient who feels warm and itchy
rows.rationale: An unstable patient and a judgment about whether this is a reaction. Both sit with the registered nurse.

rows.text: Reinforcing discharge teaching the registered nurse has already given
rows.rationale: Teaching itself is not delegable, and reinforcing a plan already taught is within the practical nurse's scope.

rows.text: Measuring and recording intake and output on all five patients
rows.rationale: Collecting the data is delegable. Interpreting what a negative balance means is not.

rows.text: Performing the scheduled dressing change on an uncomplicated wound
rows.rationale: Within scope on a wound already assessed and documented as uncomplicated.

rows.text: Suctioning an established tracheostomy on a stable patient
rows.rationale: A sterile procedure within the practical nurse's scope in most states, on a patient whose airway is not in question.

rows.text: The first assessment of the patient admitted at 0300
rows.rationale: An initial assessment cannot be assigned or delegated. The registered nurse owns assessment, and everything built on it depends on who did it.

rows.text: Helping the discharge patient dress and gathering her belongings
rows.rationale: A standard task with a predictable outcome on a stable patient, which is what makes it delegable.

items.takeaway: Assessment, evaluation, teaching and any unstable patient stay with the registered nurse. Everything else is sorted by the task, the person's scope, and whether the patient is stable.
items.strategy: Two rows look like the same task split in half: taking the pain score and evaluating the analgesia. Collecting data is delegable and judging it is not.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Pull out the nursing process steps

steps.detail: Sterile and clinical to the practical nurse.

elimination.verdict: Three to the registered nurse, three to the practical nurse, two to the assistive personnel.

items.stem: Which patient does the nurse go to first?

options.text: Room 5, because the airway comes before everything else
options.rationale: The strongest distractor, because the framework is correct and does not apply. His saturation is 95 percent, his trachea has been open four days, and he is asking rather than struggling. An airway at risk outranks everything; an airway that needs clearing does not outrank a reaction in progress.

options.text: Room 3, because he is unassessed and an antibiotic is due
options.rationale: An unknown patient is a risk and the antibiotic has an hour on it. Unknown is not the same as deteriorating.

options.text: Room 2, because warmth and itching twenty minutes into a transfusion may be a reaction and the blood is still running
options.rationale: This is the only patient receiving something that can be stopped, and the longer it runs the larger the dose of whatever is causing it. Actual and deteriorating beats unknown and beats scheduled.

options.text: Room 1, because pain of 7 of 10 is unrelieved and pain is what the patient says it is
options.rationale: It is real and it needs addressing within the hour. It is not what will harm him in the next five minutes.

items.takeaway: Ongoing harm that you can stop outranks an unknown, and both outrank anything scheduled. The ABCs decide between two unstable patients, not between an unstable one and a stable one with an airway complaint.
items.strategy: Both of the leading options cite a sound rule. Ask which patient is getting worse while you are with the other.

strategies: Ask what is actively causing harm
elimination.verdict: Room 2.

items.stem: Which actions are appropriate in the first fifteen minutes of the shift? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel for a full set of vital signs while the nurse stays in the room
options.rationale: Taking vital signs is delegable and having them taken now is faster than doing it herself. She stays, because the assessment and the decisions are hers.

options.text: Send the assistive personnel to suction the tracheostomy while the nurse deals with the transfusion
options.rationale: Outside her scope, and on an airway four days old. Right task to nobody, wrong person.

options.text: Chart the transfusion reaction in the record before going in to assess the patient
options.rationale: Documenting a reaction nobody has assessed records a conclusion rather than a finding.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing
options.rationale: Stopping ends the exposure. New tubing matters because the old set still holds blood, and saline keeps the access she will need.

options.text: Tell the daughter the teaching will happen and give her a specific time
options.rationale: Thirty seconds that buys an hour. An answer with a time in it stops the interruptions and keeps a 1000 discharge on track.

options.text: Ask the licensed practical nurse to give the 0800 antibiotic before anyone has assessed that patient at all
options.rationale: A dose given on a patient with no assessment on record leaves nobody who can say what he looked like beforehand. Assess, then give.

options.text: Assign the dressing change to the licensed practical nurse
options.rationale: Within scope on an uncomplicated wound, and it moves a task off a list that is about to get longer.

items.takeaway: Delegating well in a bad first hour means two things at once: moving every task that can move, and staying where your own judgment is required.
items.strategy: Three distractors are reasonable actions in the wrong order or to the wrong person. Check the five rights against each one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vital signs, dressing, a time for the daughter.

elimination.verdict: Stop and flush, delegate the vital signs, give the daughter a time, assign the dressing.

items.stem: Place the nurse's actions for the transfusion patient in the order she carries them out.

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank
options.rationale: Fourth. Both need to know, the provider to treat and the blood bank because a second patient may be receiving from the same donation.

options.text: Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing
options.rationale: Second. The access has to stay, and the old set is full of the blood you just stopped.

options.text: Assess the patient and obtain vital signs
options.rationale: Third. Now that nothing more is going in, find out what you are dealing with and how far it has gone.

options.text: Return the remaining blood and the tubing to the blood bank with the required specimens and paperwork
options.rationale: Last. The unit and the set are the evidence, and the investigation cannot proceed without them.

options.text: Stop the transfusion
options.rationale: First, and before anything else. Every second it runs is more of whatever is causing this.

items.takeaway: Stop, keep the line with new tubing, assess, notify the provider and the blood bank, return the unit and tubing. Stopping is first and assessment comes after it.
items.strategy: The step most students move too early is the assessment. You do not assess while the thing causing it is still infusing.

strategies: Ask what stops the harm
elimination.verdict: Stop, flush, assess, notify, return.

chartUpdate.text: Transfusion stopped at 0712, line flushed with saline through new tubing. Temperature 37.4 C, from 36.9 C before the unit. Itching reduced after a prescribed antihistamine. No dyspnea, no flank pain, urine clear. Provider and blood bank notified at 0720. Unit and tubing returned at 0735. Room 3 assessed at 0738, antibiotic given at 0752. Room 1 analgesia given at 0742, pain now 3 of 10. Room 5 suctioned by the nurse at 0746, thick secretions cleared, saturation 97 percent. Room 4 teaching started at 0755. Intake and output recorded by the assistive personnel.

items.stem: For each outcome at 0800, indicate how the nurse evaluates it.

rows.text: Pain 3 of 10 after analgesia
rows.rationale: A measured reduction after a specific intervention, which is what evaluation is for.

rows.text: Temperature risen from 36.9 to 37.4 C since the unit was stopped
rows.rationale: A rise of 0.5 C in a patient who has just had a transfusion stopped is the febrile reaction continuing to declare itself. It needs reporting rather than watching.

rows.text: Urine clear with no flank pain and no dyspnea
rows.rationale: These are the findings that would point to a hemolytic reaction, and their absence is a meaningful negative.

rows.text: Itching reduced after the antihistamine
rows.rationale: The symptom that prompted stopping the unit has responded to treatment.

rows.text: Room 3 unassessed until 0738, thirty-eight minutes into the shift
rows.rationale: The outcome arrived, late. A patient nobody had assessed in five hours should not have waited behind four other things, and the next shift's plan has to account for how that happened.

rows.text: The tracheostomy suctioned by the nurse rather than delegated
rows.rationale: She kept a judgment call about an airway. Thick secretions and a saturation that rose afterward confirm it needed her.

items.takeaway: Evaluating a shift means asking about timing as well as outcome. A result that arrived forty minutes late is not the same as a result that arrived.
items.strategy: The temperature rise is easy to read as recovery because the itching improved. Read each finding against what it is specifically telling you.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four met, two needing further action.

chart.text: 74-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer, admitted with a bowel obstruction. Oncology has offered a palliative surgical procedure with a stated 30 percent risk of serious complication. He has declined it and asked for comfort measures. Oriented, answers questions in full sentences, and can state the procedure, the alternatives and what declining it means for him. His daughter holds a durable power of attorney for health care.

Patient states he has thought about it for two days and does not want the operation. Says he wants to be at home with his dog and is not frightened. Daughter at the bedside states he is not thinking clearly, that she has power of attorney and is authorizing the surgery. Surgeon has written a note stating the daughter has consented and the case is booked for tomorrow. Patient asked the nurse whether he can still say no. A night entry from two days ago reads: patient refused medication, uncooperative with staff.
Durable power of attorney for health care naming the daughter, signed three years ago. No living will. No physician order for life-sustaining treatment. No capacity evaluation on record.

items.nursesNote: 1400: Patient states he has thought about it for two days and does not want the operation. Says he wants to be at home with his dog and is not frightened. Daughter at the bedside states he is not thinking clearly, that she has power of attorney and is authorizing the surgery. Surgeon has written a note stating the daughter has consented and the case is booked for tomorrow. Patient asked the nurse whether he can still say no. A night entry from two days ago reads: patient refused medication, uncooperative with staff.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that raise a legal or ethical concern.

segments.text: Patient asked the nurse whether he can still say no
segments.rationale: He does not know he holds the decision. A patient who has to ask whether his refusal counts is not being treated as the decision maker.

segments.text: patient refused medication, uncooperative with staff
segments.rationale: A judgment charted as a finding. Uncooperative is an opinion about a person, and this is the entry that will be produced as evidence he was not thinking clearly.

segments.text: he has thought about it for two days and does not want the operation
segments.rationale: This is the finding that resolves the case rather than complicating it. A considered, consistent refusal by a patient with capacity is a decision, not a problem.

segments.text: Surgeon has written a note stating the daughter has consented and the case is booked for tomorrow
segments.rationale: Consent has been taken from the wrong person, and a procedure is now scheduled against the stated refusal of a man who can decide for himself.

segments.text: wants to be at home with his dog and is not frightened
segments.rationale: His reasons are his own and do not have to meet anyone's standard. Reasoning the team finds unusual is not evidence of lost capacity.

segments.text: Daughter at the bedside states he is not thinking clearly, that she has power of attorney and is authorizing the surgery
segments.rationale: A power of attorney for health care takes effect only when the patient loses capacity. He has it, so her authority has not begun and she cannot overrule him.

segments.text: does not want the operation
segments.rationale: The decision itself. A refusal the team disagrees with is still a refusal.

items.takeaway: A durable power of attorney is dormant while the patient has capacity. Disagreeing with a decision is not evidence of losing the ability to make it.
items.strategy: Three segments describe the patient's own reasoning. The pull is to treat an unusual reason as a warning sign, and a reason does not have to be one you would give.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.detail: His reasons are his to hold.

elimination.verdict: The daughter's claim, the consent, his question, and the night entry.

items.stem: For each statement, indicate the ethical principle most at stake.

rows.text: The nurse told him she would make sure his wishes were heard by the team
rows.rationale: Keeping a promise made to a patient. Fidelity is what makes advocacy more than a sentiment.

rows.text: Operating on a man who has refused, with the risks that carries
rows.rationale: Harm inflicted without consent. The risk was acceptable to nobody who had the right to accept it.

rows.text: A man who can state the procedure, the alternatives and the consequences has refused it
rows.rationale: Self-determination by a person who understands what he is deciding. This is the principle in its plainest form.

rows.text: Taking consent from the daughter while the patient is able to decide
rows.rationale: His decision was bypassed, which is the violation of self-determination rather than a disagreement about his good.

rows.text: Offering pain and symptom control that fits the comfort-focused path he chose
rows.rationale: Doing good within the goals he set. Beneficence is defined by his goals, not by the team's.

rows.text: Continuing to support him after the team has been told the operation is cancelled
rows.rationale: Staying with a patient whose decision has made things awkward is what the commitment means.

rows.text: The surgeon believes the operation would relieve the obstruction and extend his life
rows.rationale: Acting for the patient's good. It is a real principle and it does not outrank a competent refusal.

rows.text: The procedure carries a 30 percent risk of serious complication in a frail patient
rows.rationale: The duty to avoid harm, and the number makes the risk of harm concrete rather than theoretical.

items.takeaway: Beneficence and autonomy collide here, and autonomy wins when the patient has capacity. Beneficence is measured against the patient's goals rather than the team's.
items.strategy: The last row looks like autonomy because it follows his wishes. Ask what the action itself is: doing good within his goals is still beneficence.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Two autonomy, two beneficence, two nonmaleficence, two fidelity.

items.stem: Which best describes the central problem?

options.text: The patient's capacity has not been formally evaluated and should be
options.rationale: The most tempting wrong answer, because a documented evaluation would help. Capacity is presumed and he is demonstrating it in front of her, so ordering an evaluation because the family dislikes the decision treats disagreement as evidence.

options.text: The family and the team disagree about what is in the patient's best interest
options.rationale: True and beside the point. Best interest is the standard used when a patient cannot decide. He can, so his wishes are the standard.

options.text: Consent was obtained without a proper discussion of risks and alternatives
options.rationale: The discussion did happen. The problem is who it ended with, not whether it took place.

options.text: A competent patient's refusal is being overridden by a surrogate whose authority has not begun
options.rationale: It states the fact that decides everything: he has capacity, so the power of attorney is not yet in effect and no one else may consent for him.

options.text: The nurse is experiencing moral distress about the booked operation
options.rationale: She may well be, and that is her response to the problem rather than the problem. Naming it this way centers the nurse.

items.takeaway: Capacity is presumed until shown otherwise, and a surrogate's authority starts only when it is lost. An unpopular decision is not a trigger for a capacity evaluation.
items.strategy: Two options sound procedurally careful. Ask whether each one accepts or quietly questions that he can decide.

strategies: Ask who the standard belongs to

steps.detail: Wrong standard for a capable patient.

elimination.verdict: A surrogate acting before her authority exists.

items.stem: Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient plainly that his refusal stands while he is able to decide, and that nothing will be done without his agreement
options.rationale: He asked the question. Answering it truthfully is both the honest reply and the thing that restores his standing in his own care.

options.text: Say nothing to the patient about the booking so that he is not distressed before the team has had a chance to resolve it
options.rationale: Protecting him from information about his own body is the same error the surgeon made, carried out more gently.

options.text: Escalate through the chain of command and request an ethics consultation if the booking is not withdrawn
options.rationale: A single conversation may not resolve it. Escalation and the ethics committee exist for a conflict that persists.

options.text: Witness the daughter's signature on the consent form so the case is not delayed further
options.rationale: Witnessing a signature from someone with no authority, on a procedure the patient has refused, puts the nurse's own license into the case.

options.text: Notify the surgeon that the patient has capacity and has refused, and that the booking cannot stand on the daughter's consent
options.rationale: The person who wrote the note has to hear it, and this has to happen before tomorrow rather than through the chart.

options.text: Sit with the daughter away from the bedside and find out what she is frightened of
options.rationale: She is losing her father and reaching for the one document she has. Her fear is treatable, and this is often what resolves the conflict.

options.text: Remove the night entry describing him as uncooperative, since it is inaccurate
options.rationale: A record is never deleted. An error is corrected by a dated, signed late entry that leaves the original readable.

items.takeaway: Tell the patient the truth, take it to the person who wrote the order, escalate if it stands, and deal with the family's fear. Never alter a record and never witness a consent you know is invalid.
items.strategy: Two distractors are kind: protecting him from distress and tidying an unfair entry. Both would be the nurse making a decision that is not hers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Answer him, tell the surgeon, escalate, and sit with the daughter.

chartUpdate.text: Preoperative checklist arrives on the unit from the surgical booking office. It asks the nurse to confirm the consent and to begin preoperative preparation this evening. The surgeon has not responded to the page. The patient is asleep. The daughter asks the nurse to start the preparation so there is no delay in the morning.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Wake the patient and ask him to confirm his refusal in front of his daughter
options.rationale: He has already stated it clearly and twice. Making him defend it to his daughter at the bedside is pressure dressed as verification.

options.text: Hold the preparation and leave a detailed note asking the morning shift to resolve it with the surgeon
options.rationale: The right first half and the wrong second half. Handing an unresolved invalid consent to a shift that arrives as the list starts leaves nobody time to stop it.

options.text: Withhold the preparation, document the refusal and the invalid consent, and escalate to the supervisor now
options.rationale: Nothing proceeds on an invalid consent. Escalating this evening is the only version that reaches someone before a morning list begins.

options.text: Begin the preparation, since it is noninvasive and can be stopped if the booking is cancelled
options.rationale: Preparation carried out on a refused procedure treats the surgery as going ahead, and by morning the momentum is a fact everyone works around.

items.takeaway: An invalid consent stops the process. Document, refuse to proceed, and escalate while there is still time for escalation to work.
items.strategy: Two options correctly hold the preparation. The difference is whether anyone with authority hears about it tonight.

strategies: Ask what happens by morning
elimination.verdict: Hold, document, escalate now.

chartUpdate.text: Entries made in the record over the past twenty-four hours are listed below for review.

items.stem: For each entry made in the record, indicate whether it would stand up to review.

rows.text: Late entry for 0200 two days ago: patient declined the 0200 dose of ondansetron, stating he felt no nausea. Entered 1900 on the following day, M. Olsen RN
rows.rationale: A late entry is correct practice when it is labeled as one, dated, timed, signed, and gives the actual finding rather than erasing the earlier one.

rows.text: 1715 Daughter states she holds power of attorney and asks that preparation begin tonight. Explained that it takes effect if the patient loses capacity. She declined an ethics consultation at this time
rows.rationale: Her request, the explanation given, and her response, all in neutral language. It documents the conversation without grading her.

rows.text: 1630 Patient states he does not want the operation. Able to state the procedure, the alternative and the outcome of declining. Surgeon paged at 1605 and 1620, no response. Supervisor notified 1635. Preoperative preparation not started. M. Olsen RN
rows.rationale: Times, the patient's own words, what was attempted, who was told, and what was not done. Anyone reading this in two years can reconstruct the evening.

rows.text: Previous entry amended by drawing a box around uncooperative with staff and writing see corrected note
rows.rationale: Obscuring the original text is the problem. An error is corrected with a single line, the word error, your initials and the date, leaving the original readable.

rows.text: 1700 Daughter being difficult and demanding about the surgery, refuses to listen to reason
rows.rationale: Two judgments and a characterization. Record what she said and what she asked for, not your view of her.

rows.text: 1830 Occurrence report filed regarding the consent, see report for details
rows.rationale: An occurrence report is never referenced in the medical record. Naming it drags an internal quality document into anything that follows.

items.takeaway: Defensible charting is factual, timed, signed, and free of judgment about people. Never reference an occurrence report and never obscure what was written before.
items.strategy: Both of the correction rows look like someone being honest. One follows the method and one hides the original.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Three defensible, three not.

case-study.title: The pill with the picture on it

chart.text: 61-year-old woman admitted with a deep vein thrombosis, discharging today on warfarin. Her first language is Haitian Creole and she speaks some English. Left school at eleven. Lives with her son, who works days and will collect her. She is right-handed, wears reading glasses she did not bring, and has mild hearing loss in the left ear.

Teaching begun. Patient nods throughout and says yes to each question. When handed the medication leaflet she holds it, turns it over and sets it down, saying she will read it at home. Asked how she will take the tablet, she says the one with the picture on it. Her son has telephoned twice to ask what time the teaching is, saying he wants to be there. Patient says she has been taking her blood pressure tablet in the morning for years and never misses it. Asked whether she has questions, she says no.

Warfarin 5 mg daily, dose to be adjusted by the anticoagulation clinic. Blood test in four days. Avoid large changes in intake of green leafy vegetables. Report unusual bruising, blood in the urine or stool, or a fall.

items.nursesNote: 1000: Teaching begun. Patient nods throughout and says yes to each question. When handed the medication leaflet she holds it, turns it over and sets it down, saying she will read it at home. Asked how she will take the tablet, she says the one with the picture on it. Her son has telephoned twice to ask what time the teaching is, saying he wants to be there. Patient says she has been taking her blood pressure tablet in the morning for years and never misses it. Asked whether she has questions, she says no.
items.stem: Highlight the cues that suggest limited health literacy.

segments.text: she has been taking her blood pressure tablet in the morning for years and never misses it
segments.rationale: Evidence of what she can do. A long record of taking a daily tablet says the routine is not the barrier.

segments.text: nods throughout and says yes to each question
segments.rationale: Agreeing with everything is the most common way an adult covers not following. Yes costs nothing and ends the questioning.

segments.text: Her son has telephoned twice to ask what time the teaching is, saying he wants to be there
segments.rationale: This is a resource rather than a deficit, and it is the strongest thing in the note. He should be at the session.

segments.text: Asked whether she has questions, she says no
segments.rationale: No questions from a woman starting a drug that needs blood tests and dietary care. Not knowing enough to have a question is itself the finding.

segments.text: she says the one with the picture on it
segments.rationale: She identifies medication by appearance rather than by name or purpose. Workable until the pharmacy changes supplier and the tablet looks different.

segments.text: she holds it, turns it over and sets it down, saying she will read it at home
segments.rationale: Handling written material without reading it, and postponing. This is close to a classic sign and it is almost never volunteered.

items.takeaway: Low health literacy shows up as agreeing with everything, postponing written material, naming drugs by appearance, and having no questions. People conceal it, so you look for it rather than ask.
items.strategy: Two segments describe things going well. The pull is to read every detail as a problem once you suspect one.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.action: Find how she identifies the drug

elimination.verdict: The nodding, the leaflet, the picture, and no questions.

items.stem: For each thing the nurse says, indicate its effect on the exchange.

rows.text: I want to make sure I explained the food part clearly. Can you tell me what you heard?
rows.rationale: The burden sits on the explaining. That framing is what makes it safe to say she did not follow it.

rows.text: Tell me how you will take this when you get home tomorrow morning
rows.rationale: Open, specific to a moment she can picture, and it produces a description rather than a yes.

rows.text: Why didn't you bring your reading glasses in with you?
rows.rationale: A why question about something she cannot now change. It asks her to account for herself at the start of a teaching session.

rows.text: You understand all of this, don't you?
rows.rationale: A leading question with the answer inside it. It asks her to agree, and she will.

rows.text: Let's do this part again together, and this time you hold the chart
rows.rationale: Repetition offered without blame and with her hands on the material. It changes who is doing the work.

rows.text: The anticoagulation clinic will go over the international normalized ratio with you
rows.rationale: It hands the hardest part to someone else and uses a term she has not been given. Both move the conversation away from her.

rows.text: Most people find this straightforward once they get going
rows.rationale: Reassurance that tells her everyone else manages. It makes admitting confusion a confession of being slower than most.

rows.text: What worries you most about starting this tablet?
rows.rationale: Open, and it invites the concern she has not raised. It assumes a worry exists rather than asking whether one does.

items.takeaway: What blocks an exchange is usually kind: reassurance, deferral, and questions that carry their own answer. Open questions tied to a specific moment are what produce information.
items.strategy: Two blocking rows sound supportive. Ask what each one makes it harder for her to say.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find the deferral and the jargon

elimination.verdict: Four therapeutic, four blocking.

items.stem: Which barrier does the nurse address first?

options.text: Teaching is being given in her second language with no interpreter present
options.rationale: Every other cue sits downstream of this one. She has been nodding through a conversation in a language she half holds, and nothing taught this morning can be relied on until it is repeated through an interpreter.

options.text: Her son's absence, since he is the one who will supervise the medication at home
options.rationale: He should be there and she is the one taking the tablet. Teaching the son instead of her makes her a bystander in her own treatment.

options.text: The absence of her reading glasses, which would explain her setting the leaflet down
options.rationale: A plausible single explanation and it does not survive the rest of the note. Glasses would not produce the nodding, the picture, or the absence of questions.

options.text: The hearing loss in her left ear, which may be why she is agreeing without following
options.rationale: Worth managing by sitting on her right and facing her, and it is mild and one-sided. It does not account for the leaflet or the picture.

items.takeaway: When several barriers are present, treat the one the others depend on. Teaching in a second language without an interpreter makes every check you run unreliable.
items.strategy: Three options explain part of the note. Ask which one explains all of it.

strategies: Find the barrier the others sit underneath
elimination.verdict: The language barrier.

items.stem: Which strategies does the nurse build into the teaching session? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give her written material at about a sixth-grade level with pictures, in her own language
options.rationale: Material she can use after the session, pitched where she can read it, and the pictures carry the actions if the words do not.

options.text: Ask her to sign that she received the teaching so the discharge is not delayed
options.rationale: It documents the delivery of teaching and evidences no learning at all, which is exactly the error already in this chart.

options.text: Limit the session to three things she must do and leave the rest to the clinic
options.rationale: Three is roughly what anyone retains in one sitting. Choosing which three is the nursing judgment.

options.text: Use her son to interpret, since he speaks both languages and knows her
options.rationale: A family member is not a qualified interpreter. He will summarize, soften and omit, most of all around anything he finds worrying.

options.text: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter and schedule the session when her son can be present
options.rationale: It removes the barrier underneath everything else, and the person who will be with her at home hears the same thing she does.

options.text: Show the actual tablet and have her demonstrate putting a dose into her own pill organizer
options.rationale: It moves the learning out of words and gives her something to do with her hands, which is also the check on whether she can do it.

options.text: Speak more loudly and more slowly throughout, since she has hearing loss
options.rationale: Volume does not make a second language easier, and raising the voice often raises the pitch into the range she has lost.

items.takeaway: Interpreter, three things, demonstration, and written material she can read. The family member and the signature are the two shortcuts that look like solutions.
items.strategy: Two distractors would speed the discharge up. Ask which actions would still be working for her on the fourth day at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Interpreter with the son present, three priorities, demonstration, readable material.

chartUpdate.text: Session held with an interpreter and her son present. Three priorities covered: one tablet daily at the same time, the blood test in four days, and what to report. Asked to explain the food advice in her own words, she says: I must not eat the green vegetables any more.

items.stem: What does the nurse do?

options.text: Ask her son to go over the dietary part with her again at home
options.rationale: It passes an uncorrected error to someone who heard the same session, and it closes the loop on paper rather than in fact.

options.text: Note the misunderstanding in the record and ask the clinic to address it in four days
options.rationale: She eats four days of meals before then. The correction costs two minutes now and the interpreter is in the room.

options.text: Correct the misunderstanding, reteach the point about keeping intake steady rather than stopping, and check that part again
options.rationale: Teach-back found a specific wrong belief, which is the method working. The loop is not finished until she can state the corrected version herself.

options.text: Confirm that she has the main point and move on, since avoiding them is the safer error
options.rationale: It is not safer. Cutting the vegetables out entirely swings her level the other way, and she loses food she has eaten all her life for no reason.

items.takeaway: Teach-back that uncovers a wrong belief has succeeded. The step people drop is reteaching and checking that part a second time.
items.strategy: Three options accept the error and manage around it. The method has one more step in it.

strategies: Ask whether the loop closed
elimination.verdict: Correct it and check again.

chartUpdate.text: Second check with the interpreter present. She states she will take one tablet every morning with her blood pressure tablet. She states she will keep eating her usual amount of greens and not change it suddenly. She locates the blood test date on a card and reads the date aloud. Shown three scenarios, she identifies blood in the urine and a fall as reasons to call, and says a bruise on her arm is nothing to worry about. Her son states he will drive her to the blood test. Asked what the tablet is for, she says to make the blood not stick.

items.stem: For each learning outcome, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: She can state when and how she takes the dose
rows.rationale: She tied it to a tablet she has taken reliably for years, which is a stronger plan than any reminder the nurse could have designed.

rows.text: She knows when the blood test is and how she will get there
rows.rationale: She found the date, read it, and her son named the transport. The plan exists outside the chart.

rows.text: She can recognize what to report
rows.rationale: She has two of three and dismissed the bruising, which is the earliest and most common sign of over-anticoagulation. A partial list is a gap in the one thing that keeps her safe between tests.

rows.text: She understands the purpose of the medication
rows.rationale: To make the blood not stick is the mechanism in her own words. Her phrasing is not the test; whether she has the idea is.

rows.text: She can read and use the written material unaided
rows.rationale: Nothing has tested this. She read a date from a card with the interpreter present, and that is not the same as working through the leaflet at home.

rows.text: She understands the dietary advice
rows.rationale: Steady intake rather than avoidance, stated in her own words after the correction. This is the reteaching having worked.

items.takeaway: Evaluate what she showed you, not what she was told. Two of three warning signs is a gap, and an outcome nobody tested is not met.
items.strategy: Her phrasing of the purpose is plain and correct, and her list of warning signs is fluent and incomplete. Judge the content, not the fluency.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Four demonstrated, two not.

chart.text: Patient is 27, admitted eight days ago after a collision in which the front seat passenger, a close friend, died at the scene. He has a fractured femur, repaired, and surface injuries. He was not at fault. No psychiatric history. Works as a joiner, lives alone, has a large circle of friends.

Reports he has not slept more than two hours at a time since admission and that the moment before the impact replays when he closes his eyes. Startles when the door closes. Declines to look at his phone, which has been face down on the locker for three days, saying he knows what the messages will say. Asked how he is, says he is fine and that he was lucky. Became tearful yesterday when physical therapy mentioned driving. Has eaten most meals. Asked the night nurse whether it would have been better if it had been him. Family visiting daily. Has requested extra analgesia four times in two days, each time with a pain score of 4 of 10.
Temperature 36.8 C. Heart rate 96. Blood pressure 128/76. Respirations 18. Oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air.

items.nursesNote: 0900: Reports he has not slept more than two hours at a time since admission and that the moment before the impact replays when he closes his eyes. Startles when the door closes. Declines to look at his phone, which has been face down on the locker for three days, saying he knows what the messages will say. Asked how he is, says he is fine and that he was lucky. Became tearful yesterday when physical therapy mentioned driving. Has eaten most meals. Asked the night nurse whether it would have been better if it had been him. Family visiting daily. Has requested extra analgesia four times in two days, each time with a pain score of 4 of 10.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that need the nurse to act rather than observe.

segments.text: Has eaten most meals
segments.rationale: A finding in his favor, and one of the few things going well.

segments.text: says he is fine and that he was lucky
segments.rationale: Said by a man sleeping two hours a night, eight days after his friend died beside him. It is the sentence that closes every conversation and it needs opening.

segments.text: Became tearful yesterday when physical therapy mentioned driving
segments.rationale: A proportionate reaction to a specific reminder. Tears at the mention of the thing that killed his friend are not a symptom.

segments.text: he has not slept more than two hours at a time since admission
segments.rationale: Eight nights. Sleep this broken for this long makes everything else worse and is itself treatable.

segments.text: Asked the night nurse whether it would have been better if it had been him
segments.rationale: This has to be followed up today, directly and without alarm. Survivor guilt phrased this way is a question about his own life and it is not answered by moving on from it.

segments.text: Declines to look at his phone, which has been face down on the locker for three days
segments.rationale: Cutting himself off from the people who would be supporting him. Avoidance that removes support is the kind that needs an intervention.

segments.text: Startles when the door closes
segments.rationale: An expected response at eight days. Worth noting and monitoring rather than intervening on.

segments.text: Has requested extra analgesia four times in two days, each time with a pain score of 4 of 10
segments.rationale: The number and the request do not match. Something other than the femur is being treated, and nobody has asked him what.

items.takeaway: At eight days, startle and tears are the expected response. What needs acting on is the question about his own life, the sleep, the withdrawal from support, and the analgesia that does not match the score.
items.strategy: The distractors are the findings that look most like trauma. Expected does not mean unimportant, and the question is which ones need an action today.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: His question, the sleep, the phone, the analgesia, and being fine.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate how the nurse classifies it at eight days.

rows.text: Keeping the phone face down for three days
rows.rationale: Avoidance that cuts off the support most likely to help him. Short-term relief at a long-term cost is what makes a strategy maladaptive.

rows.text: Answering every question with being fine and lucky
rows.rationale: Minimizing keeps him from having to feel it and keeps everyone else from helping. It is effective in the room and expensive afterward.

rows.text: Two hours of sleep at a time for eight nights
rows.rationale: Long enough to worsen mood, pain and recovery. It is treatable and it has gone unaddressed for over a week.

rows.text: Requesting analgesia at a pain score of 4 of 10, four times in two days
rows.rationale: A mismatch between the request and the report. He may be treating distress with the only thing he is offered, and that is a pattern to interrupt early.

rows.text: Asking whether it would have been better if it had been him
rows.rationale: Survivor guilt that has reached the question of whether his own life should have been the one lost. It is asked about directly, today.

rows.text: Intrusive replay of the moment before the impact
rows.rationale: Intrusive memory in the first weeks is close to universal. It becomes a disorder when it persists and disables, which cannot be judged at eight days.

rows.text: Tearfulness when driving is mentioned
rows.rationale: A proportionate reaction to a cue. It shows the feeling is reachable, which is a good sign rather than a bad one.

rows.text: Startling at a door closing
rows.rationale: Heightened arousal after a sudden violent event. Expected, and it settles for most people.

items.takeaway: Expected, maladaptive and urgent are three different judgments. Intrusion and arousal are expected early. Avoidance and minimizing are strategies. A question about his own life is urgent.
items.strategy: Several findings look alarming and are expected at this point. Ask of each one whether time will settle it, whether it costs him something, or whether it cannot wait.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find the symptoms of the event

elimination.verdict: Three expected, two maladaptive, three needing evaluation.

items.stem: What does the nurse address first?

options.text: What he meant by asking whether it would have been better if it had been him
options.rationale: He has raised the question of his own life, to a nurse, at night. It is asked about directly and today, and everything else in the plan waits on the answer.

options.text: The analgesia requests, since he may be treating distress with medication
options.rationale: A perceptive observation, and it is a pattern to interrupt over days rather than the first thing said to him this morning.

options.text: The sleep, since eight nights of broken sleep is worsening everything else
options.rationale: A real priority and the one most likely to improve the rest of the picture. It does not come before finding out what he meant last night.

options.text: The avoidance of his phone, since isolation from support will slow his recovery
options.rationale: Important, and something he will be more able to do once the heavier thing has been said out loud.

items.takeaway: When a patient raises a question about his own life, that is the conversation. Ask about it plainly, and do not treat the fact that it was said quietly as a reason to let it pass.
items.strategy: All four findings need addressing. Ask which one, if left until tomorrow, you would regret.

strategies: Ask what cannot wait

steps.action: Read what he asked the night nurse

elimination.verdict: Ask him what he meant.

items.stem: Which actions belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep his analgesia strictly to schedule and decline the extra requests until he discusses his feelings
options.rationale: It makes pain relief conditional on emotional disclosure. The mismatch is assessed, not used as leverage.

options.text: Address the sleep, including the environment, the timing of analgesia and what wakes him
options.rationale: Eight nights at two hours is treatable and it is making his mood, his pain and his thinking worse.

options.text: Explore with him what makes looking at the phone hard, and what a first small step might be
options.rationale: It works with the avoidance rather than against it, and it leads toward the support he has cut himself off from.

options.text: Arrange assessment by the team who can evaluate his risk and his mood properly
options.rationale: The nurse opens it and does not carry it alone. A referral made today is part of the response rather than a way of passing it on.

options.text: Tell him his friend's death was not his fault and that he should not feel guilty
options.rationale: True and it closes the subject. Guilt is not reasoned away, and being told not to feel it teaches him not to mention it.

options.text: Press him to describe the collision in detail now, while the memory is clear
options.rationale: Pushing a detailed account in the early weeks does not help and can make the outcome worse. He talks about it when he chooses to.

options.text: Sit down and ask him directly what he meant, without softening the question
options.rationale: Asking plainly is what gives him permission to answer. Nothing about the question makes the thought more likely; it makes it sayable.

items.takeaway: Ask plainly, refer, treat the sleep, and work with the avoidance a step at a time. Do not reason away guilt, force a retelling, or trade analgesia for disclosure.
items.strategy: Two distractors are well-meant interventions that evidence says do harm. The third makes care conditional, which is never right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Ask, refer, treat the sleep, work on the phone.

chartUpdate.text: Asked directly what he meant. He says he does not want to die and cannot see why he is here and his friend is not. Says he has no thoughts of harming himself and has not had any. Begins to cry and says this is the first time anyone has asked him anything that was not about his leg.

items.stem: What does the nurse do now?

options.text: Stay with him, let him talk, and tell him she will come back later today to carry on
options.rationale: He has just said this is the first real question anyone has asked. Staying is the whole intervention, and naming a return makes it something he can count on rather than a moment that happened once.

options.text: Leave him some time alone to compose himself and return when he is calmer
options.rationale: He is not distressed by her being there, he is distressed. Leaving at this point reads as the subject being too much for the room.

options.text: Move straight to the referral so the right person can take this on
options.rationale: The referral is going to happen and leading with it tells him he has been passed on. Make it after you have stayed.

options.text: Tell him that what he is feeling is survivor guilt and that it is a normal response
options.rationale: Naming it is useful later. Offered now it converts what he just said into a category and ends the first conversation he has had.

items.takeaway: He has told you nobody asked. Staying is the intervention, and a named time to continue is what turns one conversation into support.
items.strategy: Three options are reasonable next steps that all end the moment. Ask what he needs in the next five minutes.

strategies: Ask what each action does to the moment
elimination.verdict: Stay, and name a time to return.

chartUpdate.text: Seen twice by the mental health team, no risk identified, follow-up arranged for after discharge. Sleeping in five-hour stretches after changes to the night environment and the timing of his analgesia. Analgesia requests now match his reported scores. Has read his messages and replied to two friends; has not replied to the family of the friend who died and says he cannot yet. Still startles at sudden noise. Says the replay happens less often. Talks about the collision when he chooses to and has twice stopped himself and changed the subject. Says he does not want to talk about driving at all.

items.stem: For each outcome at two weeks, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: Contact with his support network
rows.rationale: Phone read and two replies sent. Not replying to the bereaved family at two weeks is not avoidance, it is a reasonable thing to find impossible yet.

rows.text: Startle at sudden noise
rows.rationale: Still present at two weeks, which is within the expected course. Unchanged here is not failure and it is worth saying so to him.

rows.text: Sleep
rows.rationale: Five-hour stretches from two, after a specific intervention. The change followed the plan rather than time alone.

rows.text: Intrusive memories of the moment before the impact
rows.rationale: Less frequent by his own report, which is the expected direction in the first weeks.

rows.text: His willingness to think about driving
rows.rationale: Complete avoidance of the thing most tied to the event is what tends to persist and disable. It is the item most likely to need specific work after discharge.

rows.text: Risk to himself
rows.rationale: Assessed twice with no risk identified, and this is reviewed rather than closed. Discharge removes the daily contact that surfaced it in the first place.

rows.text: The match between his analgesia requests and his pain scores
rows.rationale: The gap has closed, which suggests the distress was what was being medicated and is now being addressed directly.

items.takeaway: Most of an acute stress response settles with sleep, support and someone asking. What needs following is the avoidance that is hardening and the risk that was only ever found because someone was there daily.
items.strategy: Two rows look resolved: the startle and the risk assessment. Expected and persisting is not the same as needing follow-up, and no risk identified is not the same as closed.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find what is expected to persist

elimination.verdict: Four improving, one unchanged, two needing follow-up.

chart.text: 78-year-old man, second day after an elective hip replacement. History of hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Collar size 18. His wife reports that he snores loudly and that she has slept in another room for years. He has never been investigated for this. Lives independently and drives.

Reports he has not slept at all. Observations were taken at 0000 and 0400. Corridor light falls across the bed. The roommate's television was on until 2300. Given diphenhydramine at 2200 as a one-off for sleep. Woke to pass urine three times. Dozed for two hours yesterday afternoon. Intravenous fluid running at 100 mL per hour. Reported pain 6 of 10 at 0300 and analgesia was given at 0330. This morning he asked the nurse whether he was at home and could not say what day it was, then corrected himself.
Spot oxygen saturations overnight 90 to 92 percent on room air while asleep, 94 percent awake. Heart rate 84. Blood pressure 146/82. Temperature 36.7 C.

items.nursesNote: 0700: Reports he has not slept at all. Observations were taken at 0000 and 0400. Corridor light falls across the bed. The roommate's television was on until 2300. Given diphenhydramine at 2200 as a one-off for sleep. Woke to pass urine three times. Dozed for two hours yesterday afternoon. Intravenous fluid running at 100 mL per hour. Reported pain 6 of 10 at 0300 and analgesia was given at 0330. This morning he asked the nurse whether he was at home and could not say what day it was, then corrected himself.
items.stem: Highlight the findings the nurse acts on today.

segments.text: Reported pain 6 of 10 at 0300
segments.rationale: Pain severe enough to wake him, treated after it woke him. The analgesia schedule is not reaching through the night.

segments.text: Observations were taken at 0000 and 0400
segments.rationale: Two wakings for a stable patient. Whether he still needs four-hourly observations overnight is a decision someone has to make rather than a default.

segments.text: Dozed for two hours yesterday afternoon
segments.rationale: Worth addressing in the sleep plan and it is a consequence of the bad night rather than a finding to act on.

segments.text: he asked the nurse whether he was at home and could not say what day it was
segments.rationale: New disorientation on the second postoperative day. Correcting himself afterward is reassuring and it does not make this go unexamined.

segments.text: Corridor light falls across the bed
segments.rationale: A real contributor and one the nurse fixes tonight without it being a clinical decision. It belongs in the plan rather than in the list of things to act on today.

segments.text: The roommate's television was on until 2300
segments.rationale: Environmental, resolvable by asking, and not a clinical finding.

segments.text: Given diphenhydramine at 2200 as a one-off for sleep
segments.rationale: A strongly anticholinergic drug given to a 78-year-old. It is on every list of medications to avoid in older adults, and the confusion this morning follows it.

segments.text: Intravenous fluid running at 100 mL per hour
segments.rationale: Two and a half litres overnight into a man with an enlarged prostate. The fluid is a large part of why he was up three times.

items.takeaway: The environmental causes are real and they are the easy half. What needs a decision today is the drug he was given, the new confusion, the overnight observations, the analgesia timing and the fluid rate.
items.strategy: The light and the television are the most obvious causes of a sleepless night and the least important findings. Sort by which ones need someone's judgment.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false
elimination.verdict: The diphenhydramine, the confusion, the night observations, the 0300 pain, and the fluid rate.

items.stem: For each factor, indicate what kind of contributor it is.

rows.text: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea
rows.rationale: Repeated airway obstruction fragments sleep all night, and it explains the saturations dropping while he slept.

rows.text: A two-hour afternoon nap
rows.rationale: It reduces the pressure to sleep at night, which is his own sleep regulation working against him.

rows.text: Analgesia timed so that pain wakes him at 0300
rows.rationale: The drug and the schedule, rather than the pain itself. Moving the timing is a medication decision.

rows.text: Diphenhydramine given for sleep
rows.rationale: It shortens sleep latency and fragments the rest of the night, and in an older adult it adds an anticholinergic load on top.

rows.text: Observations scheduled at midnight and 0400
rows.rationale: A routine of the setting. Nothing about his condition required waking at those hours.

rows.text: Intravenous fluid at 100 mL per hour overnight
rows.rationale: A prescribed infusion, and the volume is what fills the bladder three times. The order is where the fix is.

rows.text: Corridor light across the bed and a television until 2300
rows.rationale: Light and noise, both outside the patient and both removable tonight.

rows.text: Waking three times to pass urine
rows.rationale: An enlarged prostate and an aging bladder, which is his own physiology rather than anything the ward did.

items.takeaway: Sorting the causes is what tells you who fixes each one. The nurse fixes the environment, the prescriber changes the drugs and the fluid, and the physiological causes need assessment and referral.
items.strategy: The intravenous fluid is written as a cause of nocturia, which makes it look physiological. The waking is physiological and the fluid filling the bladder is an order.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Two environmental, three physiological, three pharmacological.

items.stem: Which concern does the nurse raise first?

options.text: The overnight intravenous fluid causing the nocturia
options.rationale: A real and easily fixed contributor, and it does not carry the risk the drug does.

options.text: The analgesia timing that let pain wake him at 0300
options.rationale: Worth changing today and it is comfort rather than a safety problem.

options.text: The diphenhydramine, given the new confusion and the saturations overnight
options.rationale: A strongly anticholinergic drug in a 78-year-old, followed by new disorientation, in a man with likely untreated sleep apnea in whom a sedating drug also worsens the airway. It is the one finding that must not be repeated tonight.

options.text: The likelihood of untreated obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Very probable and it needs flagging for assessment and follow-up. It is a referral rather than something to resolve on day two.

items.takeaway: A sedating antihistamine given to an older adult is the finding to stop first. It carries an anticholinergic load, it worsens an untreated airway, and the order will repeat tonight if nobody cancels it.
items.strategy: All four are contributors worth changing. Ask which one, repeated tonight, could do the most harm.

strategies: Ask what happens if nothing changes tonight
elimination.verdict: The diphenhydramine.

items.stem: Which actions belong in tonight's plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Close the door, move his bed away from the corridor light, and agree a television time with the roommate
options.rationale: The environmental half, and the part the nurse can do without asking anybody.

options.text: Encourage him to stay awake through the whole day so that he is tired enough to sleep tonight
options.rationale: Limiting the long afternoon nap is reasonable; enforced wakefulness in a confused older man after surgery is not, and exhaustion raises the delirium risk.

options.text: Offer a different hypnotic so that he gets some sleep tonight
options.rationale: It swaps one sedating drug for another in a man who is already confused and desaturating while asleep. The answer is to remove causes, not to add an agent.

options.text: Ask that the diphenhydramine be discontinued and that no sedating antihistamine be used for sleep
options.rationale: It removes the drug and it stops the next nurse reaching for the same thing at 2200.

options.text: Ask about reducing or front-loading the intravenous fluid so less runs overnight
options.rationale: It addresses the nocturia at its cause rather than offering him a bottle.

options.text: Ask whether the overnight observations can be spaced or stopped if he remains stable
options.rationale: Two wakings removed by one conversation. Overnight observations are a routine that someone has to actively review.

options.text: Document that he reports not having slept and reassess the whole picture tomorrow morning
options.rationale: It records the problem for a third night and changes nothing about any of its causes.
