items.takeaway: Treat hospital sleep loss by removing causes rather than adding a drug. Most of the fix is a conversation about observations and fluid plus ten minutes on the room.
items.strategy: Two distractors propose doing something active about the sleep itself. Both add a burden to a patient whose problem is what has already been done to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Stop the drug, review the observations, change the fluid, fix the room.

chartUpdate.text: He is asleep. Snoring loudly with pauses the nurse times at up to twelve seconds, followed by a gasp. Spot oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, rising to 93 percent after the gasp. He is lying flat. No oxygen prescribed. He received his scheduled analgesia at 2200.
Respirations 14 between pauses. Heart rate 78. Rousable to voice.

items.stem: What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Reposition him onto his side with the head of the bed raised, and stay to see the effect
options.rationale: Position is the one thing that relieves an obstructing upper airway immediately, costs nothing, and needs no order. Staying to see whether it works is what makes it an intervention rather than a guess.

options.text: Record the saturation and the length of the pauses and report all of it at handover
options.rationale: The observation is excellent and the timing is wrong. He is obstructing now and nobody acts on it for seven hours.

options.text: Apply oxygen by nasal cannula to bring the saturation up into an acceptable range
options.rationale: There is no order, and oxygen treats the number rather than the obstruction. In untreated apnea it can hold the saturation up while carbon dioxide climbs, which hides the problem.

options.text: Wake him and keep him awake for a while until the pauses have stopped altogether
options.rationale: It ends the apnea by ending the sleep, which is the problem being treated. A third sleepless night is not a treatment.

items.takeaway: An obstructing airway in sleep is treated first by position. Oxygen without an order treats the number, and waking him treats nothing.
items.strategy: Three options are reasonable responses at the wrong moment or to the wrong target. Ask what opens the airway in the next thirty seconds.

strategies: Ask what relieves the obstruction
elimination.verdict: Side-lying with the head raised.

chartUpdate.text: Diphenhydramine discontinued. Overnight observations spaced to one at 0200 after review. Intravenous fluid completed by 2000 and he woke once to pass urine. Bed moved from the corridor light and the television agreed to stop at 2130. Analgesia rescheduled and he reported no pain overnight. Reports sleeping about five hours in two stretches and says he feels like himself. Oriented to place, date and situation. Still snores with pauses observed by two nurses; saturations 90 to 92 percent while asleep. A sleep clinic referral has been written for after discharge and he has been told he should not drive until he is assessed.

items.stem: For each outcome at day four, indicate the nurse's evaluation.

rows.text: His safety to drive
rows.rationale: Untreated apnea with daytime sleepiness is a driving risk, and he drives. Telling him once is where this starts rather than where it ends.

rows.text: Witnessed apneic pauses with desaturation in sleep
rows.rationale: Unchanged and undiagnosed. It was never going to resolve on a surgical ward, and the referral is the right outcome rather than a gap.

rows.text: He is receiving a medication that should be avoided in older adults
rows.rationale: Discontinued, and the reason recorded so nobody reaches for it again.

rows.text: His confusion
rows.rationale: Oriented to place, date and situation. It tracked the drug and the sleep loss, which is what confirms it was delirium rather than something new.

rows.text: Sleep is being interrupted by ward routines
rows.rationale: Observations spaced, light removed, television agreed, fluid finished before bedtime. Every environmental cause has been dealt with.

rows.text: Nocturia
rows.rationale: Once rather than three times, and the prostate is still there. Finishing the fluid earlier solved the hospital half of it.

rows.text: Total sleep time
rows.rationale: Five hours in two stretches is better and is still short, and it is being measured by his report rather than anything objective.

items.takeaway: Most hospital sleep loss is caused by the hospital and resolves when you remove the causes. What the admission uncovered, the apnea and the driving risk, leaves with him.
items.strategy: The apnea row is unchanged, which makes it look like a failure. An outcome correctly routed to follow-up is not the same as one that was missed.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Three resolved, two improved, two for follow-up.

chart.text: 19-year-old college student with no previous medical history, brought in by a roommate. Three weeks of passing large volumes of urine, constant thirst, and eating more than usual while losing weight. Reports about 6 kg of weight loss. Two days of nausea, vomiting and cramping abdominal pain, and has kept nothing down since yesterday. Takes no medications.

Alert and answering questions, drowsy between them and slow to respond. Breathing deep and sighing without effort. Breath has a sweet acetone odor. Oral mucosa dry, skin warm and flushed. Reports abdominal pain 6 of 10. Vomited 200 mL of clear fluid on arrival. Capillary refill 4 seconds.
Temperature 37.2 C. Heart rate 126. Blood pressure 92/54. Respirations 30 and deep. Oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air.

Capillary glucose 486 mg/dL. Arterial pH 7.18. Bicarbonate 10 mmol/L. Partial pressure of carbon dioxide 22 mm Hg. Sodium 131 mmol/L. Potassium 5.4 mmol/L. Chloride 98 mmol/L. Anion gap 23. Serum ketones positive. Blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL.

items.nursesNote: 1830: Alert and answering questions, drowsy between them and slow to respond. Breathing deep and sighing without effort. Breath has a sweet acetone odor. Oral mucosa dry, skin warm and flushed. Reports abdominal pain 6 of 10. Vomited 200 mL of clear fluid on arrival. Capillary refill 4 seconds. Reports eating more than usual over the past three weeks. Temperature 37.2 C. Heart rate 126 with blood pressure 92/54. Oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air.
items.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: Reports abdominal pain 6 of 10
segments.rationale: Genuine and it is a feature of the acidosis rather than a separate emergency. It resolves as the acidosis does, which is also why it is a trap for appendicitis.

segments.text: drowsy between them and slow to respond
segments.rationale: A falling level of consciousness in a young man with no history. It tracks the acidosis, and it is the finding that decides how fast everything else has to move.

segments.text: Reports eating more than usual over the past three weeks
segments.rationale: A key piece of the diagnostic history and not something to act on in the next ten minutes.

segments.text: Capillary refill 4 seconds
segments.rationale: Peripheral perfusion is already failing, which places this in the hour that matters rather than the day.

segments.text: Breathing deep and sighing without effort
segments.rationale: The lungs blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate for a metabolic acidosis. It looks calm and it means the blood is dangerously acidic.

segments.text: Breath has a sweet acetone odor
segments.rationale: Ketones leaving through the lungs. Together with the breathing pattern it names the problem from the doorway.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air
segments.rationale: Normal, and misleading. Saturation stays high in this patient while he is in serious respiratory and metabolic trouble.

segments.text: Heart rate 126 with blood pressure 92/54
segments.rationale: Three weeks of osmotic diuresis and two days of vomiting. He is profoundly volume depleted and his heart is covering for it.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2 C
segments.rationale: Normal. Worth noting, since an infection is a common trigger and this one does not point to it.

items.takeaway: The findings to act on are the acidosis and the volume loss. A normal saturation and a normal temperature do not mean a stable patient.
items.strategy: The pain is the finding most students select and the one most likely to send them down the wrong path. Ask what each finding would change in the next ten minutes.

strategies: Treat each segment as true or false

steps.detail: Eating more is diagnostic, not urgent.

elimination.verdict: Mentation, respirations, acetone odor, the heart rate with the pressure, and the refill.

items.stem: For each finding, indicate which condition it points to.

rows.text: An altered level of consciousness
rows.rationale: Both can obtund a patient, through acidosis in one and through osmolality in the other.

rows.text: Deep sighing respirations with an acetone odor on the breath
rows.rationale: Both are the body dealing with ketoacids, one through the lungs as carbon dioxide and one as acetone.

rows.text: Severe dehydration with a heart rate of 126
rows.rationale: Osmotic diuresis drives both, and the fluid deficit in the hyperosmolar state is usually the larger of the two.

rows.text: Serum ketones positive
rows.rationale: Ketones appear when there is no insulin at all and fat is being broken down for fuel. Some insulin is still present in the other condition.

rows.text: Glucose 486 mg/dL
rows.rationale: High glucose belongs to both. It is usually higher in the hyperosmolar state and the value alone decides nothing.

rows.text: Arterial pH 7.18 with bicarbonate 10 mmol/L
rows.rationale: Acidosis is the whole distinction. The hyperosmolar state runs high glucose without it.

rows.text: Glucose above 600 mg/dL with a normal pH and serum osmolality above 320
rows.rationale: Very high glucose, very high osmolality, no acidosis. That combination is the definition.

rows.text: Onset over three weeks in a 19-year-old with no prior history
rows.rationale: A rapid presentation in a young person with no diabetes is type 1 declaring itself, and this is how it usually arrives.

rows.text: A gradual onset over days in an older adult with type 2 diabetes and an infection
rows.rationale: The typical picture: slower, older, some insulin still present, and a precipitating illness.

items.takeaway: Acidosis and ketones separate the two. Glucose, dehydration and altered consciousness belong to both, so they cannot be used to tell them apart.
items.strategy: Three rows are shared features and they are the ones most often used to distinguish the conditions. Ask whether the finding could appear in both before assigning it.

strategies: Treat each row on its own

steps.action: Find the acid and the ketones

elimination.verdict: Four to ketoacidosis, two to the hyperosmolar state, three to either.

items.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
items.sentence:
The patient is most likely experiencing [[1]].

The priority problem at this moment is [[2]].

The first measure that addresses it is [[3]].

options.text: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Wrong on both counts that matter. He has a pH of 7.18 and positive ketones, and he is 19 with no prior diabetes.

options.text: hypoglycemia
options.rationale: His glucose is 486 mg/dL. The drowsiness invites this answer and the number closes it.

options.text: gastroenteritis with dehydration
options.rationale: It accounts for the vomiting and the dry mucosa and for none of the glucose, the ketones or the pH. The three weeks before the vomiting are what rule it out.

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Hyperglycemia, ketones, an anion gap acidosis and a three-week history of thirst and weight loss in a young man. Type 1 presenting for the first time.

options.text: the blood glucose of 486 mg/dL
options.rationale: The most visible number and not the most dangerous one. The glucose is the marker; the volume loss and the acidosis are the threat.

options.text: the potassium of 5.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: It needs watching closely, because it will fall sharply once insulin starts. Right now it is a number to monitor rather than the priority problem.

options.text: the abdominal pain of 6 of 10
options.rationale: A symptom of the acidosis that resolves as the acidosis does.

options.text: the severe fluid volume deficit
options.rationale: He has lost litres over three weeks and kept nothing down for a day. Perfusion fails before the glucose or the pH does, and nothing else can be corrected in a patient who is not circulating.

options.text: an intravenous isotonic fluid bolus
options.rationale: Fluid comes first. It restores perfusion, begins lowering the glucose by dilution and by letting the kidney excrete it, and makes the insulin that follows work where it is supposed to.

options.text: a subcutaneous dose of rapid-acting insulin
options.rationale: Absorption from subcutaneous tissue is unreliable in a patient this poorly perfused, and the route is wrong for an emergency that needs titration.

options.text: an antiemetic for the vomiting
options.rationale: It will make him more comfortable and treats a symptom while the underlying problem continues.

options.text: intravenous sodium bicarbonate
options.rationale: Reserved for a pH below roughly 6.9. Given above that it worsens potassium shifts and does nothing the fluid and insulin will not do.

items.takeaway: Fluid before insulin. The glucose is the number everyone looks at and the volume deficit is what is killing him.
items.strategy: The second blank is the one that separates students. Ask which problem would stop him in the next hour, not which number is furthest from normal.

strategies: Work the blanks in order

steps.action: Use the pH and the ketones

elimination.verdict: Ketoacidosis, the volume deficit, an isotonic bolus.

items.stem: Which does the nurse anticipate in the first hour of this patient's care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Capillary glucose measured hourly
options.rationale: The infusion is titrated against the number, and the rate of fall matters as much as the value.

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH
options.rationale: Not at a pH of 7.18. Giving it drives potassium into the cells on top of what the insulin is about to do, and the acidosis resolves on fluid and insulin alone.

options.text: Potassium added to the fluid immediately, before any is lost
options.rationale: His potassium is 5.4 mmol/L and his urine output is not yet established. Replacement waits for the level to fall and for the kidney to be clearing.

options.text: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every two hours in place of an infusion
options.rationale: Wrong route for a poorly perfused patient and far too blunt. Two-hourly dosing cannot be adjusted against an hourly glucose.

options.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: His potassium is high now and will drop fast once insulin starts. The rhythm is where both ends of that swing show up first.

options.text: A continuous intravenous infusion of regular insulin
options.rationale: A continuous infusion is the only route that can be titrated against hourly values, and regular insulin is the one given intravenously.

options.text: An intravenous isotonic crystalloid at the prescribed rate
options.rationale: The first and largest intervention. Everything else works better once he is perfused.

items.takeaway: Fluid, an insulin infusion, hourly glucose, and the monitor. Potassium waits for the level to fall and for urine to flow, and bicarbonate waits for a pH almost nobody reaches.
items.strategy: Two distractors are about potassium and bicarbonate, and both are correct interventions at the wrong moment. Check the current value and the urine output before either.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Fluid, insulin infusion, hourly glucose, cardiac monitoring.

chartUpdate.text: Four hours into treatment. Capillary glucose 248 mg/dL. Arterial pH 7.28. Bicarbonate 15 mmol/L. Anion gap 17. Potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Urine output 60 mL per hour. Insulin infusion running.

items.stem: What does the nurse anticipate next?

options.text: The insulin infusion stopped, since the glucose is approaching the normal range
options.rationale: The trap, and it is a dangerous one. His anion gap is still 17 and his pH is still 7.28, so the ketoacidosis is not resolved. Stop the insulin now and the ketone production restarts.

options.text: The insulin infusion rate doubled to clear the remaining ketones faster
options.rationale: It would drop his glucose and his potassium too fast. The rate is titrated, and the way to keep insulin running is to add dextrose rather than to push harder.

options.text: Transition to subcutaneous insulin at this point
options.rationale: That comes later, once the gap has closed and he is eating, and the first subcutaneous dose overlaps the infusion before it is stopped.

options.text: Dextrose added to the intravenous fluid while the insulin infusion continues
options.rationale: Around 250 mg/dL the fluid changes rather than the insulin. The insulin is there to shut off ketone production, not only to lower glucose, so you feed glucose in to keep it running safely.

items.takeaway: Insulin is stopped by the closing of the anion gap, not by the glucose. At about 250 mg/dL you add dextrose so the insulin can keep running.
items.strategy: Two options act on the glucose and the glucose is not the endpoint. Read the anion gap and the pH before touching the infusion.

strategies: Find the endpoint the treatment is aimed at
elimination.verdict: Add dextrose and keep the insulin running.

chartUpdate.text: Eight hours into treatment. Glucose 184 mg/dL on an insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluid. Arterial pH 7.36. Bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. Anion gap 12. Potassium 3.2 mmol/L. Heart rate 92. Blood pressure 112/68. Respirations 18 and unlaboured. Awake, answering fully, asking what happens next. Urine output 70 mL per hour. Abdominal pain 1 of 10. Says he has never held a syringe and does not know what he is supposed to do on a day he cannot keep food down.

items.stem: For each finding at eight hours, indicate how the nurse evaluates it.

rows.text: He has never held a syringe
rows.rationale: He is going home on insulin he has to draw up and inject himself. Not urgent tonight and not optional either.

rows.text: Respirations 18 and unlaboured
rows.rationale: The compensation is no longer needed, which is what you expect once the acidosis has corrected.

rows.text: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L
rows.rationale: It has fallen from 5.4 as insulin drove it into the cells. Below 3.5 with an insulin infusion still running is the rhythm problem of the night, and it needs replacement now.

rows.text: Arterial pH 7.36 with an anion gap of 12
rows.rationale: The gap has closed and the pH is normal. This is the endpoint the insulin infusion was aimed at.

rows.text: Glucose 184 mg/dL
rows.rationale: Inside the range aimed for during treatment, and held there by the dextrose rather than by stopping the insulin.

rows.text: He does not know what to do on a day he cannot keep food down
rows.rationale: The exact situation that brought him in. Sick-day rules are what stop the second admission.

rows.text: Abdominal pain 1 of 10
rows.rationale: It tracked the acidosis the whole way, which is the reason it never needed a separate workup.

rows.text: Heart rate 92 with blood pressure 112/68
rows.rationale: Perfusion restored. The volume deficit that was the priority eight hours ago has been corrected.

items.takeaway: Potassium falls as the treatment works, so the number that was high on arrival is the one to watch at eight hours. And a resolved episode in a patient who cannot inject is a readmission waiting to happen.
items.strategy: Five rows are moving the right way and one has crossed in the other direction. Track the finding that treatment itself changes.

strategies: Treat each row on its own
elimination.verdict: Five resolving, one immediate, two before discharge.
